prs.title: fix: show the whole reply when you reopen a TUI session
prs.body:
Closes #200408 ## What Problem This Solves In `openclaw tui`, a reply longer than 8,000 characters is complete while it streams, but after you close and reopen the session it stops mid-sentence with `...(truncated)...`. The full reply is stored, yet the TUI gives no way to see the rest, so it looks as if the model stopped early or text was lost. ## User Impact User impact: reopening a TUI session (Gateway or `--local`) shows long replies in full again. If the full text cannot be shown, the preview stays and says why, instead of ending silently. ## Why This Change Was Made The Gateway caps text in `chat.history` to keep history pages small. The Control UI already loads capped rows in full through `chat.message.get` (#122207); the TUI took the capped text as it came. The TUI now does the same as the Control UI: after loading history, each assistant row marked `truncated: true` / `reason: "display-cap"` is replaced by the stored message, newest first, four reads at a time. History pages stay bounded, and there are no protocol or schema changes. When the full text cannot be shown, the preview is kept and its marker says why: - read failed, not found, or a Gateway without `chat.message.get`: `...(truncated; couldn't load the full reply. Reopen the session to try again)...` (same advice as the Control UI's "Couldn't load the full message. Try again.") - `chat.message.get` reports the stored reply as oversized (over its ~25 MB payload limit): `...(truncated; the full reply is too large to show here)...` Local mode (`openclaw tui --local`) had the same cap. Its history read moves from `embedded-backend.ts` into `src/tui/embedded-history-messages.ts`, unchanged, and full text is loaded after the existing budgets pick the rows (the 128 KiB per-message limit and the page limit), so loading full text never drops an older row from the page. The stored message is then read in-process with the same limits as the Gateway's `chat.message.get` handler, so both modes show the same reply. A reply over 128 KiB shows in full in both. As with Gateway clients, a page with loaded replies can end up over its byte budget. The first revision of this PR loaded local full text before those budgets. A reply over 128 KiB then became `[chat.history omitted: message too large]` instead of its preview, and expanded rows could push older rows off the page. This revision fixes both. Known limit, left as is: `chat.message.get` caps text at 1,000,000 characters, so in both modes a longer reply loads its first million characters, ending in the plain `...(truncated)...` marker. Command-line runs (`openclaw agent`) are not affected by any of this: they print the run result, not history. ## Evidence Live check, Windows 11, against a running 2026.11.5-beta.4 Gateway: the session from #200408 holds an 11,532-character reply that `chat.history` returns as 8,018 characters ending `...(truncated)...`. - Before (installed 2026.11.5-beta.4 TUI, session reopened): the reply stops mid-sentence at "forest ecology", followed by `...(truncated)...`. - After (this branch built from source, same session reopened): the whole reply is shown, ending with `THE END`. Before: After (Gateway): After (`--local`): live run of this branch, `openclaw tui --local --session agent:main:proof`, Windows 11. The run used throwaway `HOME`, `OPENCLAW_HOME`, `OPENCLAW_STATE_DIR`, config and `OPENCLAW_WINDOWS_TASK_NAME`. The session holds two stored assistant replies, written with the repo's own transcript writer (`upsertSessionEntryCore` + `replaceTranscriptEvents`). An 8,000-character preview of either stops partway through paragraph 72. - 11,539 characters, ending `THE END`: after reopening, it shows in full (paragraphs 1–103 and `THE END`). - 150,078 characters, over the 128 KiB per-message limit: after reopening, it also shows in full (paragraphs 1–1,326 and its last line, `HUGE_REPLY_LAST_LINE`), as it does over the Gateway. The `src/tui/tui-pty-local.e2e.test.ts` harness times out on this Windows machine (its own existing cases too), so this was a manual run in a terminal. The retrieval-failure case can't be triggered live without corrupting storage; the unit tests below cover it.
Reopened TUI screen text (repeated middle paragraphs elided) ```text openclaw tui - local embedded - agent main - session proof session agent:main:proof Write the huge reply. Huge paragraph 1: the tide pool keeps its water between waves, and every stone holds a small world of its own. Huge paragraph 2: the tide pool keeps its water between waves, and every stone holds a small world of its own. [... paragraphs 3-1,324 elided ...] Huge paragraph 1325: the tide pool keeps its water between waves, and every stone holds a small world of its own. Huge paragraph 1326: the tide pool keeps its water between waves, and every stone holds a small world of its own. HUGE_REPLY_LAST_LINE Write the long reply. Long paragraph 1: the tide pool keeps its water between waves, and every stone holds a small world of its own. Long paragraph 2: the tide pool keeps its water between waves, and every stone holds a small world of its own. [... paragraphs 3-100 elided ...] Long paragraph 101: the tide pool keeps its water between waves, and every stone holds a small world of its own. Long paragraph 102: the tide pool keeps its water between waves, and every stone holds a small world of its own. Long paragraph 103: the tide pool keeps its water between waves, and every stone holds a small world of its own. THE END local ready | idle agent main | session proof | gpt-5.5 | deliver:off | tokens ?/200k ```
Focused tests: - `src/tui/gateway-chat.test.ts`: a capped row is replaced by the `chat.message.get` result; when the read reports unavailable, reports oversized, or is rejected, the preview is kept with the matching marker. - `src/tui/embedded-history-messages.test.ts` (new) runs the real history budgets with synthetic transcript rows: a capped reply shows its stored text; a 150,000-character stored reply shows in full; a reply the reader reports oversized, and a missing reply, keep their marked previews; loading a 30,000-character reply under a 40,000-byte page budget keeps the older 15,000-character row. The 150,000-character and page-budget cases fail when full text is loaded before the budgets (the order in the first revision) and pass here. - `gateway-chat.test.ts`, `embedded-backend.test.ts` and `embedded-history-messages.test.ts`: 172 passed. `pnpm check:changed`: typecheck, lint, format, line-cap and mock-export ratchets pass. The dead-export scan reports three exports in untouched files that are already on `main` (`approval-shared.ts`, `spawn-broker/host.ts`, `system-agent/operation-types.ts`).

prs.title: fix: preserve pending tools in watchdog stop diagnostics
prs.body:
## What Problem This Solves

A watchdog stop can report `pendingTools: []` even though a Code Mode exec was pending when the stop was selected. Recovery can abort and drain that exec before the diagnostic is built, hiding the operation that explains the stall.

## User Impact

Operators retain the pending tool names, call IDs, elapsed times, and Code Mode bridge waits from the stop decision. Turn execution, recovery policy, timeouts, thresholds, and deadlines are unchanged.

## Why This Change Was Made

The gap is between asynchronous placement recovery (`src/sessions/session-controller.operation-recovery.ts:190`) and the later diagnostic capture (`src/sessions/session-controller.operation.ts:650`). The existing watchdog now snapshots its pending-tool projection before invoking recovery and discards the snapshot if recovery resumes or the watchdog closes. This uses the existing registrations: at most five tools and at most three structure-only bridge waits per Code Mode entry, with no arguments, results, paths, or message content. It adds no public export, protocol, schema, config, or prompt change.

Example exec entry:
```json
{"toolName":"exec","toolCallId":"await-cell","elapsedMs":900001,"awaiting":[{"kind":"bridge","method":"callValue","deadlineAtMs":null,"elapsedMs":900001}]}
```

Related: #200839.

## Evidence

The existing Code Mode bridge cases now abort and fully drain exec during placement recovery, verify the live registrations are empty, and advance the fake clock before stop construction. On base both cases fail with `expected [] to deeply equal [...]`; with the fix they preserve exec and its bridge wait with the original decision-time elapsed values. The no-deadline case reports `deadlineAtMs: null`; the second retains the known deadline. An existing successful-recovery case also checks that a resumed turn discards the snapshot.

Focused command:
```sh
pnpm test src/agents/code-mode.bridge.lifecycle.test.ts --maxWorkers=1 -t 'preserves an off-VM wait when stop recovery'
```
```text
Base: Tests 2 failed | 25 skipped; pendingTools=[]
Fix:  Tests 2 passed | 25 skipped
```

Focused green wall time: 34.90 seconds including compiler preparation (Vitest 5.47 seconds). The full bridge file passed 27 tests in 51.11 seconds including compiler preparation (Vitest 16.22 seconds); the watchdog file passed 65 tests in 10.86 seconds including compiler preparation (Vitest 8.44 seconds). The worker bridge composition is necessary to prove that abort-driven settlement closes the real exec registration before stop construction. The 49-file non-live Code Mode/watchdog/prefix-stability selection passed 736 tests with 27 skipped in 190.35 seconds. Core and both affected test-graph typechecks, targeted type-aware lint, format, and `pnpm build` passed (build: 3m 3.6s). Exact-head [CI run 44205146397](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/44205146397) passed with no failed jobs (884 seconds elapsed for the run). Tests extend existing cases rather than adding another harness; net test growth is 20 lines for recovery/drain setup, the nested-tool assertion, and successful-recovery cleanup. No test ceiling change is needed.

Codex autoreview of the complete local change against base `82a38fb2fe944b76c0604bb8ee1e0697404e64cd`: scoped-clean at P0–P2, no accepted/actionable findings.

prs.title: improve(auto-reply): name the model whose connection failed
prs.body:
Closes #191299

## What Problem This Solves

When a model call fails to connect, the reply says "Couldn't connect to the AI service." (#168247) but not which model. With a fallback chain or several providers, the user can't tell which endpoint is down without the gateway logs.

## User Impact

User impact: the connection-failure reply starts with the failing model, e.g. `⚠️ gpufarm/qwen3.8-27b request failed: Couldn't connect to the AI service. ...`. The rest of #168247's copy is unchanged, including the completed-work caution. A failure without a provider or model reads exactly as before, and raw error text stays hidden.

## Why This Change Was Made

`resolveReplyFailoverFacts` already has the failover error's provider and model; the connection copy just didn't use them. It now prefixes the copy with the failing model through `modelKey`, which keeps a model id that already carries its provider as is (`openrouter/auto` is not doubled). Terminal replies and incomplete-turn replies both read `requestFailureText`, so both get the name.

When the error carries fallback attempts, the name comes only from the attempts whose own error is a connection failure, joined with ", " when there are several. A chain summary keeps the last attempt's model while its message joins every attempt's error, so taking the top-level model would blame a backup that connected and then timed out (ClawSweeper's P2 on the first head).

This partly reverses #163381 (#163368), which removed provider details from default errors to keep them short. For a connection failure, though, the failing model is the next recovery step (which server to check), not a diagnostic. Only the connection copy changes; rate-limit, auth and server-error replies are untouched. If maintainers want to keep #163381's rule here too, closing this is fine.

## Evidence

- New qa scenario `connection-failure-reply-names-model` (in this PR): real gateway, qa-channel, mock-openai with the provider's `baseUrl` set to `http://127.0.0.1:9/v1`, so every model call is refused. It sends a DM and reads the terminal reply from the bus. The reply is `isError`, so it is read directly rather than through the failure-aware transport waits, the same way `a2a-allowlist-denied-cross-agent-send` reads its expected warning.
  - main at `70c93a29f17` (this PR's base): fails with `unexpected connection-failure reply: ⚠️ Couldn't connect to the AI service. Check your connection, then try again. ...`
  - This branch at `a798fb3485e` (the scenario now requires two distinct named models before "request failed"): passes with `reply: ⚠️ mock-openai/gpt-5.6-luna, mock-openai/gpt-5.6-luna-alt request failed: Couldn't connect to the AI service. Check your connection, then try again. For details, open Settings → Logs in the Control UI or run `openclaw logs --follow`. Check the conversation for any completed work before trying again.` qa-lab configures `gpt-5.6-luna-alt` as the fallback, both on the refused provider, so this is the real fallback-chain path, and both refused models are named. The first head named only the last one: with its `request-error-facts.ts`, the scenario fails on `⚠️ mock-openai/gpt-5.6-luna-alt request failed: ...`.
  - Command: `node scripts/run-node.mjs qa suite --provider-mode mock-openai --scenario connection-failure-reply-names-model --concurrency 1 --fast`, after `pnpm build`.
- `pnpm test src/auto-reply/reply/agent-runner-failure-reply.test.ts`: 22 passed.
  - "names the model whose connection failed" covers the named copy, a provider-prefixed model id, and the unchanged copy without facts. With main's `request-error-facts.ts` it fails with `Received: "⚠️ Couldn't connect to the AI service. ..."`.
  - "names only the fallback attempts that failed to connect" builds the error with the real `throwFallbackFailureSummary`: the primary is refused and the backup times out, then both are refused. With the first head's code it fails with `Received: "⚠️ backup/llama3.3 request failed: Couldn't connect ..."`.
- 34 related test files at `e40cb6903e0`: 1,053 passed, 0 failed. They are the 13 that assert this copy or call `resolveReplyFailoverFacts` (`agent-runner-failure-reply`, `agent-runner.runreplyagent.e2e`, `incomplete-turn*`, `settled-turn-finalization*`, `payloads.errors`, `session-lifecycle-run-failure`, `server-methods`, `assistant-error-format` and others), plus `model-fallback*` and `agent-terminal-snapshot`.
- qa-lab scenario catalog tests (19 files): 145 passed, run at `fc2d656c3bc`. The scenario file is unchanged since.
- `pnpm tsgo:all` exits 0. oxlint and oxfmt are clean on the changed files, and `git diff --check` is clean.
- Test lines: main's test-line ratchet is now at its ceiling (`3855c896edd`: slack 0), so `35ed4298bdd` adds `config/test-lines-allocations/191301-connection-failure-names-model.txt` with this PR's exact net test-line growth, 61 lines. They are the tests that pin this change: Connection-failure replies name the fallback models that failed to connect. Merged onto `3855c896edd`, `check-test-lines-ratchet.mts --base 3855c896edd --no-merge-base` reads `Test lines OK: 6592429; ceiling: 6592429; slack: 0.`, and an allocation of 62 is refused. This is not a fix PR, so per the openclaw-testing guide the record needs a maintainer's approval; could a maintainer approve it?
- Test cost (`pnpm test <file> --maxWorkers=1`, Bun, the local default, macOS arm64, two runs each): `agent-runner-failure-reply.test.ts` 27.7 s (cold worker cache, 21.9 s of it compiling) and 6.5 s wall, 15 ms and 16 ms of tests. CI run 41570533435, Bun: `agent-runner-failure-reply.test.ts` 4.4 s Vitest duration, 20 ms of tests (`checks-node-changed-4`).
- Gap: the end-to-end proof is mock-openai against a closed local port. The refused-then-timed-out chain is covered by the unit test only; I did not build an end-to-end case for it. My fork runs the same naming on two bots with local models; I have not captured a live provider outage with this exact build.

prs.title: fix: keep slash commands in ordinary prose from executing
prs.body:
Related: #199841

## What Problem This Solves

Quoting slash-command instructions in an ordinary message can silently switch the session model, change runtime settings, or run a command instead of discussing it. For example, `Send /model to choose another model.` can select a fuzzy-matched model and lose words from the prompt.

## User Impact

Slash commands, directives, and shortcuts are interpreted only when the canonical sender text begins with `/`, allowing leading whitespace and channel-owned bot addressing. Mid-sentence commands and examples stay ordinary text across the shared Gateway/channel reply path. Explicit native commands, leading commands, chained directives, and `$skill-name` references retain their existing behavior.

**Control UI dependency:** #199841 fixes the separate Enter-time command extraction that happens before Gateway ingress. This backend PR alone does **not** complete the requested all-surfaces behavior until that companion lands. It was verified open at `00e64bab02267db85170b9ad0ffd48ec652e7adf`; its UI implementation is not duplicated here.

**Compatibility:** integrations that supply only a generated envelope/sender label in `Body` must instead provide clean `CommandBody` or `BodyForCommands`. Plain slash-leading `Body` remains supported. Once a message starts with `/`, existing chained parsing remains; this is not Markdown-aware quote parsing inside an admitted command message. No configuration or state migration is required.

## Why This Change Was Made

The shared reply owner captures directive admission before stripping spans. Reset/general-command preparation and early abort, native-command, bash, and compaction paths now use canonical sender text rather than turning bracketed examples or sender labels into commands. Feishu also stops treating arbitrary plaintext `@name` as removable addressing; its normalized transport mention markup keeps its existing behavior.

The inline directive parser handles model/profile/runtime selection, thinking/fast/verbosity/trace/reasoning controls, elevated/exec settings, queue behavior, and status shortcuts. General slash-command dispatch and explicit skill references remain separate. No new parser, helper, state, configuration, or public field was added; the seven production files have a combined net growth of five lines.

## Evidence

- The exact fuzzy-model sentence failed on base with a synthetic visible catalog entry and passed with the fix. Canonical-admission owner regressions produced 14 intended failures before repair; 282 core owner/consumer tests passed. A required test-only extraction then moved the command-source contract into a coherent sibling suite; the original and new session suites passed 95 tests afterward.
- Feishu plaintext mention regressions produced two intended failures before repair; its command, sequential-key, and ingress suites pass 29 tests across three files, including actual transport-mention controls.
- Shared downstream command tests cover Discord, Slack, Telegram, WhatsApp, Signal, iMessage, and WebChat. Representative Discord, Slack, and Telegram adapter suites passed 47 tests; unchanged-input adapter proof was retained rather than restarted.
- After the canonical cutover, Gateway ingress and prompt-prefix stability suites passed 42 tests across two files. The ingress table exercises Control UI/WebChat and macOS/iOS/Android client identities with ordinary slash prose and leading-command controls.
- Before the canonical-prefix follow-up, temporarily composing the UI-only diff from companion #199841 at the pinned head with the directive-gate candidate passed 201 UI unit tests across composer mentions, suggestions, chat view, and command parsing. The exact temporary patch was reversed and `ui/` is unchanged in this PR. This is source-level frontend compatibility proof, not a single live UI-to-provider flow.
- Targeted canonical messaging, Gateway-methods, and Feishu-package typechecks; focused lint, formatting, four-doc MDX validation, line-cap and mock-export ratchets, and `git diff --check` passed.
- Independent local autoreview completed with `scoped-clean` and no P0–P2 findings over base `346d231275b3930848b8e31239c74f689d361436` through the complete uncommitted candidate (binary diff SHA-256 `799879246ff696e35aaf78ba1a4793de2106dbbd0810d41dfb1fc5592010c61a`). The review was static; it does not certify omitted source or runtime behavior. Local ClawSweeper was unavailable because the retained runner checkout was dirty; the shared autoreview route was used instead.

### CI consumer repair

[CI run 44033378790](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/44033378790) and the hosted review identified three stale assertions expecting mid-sentence model, alias, or exec directives to execute. The test-only follow-up retains those prose inputs as negative controls and adds slash-leading controls for unknown-skill/model selection, the `list` alias, and per-turn exec policy without placement or persistence changes. All 28 tests in the two affected suites pass, along with targeted messaging typecheck, lint, formatting, and `git diff --check`. Production code is unchanged.

Independent local autoreview of this two-file follow-up against `7fc364235e9dec21091579284dc1e87a3c090469` also completed `scoped-clean` at P0–P2 (delta SHA-256 `d340fd00d4c7052aef3dbe57a2b353bad1e73d83549b27b9911916ba12187b7a`). New-head CI must finish separately; prior-head CI is not claimed for this follow-up. The small shared surface matrix is retained to protect surface-dependent command routing; separate adapter-boundary regressions remain in place.

**Coverage limits:** real provider/channel E2E, physical/native app builds and device runs, and a full package build were not run. Native coverage exercises Gateway ingress under Control UI/WebChat and macOS/iOS/Android client identities, not those app binaries. Other bundled channels inherit the shared-path admission fix; they were source-audited rather than each live-tested. CI and required GitHub approvals remain separate.

### Contributor credit

Requested and co-authored with @Patrick-Erichsen.

## Work sessions

Linked for team reference; these sessions aren’t public.

- [Original discussion with @Patrick-Erichsen](https://team.openclaw.ai/chat/roboclaw)
- [Implementation and verification](https://team.openclaw.ai/chat/roboclaw/73c133d73efd48f48d01da527fdfb8b6)
- [Backend implementation and verification helper](https://team.openclaw.ai/chat/roboclaw/~key/subagent/c2ceaa6f-c832-47d0-a1ca-c125de8ee45b)

prs.title: feat(location): consume location.update events; notify on fence crossings
prs.body: # PR description draft — location.update significance + event-driven APNs delivery Resolves #163480 ## What Problem This Solves iOS nodes emit `location.update` events on significant location changes, but the gateway drops them as `unsupported_event` — verified by two independent users on current builds (#163480). This PR makes the event consumable and closes the full chain: **fix → significance detection → event-driven APNs notification**, with no heartbeat, no session turn, and no coordinates in logs. - **Gateway:** `location.update` is validated, dispatched to the node-event consumer registry, and instrumented at the dispatch boundary. The response ack path no longer crashes (`logGateway.info` → `warn` — every event ack previously failed with `UNAVAILABLE` after dispatch). - **Plugin surface:** `registerNodeEventConsumer` — a plugin-API subscription hook for gateway-validated node events (currently allowlisted to `location.update`). This is the "plugin hook" requested in #163480. - **memory-core consumer:** armed location intents evaluate each fix against fence geometry. Enter fences fire on the first inside fix when armed from afar (previously required a 0→1 crossing that never happened when the intent was armed while already outside); stale-facts-cache reads no longer mask fires. - **Direction-gated crossings (bug fix):** an exit fence no longer fires on an arrival fix, and an enter fence no longer fires on a departure fix — see below. This was found during live verification, not by the test suite. - **Delivery:** fires push an APNs alert at fire time (new plugin-SDK surface `sendNodeIntentAlert`, category `openclaw.location-intent`) — delivery no longer waits for the target session's next turn. The routed system-event enqueue is retained as an in-session record; push failures are logged and never re-arm the one-shot. ## Direction-gating bug (found and fixed during live verification) `decideLocationFire` gated only *one* side of each transition on direction. The inside branch fired for `previous === 0` regardless of direction, and the outside branch fired for `previous === 1` regardless of direction. Consequences observed on real drives: - **2026-11-13 06:33** — a Göteborg *arrival* fence fired on the user's morning *departure* from inside the fence. - **2026-11-16 15:29** — a home *exit* fence fired while the user was *arriving* home (the fix that also correctly fired the Göteborg arrival fence in the same second). Both branches are now direction-gated: `enter` fires only on 0→1 (including the first inside fix when armed from afar), `exit` fires only on 1→0. Each branch carries the live-fire evidence in a comment, and two regression tests cover both directions — the existing test's comment promised this behavior but never asserted it, which is how the bug survived review. ## Evidence - **2026-11-14, live drive:** Skene fence (1.5 km, enter) fired on a real outside→inside crossing from an unsolicited background fix; the APNs alert appeared on the owner's phone (screenshot-timestamped, matching the log fire and the intent description text). Exactly one fire, no duplicates. - **2026-11-16:** home-exit fence (200 m) fired on a real departure; the ack-crash fix verified live (three fixes traced, zero `UNAVAILABLE`). - **2026-11-17, full drive test (3/3 fences, 0 evaluation errors):** | Time | Fence | Fix distance | Accuracy | Outcome | |---|---|---|---|---| | 10:58:46 | home exit (200 m) | 7 m *inside* | 16 m | baselined, **no fire** ✓ | | 11:21:49 | home exit (200 m) | 512 m outside | 46 m | **fired** — correct direction | | 11:37:28 | store (1000 m) | 427 m from store | 11 m | **fired** | | 11:42:51 | destination (1000 m) | 52 m from center | 34 m | **fired** | All three notifications owner-confirmed on the phone (screenshots matching the log timestamps). The exit fence baseline-then-fire sequence is the live proof of the direction-gate fix; the destination fire (52 m from a decoded Plus code) validates arrival geometry end to end. - Consumer tests assert: single push per fire, fire-on-first-inside-fix, no re-arm on push failure, and both direction gates. ## Known limitation: fence radius cannot buy lead time at driving speed Reported by the owner on the 2026-11-17 drive: the store fence fired **after** he had passed the store. Measured along-track against the store→destination leg, the firing fix was **+404 m past** the store (137 m cross-track, 427 m straight-line — i.e. comfortably *inside* the 1 km circle, 573 m from the edge). The cause is fix cadence, not fence logic: - 4.28 km travelled between consecutive fixes → 49 km/h on a ~5-minute significant-change cadence - a 1 km circle is a 2 km-wide band; at 4.28 km spacing the chance any given fix lands inside is only ~47%, i.e. whether it fires before or after the POI is close to a coin flip **Enlarging the radius does not fix this.** To gain one fix-interval of lead you would need R > 4.2 km at 50 km/h and > 6.7 km at 80 km/h. At that size the notification fires while the user is kilometres away, so "you're passing the store" becomes false. Radius trades precision for reliability; there is no setting that delivers both at driving speed. This is a property of the fix-delivery platform, not of the fence evaluator. The mechanism that actually fixes approach timing is **device-side region monitoring** (`CLCircularRegion`, 20-region limit): the OS surfaces a callback *at the boundary crossing*, independent of the significant-change cadence. That is the planned device-fence direction, and this drive is its concrete justification. Until then, a fence that fires shortly *after* a high-speed POI is behaving as designed given the fixes it receives. ## Consent and privacy (answers the labels on #163480) - **Consumption is consent-scoped:** fixes are evaluated only against location intents the user explicitly armed ("notify me when I arrive at X"). No armed intents → no consumption into anything user-visible; fixes are evaluated and discarded. - **No precise-location persistence:** coordinates are never written to gateway logs, prompts, or system events. The dispatch-boundary log line records the event name and node id only. (The prior closed PR #50936 was flagged for passive precise-location delivery; this design evaluates and discards.) - **No autonomous turns:** a location fire pushes a notification and enqueues a passive in-session record. It never starts an agent turn — consistent with the passive device-event direction (#196989). Any follow-up ("lets stop by X") is a user-initiated turn. - **Existing consent basis:** the event only exists when the user has granted iOS Always location to the app; this PR consumes that signal purpose-scoped, per #163480's discussion. ## Scope boundaries - One consumer per event by design (registrar rejects a second subscriber for `location.update`; dispatch uses first-match). Fan-out to multiple consumers is a deliberate follow-up, not included here — it widens the location access surface and deserves its own security review. - No fix history is stored; fixes are evaluated against armed intents and dropped. A bounded presence/fix store is a separate proposal. - The event-driven push is the interim surfacing policy ("fired ⇒ notify"). Whether and how to notify is a policy layer question; the follow-up direction (below) explores a tunable local judge for it. - Device-side region monitoring (the fix for the lead-time limitation above) is out of scope for this PR. - **File structure is ratchet-driven, not stylistic.** `location.update` handling lives in `server-node-events-location.ts` alongside the existing `server-node-events-*.ts` handlers. The chat `subscribe`/`unsubscribe` arm moved to `server-node-events-chat-subscription.ts` for one reason: the dispatcher is grandfathered in `config/max-lines-baseline.txt`, and that ratchet rejects *any* growth, so a two-line case arm plus its import had to be offset. That extraction is behaviour-preserving and covered by the existing chat subscribe/unsubscribe tests, but it is unrelated to this feature — call it out if you would rather it land separately. ## Follow-up direction (not in this PR) Significance is currently declared geometry. The next layer separates geometry (deterministic, in code) from interruption policy (a local decision model, evaluated only on events, with the fence verdict as the fail-open baseline). An 11-case eval (incl. negative controls and a conjunction scenario: "passing a store × open shopping-list need") found local decision models (`clef-flash`, `d3:2b` via Ollama's `/v1/systemone`) that discriminate correctly with ~160-token calls. Full methodology and results: https://gist.github.com/zigit/8c765c33d1edea1435f9b26d6d22c896 This PR intentionally ships only the deterministic layer. ## Why this shape (the box, not the cloud) > "It ain't gonna be some cloud… then I don't know who has my shit. It will be > like a box that knows what I need, and when I pass by Ralph's on my way home > I get a message: 'You know we ain't got no milk.' That's what I expect we > have in the future." > > — will.i.am, on stage at CES 2013, as recalled by this PR's author That quote is the reason this PR is shaped the way it is, and the reason the example notification in the drive-test screenshot reads *"We ain't even got no milk."* Thirteen years later the box is an OpenClaw gateway on a Mac, the milk is a reminder in a local database, and the message arrives within a few hundred metres of the store — verified on a real drive, with the notification landing on the phone as the car passed. Two parts of the quote turned out to be design constraints rather than rhetoric: - **"not some cloud… I don't know who has my shit"** — fixes are evaluated against armed intents and discarded; coordinates never reach a log, a prompt, a system event, or a third-party API. The follow-up judge layer runs on a local decision model precisely so that the one component that reasons about *where you are* does not require sending *where you are* anywhere. - **"knows what I need"** — the trigger is a conjunction the user declared (an armed intent, an open shopping need), not an inference over harvested behaviour. Consent is the mechanism, and it is per-intent and revocable. This PR ships the deterministic half: geometry in code, significance declared by the user. The contextual half — a small local model deciding whether a crossing is worth interrupting you — is the follow-up below. ## Change type - [x] Bug fix (ack-path crash; enter-fence miss when armed from afar; direction-ungated crossings) - [x] Feature (node-event plugin hook; event-driven location-intent push) - [ ] Refactor - [ ] Docs - [ ] Tests (covered by existing consumer tests; new asserts added for both direction gates)

prs.title: fix: shorten pauses after workspace-changing commands
prs.body:
## What Problem This Solves

After #200787 removed disposable command-checkpoint snapshots, changing many workspace files could freeze the guest while Git payloads were prepared and written. A 62,000-file synthetic workspace reproduced roughly five-second pauses for 5,000 changed files.

## User Impact

Prepare changed Git blobs while the guest runs, then verify the current filesystem and publish the immutable result under the existing pause owner. In five paired APFS runs, changed-command pause p99 fell from **5.16 s to 1.78 s**, preserving zero command snapshots/removals and unchanged-command skips.

Owner accepts +7.3% finalization time, +11% CPU, +13.1% allocation (background finalization) and +117 ms on ten-file pauses, plus +137 production LOC, in exchange for changed-command guest-pause p99 5.16 → 1.78 s (APFS) while keeping zero per-command btrfs snapshots/retirements. Production context: on Team, 93d84036 checkpoint pauses run p50 1.39 s / p99 3.75 s without this fix; per-command snapshots previously forced global btrfs commits (Gateway SQLite waits up to 19.6 s).

Native btrfs is unmeasured. The owner has accepted the replay/recovery evidence below and explicitly declared the apply-failure gate satisfied. This is not a hard two-second bound: a diagnostic run under concurrent local validation load reached **3.50 s**.

One candidate trace aborted during canonical apply with `Local workspace custody has ended`, after a 1.68 s pause. Recovery preserved and applied its retained result. Candidate and baseline diagnostic runs then completed without reproducing the underlying mutation failure. This failure is **unexplained**, not claimed fixed or inherited; it is retained separately from the five completed pairs.

## Apply-failure replays and owner resolution

Five matched fresh-process traces per arm completed: **baseline 0/5 failures, candidate 0/5 failures**. Each arm completed twenty measured changed-command captures and eighty unchanged-command skips, with zero snapshot/removal calls and every changed file verified. Sources are the exact parent `e1e108c7e4711959b287aff7acab1ac085ea2533` and production code at `343e0d796c1f68c203302b336304bbd2b384377d`; both diagnostic capsules add the same error print before a failed mutation loses its underlying exception during custody cleanup. No runtime behavior was altered for these diagnostics.

Each A/B pair used identical explicit content seeds, a fresh APFS clone of the same isolated synthetic fixture, the original 10/100/1,000/5,000-file edit sequence, and two measured turns. Order: AB/BA/AB/BA/AB. The benchmark now prints and records its seed and accepts `--checkpoint-seed` for replay. No task-owned builds/tests overlapped. The original failed run used an unrecorded random seed and produced no final load report; its exact bytes/load cannot be reconstructed. Background host load was recorded rather than controlled (one-minute load 5.1–13.6 on 32 cores).

Owner resolution, recorded verbatim:

> One recovered apply failure observed in an unseeded early run; not reproducible in 10 seeded matched replays (0/5 baseline, 0/5 candidate); recovery path exercised and correct; replay-seed support added (eb05d694) so any recurrence is replayable.

The owner explicitly declares the gate satisfied on this evidence and authorizes landing after fresh exact-head CI and ClawSweeper clearance. The underlying early mutation error was not recovered; no baseline-inheritance or newly fixed root-cause claim is made. The original failed observation and retained-result recovery evidence remain intact.

## Why This Change Was Made

The projection operation owns speculative preparation. Existing manifest and Git staging workers carry prepared entries and object IDs through that one operation. The final scan checks current namespace membership and file identity (including ctime); recent or changed observations are rehashed, and only matching content reuses prepared objects. Blob-only import creates no result ref or accepted checkpoint. Recovery bypasses speculative preparation, and normal durable result publication still precedes resume.

The original-read ctime safety window is preserved: an unsafe observation cannot become trusted merely by aging. Immediately written files may therefore all need hashing again under pause. The measured improvement predominantly removes payload/object staging: its paused wall time fell from 4.57 s to 0.34 s per trace, while paused scans remained near four seconds across four captures. No schema/config changes, retained cache, host changes, or provisioned-copy/base-refresh behavior changes. Existing manifest read/repair logic moves to the inventory module to keep the state owner within its line limit. Production diff: **+170/−33 = +137 lines**, needed for the preparation/verification handoff through existing owners.

The apparent checkpoint-frequency increase in pause logs is not evidence of more captures: #200787 changed previously pause-free snapshot captures into paused captures. Its unchanged probe, mutation gate, pending-checkpoint key and capture boundary did not change. Matched traces still capture four changes and skip sixteen unchanged commands; no cadence throttle is introduced.

## Evidence

Predeclared workload: 62,000 files × 17,742 bytes (1.10 GB), 10,001 synthetic sessions; unique incompressible edits rotating 10/100/1,000/5,000 files. Two baseline controls, then five serial counterbalanced pairs; twenty changed-command samples per arm. Every changed file is verified after finalization. Nearest-rank p99 is the observed maximum at this sample count. Synthetic engine seam, APFS; no production data or native container/btrfs latency claim.

| Metric | Baseline | Candidate |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| Changed pause p50 | 1,512 ms | 943 ms |
| Changed pause p95 | 5,095 ms | 1,766 ms |
| Changed pause p99/max | 5,158 ms | 1,784 ms |
| 10-file pause median | 792 ms | 909 ms |
| 100-file pause median | 837 ms | 869 ms |
| 1,000-file pause median | 1,795 ms | 1,021 ms |
| 5,000-file pause median | 5,075 ms | 1,718 ms |
| Total finalization / 20-step trace, median | 40.262 s | 43.211 s |
| Whole-trace process CPU, median | 31.115 s | 34.537 s |
| Main allocated bytes / 10-step turn, median | 159,251,928 | 180,145,376 |
| Captures / unchanged skips per 20 steps | 4 / 16 | 4 / 16 |
| Snapshot / removal calls | 0 / 0 | 0 / 0 |

A/A control 5,000-file pauses were 4,668 and 4,753 ms. Their mixed-size p50s were 766 and 780 ms, below the candidate’s 943 ms. One 100-file baseline outlier shifts the paired mixed-size p50 across the small/large-edit boundary; do not treat its apparent improvement as robust. The per-size medians and large-edit tail are more informative. Candidate median CPU is 23.7% above the faster A/A control (11.6% above the other); paired CPU increases range from 4.2% to 17.2%, consistent with the additional preparation scan. This is disclosed added work, not a zero-cost move. CPU includes Node workers and excludes native Git children; allocation covers the main isolate only. Whole-trace CPU/allocation include synthetic command and verification work. Finalization wall time brackets the actual owner. The synthetic agent DB is 8.1 MB; this exercises filesystem capture, not a 35 GiB transcript workload. Physical writeback is unmeasured.

The first two candidate pairs precede only a behavior-preserving reader extraction and mechanical lint fixes; three subsequent pairs use the final implementation. Source hashes and all raw observations are retained locally, including the failed trace and excluded diagnostics.

Validation: 54 shared manifest/staging tests; 16 focused checkpoint/recovery/retirement tests; the final direct-checkpoint ordering regression. The payload-preparation assertion fails on the parent and passes with this change. Same-size rewrites with restored mtime, additions/deletions during preparation, interrupted acceptance, and retirement retry remain covered. A separate coarse-timestamp regression failed on the unsafe initial candidate and passes after retaining original-read eligibility. Independent Codex review is scoped-clean at P0–P2.

`pnpm check:changed` initially found the file cap and four lint violations. Those were fixed, targeted replays passed, and the final full `pnpm check:changed --base e1e108c7e4711959b287aff7acab1ac085ea2533` rerun passed on the committed candidate. The first CI run exposed four test-fixture assumptions that treated speculative preparation as final capture or injected rejection into blob-only staging. Those failures reproduced locally. Test observers now distinguish preparation from capture, and rejection injection remains at durable staging; all original assertions and expected capture counts are unchanged. All four affected cases, focused lint/type checks, and independent Codex review passed. Production code is unchanged by this correction. Production-head CI passed at `343e0d796c1f68c203302b336304bbd2b384377d` ([run 44196225055](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/44196225055)); the native watcher exited 0/GREEN with zero pending checks, excluding ten superseded checks. The subsequent harness-only seed replay change at `eb05d694b5bb7fab26d2c291821d395cb0bd055e` passed `pnpm check:changed --base HEAD` before commit and independent Codex P0–P2 review. Exact-head CI was verified GREEN before landing (attached CI run 44202827250; native watcher exit 0, no pending checks, 27 superseded checks excluded). Owner acceptance and the apply-failure gate resolution are recorded above. Final-head ClawSweeper review at 00:12:06 UTC had zero open items and no findings. The exact reviewed head was merged as `d4faf614e6eb21c68f62d81c3ceff709b5849114` at 00:15:30 UTC on November 18 (16:15:30 PST November 17), through the native maintainer workflow without an inherited-CI exception. No Control UI imports of changed modules were found.

Reproduction (freeze baseline and candidate with the same harness first):

```sh
node --expose-gc --import ./scripts/tsx.mjs scripts/perf/local-workspace-checkpoint-measure.ts \
  --source-root <frozen-source> --mode turn-loop --output <owned-fixture> \
  --reuse-fixture --files 62000 --file-bytes 17742 \
  --checkpoint-changed-files 10,100,1000,5000 --requests 2 --burst 1 --report <arm>.json
```

prs.title: fix: stop updates failing with "database is locked" when another OpenClaw process is writing
prs.body:
Related: #197083

## What Problem This Solves

Updating OpenClaw can fail at the very end with "database is locked" even though the update's data migration already finished. This happens when another OpenClaw process, such as a status check, the old updater, or a CLI command, briefly holds the state database. The update then reports `post-update-failed`. In some runs the Gateway is also left stopped with "data at risk", and the user has to run `openclaw update repair`.

## User Impact

User impact: updates and `openclaw doctor --fix` no longer fail when another OpenClaw process holds the state database for a few seconds, and a step that finished its work is no longer reported as failed.

## Why This Change Was Made

Doctor's maintenance steps (media persistence, plugin session repair, transcript directives) run while holding a state lease. Releasing that lease retried SQLite lock contention for only 2 seconds, then threw the raw lock error. Every other shared-state writer waits 5 seconds. So a step whose work had already committed failed with a bare "database is locked". The lease row also stayed behind, so the next step waited on it and failed with "lease … is held by …".

Releasing a lease now waits the same 5-second busy bound as any other writer, but only for plain SQLite lock contention; offline-maintenance contention keeps its 2-second window. If a writer still holds the lock past that, lease cleanup retries in the background, as it already did for offline-maintenance contention, so an unreleased lease no longer blocks later steps until it expires.

## Evidence

- **Reproduced on Crabbox AWS Linux.** Each lane updated from published 2026.11.4 to main `237e3e4fe0d` through the Gateway's `update.run`, with a 400 MB state database and an outside writer holding the write lock.
  - Writer holding 2 s out of every 3 s: 1 of 14 lanes failed. Transcript directives failed with "database is locked", ending in `state-migrated-no-rollback` with the Gateway stopped.
  - Writer holding 2 s out of every 2.2 s: 9 of 14 lanes failed `post-update-failed`, with "Plugin session repair did not settle: database is locked" or "plugin lifecycle lease … is held by …".
- **Instrumented build.** In each failed lane, the same Doctor process logged the lease-release lock error about a second before the step failed.
- **Fix lanes:** the same high-contention lanes on the fixed build (base `237e3e4fe0d` plus this patch) passed 11 of 12, against 12 of 18 failing on base. The one remaining failure has a different cause: the old 11.4 Gateway acquired a plugin lifecycle lease during its own startup maintenance and was stopped for the update without releasing it, so main's Doctor met a lease held for up to 300 s. It is tracked as a separate follow-up.
- **Latest stable:** the same lanes from published 2026.11.5 failed 4 of 4 on base. In each, the lease-release lock error was followed by "Plugin session repair did not settle" in the same Doctor process. With the fix they passed 4 of 4: core ready, Gateway active, config intact, and all 1,024 synthetic state rows present in the 425 MB database.
- **Regression tests** in `src/state/openclaw-state-lease-contention.test.ts`:
  - A writer holding the lock longer than 2 seconds during release. Red on base with the same bare `database is locked` (errcode 5); green with the fix.
  - Background retry releasing the lease after the writer commits.
- **Other checks:**
  - Lease suites pass, including contention, maintenance-retry, native-cleanup, and worktree capacity.
  - `pnpm tsgo:core`, oxlint, and oxfmt are clean.
- **Reviews:** autoreview came back scoped-clean at P2. An independent codex review found nothing.
- **Size:** production +16/−9; tests +97.
- **Head:** rebased onto current main only to resolve an append-only conflict in the test file; the production diff is unchanged from the build the lanes ran.

prs.title: fix: stop a long Claude CLI turn from redoing its tool work on the fallback model
prs.body:
Root cause: `src/agents/cli-runner.ts:410` (main 91614b5c3778) handles a refused CLI stream (`CLI JSONL output exceeded …`) by keeping the first-turn session and rethrowing, but never applies the existing rule that a turn which already ran tools must not be replayed on another model (`cli-runner.ts:466-472`, from #162567). The executor also rethrew the refusal without the run's tool facts, so model fallback sent the same user message to the fallback model, which ran the completed tools again.

Fixes #200744

## What Problem This Solves

A long Claude CLI turn can edit files and run commands, then produce more output than OpenClaw will parse. OpenClaw refuses that output and, when a fallback model is configured, hands the same request to the fallback model. That model starts from scratch and repeats the work on top of half-applied changes, while queued messages wait behind it. Thanks @jzmudzinski for the detailed report (a 54-minute turn replayed this way).

## User Impact

User impact: when a `claude-cli` turn that already ran a tool hits the stream output limit, the run stops with the limit error instead of replaying the request on another model, so finished tool actions are not repeated. A turn that hits the limit before running any tool still falls back as before.

## Why This Change Was Made

OpenClaw already refuses to fall back after tool effects when a CLI turn ends with an empty answer. The output-limit refusal never reached that check, because the refused output did not carry the run's tool summary. The executor now attaches the tool summary and accepted session spawns to the refused output, and the runner applies the same stop to both failures. The refused first turn's native session is still kept for the next message (#192838 unchanged).

The issue also suggests a new failover reason for output budgets. This keeps the existing reason and uses the existing fallback stop, so failover reasons and their consumers stay unchanged.

Fix by @fede-kamel (d2169a3fb5), kept as is; on top: a merge of current `main` and a shorter regression test.

## Evidence

Real Gateway, real Claude Code 2.1.322 as the `claude-cli` backend, built `dist/`, isolated state. Claude Code talks to a local Anthropic Messages fixture; the fallback `stub/stub` is a local OpenAI-compatible fixture that starts the request from scratch. The turn runs `exec` once (appends a line to a marker file) through the Gateway's MCP, then streams 10 MiB of reply text.

| Build | Result | `exec` runs |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `main` 91614b5c3778, run 1 and 2 | output refused, fallback `stub/stub` runs `exec` again and answers | **2**, **2** |
| this PR, run 1 and 2 | output refused, run fails with `CLI JSONL output exceeded 8388608 characters`, fallback never called | **1**, **1** |
| this PR, no tool before the overflow | output refused, fallback to `stub/stub` as before | 0 from Claude Code |

Regression test: `execute.output-limit.test.ts` › "stops model fallback when a turn that already ran a tool exceeds the output limit" fails on `main` (`expected false to be true`) and passes here; the existing first-turn refusal test now also checks that a refusal without tools records no stop.

Gateway and fixture logs: https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/200801#issuecomment-6963273381

Merge danger: two-way door. Reverting restores the old fallback behavior; nothing is written or migrated. Blast radius: `claude-cli` turns that hit the output limit after running a tool now end with the error instead of falling back.

prs.title: feat: confine native node worker filesystem access
prs.body:
## What Problem This Solves

OCE OpenClaw node workers cannot safely use writable OpenShell PVC ancestors unless model-controlled processes are also prevented from replacing them.

## User Impact

Adds opt-in `nodeHost.workerRuns.isolation: "filesystem"` for Linux workers, alongside the scoped writable-ancestor exception. The worker and its descendants can write their admitted workspace, model HOME and scratch directory, but cannot replace those roots through their parents. Unsupported kernels/helpers reject launch; existing defaults remain unchanged.

The PR now pins the published packages `@openclaw/proc-safe@0.6.0` (includes [#39](https://github.com/openclaw/proc-safe/pull/39)) and `@openclaw/fs-safe@0.28.1`. Operators must stop existing workers and exclude all other unconfined untrusted writers, including same-UID processes, for the entire workspace lifetime. A dedicated Pod or PVC alone is insufficient.

Josh’s [#198073](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/198073) is included. The node now rejects writable roots that overlap trusted runtime or shared storage before launching a worker. An explicitly assigned workspace remains usable.

At [`1a639e0`](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/commit/1a639e0e6d3b2f6fd25849071efb37a4a4841af7), the default supervisor loads the filesystem launcher only when filesystem isolation is selected. With the PR’s locked proc-safe 0.4.2 and fs-safe 0.27.1, 27 Linux worker supervisor and workspace retention tests passed, including launching a downloaded worker through the standalone executable. With a locally packed proc-safe launcher and fs-safe 0.28.0, all three Linux filesystem supervisor tests passed. The latter run used local packages and does not qualify a published install.

At [`2d3e3d4`](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/commit/2d3e3d4e3bfc28f649dad6840dee113c07aa98c2), the Git cancellation test expects the existing `-c core.fsmonitor=false ls-files` invocation. The manifest suite reproduced the CI failure on the parent and passed all six cases on Linux after this test-only change ([CI](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/43506279639)).

## Why This Change Was Made

Pre-exec Landlock confinement covers model-launched subprocesses while keeping existing Git transfer/publication APIs and process ownership. Descriptor-relative fs-safe I/O could harden its own operations, but subprocess and lifecycle integration would still need additional work. This approach requires Linux Landlock ABI 3+; inherited descriptors and other sandbox boundaries remain the caller's responsibility.

The real repository path also needs named-device dispatch to preserve its profile and use existing device eligibility. Trusted Git inventory disables repository fsmonitor/lazy fetch; anonymous credential checks retain explicit hostname selection without ambient `GH_HOST`. No new recovery manager or state is introduced.

## Evidence

- Follow-up `efe8729cb56` selects worker scratch using the same strict ancestry rules as the child process. The regression test failed on the prior commit, then passed with the fix. All 69 focused Linux tests and the targeted TypeScript check passed with the locked published dependencies. The managed OpenShell run below covers the preceding commit.
- The [merged commit](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/commit/ef0b4dbf2c3f47105141d42dffc672a507de1495) has Git tree `1af3c007cc4b`, identical to the locally tested combination of `a17be0e` and `f912389`. All 41 focused Linux tests passed, covering overlap rejection and assigned-workspace admission. The affected typecheck passed.

<details><summary>Redacted managed OpenShell 0.1.8 run output for the merged tree</summary>

From the test runner and its before/after receipts. Session, node and Pod identifiers are omitted.

```text
candidate passed
restart passed

before.gatewaySha256      34239c36b1f7bd051dabd809b0ce0264f29610dbe6c1f7b8e2457be346aa1e57
after.workerCommitSha256  34239c36b1f7bd051dabd809b0ce0264f29610dbe6c1f7b8e2457be346aa1e57
downloadPackPresent = false
transferSiblings = []
publicationScratch = []
uploadScratch = []
```

</details>

- In managed OpenShell 0.1.8, the deployed Gateway and node host both reported the combined build with published fs-safe 0.28.1 and proc-safe 0.6.0. A dedicated worker committed a file and the Gateway served its contents. After a normal stop/start changed the Pod UID, the same session read the same Git commit without redispatch. The published and committed file hashes matched on both sides of restart. Transfer, upload and publication scratch were empty. The fixture includes the downstream OCE integration patches.

- [9ed8cec](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/commit/9ed8cec68480be6ed53bb028f78d9497a9c3a926) updates the two dependencies across the workspace. All 22 published tarballs matched the SHA-512 values in the lockfile. A clean frozen install on Linux arm64 resolved both native packages and the launcher export. All 20 tests passed across filesystem supervisor, workspace admission, and workspace manifest. 
- On managed OpenShell 0.1.8 with the downstream integration patches, a real dedicated worker received its workspace context and executed a model-requested command. A repository session checked out the requested commit, made a local commit and published a file whose SHA-256 matched the committed contents. The staging pack, upload and publication scratch checks passed.
- At 9ed8cec a normal managed stop/start could leave the next `sessions.send` turn unable to commit its transcript. The Gateway treated a pending writer update as an access change. A regression test fails on the PR base (4940240). The full base runtime hit an earlier worker setup failure in the same managed deployment.
- [a17be0e](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/commit/a17be0e38cd16424e744278e3e04915a0aad7678) uses the existing session-access check for `sessions.send`. Pending visibility changes still reject the grant. Two real repository sessions each continued after a managed stop/start without redispatch. One read the pinned Git HEAD on both sides. The other committed a file, published it, and read back the same commit and content hash after the Pod UID changed. Transfer and publication scratch were clean. Both targeted suites passed (34 tests). Local autoreview of the two-file change against 9ed8cec found no P0–P2 issues.
- [CI on efe8729](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/43970508302) finished with six failing test groups. The failing suites were browser CLI error output, the FaceTime child-process mock, Codex auth bridge, Codex context-engine lifecycle, Windows update lifecycle and QA quota reset. Each also failed in a separate run on unmodified `main@bd25e9ef60cc`. The worker GitHub initial-launch suite passed all three cases on this head. The [required CI gate](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/43970508302/job/133678629571) reports failure and classified the shards as unknown because no corresponding main jobs matched.

<details><summary>CI failure signatures reproduced on the unmodified baseline</summary>

- **Browser CLI.** JSON failure returned the test runtime exit error instead of the original request error. [Job](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/43970508302/job/133662824583)
- **FaceTime.** The child process mock supplies spawn only. Importing the runtime executable resolver also requires execFile. [Job](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/43970508302/job/133662824614)
- **Codex auth.** The scoped login/refresh test rejected with an auth-profile refresh error instead of resolving. [Job](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/43970508302/job/133662830554)
- **Codex context engine.** The startup-buffering test expected zero markSentToProvider calls and recorded one. [Job](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/43970508302/job/133662830927)
- **Windows update lifecycle.** Snapshot startup hit mkdir EEXIST in the spawn broker; several update and service lifecycle assertions failed. [Job](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/43970508302/job/133662830316)
- **Quota fallback.** The QA fallback expected ok and returned error. Gateway logged a missing prompt projection before provider dispatch. [Job](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/43970508302/job/133662824334)

The [classifier](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/blob/efe8729cb563f9508e4f91963f7585a3d12891ff/scripts/ci-known-main-red.mjs) looks for a main job with the same name before comparing its failure signature. The CI report found no matching job for these six shards. The [maintainer guide](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/blob/main/.agents/skills/openclaw-pr-maintainer/references/landing.md#authorized-pre-existing-failures) documents the landing procedure for independently attributed failures.

</details>

- Upgraded published OpenClaw 2026.11.4 to the packaged PR head on Linux through the external package manager and ran fresh Doctor. The configured CLI plugin worked before and after the upgrade. The candidate Gateway returned both the user and assistant messages from the session created by the published binary, and a new session passed the same history check. The release and candidate share a version string, so the test also checked the installed build commits. This covers the external upgrade path. In-process self-update was untested.

<details><summary>Redacted upgrade runner output</summary>

```text
Published baseline build 2026.11.4 d843d6af39a42cd3c30084edbeabeece732fd93a
Installed candidate build 2026.11.4 efe8729cb563f9508e4f91963f7585a3d12891ff

Candidate session history: persistedUserAndAssistant = true

Release upgrade user journey passed: external package-manager installation and fresh Doctor.
```

</details>

- Synchronized with main at `3bd03dafb94` in `b1f3d73d551` to resolve the generated config baseline conflict. Regenerated and passed `pnpm config:docs:check`. [Current CI](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/43491101538).

- At `fdd1f60b497`, fixed the missing filesystem-policy module in the PR tooling source inventory. Replayed the import graph (one missing file before, none after) and passed the repo’s `test/scripts/pr-wrapper-source-closure.test.ts` on Node 24.19.0. [CI for the updated head](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/43489710410).

Using the repository’s source counter, verified 463 names against the proposed budget of 463. The +2 is submitted for repository-owner review.

This included admission of an approved device folder with its assigned private HOME, refusal when a folder changed during admission, and preserving IPC and process cleanup with the filesystem launcher. Same candidate dependency setup as below. These focused suites do not establish a full managed OpenShell E2E on this combined tree.

- At `8383df24c18`, merged upstream main `f5c5984f734`, regenerated the config baseline, and passed `pnpm config:docs:check`. Linux arm64 ran all 44 tests from the workspace-admission, worker-supervisor runtime, and temp-directory suites using fs-safe 0.28.0 and locally packed proc-safe with the native artifact from [proc-safe #39 at 6ab653c](https://github.com/openclaw/proc-safe/actions/runs/43487021774). The macOS tooling checkout had mismatched fs-safe native dependencies and its test run failed. [Hosted CI for this head](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/43488320015).


- Cleanup repair `1632274c789`: a real worker under UID 10001 leaves an unreadable scratch subdirectory; the old code rejects its extinction promise with EACCES, while the fix warns and preserves the confirmed exit. All three filesystem-owner cases pass on the final code. Startup/idle coverage also passed during the repair (50 tests total), with affected type graphs, formatting and lint passing. ## Evidence

prs.title: fix(worktrees): report when provisioning falls back from reflinks
prs.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Managed-worktree provisioning uses GNU `cp --reflink=auto`, which can silently copy file contents when cloning is unavailable. Existing diagnostics report selected bytes and elapsed time but cannot distinguish inexpensive clones from potentially large byte copies.

## User Impact

Operators can see confirmed cloned and copied file/byte counts, plus the first reported reflink fallback reason, in existing provisioning diagnostics. GNU coreutils older than 9.2 and incomplete reports explicitly count unreported work. No configuration or migration is required. This change adds visibility; it does not claim to reduce filesystem writes or change fallback behavior.

## Why This Change Was Made

Read GNU cp's existing transfer-method reports at the batch owner, carrying the already-admitted source sizes into the existing `copyDetails` event. Counts describe logical source bytes in completed batches, not physical IO. Contents, modes, timestamps, descriptor pinning, destination skipping and cancellation settlement retain their current behavior.

The source walk rejects symlink files and directories; `-L` follows the pinned descriptor paths. A nested source mount or incompatible filesystem policy can still prevent reflinking. Native template snapshots are a separate path and already use filesystem-native cloning, so this change does not modify them.

The simplify pass retained the existing batching and diagnostic owners, without a new cache, queue or fallback policy. Production code grows by 44 net lines to parse the observed transfer method and expose seven optional diagnostic fields.

## Evidence

Three new regression cases fail against the original helper because transfer counters are absent, then pass with this change. They cover mixed clone/fallback reports, fragmented output, legacy output and incomplete reports. Existing generic copy-detail forwarding coverage is reused; the redundant per-field assertion was removed after review.

Focused Node validation passed: 3 test files, 13 tests; 8 existing Linux-only tests are skipped on macOS. The default Bun runner failed before test collection in its local SQLite-library probe; the documented Node runtime route was used.

A real GNU cp 9.12 probe on APFS reported a 3,072-byte same-filesystem clone and a 5,120-byte distinct-filesystem copy, including `Operation not supported` as the fallback reason. Contents and timestamps matched. It exercised the production shell/stream protocol with a synthetic descriptor-link table in place of Linux procfs. Linux/btrfs live validation is unavailable locally; that limitation is not treated as a pass. [Linux CI on the first head](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/44198581864/job/134447449077) passed all 14 real-file provisioning cases, including native and cross-filesystem copies, symlink-swap protection, helper failure and cancellation settlement. This is owner-boundary proof, not a full Gateway creation capture on btrfs.

The prior 62,000-file APFS A/A/B experiment did not justify serialization: two concurrent copies completed in 109.524/109.532 seconds versus 225.224 seconds serialized, with unchanged file counts and similar CPU/allocation. Warm reuse copied zero files. No performance reduction is claimed for this diagnostic patch.

Independent Codex autoreview: scoped-clean for P0–P2 on the complete candidate. `OPENCLAW_VITEST_RUNTIME=node pnpm check:changed` passed on `a0503c89bc0453282286111152ab523e65427201`, including core/test typechecks, lint, dead exports and repository guards. That head also passed exact-head CI. The follow-up only removes a redundant test assertion and fixture fields; all 7 affected focused cases and a fresh Codex cleanup review pass. Production code is byte-identical. Exact-head CI and hosted review are required again on the final head before landing.

prs.title: fix(macos): keep attach-only save failures visible
prs.body:
Closes #190153

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes the macOS Debug "Attach only" toggle silently failing when it cannot save the setting.

## User Impact

The toggle reports a failed save and returns to its saved value. A permission problem can be corrected and retried without the rollback erasing the error.

## Why This Change Was Made

The marker write now throws on failure. A user-action binding owns persistence, so updating the displayed value after a failed save cannot trigger another write that clears the error. There are no new settings or storage formats.

## Evidence

- On unchanged main `c8f87b2e516`, a non-root disposable macOS 27.0 guest exercised the real marker setter against a task-owned read-only directory. The new creation regression failed because the setter returned nil even though the marker did not exist. The complete owner suite finished with 24 tests and this one expected failure, 0.062 seconds.
- With the repair, all 111 tests in GatewayLaunchAgentManagerTests, GatewayProcessManagerTests, and GatewayAutostartPolicyTests pass in the guest, 17.267 seconds. The new table covers both write directions, unchanged saved state after failure, successful retry, and idempotency.
- The native app and test bundle compile with `swift build --package-path apps/macos --build-system native --build-tests --disable-automatic-resolution`, 101.86 seconds.
- Pinned SwiftFormat 0.63.1, SwiftLint 0.65.1, and `git diff --check` pass. Fresh independent source review found no actionable P1/P2 findings.

The full macOS formatting check passes. The full lint script reports two inherited file-length violations in unchanged DashboardManager.swift and GatewayConnection.swift; both files are byte-identical to the base. The local sandbox also prevented SwiftLint cache writes. Lint of every changed file passes without a cache.

Actual-app before/after proof was captured in the disposable guest on November 2. With the task-owned state directory at mode 0500, the baseline app's failed removal returned the toggle to on and erased the error. The fixed app kept the saved on state and displayed the permission error. Restoring mode 0700 and retrying turned the control off, removed the marker, and cleared the error. Failed creation likewise kept the control off and showed an error; a writable retry recreated the marker. The test directory is back at mode 0700. This was a new offline profile with no running Gateway, operator credentials, or live account data.

![Before: failed-removal rollback silently clears the save error](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/5e1dabea-74b4-4fbd-ac50-8d2a48392281)

![After: failed removal retains the saved state and permission error](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/8e917158-e598-4700-bfd2-df8d0d93211a)

![After: failed creation reports the save error and stays off](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/70a7209b-cdb0-4005-a941-2a93b63bc54f)

![After: restoring write access lets the retry succeed and clears the error](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/d38548c9-6e09-4350-9228-ed8fedbf563a)

The production change removes one net line; the regression adds 23 Swift test lines. Release-note context: macOS attach-only preference save failures remain visible and can be retried.

AI-assisted. Thanks to @anmol0b for reporting both failure paths.

prs.body:
Closes #190151

## Maintainer disposition (November 9, 2026)

Approved for landing as submitted at unchanged head `4a375b5278d0`, using the existing Launch Services regression evidence. No additional VS Code installation or manual test is required. VS Code remains the selected editor, with the existing Finder fallback. The earlier maintainer draft hold is lifted; normal native merge gates remain in force. No product code changed for this approval.

### Current gate status

[CI run 42583866182](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/42583866182) succeeded at the unchanged head. The separate [Periphery run 42583865961](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/42583865961) failed: both builds stopped during tool installation with HTTP 504, and downstream scans had no artifacts. Periphery is not being reported as green.

The actual checkout was merge `b73d6fee312d` (main parent `b6d8eb287e08` plus this PR head). The Periphery workflow and its three tool installers are byte-identical to that parent. These are setup failures before source compilation, not dead-code findings against this change.

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes the macOS session menu's "Open Session Log" action doing nothing when VS Code is installed without its `code` command on the GUI search path.

## User Impact

Session logs open in the installed VS Code app, or appear in Finder when the editor is unavailable or cannot open them.

## Why This Change Was Made

Resolve VS Code through macOS Launch Services and observe the open result through the existing app-activation owner. This preserves the activation policy and Finder fallback.

## Evidence

### November 8: complete before/after recordings and both Finder fallbacks

[Current native proof and four recordings](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/190645#issuecomment-6724704903) supersede the earlier recording/open-error coverage limits below. At unchanged head `4a375b5278d01e90346e586b7ebf0020e85e968a`, the actual development app's production menu opens the synthetic transcript in real VS Code, selects it in Finder when editor lookup is absent, and selects it in Finder after a real asynchronous editor launch failure. A baseline recording shows the original missing-`code` failure. The comment includes two new Finder stills, preconditions, separate native API error confirmation, restoration, and validation limits.

The transcript is explicitly staged synthetic data. These are unbundled development executables, not signed release-package validation. No product code changed or fresh unit suite was run for this proof update. [ClawSweeper's completed November 8 re-review](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/190645#issuecomment-6563334241) rates overall readiness, proof and patch quality Diamond 5/6, with sufficient native evidence and no findings. It inspected the Finder stills and supplied diagnostics; video playback was unavailable in its review environment. Its sole before-merge item is Vyctor's decision on the draft hold. [Vyctor has been asked to assess the new reproduction](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/190645#issuecomment-6724806560); the PR remains draft.

### Earlier November 1 evidence (retained for history)

### Attached production-menu screenshots

These are saved, unedited window captures from a repeat of the same production-menu checks on November 1 at 4:54–4:55 PM ET. Brian clicked the native menu and saved the Screen Sharing window; I inspected both PNG files before uploading them. They contain only the disposable guest and synthetic fixture.

The native executable is still at reviewed head `4a375b5278d01e90346e586b7ebf0020e85e968a`, SHA-256 `d1442816618c18cf3643d8a0af3a7dfeaad0c98ebb939ded1796ffdeba3eacd6`. Finder abbreviates the selected icon label; the full matching filename remains visible in the editor tab behind it. This was the menu's reveal action, not a separate manual Finder selection.

![Finder selecting the synthetic JSONL after the same production menu action with the editor unavailable](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/834a0670-ef43-4949-8cc2-10ca8336edba)
