prs.title: improve(codex): reduce delays before replies in long sessions
prs.body:
Related: #185111

## What Problem This Solves

On the Codex runtime, OpenClaw read the whole mirrored session history in places where nothing used the result. On long sessions each of these reads is history-sized (seconds at 200,000 events). This PR removes two of them:

1. **Compaction hooks with no listener.** Every native Codex compaction read the whole history twice, before and after the compaction, to feed `before_compaction` and `after_compaction`, even when no plugin registered either hook.
2. **Context-engine bootstrap that changed nothing.** Before every Codex turn with an active context engine (for example Lossless Claw), the attempt read the whole history, ran the engine's bootstrap and bootstrap maintenance, then read the whole history again, even when maintenance reported no change. The re-read came back identical under the same read fence.

## User Impact

- Long Codex sessions with no compaction-hook listener no longer pay two full-history reads per compaction. With a listener nothing changes: `before_compaction` still receives the mirrored messages and `after_compaction` the message count and metadata.
- Codex sessions with a context engine do one full-history read before each turn instead of two whenever bootstrap maintenance reports no transcript change. The #185111 follow-up report on 2026.11.3 shows two consecutive `session context snapshot read` holds of 8,267 ms and 8,349 ms before one turn with Lossless Claw active (the reporter notes these include application work inside the transaction, not only disk reads); this PR skips the second read when bootstrap maintenance reports no transcript change. Lossless Claw at `15548bfcdd` returns `changed: false` during foreground bootstrap maintenance without rewriting OpenClaw's transcript; compaction work requires background execution. With that version, this PR skips the second history read on successful pre-turn setup. Bootstrap or maintenance failures still trigger a reread.
- When maintenance rewrites the transcript, fails, or bootstrap throws, the history is read again as before.

This is part of #185111, not all of it. The remaining pre-turn read on the Codex path still scans the whole transcript, because Codex compactions are recorded as display notes, not compaction boundaries. That needs a separate change and a Codex-runtime decision.

## Why This Change Was Made

**Compaction hooks.** The embedded compaction path already checks `hasHooks("before_compaction")` / `hasHooks("after_compaction")` before running those hooks (`src/agents/embedded-agent-runner/compact.queued-execution.ts`). The Codex event projector read the mirrored history first and only then called the shared hook helper, which checks for listeners itself. Codex now runs each compaction hook through one small sibling module, `event-projector-compaction-hooks.ts`: check for a listener with the public `getAgentHarnessHookRunner()`, read the history only then, skip the hook if the projection stopped during the read (as before), and run the shared helper.

**Bootstrap re-read.** Pre-turn bootstrap receives no `rewriteTranscriptEntries` capability (`preparePreTurnRuntimeContext` strips it), so only bootstrap maintenance can change transcript rows, and `maintain()` returns `changed`. `bootstrapHarnessContextEngine` now resolves whether the transcript may have changed: `true` when maintenance reported a change, when maintenance failed (it resolves `undefined` after a logged failure, and a partial rewrite is possible), or when bootstrap threw; `false` when there is no transcript, no bootstrap/maintain, or maintenance reported no change. The Codex attempt re-reads only on `true`. The other bootstrap callers (embedded runner, CLI runner, worker prompt) ignore the value; the embedded runner keeps a live session manager and never re-read. The context-engine docs now say engines must return `changed: true` when maintenance rewrote the transcript.

Accepted edge case: an engine that rewrites the transcript in bootstrap maintenance but returns `changed: false` would give the Codex turn the pre-rewrite history for that turn only; the next turn reads fresh rows. The documented pattern returns the rewrite helper's own result.

No plugin SDK contract is removed; `bootstrapHarnessContextEngine` now returns `Promise<boolean>` instead of `Promise<void>`.

## Full-product repro on main

Isolated Gateway built from `main` (`292a425338a`), the real Codex app-server on the Codex runtime, the QA channel and the QA mock model, with a test context-engine plugin selected through `plugins.slots.contextEngine`. The plugin declares current-turn fencing and atomic turn advancement (as real engines do), has `bootstrap()` and a `maintain()` that reports no change, and logs each call with a timestamp. A 200,000-event session (six resets in the first half, as in the report) is seeded for the DM's session key; three messages follow. Each message ran two Codex attempts, so each run has six bootstrap-to-assemble gaps. The reliable result: on `main` every attempt reads the whole history twice (once before bootstrap, once after `maintain` reported no change); with the fix it reads once (the unit test below counts the reads). The timings are observations from these runs: the gap between `maintain` returning and `assemble` starting contains the second read plus the other preparation work between them, so it is not a measurement of the read alone.

| Tree | Observed gaps between `maintain` returning and `assemble` starting | Message times |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `main`, run 1 | 679, 387, 412, 369, 388, 364 ms | 14.1 / 11.2 / 10.7 s |
| `main`, run 2 | 665, 376, 391, 363, 400, 361 ms | 14.1 / 11.0 / 10.6 s |
| fix | 283, 17, 29, 13, 25, 14 ms | 12.8 / 9.5 / 9.3 s |

Second message on `main` (run 1), from the proof's evidence file (engine calls with millisecond timestamps; message counts dropped). `maintain` returns at …168 and …902, `assemble` starts 412 ms and 369 ms later:

```
[repro-185111] turn-2 ms=11197 engineCalls=[{"call": "bootstrap", "at": 1794760269168}, {"call": "maintain", "at": 1794760269168}, {"call": "assemble", "at": 1794760269580}, {"call": "bootstrap", "at": 1794760273901}, {"call": "maintain", "at": 1794760273902}, {"call": "assemble", "at": 1794760274271}, {"call": "commitTurn", "at": 1794760274820}, {"call": "maintain", "at": 1794760274830}]
```

On the first turn the Codex `context` preparation stage (from `diagnostics.flags: ["codex.profiler"]`) took 4,333 / 4,255 ms on `main` and 3,762 ms with the fix. With the fix the first gap of the run was still 283 ms, the later ones 13-29 ms. On this machine the second read follows the first closely and is much cheaper than the first; the 2026.11.3 report shows two consecutive holds of about 8 s each, which include application work.

## Gateway proof with the scripted model: fix vs main

Same Gateway, Codex app-server, test engine and seeded session, built from `main` + this PR. Second message: `assemble` started 29 ms and 13 ms after `maintain` returned (412 ms and 369 ms on `main` in the same position), and the message took 9.5 s (11.2 s on `main`, run 1):

```
[repro-185111] turn-2 ms=9457 engineCalls=[{"call": "bootstrap", "at": 1794760826145}, {"call": "maintain", "at": 1794760826145}, {"call": "assemble", "at": 1794760826174}, {"call": "bootstrap", "at": 1794760830036}, {"call": "maintain", "at": 1794760830037}, {"call": "assemble", "at": 1794760830050}, {"call": "commitTurn", "at": 1794760830565}, {"call": "maintain", "at": 1794760830572}]
```

## Real model run (fix vs main)

Isolated Gateway started from the tree, the real Codex app-server and the real OpenAI model `openai/gpt-5.6-luna` on the Codex runtime, the same test context engine and a seeded 200,000-event session; three short turns through `/v1/responses`, all HTTP 200, no engine degradation. `main` = `292a425338a`, fix = this branch. Slow reads are `session context snapshot read` holds the Gateway logged as over 1 s; `context` is the Codex preparation stage.

| Tree | Slow history reads in three turns | `context` stage, turn 1 | Observed `maintain` -> `assemble` gap, turns 1 / 2 / 3 | Turn times |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `main` | 4 (4,788 / 3,922 / 4,785 / 4,810 ms) | 9,510 ms | 4,206 / 443 / 381 ms | 15.2 / 9.7 / 8.5 s |
| fix | 3 (4,705 / 4,977 / 4,763 ms) | 5,416 ms | 243 / 26 / 16 ms | 11.4 / 8.5 / 7.2 s |

On `main` the first turn logged two consecutive slow history reads (the second 3,922 ms, after bootstrap maintenance reported no change); with the fix it logged one. Turn times include the model's own latency, which varies run to run. Captured lines (turn 1 and the summary; text and usage fields dropped):

`main`:
```
[repro-185111] turn-1 {"ms":15160,"status":200,"engineCalls":[{"call":"bootstrap","at":1794765760669},{"call":"maintain","at":1794765760671},{"call":"assemble","at":1794765764877},{"call":"commitTurn","at":1794765768325},{"call":"maintain","at":1794765768332}],"preparation":["stage=context outcome=completed totalMs=9761 stages=connection:18ms@18ms,runtime:15ms@33ms,tools:218ms@251ms,context:9510ms@9761ms"]}
[repro-185111] proof {"model":"openai/gpt-5.6-luna","turns":[15160,9723,8510],"slowSnapshotReadMs":[4788,3922,4785,4810],"degraded":0}
```

fix:
```
[repro-185111] turn-1 {"ms":11434,"status":200,"engineCalls":[{"call":"bootstrap","at":1794766635424},{"call":"maintain","at":1794766635425},{"call":"assemble","at":1794766635668},{"call":"commitTurn","at":1794766638959},{"call":"maintain","at":1794766638971}],"preparation":["stage=context outcome=completed totalMs=5759 stages=connection:31ms@31ms,runtime:23ms@54ms,tools:289ms@343ms,context:5416ms@5759ms"]}
[repro-185111] proof {"model":"openai/gpt-5.6-luna","turns":[11434,8499,7209],"slowSnapshotReadMs":[4705,4977,4763],"degraded":0}
```

## Evidence

- Regression tests, red on `main`, green with the fix:
  - `event-projector.compaction-usage.test.ts` runs two Codex compactions with no hook registered and asserts the mirrored history is not read. On `main`: "expected readCodexMirroredSessionHistoryMessages to not be called at all, but actually been called 4 times".
  - `run-attempt.context-engine.test.ts` runs a Codex attempt with a context engine whose bootstrap maintenance (a) leaves the stored transcript unchanged, (b) writes a new message to it and reports the change, (c) writes a new message and then throws. It counts mirrored-history reads before the native turn starts (1, 2, 2) and checks that the message written during maintenance reaches the requests sent to Codex in (b) and (c). On `main` case (a) fails: "expected readMirroredSessionHistoryMessages to be called 1 times, but got 2 times".
- `context-engine-source-scope.test.ts` now expects a failed bootstrap to resolve `true` (re-read) instead of `undefined`.
- Existing hook tests still pass (`event-projector.verbose-hooks.test.ts`), as do the context-engine lifecycle, source-scope and transcript-cursor suites. Type-check, lint and format (`pnpm check:changed` against `main`) pass; its dead-export scan fails the same way on `main`.
- Test lines are net +36 against `main`: one three-row table pins the re-read decision for unchanged, rewritten and failed maintenance at the Codex attempt boundary, plus Fix A's spy and assertion in an existing compaction test; no existing suite counted these reads. The Fix A allocation record is removed (within the per-PR allowance).

### Compaction hooks: Gateway proofs (from the first revision)

Real model: an isolated Gateway, the real Codex app-server and `openai/gpt-5.6-luna` on the Codex runtime, a seeded 200,000-event session, three turns, Codex auto-compaction set to a small growth limit so it compacts once. Base `ca07e1c03c5`, fix `e8f8798a6f5`.

| Tree | Compaction hook listener | Real Codex compactions | Slow history reads in three turns |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| base | none | 1 | 4 |
| fix | none | 1 | 3 |
| fix | `before_compaction` + `after_compaction` (test plugin) | 1 | 4 |

Scripted model (QA mock, `codexMockAutoCompactTokenLimit: 1`), two turns, one compaction:

| Tree | Compaction hook listener | Slow history reads in two turns | Second turn |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| base, run 1 / run 2 | none | 3 / 3 | 10.3 s / 9.9 s |
| fix, run 1 / run 2 | none | 2 / 2 | 5.8 s / 5.2 s |
| fix | `before_compaction` + `after_compaction` (test plugin) | 3 | 9.9 s |

With a listener the plugin's `before_compaction` received 1,627 mirrored messages and `after_compaction` a count of 1,627, as on the base.

Proof artifice: the session history is seeded; the context-engine proof uses a test engine plugin and the QA mock model; the compaction proofs force a low Codex compaction limit.

Proof gaps: the context-engine proofs use a test engine, not Lossless Claw itself; the ~8 s holds come from the reporter's log, not from this machine. The remaining cold pre-turn read that #185111 reports is unchanged.

prs.title: fix(release): recover failed plugin artifact preparation
prs.body:
## What Problem This Solves

A runner loss during plugin package preparation leaves Full Release Validation unable to recover: its controller discovers core npm and Docker producers but silently omits the original plugin producer. This currently blocks qualification of 2026.10.33.

## User Impact

Release operators can recover the original plugin preparation pipeline without replacing the release candidate or mixing packages and verification evidence from different attempts. No runtime behavior, publication permission, or waiver changes.

## Why This Change Was Made

Discover and authenticate the original plugin producer using its exact workflow, repository, tooling SHA/ref, target, dist-tag, dispatch identity, run, and attempt. Retry its planning root and dependents so packaging, readback, and the final artifact seal share one attempt. Preserve green validation children and the existing parent reseal/strict-verification path.

## Evidence

- Regression reproduced on unchanged main: preflight omitted the original failed plugin producer. It passes with this change.
- 276 focused FRV/artifact tests passed, including full recovery selection, identity-drift rejection, both dist-tags, repeated log headers, and conflicting tags.
- Tooling test typecheck, targeted lint, formatting, and diff checks passed.
- Fresh independent review: no substantive findings after fixing two initial findings; reviewer additionally passed 151 FRV tests and 76 continuation/plugin-workflow tests.
- Canonical local autoreview, OpenClaw engine (`openai/gpt-6.1-sol`), P0–P2, base `66273da9a395ec9f91f7fb0a687fc8949ec8e371`: scoped-clean. Its supplied diff lacked unchanged workflow context; the independent source review covered those contracts.

The mocked controller test does not prove live GitHub dependent-job execution or final artifact adoption. The required post-merge FRV Proof Broker/Fixture must pass before this controller is used on the real release. No real producer retry or publication has been performed with this patch.

prs.title: feat(message): let operators confine group-turn sends to the current conversation
prs.body:
Related: #190557

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes: a group turn's `message` send can reach the owner's DM or another chat when the operator wants group turns kept in their own conversation, because the existing `crossContext` switches confine every kind of turn or none.

## User Impact

User impact: existing configs behave exactly as on main; no default changes. An operator who sets `tools.message.crossContext.confineChatTypes: ["group", "channel"]`, globally or per agent, gets group and channel turns that can only send to their own conversation. Any other target, on the same provider or another one, fails with `message_cross_context_denied` before a transport call. DM turns keep their current permissions. Separately, under the existing `allowWithinProvider: false`, a Telegram forum-topic send or poll that names the chat id with the current topic's `threadId`, or inherits it, is no longer denied. Other actions from a topic turn, such as renaming a topic, still have to name the current topic, as on main. Two deliberate tightenings apply under `allowWithinProvider: false`, or when group turns are confined. A turn in a Telegram forum topic can no longer create a forum topic in that chat, even through its own topic target, which main allows; the new topic is a sibling conversation in the base chat, and a turn bound to the chat itself still can. Telegram topic creation and topic edits that name another chat through `chatId`, `chat_id` or `channel_id` are denied. In every mode, a target that disagrees with one of those fields is refused as conflicting input. A numeric `target`, `to` or `channelId` is now read as its string, so it follows the same rules as the string: with a target the target wins, and alone it is the destination the check judges. Before, a numeric `channelId` skipped the check and Telegram acted on it, and a numeric `to` or `target` was dropped for the current conversation. A number that is not a safe integer is refused.

## Why This Change Was Made

The first revision (4b90fc67b80) flipped the shipped `allowWithinProvider` default to deny. That was the wrong shape. It reversed a deliberate default (#149875, #150157), it broke the required-delivery and context-isolation fixtures, and it changed bound broadcasts. My claim in the old body that broadcasts were exempt was wrong: child sends carry `toolContext` into the same check. Review also found a real matcher bug: the same-provider check ignored `threadId`, so a same-topic Telegram send could be denied.

This revision keeps the default and adds an opt-in inside the existing owner, `enforceCrossContextPolicy`:

- `confineChatTypes` keys on the conversation kind the host reports for the turn (`toolContext.currentChatType`). A listed kind may only target its own conversation; this overrides both `allowWithinProvider` and `allowAcrossProviders`. Unlisted kinds, and turns with no reported kind, keep those flags. A `POST /tools/invoke` call bound by the conversation headers reports the bound target's kind, so it is confined like a turn from that conversation. A per-agent list replaces the global one through the existing per-agent merge; `[]` lifts it.
- Broadcast child sends already go through this check, so a confined broadcast delivers the current conversation and reports a denial for every other target. There is no runner change.
- When same-provider sends are restricted, the check resolves the thread the send will actually use, with the same `resolveAndApplyOutboundThreadId` that delivery uses (on a copy of the params), and names the destination with the channel's own `resolveCurrentChannelId`. Policy and delivery now judge the same destination. Only `send` and `poll` are judged by that thread alone, because the runner delivers them into it. Other guarded actions only hand the thread to the plugin, so they are judged on their requested target as on main, and a thread they carry can only narrow that. `topic-create` must also name the current conversation through its parent chat, resolved with the channel's own conversation grammar (core's `resolveSessionConversation`, which asks `messaging.resolveSessionConversation`), because Telegram creates the topic in the base chat whatever topic or thread the request names. Telegram declares `chatId`, `chat_id` and `channel_id` as delivery-target aliases for `topic-create` and `topic-edit`, because its handler takes the chat from them ahead of the target. Normalization therefore canonicalizes them before the check, the same way the thread spellings are folded. Normalization also stringifies exact integer values of `target`, `to` and `channelId` before folding them: Telegram's chat reader accepts numbers, while the fold and the check read only strings.
  - When a Telegram target's encoded topic and an explicit `threadId` disagree, the check follows Telegram's delivery precedence: the explicit thread wins. Telegram's `resolveCurrentChannelId` now goes through `formatTelegramDeliveryTarget`, the helper Telegram already uses to name a delivered send (moved unchanged into `targets.ts`).
  - The shared param readers accept each key's snake_case form, and Telegram's handler reads `messageThreadId` or `message_thread_id` before `threadId` or `thread_id`. Action normalization now folds every one of those four spellings into one string `threadId` before any check, including a numeric `threadId`, which core's string reader would otherwise skip. Values that disagree are refused, and so is any value alongside an explicit `threadId: null`. On any channel, an action carrying only an alias, or a numeric `threadId`, gets that value as its string `threadId`.

What changed since `1cb5e029db3` (2026-11-10): `POST /tools/invoke` now reports the kind of the conversation its headers bind it to, so `confineChatTypes` applies to header-bound direct calls as it does to a turn from that conversation (`9aadc2bbc5c`). The Bot API traces at `1cb5e029db3` showed the gap: with only `confineChatTypes: ["group"]` set and the topic-A headers, all nine direct calls were delivered, including a `sendMessage` to the owner DM and `editForumTopic` and `createForumTopic` on it. `src/gateway/tool-resolution.ts` now sets `currentChatType` on the direct-invocation surface from the bound target, with the resolver outbound target resolution already uses, `inferChatTypeFromTarget` (now exported from `src/infra/outbound/targets.ts`; for Telegram it asks the plugin's `parseTelegramTarget`). Calls without the headers, the RPC `tools.invoke` and the MCP loopback surface are unchanged. `src/gateway/tool-resolution.direct-invoke-confinement.test.ts` fails on `1cb5e029db3` (`promise resolved "{ content: [ { …(2) } ], …(1) }" instead of rejecting` for a sibling-topic send from a header-bound call) and passes on this head; `92aee940aa8` raises the test-line allocation by its 62 lines.

pr-simplify: compared with the first revision, the default flip and its three default-denial tests are gone. No new plugin API, no runner or broadcast changes. Every remaining test group fails on a named control (below). The remaining growth is one config field (4 schema paths), the denial reason text, thread-aware matching, the tests (493 net test lines, allocated in `config/test-lines-allocations/message-cross-context-confine-chat-types.txt`), and one qa-lab scenario. Against main `9a5df3d60f1`, which this branch is rebased on:

- production source +194 −37 (`outbound-policy.ts` +86 −11; `tool-resolution.ts` +11 −1 and `targets.ts` +2 −1 for the direct-invocation kind; Telegram `targets.ts`, `channel.ts` and `action-runtime.ts` +40 −24 for the moved delivery-target helper and `channel-actions.ts` +11 for the topic chat aliases; `message-action-normalization.ts` +33; +11 across schema, help and labels)
- tests +493 (`tool-resolution.direct-invoke-confinement.test.ts` +62)
- qa-lab scenario +172
- docs +18, plus the regenerated config baseline counts and hashes

## Evidence

Focused suite (measured at `470c81210da` against its merge base `19aff5bfd42`; the current head's checks are below): `outbound-policy.test.ts`, `message-action-routing.send-policy.test.ts`, `message-action-runner.broadcast.test.ts`, plus the existing context-isolation fixtures in `message-action-routing.context.test.ts`.

- With the change: 51 of 51 pass, and the 15 context-isolation fixtures pass.
- `outbound-policy.ts` at the merge base: 8 fail, 43 pass.
  - The confined cross-provider, confined same-provider, and confined broadcast cases fail. The broadcast case gets `expected [ 'first', 'second' ] to deeply equal [ 'first' ]`.
  - 5 of the 6 Telegram topic cases fail: the chat id with the current `threadId`, and the chat id inheriting the topic, are falsely denied (`target="telegram:-1001234567890" while bound to "telegram:-1001234567890:topic:42"`). Another `threadId`, another topic target, and `topLevel: true` are let through.
  - The in-band current-topic target passes either way.
- Default flipped to deny (the first revision's shape): 6 of the 51 fail.
  - The existing `preserves required delivery when message-tool-only sends target another conversation` gets the denial instead of `missing reconcileUnknownSend`.
  - The default-delivery cases for sends and broadcasts fail, and so do the direct, untyped and per-agent `[]` cases.
  - 3 of the 15 existing context-isolation fixtures also fail with `Cross-context messaging denied`: `allows directchat target mismatch`, `allows localchat target mismatch` and `blocks cross-context UI handoff for thread-reply to another workspace channel`.

The Telegram cases run the bundled Telegram plugin's real threading code (dry run), under both `confineChatTypes: ["group"]` and `allowWithinProvider: false`.

Conflicting thread inputs (review P1), bound to topic 42:
- `-1001234567890:topic:42` with `threadId: "99"` is denied; on `7742e779d2e` it resolved.
- `-1001234567890:topic:99` with `threadId: "42"` is allowed; on `7742e779d2e` it was denied with `target="telegram:-1001234567890:topic:99" while bound to "telegram:-1001234567890:topic:42"`.
- A topic-42 target with `messageThreadId: "99"` is denied; on `5afec105d94` it resolved.
- A topic-42 target with `message_thread_id: "99"` is denied; on `470c81210da` it resolved. A dry run of the bundled Telegram plugin against a loopback Bot API delivered that send into topic 99 (`sendMessage` with `message_thread_id` 99) in 5 of 5 runs at `470c81210da`.
- A topic-42 target with a numeric `threadId: 99` is denied; on `ee49182a9c1` it resolved (`promise resolved "{ kind: 'send', …(9) }" instead of rejecting`). Through the message tool the schema already turns that number into a string, so this covers callers that pass a number to `runMessageAction`.
- Normalization: `message_thread_id`, `thread_id` or a numeric `threadId` alone becomes a string `threadId`. `{threadId: "42", messageThreadId: "99"}`, `{threadId: "42", message_thread_id: "99"}`, `{thread_id: "42", messageThreadId: "99"}` and `{threadId: null, message_thread_id: "99"}` are refused. The spelling cases fail on `470c81210da` (7 failed, 43 passed). One of them, `threadId` with `messageThreadId`, was already refused there and fails only on the new error text. `thread_id` alone was never a bypass, because core already read it. The numeric cases fail on `ee49182a9c1` (2 failed, 50 passed), and all 52 pass here.

Effect-scoped judgement (review P1) and Telegram chat aliases, through the bundled Telegram plugin under both `confineChatTypes: ["group"]` and `allowWithinProvider: false` (the Telegram table is now 30 rows x 2 switches):
- `topic-create` to `-1001234567890` with `name` from a turn bound to topic 42 is denied; on `561a13dd1af` it was allowed (the review repro), and main denies it under `allowWithinProvider: false`.
- `topic-create` through the topic-42 target, with or without `threadId: "42"`, is denied; main and `af58c646aea` allowed it. From a turn bound to the chat itself, `topic-create` to the chat id is allowed and through a topic-99 target is denied, as on main.
- `topic-edit` naming topic 42 but `chatId` or `channel_id` of another chat is refused as conflicting input; `topic-edit` or `topic-create` with only `chatId` of another chat is denied. All four were allowed on main and on `46c40dc35e6`. A same-chat `chatId` stays allowed. That Telegram acts on the other chat comes from reading the handler; a recorded non-dry handler run shows that chat reaching it.
- Numeric target keys (review P1 at `3a79b762bb7`): from a group turn bound to `-1001234567890`, `topic-create` with target `-1001234567890` and numeric `channelId: -1009999999999` now reaches Telegram's handler with only the chat target; a recorded non-dry handler run shows `channelId` dropped (at `3a79b762bb7` and on main it carried the other chat). Numeric `channelId` of another chat alone is denied for `topic-create` and `topic-edit`; the same chat's numeric id stays allowed. Normalization turns numeric `target`, `to` and `channelId` into strings and refuses `2 ** 60` and `1.5`. Through the model's message tool the agent loop already coerces the number to a string before `execute`, and Tool Search and Code Mode reject it, so a real-Gateway dry run sent `editForumTopic` to the turn's own topic. This covers callers that hand a number to `runMessageAction` or call the tool's `execute` directly (the Gateway's tool-invoke path and in-process callers), as with the numeric `threadId` case.
- Red: 3 of 29 at `561a13dd1af`, 2 of 33 at `af58c646aea`, 4 of 39 at `46c40dc35e6`, 9 of 78 at `3a79b762bb7` (normalization and send-policy tests together); all pass now. Ten mutation controls (dropping each rule or alias, making the parent check always deny or parent-only, leaving `channelId` numeric, or stringifying inexact numbers) are each caught.
- Action by action, under a restricting switch: `send` and `poll` are judged by the resolved thread; `sticker`, `edit`, `delete`, `topic-create` and `topic-edit` by the requested target plus any thread it carries (and `topic-create` also by its parent chat); `react`, `read`, `emoji-list` and `sticker-search` are not guarded.

qa-lab, `qa suite --provider-mode mock-openai --scenario message-cross-context-confine-group` (qa-channel, real gateway child, mock-openai):

- With the change: pass, at `79dbe06abbe`, `3a79b762bb7`, `561a13dd1af` and `ee49182a9c1` (merged with main), `470c81210da` and `7742e779d2e`.
  - With no config, a group turn's send reaches the DM.
  - After `config.patch` sets `confineChatTypes: [group]`, the same send returns `Cross-context messaging denied: action=send target="dm:alice" while bound to "group:qa-confine-group" (channel=qa-channel). tools.message.crossContext.confineChatTypes keeps group turns in their current conversation.`, and 0 DM deliveries follow.
  - The group's own sends and a DM turn's send to another group still deliver.
- Policy reverted: fail at the confined step. The DM was delivered.

Compatibility: `confineChatTypes` is optional and empty by default, and omitted policy behaves as on main. Two existing-setting changes, both only when same-provider sends are restricted: the `topic-create` tightening, and `chatId`/`chat_id`/`channel_id` on Telegram topic actions being judged as the target. Changes in every mode: a Telegram topic action whose target disagrees with one of those fields is refused as conflicting input, including the same chat spelled two ways; a numeric `target`, `to` or `channelId` is used as its string (a numeric `to` or `target` alone was dropped for the current conversation before), and a number that is not a safe integer is refused. Other consistent inputs behave as before when no policy is set. The fixtures that the first revision broke pass unchanged.

Not covered: a run on real Telegram. The runs above use the real Gateway and Telegram plugin with a loopback Bot API.

Revocation (measured with a real model, loopback Bot API). Tightening the policy applies from the next turn; a turn that is already running keeps the config it started with. One topic turn sent to the DM, waited 25 s in `exec`, and sent again; I tightened the policy with `config set` while it waited.

| Build | Key set mid-turn | Hot reload applied | Second send (planned) | Next turn |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 2026.11.1 | `allowWithinProvider: false` | 07:02:59.062Z | delivered (07:03:23.5Z) | denied |
| this branch | `confineChatTypes: ["group"]` | 07:04:25.367Z | delivered (07:04:49.8Z) | denied |
| this branch | `allowWithinProvider: false` | 07:05:41.236Z | delivered (07:06:10.8Z) | denied |

The message tool reads the turn's config, `getConfig: () => options?.config ?? getRuntimeConfig()` (`src/agents/tools/message-tool-execution.ts:155` at main `3855c896edd` and at this head). `config-reload-plan.ts:263` documents the `tools` prefix as "Prospective operation policy; retained turns and resources keep their own lifetime". So `confineChatTypes` behaves like every existing `crossContext` setting, and like the in-flight cases in #103900 and #189752.

## Bot API traces (2026-11-10)

On this head `92aee940aa8`, built alone, a topic-A turn under `confineChatTypes: ["group"]` puts its same-topic poll and topic rename into topic A. The sibling-topic, other-chat, alias and topic-create calls make no Bot API request at all: after each refusal, the only request is the turn's own reply in topic A. Direct calls through the Gateway's `POST /tools/invoke` that carry the conversation headers for topic A are confined the same way: under `confineChatTypes: ["group"]` alone, and under `allowWithinProvider: false`, every call that names another topic or chat is refused with no Bot API request, where main `9a5df3d60f1` (this branch's merge base) sends the numeric ones to topic 99 or acts on another chat. I ran everything twice, and both runs made the same Bot API requests (method, chat, thread, status) with the same results in all 49 recorded turns and calls.

Setup:
- The real Gateway with the bundled Telegram plugin, built from this head alone (`pnpm build`, buildstamp head `92aee940aa8`, `inputsClean: true`), and main `9a5df3d60f1` built the same way. Every Gateway log line in both runs, 2,981 of 2,981, reports runtime `node` `26.12.1` (macOS arm64).
- The Gateway polls a loopback Bot API (Crabline 0.2.0) through a recording proxy that logs each Bot API request the Gateway sends, with all of its parameters. These are HTTP requests from the Gateway, not the plugin's dry-run mode. Crabline has no `sendPoll`, so the proxy answers that one method itself, with a poll message in the requested chat and thread.
- The model is QA Lab's mock OpenAI provider, in its own process, playing a fixed list of `message` tool calls per turn. Each turn starts from a user message in topic A (thread 42) of a forum supergroup; topic B is thread 99. Chat ids are replaced with `<group>` (the supergroup) and `<owner-dm>` (a private chat).
- Run 1 18:06:58Z to 18:12:07Z, run 2 18:12:07Z to 18:17:13Z.

Topic-A turns under `tools.message.crossContext.confineChatTypes: ["group"]`:

| Case | `message` call | Tool result | Bot API requests in the turn |
|---|---|---|---|
| Poll (allowed) | `poll`, target `<group>:topic:42` | `ok` | `sendPoll` to `<group>` with `message_thread_id: 42`, then the reply |
| Topic edit (allowed) | `topic-edit`, target `<group>:topic:42`, `threadId: "42"` | `ok` | `editForumTopic` on `<group>` with `message_thread_id: 42`, then the reply |
| Sibling topic | `send`, target `<group>:topic:99` | denied: `target="telegram:<group>:topic:99" while bound to "telegram:<group>:topic:42"` | the reply only |
| Sibling topic, other spellings | `<group>` with `threadId: "99"`; `<group>:topic:42` with `threadId`, `messageThreadId` or `message_thread_id` `"99"`, or `threadId: 99` as a number | denied, 5 of 5, each naming topic 99 | the reply only |
| Other chat | `send`, target `<owner-dm>` | denied: `target="telegram:<owner-dm>"` | the reply only |
| Other-chat aliases | `topic-edit` of `<group>:topic:42` with `chatId`, `chat_id` or `channel_id` set to `<owner-dm>` | `Action topic-edit received conflicting target and delivery alias values.`, 3 of 3 | the reply only |
| Alias alone | `topic-edit` or `topic-create` with only `chatId: "<owner-dm>"` | denied: `target="telegram:<owner-dm>"`, 2 of 2 | the reply only |
| Topic create | `topic-create` with target `<group>`, with target `<group>:topic:42`, and with `<group>:topic:42` plus `threadId: "42"` | denied, 3 of 3 | the reply only; no `createForumTopic` |
| Main control | the sibling-topic send on main, no `crossContext` settings | `ok`, `threadId: "99"` | `sendMessage` with `message_thread_id: 99`, then the reply |

"The reply" is the turn's answer, a `sendMessage` to `<group>` with `message_thread_id: 42`. Every turn also sends one `sendChatAction` (typing) to thread 42. Each denial ends with `tools.message.crossContext.confineChatTypes keeps group turns in their current conversation.`

Direct calls: `POST /tools/invoke` with the `message` tool, the topic-A session and the Gateway's conversation headers (`x-openclaw-message-channel: telegram`, `x-openclaw-message-to: telegram:<group>:topic:42`, `x-openclaw-thread-id: 42`), once with only `confineChatTypes: ["group"]` set and once with only `allowWithinProvider: false`. This path passes the arguments to the tool's `execute` as sent, so a number stays a number.

| Arguments | This head, `confineChatTypes: ["group"]` | This head, `allowWithinProvider: false` | Main `9a5df3d60f1`, `allowWithinProvider: false` |
|---|---|---|---|
| `send`, target `<group>:topic:42`, `threadId: 42` (number) | `sendMessage`, thread 42 | `sendMessage`, thread 42 | `sendMessage`, thread 42 |
| same target, `threadId: 99` (number) | refused, no request | refused, no request | `sendMessage`, thread 99 |
| same target, `threadId: "99"` | refused, no request | refused, no request | `sendMessage`, thread 99 |
| `send`, `to: <owner-dm>` (number) | refused, no request | refused, no request | `sendMessage` to `<group>`, thread 42 (the number was dropped for the current conversation) |
| `send`, `to: "<owner-dm>"` | refused, no request | refused, no request | refused |
| `topic-edit`, `channelId: <owner-dm>` (number), `threadId: "42"` | refused, no request | refused, no request | `editForumTopic` on `<owner-dm>` |
| same, `channelId: "<owner-dm>"` | refused, no request | refused, no request | refused |
| `topic-create`, `channelId: <owner-dm>` (number) | refused, no request | refused, no request | `createForumTopic` on `<owner-dm>` |
| same, `channelId: "<owner-dm>"` | refused, no request | refused, no request | refused |

On this head the Gateway logs each refusal. Under `confineChatTypes` it ends with the confinement reason, for example `MessageActionDeniedError: Cross-context messaging denied: action=send target="<group>:topic:99" while bound to "telegram:<group>:topic:42" (channel=telegram). tools.message.crossContext.confineChatTypes keeps group turns in their current conversation.`; the `to`, `topic-edit` and `topic-create` rows name `target="telegram:<owner-dm>"`. The HTTP caller gets `500` with `{"type":"tool_error","message":"tool execution failed"}` for a refusal, on main as well.

What these runs also showed, and what they do not cover:
- At `1cb5e029db3` the `confineChatTypes` column was all delivered: with only `confineChatTypes: ["group"]` set and the same headers, all nine calls went out, including a `sendMessage` to `<owner-dm>` and `editForumTopic` and `createForumTopic` on `<owner-dm>`, because `/tools/invoke` reported no conversation kind. `9aadc2bbc5c` makes it report the kind of the conversation its headers bind it to, which gives the refusals above.
- Without the conversation headers, `/tools/invoke` has no current conversation on either build (`Action send requires a target. This turn has no current conversation; pass an explicit target, or reply in normal text.`), so no `crossContext` switch applies. This is unchanged by `9aadc2bbc5c`: in both runs on this head, under `confineChatTypes`, a `threadId` of 99, string or number, went to topic 99, as it does on main. `topic-edit` with `channelId` `<owner-dm>` acted on `<owner-dm>` as a string on both builds, and as a number on this head; main refused the number with that "requires a target" error.
- The Bot API is a loopback, not Telegram. The traces show what the Gateway sent, not how Telegram would answer.

prs.title: fix(ui): keep lazy panel menu actions ready for selection
prs.body:
Dashboard options can ignore Expand Dashboard or Restore split just after opening.

## Work sessions

Linked for team reference; these sessions aren’t public.

- [Implementation and verification](https://team.openclaw.ai/chat/roboclaw/~key/dashboard/6a1b6fef-8de4-46d1-8db7-8a8e43aa305c)

## What Problem This Solves

When lazy panel-menu content is already loaded, enabled rows can render before their selection handlers are registered. Clicking one then silently does nothing and leaves the root menu open. Five unrelated UI E2E jobs fail in the same layout-preservation test: three select Restore split and two select Expand Dashboard.

## User Impact

Dashboard and Layout menu actions become available together with their handlers, so the first actionable click can change the layout and dismiss the menu even during its opening phase.

## Why This Change Was Made

Rendering and activation now share the registered handler snapshot. Until it is ready, both use the existing disabled Loading row. This removes the independent body-rendering path that exposed actions before activation could find them. The shared test helper and its menu-hidden assertion are unchanged.

One shared panel-menu factory owns registration, loading items, lazy group rendering, error recovery, selection, and focus handoff for both consumers. The lazy components register their handlers; the factory renders only registered rows. This removes duplicate group renderers, the unused render callback bridge, and the separate boundary wrapper, preserving the readiness fix and unchanged regression. Production is net 38 lines smaller than the original base; the regression adds 105 lines. No budget or baseline file changes.

## Evidence

- A deterministic Node/jsdom regression exercises the real Dashboard menu, primes its lazy component in a separate mount, then clicks the first enabled connected leaf while frame callbacks are held in `opening`. It does not mock `onReady`, menu activation, or selection. Both labels fail on the base with no `menu-select` event and pass with the fix, including the expected layout update and menu closure.
- Final regression: 2/2 pass in 0.861 s Vitest wall time (179 ms in test callbacks); the exact regression fails 2/2 on original production source in 0.957 s. The CI Bun run also passed both cases in 256 ms total (193 ms / 63 ms).
- The current follow-up plus existing pane-header and dashboard-presentation consumer suites: 80/80 pass across three named files in 4.47 s. The readiness regression is unchanged.
- Touched-file type-aware lint, formatting, and `git diff --check` pass. Lint reports existing warnings in the unchanged layout-model function.
- Strict touched-file typecheck was attempted but stopped before checking source because the repository wrapper rejects a compiler outside the worktree; the existing dependencies are in a shared cache. No compiler guard was bypassed. CI production and test typechecks subsequently passed; the local placement limitation remains recorded.
- Fresh follow-up Auto Review (Codex, P0–P2) reviewed the complete local candidate, including the shared helper and unchanged regression, against `9f441adcf1e7307e1dfd0a496660106c4922dfe8` with the menu, machine, overlay lifecycle/control, and lazy-content owners supplied: scoped-clean, no findings. Local ClawSweeper is unavailable.
- No browser, Chromium, container, dependency installation, or broad local sweep was run on the Team Gateway host. The CI artifacts identify the matching root-menu state but do not retain activation history for the original five failures; exact-head PR CI must supply the browser result.


### Sizing acceptance for the follow-up

The normalized **chat boot JS gzip** measurement in PR CI's existing `pnpm ui:check-performance:base` head/base build comparison must have **head minus base <= 0 bytes**. Use that CI pair for the same workload and normalization; the preceding candidate was +30 bytes. This is an artifact-size comparison, not a latency sample. No local UI build or performance/packaging script is run on the Team Gateway host. No budget or baseline changes are permitted.

Current candidate: `7016bddcdba19b81ae033da6e96be93058e72a53`. [Its control-ui-performance check passes](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/44012963534/job/133804985780): normalized chat boot JS gzip **1,324,689 → 1,324,606 bytes (−83)**, **85 bytes below** the unchanged 1,324,691-byte ceiling. The CI pair uses base `a564030a2b6ea08a2198a16d6865f1d9928dd496` and merge checkout `64c6fd806b805ecb09818b5d99345a7ad2012bb1`, with Node v24.22.1 / Vite 8.3.5 / Pako 3.0.3. This meets the <=0-byte acceptance rule.

Fresh P0–P2 Auto Review of the complete candidate is scoped-clean; all 80 focused tests and touched-file type-aware lint/format pass. [Exact-head production types](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/44012963534/job/133805937383) and [selected UI E2E smoke shard](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/44012963534/job/133804985754) pass. Test types, CI lint and UI unit shards were still running at the result capture; no full-CI success claim is made. The original browser layout caller remains outside the observed smoke selection.

[The preceding fdda84cb performance check](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/44011903578/job/133801349082) measured **1,324,689 → 1,324,707 bytes (+18)**, against base `f52f728d34158e66c0d11ce48cc7fb1c7a0cd6a7`; the current shared renderer addresses that remaining growth. Production and test typechecks and the selected UI E2E shard passed on that prior head. Its performance failure was not rerun.

[The cf709361 performance check](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/44010220663/job/133795978659) measured **1,324,689 → 1,324,703 bytes (+14)**, 12 bytes above the 1,324,691-byte ceiling. This supersedes the earlier +30-byte candidate but still fails the acceptance criterion.

[The latest main run that actually ran performance](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/44010442679/job/133796400798), at `054fd9788bc0f86303e161ca3b2ab36a1ed8cd65`, measured **1,324,689 bytes**, 2 bytes below that ceiling. Newer main push runs skipped the performance job or had no such job. Thus cf709361 adds 14 bytes against the same measured main/base; its gzip failure is attributable to this diff. Exact byte figures come from only the scalar comparison lines in the job output; the check summary has no byte figures. No full logs or local builds were used.

### Prior-head PR CI results

[CI run 44007450967](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/44007450967) covers head `80923235eae1b1762d024709fe000d738801f5e4` through merge checkout `3a2e5808f80a2a109c114995b63c545dffbaa704`.

- [UI shard 1/3](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/44007450967/job/133786879688) passes, including both new readiness cases on Bun. UI shard 3/3, production/test typechecks, architecture guards and baseline ratchets also pass.
- [UI E2E shard 1/2](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/44007450967/job/133786879480) passes: 12 tests across five selected smoke files. This selection does **not** include `chat-panel-layout.e2e.test.ts`; the original browser caller remains unrerun. No Chromium/Playwright run was attempted on the Team Gateway host, and blocked remote credentials were not bypassed.
- [UI shard 2/3](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/44007450967/job/133786879718) fails `chat-position-rail.test.tsx > conversation position rail > keeps the focused run marker through streaming and retargets its persisted answer` (`expected false to be true`). The fixture mounts only ChatThread/transcript and ChatPositionRail; it never renders or calls the panel-menu factories changed here. The new readiness test ran in shard 1/3, a separate process from this shard. This failure is unreachable from this diff and is left untouched; it is not the l74 wheel/layout assertion.
- [Control UI performance](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/44007450967/job/133786879735) fails. Its own head/base comparison reports chat boot JS gzip **1,324,689 → 1,324,719 bytes (+30)** against a 1,324,691-byte limit, so this change crosses that budget by 28 bytes. Both builds also violate the shared CSS ceiling (59,191 vs 58,315 bytes) and chat request count (21 vs 20). No budget, baseline, or exception was changed.

That prior-head CI run completed with failure. The PR remains ready and unmerged; the follow-up is measured by a new automatic PR run after its source commit.

### Supplemental release regression proof — November 17, 2026

Actual Chromium captures compare parent `cc6c3a733dfa9e226efcf4b2c221c45fe40f9acc` with merged repair `8a82b5e0b29108b804ea9267f04409cb7a9950f3`. Same synthetic fixture, light theme and 1440×900 viewport; mocked Gateway data, not real-backend proof. Priming one session menu then opening a new session reproduces the warm-module/new-owner race. Both clicks occur at the first enabled DOM observation during opening: before remains open/split; after dismisses and expands. Clean and annotated images below were inspected and sanitized. No DOM fabrication or frame scheduling manipulation. Exact release backport `f41b66c8f5f557fb8d6713a78d9a6839d27c4821` additionally passes the original panel browser suite (3/3). Full candidate qualification remains outstanding.

![Before: first enabled click leaves menu open and dashboard split](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/82e60a88-e954-4d3e-b929-6a01abb8797a)

![After: first enabled click closes menu and expands dashboard](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/10491c2b-5ce6-47b0-a9db-188d1ece0ebb)

![Before annotated: menu remains open](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/d4746649-0d50-4245-8207-d50bfc94c7b4)

![After annotated: dashboard expands](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/c2299da6-0b91-45fc-8afa-ad4a16d49ba7)

prs.title: fix: let gateway restart wait for a Gateway that is still starting before its port opens
prs.body:
Root cause: src/cli/daemon-cli/restart-health.ts:527 renews the restart readiness window only on signals the replacement can send after it opens its listener (or on a same-process migration lease), so a replacement that is still working before its listener, such as the copy-and-swap state upgrade or plugin loading, gets a fixed 60 s window and is reported as `still-starting` on a restart that succeeds.

Related: #161158. This fixes the false `still-starting` result when the new Gateway is slow before it opens its port. Two parts of that issue stay open: how the source updater handles a native exit 2 from its restart callback, and a Gateway whose listener is open but doesn't answer its probes.

## What Problem This Solves

`openclaw gateway restart` gives up after 60 seconds when the new Gateway is slow to open its port, even though the same process becomes ready a minute later. This happens after an upgrade, when the Gateway upgrades its state before it opens its port, and on slow hosts that load plugins for longer than 60 seconds. Scripts and operators see a failed restart that actually worked.

## User Impact

A restart now waits for the Gateway the service manager started, for as long as that same process is still running and has not opened its port yet. It succeeds with exit 0 once the Gateway is ready. The existing five-minute cap still applies. A Gateway that exits or is replaced by the supervisor still fails with exit 1, and one still unready at the cap is still reported as `still-starting` (exit 2). No new options or messages.

## Why This Change Was Made

Before its listener opens, the Gateway has no `/startupz` endpoint, so the CLI cannot see startup phases. The only real signal is the service manager's own process: the same PID running without a restart. The readiness wait now treats that as startup progress until the listener opens. After that, the existing rules apply: the listener, identity and new phases renew the window. Phases from a different PID, or a supervisor's next process, still don't count.

The same-process migration-lease renewal was a narrower version of this signal: startup migrations only run before the listener, in the same process. It is now covered by the general rule, so this PR removes it, along with the lease-activity callback that only it used. The lease poll stays for the `startup migration` phase label and the diagnostic absence checks.

The reporter's exit 0 does not reproduce. `fail()` in `src/cli/daemon-cli/response.ts` has exited 1 (or 2 for `still-starting`) since v2026.9.6. The control run below shows exit 1 for a restart that really fails.

Doctor restoration and update readiness use the same wait. Explicit deadlines (`gateway start`, update budgets) are unchanged. Out of scope here: when the source updater gets a native exit 2 back from its restart callback (`scripts/update-gateway-build.mts`), it treats that as a failed update. That gap was raised in the issue comments and is update-owned.

Thanks @Angelojiang11 for the report, and @Tosko4 and @hannesrudolph for the slow-start measurements.

## Evidence

Real systemd user unit on Debian 12 (node:24.22.1, systemd as PID 1, user `pi`), secretless container. `openclaw@2026.11.3` from npm onboards with `--install-daemon`, then the package is upgraded in place to this tree and the new CLI runs `openclaw gateway restart`. The container has 0.5 CPU (a slow host). The replacement runs the natural copy-and-swap state upgrade (`cli.bootstrap.state-upgrade` about 56 s), then opens its listener. `/readyz` is polled from a separate loop.

- Base b60b11474606, two runs: `Gateway service is still starting after 60s. Last observed startup phase: waiting for Gateway listener.`, `RESTART rc=2 after 70s`; the same PID reaches `/readyz` 200 at 119 s and 133 s, with `NRestarts=0`.
- Candidate, two runs: `Restarted systemd service: openclaw-gateway.service`, `RESTART rc=0 after 145s` / `READYZ 200 at t=145s` and `RESTART rc=0 after 111s` / `READYZ 200 at t=111s`, same PID, `NRestarts=0`.
- Control, both sides: a syntax error in `openclaw.json` makes the replacement refuse startup (exit 78). `Gateway restart failed after 15s: service stayed stopped and health checks never came up.` with `RESTART rc=1` (base 19 s, candidate 22 s).
- Unit: `restart-health-progress.test.ts` "bounds a silent startup before its listener" fails on base (`still-starting` at 60 s) and passes here (`healthy` at 120 s). A supervisor's next process before the listener still stops at the old bound.
- Lines: production -31 net (+17/-48) (restart-health.ts, startup-migration-checkpoint.ts); tests -93 net. Removed only the migration-heartbeat stall cases, whose behavior is now covered by the pre-listener rule.
- Upgrade on the same state (requested by review): released `openclaw@2026.11.5` refuses as a downgrade (`Refusing to restart the gateway service because this OpenClaw binary (2026.11.4) is older than the config last written by OpenClaw 2026.11.5.`, rc=1), because main is still 2026.11.4. So I used released `openclaw@2026.11.4` (d843d6a): it onboards the systemd service, a setting is written with it (`agents.defaults.timeoutSeconds 1611`), and the package is upgraded in place to this candidate on the same state. Then `openclaw gateway restart` at 0.5 CPU. The old Gateway took 330 s to stop (killed at its stop timeout; separate from this change). The replacement ran `cli.bootstrap.state-upgrade 58313ms` before its listener, then `RESTART rc=0 after 452s`, `READYZ 200 at t=452s`, same PID, `NRestarts=0`. Settings and data before and after: `gateway.bind=loopback`, `timeoutSeconds=1611`, agent `main` listed, 3 SQLite databases present, all unchanged.

prs.title: fix: avoid false identity errors when unlinked channel users create sessions
prs.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes independent session creation failing for an admitted, unlinked channel sender when the agent supplies a Team profile ID discovered outside the current request.

## User Impact

Admitted unlinked senders can use the same restricted creation path as calls that omit `user`. Valid linked-participant selection remains available; invalid or revoked linked selections remain errors. No new permissions, configuration, or account-linking requirement.

## Why This Change Was Made

Keep the optional selector and existing creation owner. Determine fallback eligibility from the ingress owner's original authenticated sender/account linkage result, not a model-supplied ID, another session's owner, or the absence of a current profile. Carry that fact privately to the admitted request and use it only for this independent-creation fallback.

The original refusal correctly prevented an unsupported identity selection; it was not a privilege escalation. This avoids an unnecessary failure without removing collaborative participant selection.

## Evidence

- **Red/green:** at the base, omitted-user creation passed while the same admitted unlinked source with a supplied unrelated profile failed before creation. The fix makes both use the existing contained creation path.
- **Final candidate:** 16 owning-boundary, reply-producer, and lifetime tests plus all 8 channel-admission tests passed. These exercise ingress, private handoff, run admission, the real tool/router, and SQLite creation. Restrictions remain inherited; mismatched, linked-without-grant, unverified, internal, serialized, known-bot, and retired sources do not gain fallback eligibility. Original-source revocation and admitted-owner closure still refuse. Other tools retain explicit-user validation.
- **Sibling coverage:** 200 affected-consumer tests and 78 selected collaboration/native tests passed, including stable tool definitions, original-requester defaults, valid Bob selection, revocation, overlapping Alice/Bob calls, and queued custody. These broader results preceded the final private-handoff simplification; unchanged-input proof was reused. The final 16-test batch and 8-test admission suite cover the changed handoff and lifetime contracts.
- **CI repair:** the first revision introduced a session-identity ratchet failure. The repair removes the duplicate guard and reuses `resolveAdmittedRunActiveAssertion`; no diagnostic rename, baseline change, suppression, or weakened lifetime check. The ratchet passes locally and in the corrected revision's CI.
- Targeted typecheck, lint, formatting, diff checks, and commit hooks passed.
- **Independent review:** shared autoreview using Codex CLI completed P0–P2 review of the full candidate against base `b9a72b5bef8d648024f89b66af9579691ae40ce1`, then a fresh P0–P2 review of the CI-repair delta against `9ab2e2653ad4491a9c21ec30946cb79630708f7a`. Both returned `scoped-clean`, no findings; committed diffs match their reviewed snapshots. Local ClawSweeper was not used because its available checkout was dirty/ambiguous; it was left unchanged. The independent reviewers did not run project tests.
- **Published-head CI:** [CI run 44037524592](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/44037524592) completed successfully for `6d7f6eeded072fdafcca031430e2c81b1198f072`. The complete 128-entry check rollup had no failed or pending entries. The published tree exactly matches the reviewed and locally tested candidate.

**Limitations:** these are isolated production-owner/composition tests with fixed or mocked model/transport I/O, not live Discord/real-model end-to-end proof. No restart, upgrade, or native-engine E2E claim is made. The private finding deliberately does not survive serialization, restart reconstruction, or another operational run; those paths keep normal selection validation.

### Original failure

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
  participant Sender as Admitted unlinked sender
  participant Agent as Agent
  participant Tool as sessions_create
  participant Runtime as Trusted runtime
  Sender->>Agent: Create an independent session
  Agent->>Agent: Copy profile ID from another session's owner
  Agent->>Tool: Create with user set to copied ID
  Tool->>Runtime: Resolve admitted participant
  Runtime-->>Tool: No person authority for supplied ID
  Tool-->>Agent: Refuse before creation
  Note over Tool,Runtime: Correct identity guard; no security bypass
```

### After: preserve valid selection and the unlinked path

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  A[Admitted messaging-service request] --> B[Ingress owner resolves sender and account linkage]
  B -->|Originally unlinked source| C[Retain private direct-source unlinked finding]
  C --> D[sessions_create ignores supplied user]
  B -->|Linked requester| E[Keep existing participant selection]
  E -->|Unknown or revoked selection| F[Refuse without creation]
  E -->|Valid selection or original-requester default| G[Existing creation owner]
  D --> G
  G --> H[Inherit sandbox, tool limits and permission ceiling]
  H --> I[Create independent session]
  J[Missing or unsupported source evidence] --> K[No fallback; existing validation applies]
```

### Identity, assignment, and permissions remain separate

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
  participant Human as Linked requester or authorized administrator
  participant Runtime as Admitted runtime
  participant Create as Creation owner
  participant Assign as Ownership assignment
  Human->>Runtime: Request creation
  Runtime->>Create: Validated requester or allowed unlinked context
  Create->>Create: Enforce inherited permission ceiling
  Create-->>Human: New session with normal ownership rules
  Human->>Assign: Assign to another person, if authorized
  Assign->>Assign: Change responsibility metadata
  Note over Runtime,Assign: Assignment does not replace requester identity or transfer authority
```

Worked on by:
- @Patrick-Erichsen

## Work sessions

Linked for team reference; these sessions aren’t public.

- [Original discussion with @Patrick-Erichsen](https://team.openclaw.ai/chat/roboclaw)
- [Design and implementation discussion](https://team.openclaw.ai/chat/roboclaw/~key/dashboard/bfd3fabc-af92-4506-8c7f-0e2043c807a0)
- [Implementation and verification](https://team.openclaw.ai/chat/roboclaw/~key/subagent/00a0b766-1992-4358-a87a-45da91109d4b)

## Worked on by

- @Patrick-Erichsen

Full Release Validation automatically includes upgrades from the outdated `2026.6.34` release because it is pinned as the oldest supported qualification baseline.

## User Impact

Runtime update behavior, explicit historical/manual June selection, and frozen historical release behavior remain unchanged.

Preserve the existing June capability threshold for the legacy operator-state scenario. Update only existing fixtures and expectations and the two workflow descriptions; no new tests or scenarios were added. The candidate fixture includes a July extended-stable predecessor as registry data, not as a replacement floor.

## Evidence

- 96 existing tests passed: candidate-owned full release dispatch (27), upgrade survivor baseline selection (34), release baseline resolution (20), and catalog parsing (15). Removed the obsolete pinned-floor error case.

prs.title: fix: name paused Code Mode waits in stall diagnostics
prs.body:
## What Problem This Solves

When a Code Mode `exec` pauses for an off-VM operation and the reply watchdog stops the turn, diagnostics identify only the outer `exec`. Operators cannot tell which bridge operation is still pending or whether it published a deadline.

The gap is the bridge frontier retained by `src/agents/code-mode-state.ts:44–50`, which was absent from the stop projection at `src/sessions/session-controller.watchdog.ts:440–447` on base `0e04f4813bf21577186237e87e742065e401e9ca`.

## User Impact

Stall diagnostics now name the awaited bridge operation in the existing `pendingTools` entry and lane-task-error log. Watchdog timing, thresholds, execution allowances, prompts, tool definitions, protocol, config, and public SDK are unchanged.

## Why This Change Was Made

The Code Mode owner projects its existing pending frontier through the existing invocation liveness carrier. A stop captures at most three outstanding entries. Each entry contains only `kind: "bridge"`, a fixed bridge method, `deadlineAtMs` (or `null` when unpublished), and `elapsedMs`. Nested execution-owner deadlines and existing timer deadlines are observed without creating a watchdog allowance. Settlement and invocation cleanup release the diagnostic reader; there is no second wait registry.

For example:

```json
{"awaiting":[{"kind":"bridge","method":"callValue","deadlineAtMs":null,"elapsedMs":900001}]}
```

No arguments, results, paths, guest strings, or user content enter this field. The fixed method vocabulary and three-entry cap keep the payload bounded independently of guest activity.

The author simplification pass retained the existing owners and one boundary regression table. Net change: +119 production lines, +83 test lines, +8 documentation lines. The test growth covers no-deadline and known-deadline stops plus two fields in an existing fixture; existing distinct lifecycle coverage remains intact. No test ceiling or allocation changed.

## Evidence

A real Code Mode executor and subscribed lifecycle harness pause on an external operation under fake timers, then the production watchdog stops the turn. The stop error identifies `callValue` with `deadlineAtMs: null`; the second case preserves `1800000`.

- Red on the base: `pnpm test src/agents/code-mode.bridge.lifecycle.test.ts --maxWorkers=1 -t 'names an off-VM wait'` → `Tests 2 failed`; the expected `awaiting` array was missing from the actual `exec` entry.
- Green after the fix: same focused command → `Tests 2 passed | 25 skipped`.
- Full changed lifecycle file: `pnpm test src/agents/code-mode.bridge.lifecycle.test.ts --maxWorkers=1` → 27 passed; 15.33 s Vitest duration, 46.12 s wrapper wall time including cold worker preparation. The two new cases took 341 ms and 93 ms in the broader run.
- Changed fixture file: `pnpm test src/agents/code-mode-worker-lifecycle.test.ts --maxWorkers=1` → 3 passed; 8.41 s Vitest duration, 10.69 s wrapper wall time, mostly transform/import cost.
- All 50 explicit non-live Code Mode, watchdog, liveness, and prompt-stability files: 49 passed, 1 existing file skipped; 740 tests passed and 27 skipped across five shards (160.27 s wrapper wall time).
- Core and targeted agents-tools test typechecks, targeted oxlint, format check, and `git diff --check` passed.
- `pnpm build` passed (2 m 44.3 s), including declaration output and Control UI; existing advisory bundle-size warnings remain non-failing.

CI timings will be available on this PR. No production systems were accessed.

Local review: Codex autoreview, complete local diff against `0e04f4813bf21577186237e87e742065e401e9ca`, P2 and higher, `scoped-clean` with no accepted/actionable findings. The final attempt verified unchanged source before publishing its result.

The first CI attempt (`44195897400`) caught a type-only import cycle introduced by the diagnostic type. The unchanged type now lives in the existing watchdog leaf contract. The exact failed Madge guard passes locally with zero cycles; core typecheck, focused boundary/watchdog/liveness tests, lint, and format are rerun on the correction. Codex autoreview of that correction is scoped-clean with no actionable findings.

prs.title: fix: update bundled Codex for newer ChatGPT models
prs.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Native Codex model discovery uses the Codex client version. The bundled 0.164.0 runtime is behind the 0.169.0 CLI that @VACInc reports can see `gpt-6.2-sol` and `gpt-6.2-astra`. This updates the bundled runtime and matching protocol so the old native client does not hold back discovery.

Related: #200766 supplied the GPT-6.2 catalog and provider-transport support. Ben’s #197768 supplied native catalog forwarding through the inference relay and is now merged as [ed3230dd29d1](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/commit/ed3230dd29d1e162d814e38eff00f64dc77af64e). This PR includes that commit as an ancestor: it no longer contains the relay production changes and retains additional native-discovery and cleanup regression tests. It also preserves the subsequently merged #200811: the subscription picker independently requests `client_version=99.0.0`, while native app-server discovery still uses its actual binary version. The remaining OpenAI version fallback applies to Platform access-program discovery. These are complementary paths; actual native availability still depends on the account and backend.

## User Impact

Bundled Codex and the Platform access-program version fallback report version 0.169.0. Matching protocol validation accepts uploaded audio-file references without dropping a completed turn. This does not add GPT-6.2 catalog entries, change default models, or change authentication policy.

**Context limits stay unchanged:** the merged GPT-6.2 catalog records a 1,050,000-token model window, a 272,000-token default working budget, and a 128,000-token maximum output for Astra and Sol. User-selected limits and native context reporting remain unchanged. No files overlap the catalog/transport changes from #200766.

## Why This Change Was Made

- Update the package, lockfile, existing ACP version-parity override, runtime constant, OpenAI discovery fallback and documented version to 0.169.0.
- Regenerate the selected upstream schemas and standalone validators from `rust-v0.169.0`, using the existing repository generator helpers.
- Protect failed-turn settlement and visible errors for `modelNotFound`, `policyCapacityUnavailable` and `inferenceHookDenied`, including completed snapshots containing the new audio `fileId` representation.
- Recognize the new native `execve` launch diagnostic only when its path matches the native binary. Repair an HTTP test fixture that dropped shell arguments; production cleanup and permissions are unchanged.

<details>
<summary>Protocol compatibility and generation provenance</summary>

No client request methods were removed. Selected response roots retain their required fields; dynamic-tool call parameters and model-list responses are unchanged. Optional item timestamps, agent-message moderation, image generation IDs and thread attachment IDs require no consumer change. The regenerated mirror includes Account’s `gcp` variant, optional ChatGPT `workspaceName` and optional GetAccountResponse `userId`, without enabling new authentication behavior. Optional `ModelListParams.modelProvider` remains omitted to use the configured provider. New memory, guardian, approved-plan, provider/GCP/account/security setup methods are not called. Audio URL and uploaded-file variants both validate.

Source: [rust-v0.169.0](https://github.com/openai/codex/tree/d32063f96c2dff1dc96af839b3952abb6acfeda4/codex-rs/app-server-protocol/schema), commit `d32063f96c2dff1dc96af839b3952abb6acfeda4`. Used the checked-in experimental export archive with existing materialization, staging, compaction and formatting helpers, then `scripts/generate-codex-validators.mts`. All eight selected JSON schemas round-trip to those exports. No generated schema or validator was hand-edited. Rust/Cargo is unavailable here, so the Rust fixture compilation stage of `protocol:sync` was not rerun.

</details>

## Evidence

After rebasing onto Ben’s landed repair, focused protocol, failed-turn, terminal-error, HTTP-relay and native-binary tests passed: **94 passed, 1 optional live test skipped** across five files. The relay conflict retained 0.169.0 and the additional disconnect/shutdown regressions. The subsequent #200811 conflict retains the new broad subscription-picker test and removes this PR’s now-obsolete picker-version expectation. Codex and dependency file contents remain byte-identical to the tested candidate. After integrating #200811, the subscription-discovery, provider, Platform access-program and version-contract tests passed. Formatting and `git diff --check` passed.

An independent **P0–P3 review of the complete candidate after the relay rebase** returned `scoped-clean` with no actionable findings. That evidence is retained for the unchanged Codex/dependency delta; the later integration only removes an obsolete picker test and incorporates #200811’s existing behavior. No hostile behavior was identified in the reviewed delta; this is not an audit of all upstream dependency source.

The real pinned app-server requests its catalog through OpenClaw’s RPC client and loopback relay. Removing Ben’s repair causes 502 and no upstream request; restoring it returns a remote-only synthetic model through `model/list`, preserving native account headers. The external fetch boundary is mocked; separate real-HTTPS tests cover forwarding, auth separation, upstream errors and cleanup. Prior relay-family tests passed **88 tests**, with one optional live skip, plus extension-test typecheck and targeted type-aware lint.

Protocol-source/version contracts and affected OpenAI discovery/provider tests passed **68 tests**. Validator regeneration, targeted lint and the repaired HTTP fixture passed. Installed package reports `codex-cli 0.169.0`.

**Explicit base-fail/head-pass comparison:** the same failed-turn fixture with `codexErrorInfo: "modelNotFound"` and audio `{ "type": "audio", "fileId": "file-audio-1" }` was passed directly to the unchanged generated validators read from Git. Both `isCodexTurnCompletedNotification` and `isCodexTurnStartResponse` reject it at base `0a27bd7f85fa6af2964182a8c54a709b143fdefe` and accept it at published head `d2496ff4de05b0365d010783eea25b06affaaf3e`. The committed consumer regressions also pass on the head.

**Important scope of the regression:** new error-name strings alone already pass the old open-enum validator; the comparison confirms `modelNotFound` error notifications pass on both revisions. We do not claim those strings alone reproduced a hang. The concrete old-schema failure is a completed failed turn containing audio `fileId`; regeneration makes it validate and the tests protect error display and terminal settlement.

**Current-head hosted validation:** [CI run 44188975323](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/44188975323) completed successfully for `d2496ff4de05b0365d010783eea25b06affaaf3e`. The remaining Apple checks also completed successfully, including [Periphery](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/44188974909). At the final check, the only nonpassing statuses were `openclaw/dependency-review` and its combined `openclaw/ci-gate`: a repository admin or active SecOps member must approve this revision’s dependency change. This is not a claim that all required gates are green.

[ClawSweeper’s current-head review](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/200784#issuecomment-6960325018) reports no actionable code findings, confirms the runtime/protocol approach and resolved relay dependency, and retains the same approval gate. The PR remains open, with no auto-merge enabled.

<details>
<summary>Earlier validation and proof limitations</summary>

The initial full Codex suite ran 5,486 passing, 10 failing and 10 skipped tests. Focused follow-ups fixed all ten: version parity, the native launcher’s new diagnostic, dropped shell arguments in the HTTP fixture, and an isolated native test’s inherited certificate environment. Assertions, production permissions and timeouts were not weakened. A later audio-fixture type failure was fixed by explicitly typing valid JSON variants; extension-test typecheck and all 25 protocol-validator tests passed. The local full suite was not rerun merely to repeat passing work.

The prior published head `9fe8974589c5657ee79660a5e48de9c6ab84f368` also has a successful hosted CI check from [run 44182663362](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/44182663362). Earlier Darwin tooling EPERM is not claimed as a code repair; current-head evidence above supersedes that prior-head CI result.

ClawSweeper also asks for installed-Gateway live discovery, turn completion and stable-upgrade evidence. Those flows were not performed. The native binary, separate HTTPS and direct old/new validator evidence support this scoped compatibility change, but do not prove live entitlement, a live GPT-6.2 turn, or a complete installed-Gateway upgrade. No such proof is claimed.

</details>

Credit: @VACInc reported the missing models and specified this upgrade and its regression coverage. @bdjben authored the catalog relay repair now landed in #197768; this PR builds on it and adds native discovery and cleanup proof.

## Work sessions

Linked for team reference; these sessions aren’t public.

- [Discussion, implementation and verification](https://team.openclaw.ai/chat/roboclaw/~key/dashboard/e82f8ffc-8027-4d19-9da2-1766c7cff1b7)

prs.title: fix: stop doctor idling forever when a plugin capture stalls
prs.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Doctor's `Config repairs` phase could idle forever at zero CPU when a plugin-generation **capture** wedged (#178359). Captures were the only generation-worker tasks with no timeout:

- async host: `(command.operation === "capture" || sourceCapture ? {} : { timeoutMs: 120_000 })`
- sync host: `(sourceCapture ? {} : { timeoutMs: 30_000 })`

Every other operation was bounded; a capture whose preparation worker went silent (native-load child spawn, sqlite staging copy) left the host waiting indefinitely. On affected hosts this stranded `openclaw doctor --fix --non-interactive` mid-run with the gateway service left stopped/disabled and no output naming the stuck stage.

## Evidence

Runtime evidence from #178359 (two hosts, both matching this fix's failure shape):

- macOS report: doctor child held a fresh 0-byte `tmp/plugin-captures/<uuid>/owner.sqlite` + journal (capture staging frozen mid-write); parent parked in `uv__work_done`; plain SIGTERM stopped it cleanly.
- Windows re-test on 2026.11.5: `Config repairs (428s elapsed)`, **0.000 cores** across all 8 doctor node processes, only `gateway.state.lock` + `openclaw.sqlite-wal` touched, no terminal state after 28 minutes.
- Healthy-host control (2026.11.5, Windows 11): the identical flow — live service, doctor-stopped gateway, invalid config, plugin inventory — completes cleanly and restores the gateway, isolating the trigger to a wedged capture meeting an unbounded wait.

Focused test evidence (this patch):

```
Plugin capture did not complete within 1.0s (capture 1, root /…/installed); the preparation worker stayed silent. Raise OPENCLAW_PLUGIN_CAPTURE_TIMEOUT_MS for slower hosts, then retry.
```

New regression test: a capture whose worker never receives the input rejects with the stage-naming error within the configured budget (`config/test-lines-allocations/plugin-capture-deadline.txt` allocation included).

## Fix

- Capture and source-capture operations now use a generous but finite budget (default **15 min**), replacing the unbounded wait. Ordinary sync methods stay at 30s, async at 120s.
- `OPENCLAW_PLUGIN_CAPTURE_TIMEOUT_MS` (clamped 1s–1h) lets operators raise the budget for slow hosts, preserving the original concern that captures scale with package size and filesystem latency.
- On expiry the error names the capture, the plugin root, and the override — the "bounded timeout that names the stage" behavior requested in the issue.

## Compatibility

- The existing "finishes a capture after more than two minutes without retiring its worker" test still passes: host-side publication waits (the owner-controlled lifetime that motivated the unbounded design) are unaffected — the deadline applies to the worker task wait, and 120s < the 15 min default.

## Testing

- `src/plugins/plugin-generation-worker.test.ts`: 25/25 (incl. the two-minute publication-gate test)
- `plugin-module-generation.work.test.ts`, `loader.async-preparation.test.ts`, `plugin-generation-artifact.test.ts`: 51/51
- oxlint + oxfmt clean on changed files

Refs #178359
