prs.title: feat(telegram): prepare attachments before native message handling
prs.body:
### Main synchronization · November 17

Merged main `7c6f38d4` into `b31990d8a3b6`. The hook dispatcher retains both main's before-agent-finalize merge helper and the attachment-load runner. The 1,596 regression lines use 1,196 allocation credits beyond main's new 400-line allowance.

Git diff whitespace and the test-line counts were checked on the merge tree. Runtime tests are pending hosted CI.

Telegram plugins need to prepare an admitted message before native attachment loading, while preserving Telegram's sender admission, command handling, deduplication and retry ownership. This proposes the optional `before_channel_attachment_load` hook for ordinary noncommand singleton messages and edits; commands, native command config grants and albums retain their native paths.

The hook returns prepared text and an optional attachment-suppression flag. It receives an event-owned provider DTO and a scoped cancellation/heartbeat context; it cannot rewrite native message identity or routing. This proposal still requires SDK/security owner acceptance.

## Integration with current main

Reconciled with `25559c47700485ad17899307f8cf05d010346ae0`. Main's `before_channel_ingress` contract is preserved; this unreleased attachment-preparation proposal remains `before_channel_attachment_load`. An eventual consumer must adopt that name; this update activates no consumer.

The merge adopts main's `runOutsideAdmittedGenerationScopes` for subagent completion delivery and its existing regression, removing this PR's superseded implementation, duplicate test/helper and test-line allocation. It also adopts main's CLI model-picker initialization wait and removes our redundant fixture helper. The proposal-specific channel delivery scope repair and its raw/prepared/error regressions remain.

Main now runs the PostgreSQL 16 smoke in its own CI job. This removes the combined workload that reached the previous job's 30-minute limit after all tests passed. The old run remains cancelled/failed, and both author rerun credentials were denied; the new meaningful merge triggers its own CI.

## Current evidence and remaining gates

Current head: `bd1f92097c9c191f305ff90607f0b3dcbcf564c9`, tree `5e54bfe84988a7eb8fb0b0d9361ef12d6ef3b6d4`. GitHub reports no merge conflicts. [CI 43452231393](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/43452231393) is `action_required`, with zero jobs started: upstream approval of the fork workflow is required. The author attempted approval and received HTTP 403 (admin rights required). This is not a passing CI verdict.

- Native test-line budget and SDK export consistency pass on this integration candidate. The redundant subagent allocation is removed; 1,596 counted regression lines have 1,596 allocated lines (1,546 attachment preparation plus 50 channel delivery), with shared ceilings unchanged.
- 175 focused tests passed across seven files, including 112 subagent-delivery, 26 Telegram integration and 20 channel-delivery cases. The refreshed Telegram bot type then exposed a missing `api.raw` in our test fixture; that field was added without changing assertions or production, and all 10 owning-file cases passed on replay. Core production types, extension test types, the plugin-SDK test graph, targeted core/extension typed lint, formatting and unchanged size ratchets pass. The 30 publication inputs match the isolated validated source bytes.
- SDK/security owner acceptance is still required. Earlier standalone SDK surface measurements exceeded unchanged policy limits, with inherited excesses and proposal-specific growth; no policy increase or public-contract approval is claimed.
- Previous-head tests and diagnostics below retain their original scope. No live Telegram/transcription acceptance, consumer activation, production deployment, merge or release follows from this PR update.

<details>
<summary>November 10–11 integration evidence (previous head e3f1e131)</summary>

## Integration with current main

Reconciled with `a2879ad0a140654acae1f807db4021fec6b5017d`. Main now owns a separate `before_channel_ingress` hook before durable storage. This PR preserves that existing contract and gives its previously unreleased attachment-preparation proposal a distinct name, `before_channel_attachment_load` (`PluginHookBeforeChannelAttachmentLoad*`, `runBeforeChannelAttachmentLoad`). Historical evidence below uses the old proposal name and does not redefine main's hook. An eventual consumer must use the renamed contract; no private consumer was activated by this update.

The unrelated before-agent-finalize reducer extraction was removed in the simplification pass. The new hook owns its own module, the shared await helper resides with timeout handling, and reusable test payloads/channel registration live in sibling fixtures; no scenario or assertion was removed. The integration also includes the already qualified completion-routing fix from #178125: completed turns leave their closed plugin invocation scope before the host resolves and sends a subagent announcement. The affected main files are unchanged from that reproduction, and the regression is rerun here.

## Current evidence and remaining gates

Current head: `e3f1e1319bcb0984b59ec437870d9600dd41679a`. [Hosted CI 42925137136](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/42925137136) is blocked by the 30-minute timeout of PostgreSQL conformance (1/3): 165 jobs succeeded, 21 were skipped, that job was cancelled and the aggregate CI gate failed. Every test reported by the cancelled job passed, including all eight PostgreSQL 16 Gateway smoke cases; its wrapper reported success at 00:11:03 UTC immediately before cancellation. This is not a green workflow verdict. A maintainer must rerun [job 130210356991](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/42925137136/job/130210356991); both available author credentials were denied Actions rerun permission (HTTP 403). No test, timeout, ceiling or production code was changed to mask that result. Public-contract acceptance remains outstanding.

The previous CI exposed four compatibility/check issues and one delivery defect. This update removes an obsolete logger field and max-lines exemption entry, updates two strict assertions to main's compact JSON encoding, and fixes the delivery defect. On this PR's attachment-preparation candidate, after provider failure, the queued final response inherited a closed producer plugin invocation scope and could not enter the channel's bound callbacks. This candidate reproduction does not establish that provider-failure delivery is broken on unmodified main. Raw delivery, prepared delivery and error observation now leave that producer scope before entering their existing channel owner. Plugin-instance admission and disposed-instance checks remain intact; no delivery retry, timeout or duplicate-send rule is relaxed.

- The native Telegram provider-failure scenario on the PR candidate reproduced no public reply with `Plugin invocation scope is closed`. A bounded causal diagnostic of the built runtime passes after changing only the delivery scope boundary, preserving the original silent-error text, retries, request-deduplication and private-detail assertions. Hosted CI on `9c83fe3e` also passes this original Telegram end-to-end scenario.
- Maintainer follow-up on 11 November: [six synthetic Gateway runs on main `ff392dbeb0`](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/171315#issuecomment-6783529089) delivered the existing provider-failure notice without a closed-scope error. The attachment-preparation hook is a possible source of the candidate-only failure; that causal attribution has not been established. The separate subagent-announcement fix was split upstream into #196940, according to the maintainer. These are distinct findings; neither is SDK acceptance or live Telegram proof.
- New raw/prepared/error callback regressions all fail before the source fix. Owning-file result: all 20 cases pass, including those three regressions.
- Native CLI model-picker test: a separate intermittent failure was reproduced in isolation. Prepared UI rows can appear while refreshable CLI discovery is still pending; the fixture now waits for its initialize receipt before snapshotting the calls. The unchanged menu/argument/request/provider-isolation assertions pass in the targeted case, with the other two cases filtered. Root E2E types, lint and size ratchets pass. The allocation decreases from 50 to 47 after consolidating three snapshot lines into the existing fixture; no timeout or ceiling increases.
- Codex native hook relay: all 12 owning-file cases pass after matching main's compact JSON. Telegram ask-user loopback: its case passes with unchanged request/delivery assertions and compact JSON expectation. Extension test typecheck passes after the obsolete logger property is removed.
- Earlier isolated qualification against `8bac830dcb8ff99055ba71558dd369a989cc7881`: 155 focused tests pass, including 26 Telegram/SQLite integration cases, hook access/cancellation, transport preparation and 111 subagent-delivery cases. These are retained scoped proofs, not represented as a fresh full-suite run against the later main.
- Native SDK export check, focused typed lint, production typechecks and unchanged size/test-line ratchets: passed in the scoped checks (including the actual plugin-SDK test graph after correcting the two asynchronous fixture signatures). Test-line allocations account for exact formatted regression growth; the global baseline and policy ceilings remain unchanged.
- The separate SDK surface policy remains unresolved. At the initial reconciliation base, native control measured 162 entrypoints / 3880 exports / 2239 callable exports / one wildcard; the proposal measured 163 / 3884 / 2240 / one wildcard. Limits remain 162 / 3865 / 2235 / zero. Three excesses were inherited; the proposal adds one entrypoint, four exports and one callable. No policy increase or SDK/security owner approval is claimed.
- Hosted lint, test types, all Node shards, Android checks and the other two PostgreSQL conformance groups passed on this head. The separate CodeQL summary is neutral because 15 configurations from main were absent; it is not a complete code-scanning verdict.
- Initial full local lint exceeded the isolated 6 GiB budget and is not a passing proof. Local API-diff stopped during dependency setup with networking disabled and supplies no API verdict. Author simplification/review is complete; no fresh independent autoreview/ClawSweeper review, live Telegram/transcription acceptance or production readiness is claimed. Maintainer/public-contract decisions remain open.

</details>

<details>
<summary>Historical qualification, with original heads, scopes and unresolved outcomes</summary>

## What Problem This Solves

A voice-transcription adapter cannot provide prepared text and suppress the original Telegram attachment before native media processing. Existing dispatch hooks run too late. This PR proposes an optional `before_channel_ingress` hook for admitted ordinary noncommand singletons.

## User Impact

A registered preparer can return text and `suppressAttachments: true`; Telegram retains the original sender, chat/topic, message/update identity, reply context, dispatch claims and retry ownership. Original control commands, command-config grants and all album members bypass preparation and retain their native authorization and collective media owners. Installations without a preparer keep existing handling.

## Why This Change Was Made

The transport factory binds preparation to the exact update and invokes it after native sender authorization and accepted fresh-message dispatch claims, before attachment I/O. Edits retain their existing silent authorization path. The event carries copied transport facts, not authority. Consumers must enforce their own current binding and consent after awaited work and before private effects.

Native cancellation, scoped liveness, claim rollback and late-result fencing stay with their existing owners. Failed rollback remains nonretryable. The focused `plugin-hook-runtime` subpath exposes the existing runner getter; generated package/entrypoint metadata stays aligned. Telegram exposes its existing native fetch bridge and token-scoped throttler. Small unchanged DTO/reducer blocks are extracted to preserve existing source-size ratchets.

The concrete consumer is our privately maintained personal-assistant voice adapter, implemented as a source candidate. It uses its selected account’s read-only file client and existing audio request/result receipts, waits for the audio owner, then supplies prepared text to avoid duplicate native media work. It adds no poller, sender, consent store or inference authority. Consumer source preparation is not an activation or migration claim. Maintainer acceptance of this public contract remains required.

## Evidence

### Current control-caption correction — October 21

Current ready head: `d9b6e3ff2055d042be440410524e60beefd884fa`, tree `f0c70e7af063f567962daa1931e185038ce78d0b`. A valid DM voice caption containing disabled `/config show` could reach preparation and private file lookup; admitted actors denied command access also lacked an early DM-media command gate. The correction reuses native command authorization before DM media processing and keeps known disabled commands with their native owner for fresh messages and edits. It adds no public API, configuration, persistent state, or client activation.

[Source qualification and native admission receipts](https://github.com/ChuLaiTheGreat/openclaw/actions/runs/39678791103): the two new DM-caption regressions fail causally on the original production files; the corrected entire owning integration file passes **26/26**, including those two cases. Scoped native typed lint and pinned formatting pass. The three unchanged consumers remain qualified at byte-identical production parent `1bc2c3dd27fa1aaaf6347dad838ce616538987f8`: admission **1**, pipeline **3**, media **9**, from [the preceding run](https://github.com/ChuLaiTheGreat/openclaw/actions/runs/39676414713). Those 13 cases are attributed, not counted as fresh executions. The current source-quality containers exit 0, PID zero, no OOM; the expected causal baseline exits 1 with exactly two assertion failures.

The same head's clean native `qaRuntime` build runs the actual Gateway, authenticated Telegram webhook and durable SQLite ingress. Four synthetic negative cases (unknown actor, text command, enabled control caption, disabled control caption) complete without invoking the registered SDK preparer or performing a file lookup/download. An ordinary admitted voice reaches that preparer and one synthetic file lookup as a positive reachability control. **This establishes the tested admission/private-media boundary with a synthetic SDK consumer; it is not real Telegram/model/transcription/suppression acceptance.**

**The enclosing recipe still fails at shutdown.** The positive control is deliberately held before final dispatch; its native caller aborts and its queue row remains pending. Gateway shutdown then exits **1** with `ERR_SPAWN_BROKER_UNAVAILABLE` / native spawn-broker cleanup failure. The cause has not been classified against a baseline. The fixture container exits 1 without OOM; its producer removes all owned containers and source/dependency/cache payloads. The completed negative cases are retained separately; no whole-CI, clean-shutdown, cancellation/replay or final-dispatch success is claimed. The pending synthetic update is not replayed.

Earlier local fixture setup failures (recorder classification, self-echo identity and invalid Telegram message shape) are not passing product proof. A corrected original-head fixture exposed the actual disabled-caption defect. A local unit attempt exhausted bounded worker memory before executing any cases. The first hosted recipe passed 26 owning-file and 13 consumer cases but native lint rejected the test owner at 1005 lines against the unchanged 1000-line ceiling. Removing an unreachable preparer return stub and a cache assertion redundant with zero dispatch-dedupe entry preserves denial/preparation/media/file/dispatch observations; command entities now use their actual token lengths. Only that test file changes from the qualified production parent, and the current recipe rechecks its causal baseline and complete owner. No limit was raised.

Remaining local work: permitted transcription/attachment suppression, authority withdrawal during waits, cancellation/replay (including diagnosis of the shutdown failure), and real model/Telegram delivery. SDK/security owner acceptance remains separate. No client credential, runtime deployment, merge or release is inferred. Historical qualification below retains its original heads and scopes.

<!-- control-caption-repair-20261021-d9b6e3ff2055d042be440410524e60beefd884fa -->

### Current upstream CI diagnosis — October 22

<!-- ci-diagnosis-cdf30635-20261022 -->

The contribution head remains `d9b6e3ff2055d042be440410524e60beefd884fa`. [Original upstream CI 39681148547](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/39681148547) tested merge `b52838fa656964d11d7e860801ff926edd83d917` into base `9bd9b07fe1d59a2fa148da45609c581a033017e5`. Its six failing leaf jobs and aggregate gate are retained; this follow-up requested no upstream CI retry or contribution push to seek a green result.

[Exact base/merge controls](https://github.com/ChuLaiTheGreat/openclaw/actions/runs/39694221341) use native repository wrappers, frozen separate installs, Node **24.19.0**, and the CI-pinned OpenClaw Bun fork in finite, secretless 9-GiB/four-CPU containers. Results below are per lane; cases excluded by a name filter are not counted as passes.

| Original failure owner | Exact base | Exact tested merge | Assessment |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Changed-test planner | One targeted pass | Same target fails, expected 2 / received 1 | Upstream fixture falsely requires the full parent's concurrency for an intentionally serialized projection; causal repair proof below. |
| Packaged IMAP service | Same targeted deadline failure | Same targeted deadline failure | Inherited: the original CI's command sequence and service-log payload reproduce identically on both lanes; owning source/test blobs are unchanged. |
| SDK surface report | Six passes | Four passes, two failures | The proposed public surface exceeds unchanged limits; SDK/security owner acceptance remains required. |
| Feishu body cancellation | One targeted pass | One targeted pass | Not reproduced in focused isolation; 28 other cases per lane were excluded. |
| Levanto registration | 28 passes | 28 passes | Complete isolated owning file passes on both lanes. |
| Codex catalogue backoff | One targeted pass | One targeted pass | Not reproduced in focused isolation; 13 other cases per lane were excluded. |

The Feishu, Levanto and Codex results do **not** establish an inherited or intermittent cause, repair the original shards, or make the whole PR CI green. No unrelated production correction, timeout increase or blind shard replay was made.

The SDK report observes **158 public entrypoints against 157**, **3,817 exports against 3,813**, and **2,211 callable exports against 2,210**. Those ceilings remain unchanged. This quantifies the existing public-contract decision; it is not owner approval.

#### Planner assertion: existing upstream repair verified

The production planner intentionally normalizes singleton jobs to serial execution while retaining their child worker ceiling. The failing fixture checked effective child environments correctly, then incorrectly required the full parent's parallel `planConcurrency`. [Upstream commit `352b23dd3407`](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/commit/352b23dd3407ac04b60fe00d11d0781cd37e2fa0), already present in the inspected target main, restores its existing `isSerialNodeTestProjection` expectation.

[Causal qualification 39698326410](https://github.com/ChuLaiTheGreat/openclaw/actions/runs/39698326410) reproduces the one intended assertion failure on the exact original CI merge. Applying **only that upstream test change** — two additions, one deletion, with the final fixture byte-identical to inspected upstream main — then passes **all 77 owning-file cases, none skipped**, plus pinned formatting. Production source is unchanged; the explicit two-worker, configuration, memory and isolation assertions are retained. This credits and verifies an existing upstream repair; the contribution branch remains unchanged. The separate earlier local 77-case base run is not added again to these counts.

All hosted phase containers have recorded terminal native outcomes, zero remaining PID and no OOM; their owned containers and temporary payloads are removed. Earlier preparation failures remain failures: the local 4-GiB Feishu worker compilation was OOM-killed before any case, then two hosted setups stopped on missing staging tools and noexec temporary execution. A subsequent whole-file attempt reached 76/77: its remaining synthetic import-graph fixture was nested under the real checkout through TMPDIR, so Git discovery read the parent's empty fixture inventory. That failed attempt is retained. The final recipe uses a private executable temporary mount outside the checkout, explicitly verifies Git isolation, and executes the unchanged assertions. Setup success alone is not product evidence.

The aggregate CI remains red. Gateway/model/Telegram behavior, suppression, withdrawal, cancellation/replay and the SDK/security contract decision remain separate, open requirements. No client installation, migration, merge or release follows from this diagnosis.

<details>
<summary>Historical qualification, attributed to its original heads</summary>

Historical ready head before the control-caption correction: `e3c9c0e22ce9b71822c04b2f5efc7e1142276704`, tree `94b0900bb516132108b3d5e8297201b789c8f22f`. The command/media P1 is fixed. This head removes only the requested nondiscriminating factory case: 16 deleted lines, no additions/import changes. Every other tracked byte and mode, including production, manifests and the integration fixture, matches parent `7b1b60779992eee09d73fb174f1a2b18e28f8bcf`.

- Ten remaining factory cases, their owning test type graph, format, assertion/mock/source-cap ratchets pass on the current head. Six native containers settle at zero, PID zero, no OOM, and are removed.

- The identical final 22-case integration fixture gives 13 passes/nine causal failures before the two command/album eligibility guards and 22/22 after. Registration, hook runner, grammY, authorization, SQLite, dispatch claims and keyed album ownership are real; downstream services are synthetic. Allowed albums resolve two file IDs into one two-media delivery. Plain command cases prove original delegation/preparation bypass, not a final command-delivery assertion.

### Concrete consumer authority correction

The consumer review exposed a real local race: preparation queued behind another download could later start file lookup/download using stale consent. The private correction rechecks its existing consent owner after waits and before the next lookup, download, body consumption, write transaction and transcript handoff. Withdrawal returns the existing terms placeholder without waiting for a job never accepted. Already accepted transactions and receipts remain intact without inference replay.

The actual registered consumer, preparation adapter, selected-account read-only client, consent-status reader and audio artifact owner were exercised together with synthetic external transport/status responses. The identical ten regressions have seven causal failures before repair; all **33 focused tests pass** after repair in isolated Node 24.22.0 containers: network disabled, read-only source, 512 MiB/one CPU, terminal PID zero/no OOM, removed. Cases include account mismatch with zero effects, queued withdrawal, withdrawal during lookup/response/body/result adoption, service stop, terminal placeholder without polling, exact-once download and unchanged accepted receipts. All fourteen published private module/test blobs match the final fixture. Its zero-read-ahead body case also fails causally when only the pre-write consent guard is removed: the forbidden pending artifact exists; this is the same distinct case, not an additional passing test.

This is concrete source-boundary proof, not an installed Gateway/model/Telegram result. A status read cannot atomically revoke an I/O already started with valid authority; subsequent effects and handoff are fenced.

### SDK qualification

[Complete eight-phase run 39510326876](https://github.com/ChuLaiTheGreat/openclaw/actions/runs/39510326876) **succeeded**, terminal 23:54:43 UTC, on exact production-bearing parent `7b1b607`, tree `0f411c8e3367a04462077192003a7cfa4e8e01f8`, against pinned main `5a0b5006`. This is not an exact build of test-only child `e3c9c0e`; the byte-identical production and the separately qualified test deletion are attributed above.

The database guard runs its original 4096 MiB Node command: T1 calls **171 → 171**, deprecated-only compatibility calls **15 → 15**. The API report records one new entrypoint, four added/169 affected exports and ten reachable declaration changes; acknowledgement digest `493581ec` is report metadata, not owner approval. The unchanged head `e3c9c0e22ce9b71822c04b2f5efc7e1142276704` now has its own successful native `qaRuntime` build in [run 39621479405](https://github.com/ChuLaiTheGreat/openclaw/actions/runs/39621479405). The unchanged head `e3c9c0e22ce9b71822c04b2f5efc7e1142276704` now starts its isolated built Gateway with the concrete Clarity ingress consumer, rather than a substitute preparer. ### Fresh native cancellation/recovery control — October 22

One new isolated scenario passes against the exact built head `d9b6e3ff2055d042be440410524e60beefd884fa`. The archive hashes and all 58,301 tracked source blobs match; the recorded concrete-consumer modules are unchanged. The Gateway receives a fresh authenticated **synthetic** webhook, enters the consumer's awaited file lookup, then receives SIGTERM. ### Prepared transcript and connected-model boundary — October 22

One fresh isolated scenario passes on unchanged head `d9b6e3ff2055d042be440410524e60beefd884fa`. Archive hashes, all 58,301 tracked blobs and both clean runtime stamps match that head. An authenticated synthetic webhook enters durable native ingress and the unchanged concrete Clarity consumer. Its selected-account read client performs one synthetic lookup and one synthetic byte download. The expected answer occurs only in the prepared user transcript, not the fixture system instruction. The provider returns HTTP 200 with a completed response; the exact expected answer reaches one native `sendMessage` to the **synthetic** Bot API. The durable event completes. The transport controller exits **1** when its allowlist rejects an auxiliary model request before any external forwarding. That guard outcome is recorded separately from the successful native scenario. Only the authorized primary inference was forwarded, once; no fallback or inference replay was used, and no credential was exported to contribution code.

This closes the isolated prepared-text → connected-model → native outbound boundary only. Bot API, actor identity, consent/status, capture RPC, audio bytes and transcription receipt are fixtures. **Real transcription, live Telegram delivery, complete consent/account withdrawal, and real-path cancellation/replay remain open**, as do the SDK/security decision and previously disclosed CI failures. prs.title: fix: avoid unrelated plugin setup on first reply
prs.body:
**Outcome: not landing.** All 20 plain browser trials completed normally. The candidate was faster in 6/10 pairs, below the predeclared 7/10 requirement. The latency gate failed, so CPU/RSS/heap populations were intentionally not run and no no-growth claim is made.

## What Problem This Solves

On the first reply, validated defaults can invent empty configuration entries for plugins the operator never configured. Those entries then trigger unrelated plugin setup discovery.

## User Impact

Fresh sessions avoid setup work caused by synthetic empty settings. Explicit settings, including an authored empty object, and real schema defaults retain their behavior.

## Why This Change Was Made

Keep schema validation and native-catalog adjustment, but materialize an absent plugin configuration only when validation produces a nonempty object. Plugin runtime registration still validates absent settings and supplies its own defaults.

## Evidence

- The new absent-settings and policy-only regressions fail on the original code; the other nine cases pass. With the fix, all 68 focused validation and auto-enable tests pass.
- Core production types, the selected config/CLI test type graph, scoped lint, formatting, and whitespace checks pass.
- Independent local autoreview of the complete two-file diff: P0–P2, no actionable findings. The reviewed patch is committed as `46fec6fc17abca06497828175f89b2d5929bbf38`. Local ClawSweeper remains unavailable after its recorded prerequisite scan failure (`incomplete_source`); it has not reviewed this range. One hosted review will be requested when ready.
- Native runtime build passed in 6m31s with the expected commit identity; Control UI content-cache reuse and 1,058 finalized sidecars verified. Both UI trees contain the same 5,025 files; JS/CSS match and HTML differs only in native build identity. The latency gate failed; resource populations were not run.

Native V8 coverage on one successfully completed browser turn per build confirms the removed work:

| Operation | Baseline | Candidate |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| Main-isolate setup registrations | 95 | 3 |
| Worker-isolate setup registrations | 2 | 2 |
| Plugin-schema validation calls | 3 | 3 |

These are separate instrumented count probes, not latency measurements. An earlier source-hook diagnostic exceeded the fixed startup budget and required forced cleanup; it remains recorded outside the comparison population. A separate uninstrumented baseline qualification and both native coverage probes completed normally. The paired latency population failed its predeclared rule; resource populations were intentionally not run.

### Completed latency result

| Metric | Baseline | Candidate |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| Median first visible text | 2535.15 ms | 2487.25 ms |
| p95 (nearest rank) | 2584.90 ms | 2658.70 ms |
| Range | 2409.50–2584.90 ms | 2410.00–2658.70 ms |

Median difference: -47.90 ms (-1.89%); paired median difference: -53.45 ms. Candidate lower in 6/10 pairs. No trials were replaced or excluded. Frozen source/build, controller, Node and browser identities were checked per trial.

### Performance acceptance, declared before comparison

Use the committed cold-TTFT controller at `105bd4d68d26488773abfad237fd551450def1a3`, a real built Gateway, a fresh state/workspace for each trial, default tools, the deterministic OpenAI SSE fixture, and the real browser Start session flow. Frozen baseline: `9122a49bd8a12baf734ec7bb78337bd556fcbef8`. OS caches are uncontrolled.

1. Confirm that the first-turn setup selection drops from 93 candidates to the one candidate with actual defaults. Diagnostic runs are separate from timing runs.
2. Run ten latency pairs, alternating AB/BA. Candidate and paired medians must improve by at least 25 ms or 5%, and the candidate must be faster in at least seven pairs.
3. Only after latency passes, run six pairs for each separate mode: lifetime Gateway CPU, external peak process-tree RSS, and instrumented heap. Candidate and paired medians must show no increase in each population. Heap is the maximum of post-completion and one-second-idle main-plus-direct-worker samples; missing tracked-worker heap samples invalidate a trial. These are sampled heap observations, not continuous heap peaks. The separately owned browser is excluded from Gateway resource totals.
4. Retain every trial. Stop after the first invalid trial or completed population that fails its gate; do not replace samples. No concurrent build, test, or review runs during measurement. Pin controller, source/build, Node, and browser identities throughout.
5. After acceptance, verify all four surfaces and selected live OpenAI models before landing.

The common trial command is:

```sh
node --import "$OPENCLAW_CHECKOUT/scripts/tsx.mjs" \
  scripts/perf/cold-ttft.mjs --openclaw "$OPENCLAW_CHECKOUT" \
  --surfaces browser --runs 1 --tools default --output "$RESULT"
```

The resource populations add `--lifetime-cpu`, `--rss`, or `--resources` separately. No speedup or no-growth result is claimed until these gates complete.

prs.title: fix(macos): unblock release audits of direct sleep continuations
prs.body:
## What Problem This Solves

The macOS release audit rejects a valid Swift sleep continuation emitted in the 2026.11.5 universal binary, blocking packaging before notarization. The captured instruction is a direct tail branch whose symbol name appears at eight different addresses.

## User Impact

Release operators can audit this emitted continuation without disabling the async-frame safety check. This changes the packaging analyzer only, not the app runtime or published release identity. Unknown transfers and undersized frames still fail.

## Why This Change Was Made

Decode the concrete ARM64 branch target from the executable and admit only the matching Tgq-to-Tg specialization with the same TY continuation. Follow it with the original descriptor, register/slot state, and accumulated stores. No name-only resolution, allocation substitution, or general unknown-instruction allowance.

Simplification pass retained one existing audit owner: 32 production lines added and 8 removed, plus a focused synthetic Mach-O regression. The decoder is named independently because it owns instruction decoding; no new parser framework or compatibility path.

## Evidence

- Real failure: openclaw/releases run 44116257970, attempt 1, universal job 134159855258, artifact 14357815854. Captured binary SHA-256: `408d1dd6568f488dd79f6a220200b084b586120d09dbfd44fab341756613a2fd`.
- Independently verified all 1,561 captured instruction encodings against that binary. Unchanged analyzer fails at `0x101470350`; patched captured-disassembly replay passes all 10 descriptors, preserving the affected descriptor at 128 allocated / 120 required bytes.
- Regression exercises the real analyzer entry point on a synthetic Mach-O: concrete resolution among duplicate symbols, register/stack/frame/context preservation, earlier stores, historical 112/120 out-of-bounds rejection, and unknown-transfer rejection. Red on the base, green with this repair.
- Focused Vitest regression passed; packaging consumer suite: 16 passed, 9 platform-gated tests skipped on Linux. Tooling test typecheck, targeted lint, formatting, and `git diff --check` passed.
- Fresh independent review and local autoreview (OpenClaw engine, P0–P2) of the complete local snapshot based on `fb9337a26b5a6ae6d2ec16154df938efdbf07f6d`, committed unchanged as `d76704b92ff0c8b40ed1e9f6adab60d8fcf15821`: no actionable findings. Local ClawSweeper was unavailable; hosted ClawSweeper acknowledged the ready PR.

**Remaining qualification:** captured Linux replay is not fresh native `xcrun llvm-objdump` proof. Matching-source macOS preflight and release validation are required before promoting release assets. Existing validation for the original frozen source does not validate this repair.

prs.title: feat(ui): edit an agent's thinking default from its Overview
prs.body:
Closes #198371

## What Problem This Solves

The agent Overview page shows an agent's **Thinking default** as plain text, so setting one agent's level (for example a `coder` agent) means using the config editor or the CLI.

## User Impact

Operators who can edit config can pick an agent's thinking default in **Agents → agent → Overview → Model selection**. The menu lists only the levels that agent's model accepts, plus **Inherit default (level)**, which removes the agent's own setting. Choices save to `agents.entries.<id>.thinkingDefault` through the page's existing autosave and affect only that agent. Message and session thinking overrides still take precedence.

## Why This Change Was Made

- The levels come from the agent's row in `agents.list` (`thinkingLevels`), which the Gateway already resolves for that agent's model and runtime.
- **Schema change (additive):** `agents.list` agent rows gain an optional `thinkingInheritedDefault`. The Gateway sends it only when the agent sets its own `thinkingDefault`. It is the level that clearing the override resolves to, using the same resolver as runs: per-agent model params, shared model params, the global default, the model's own default, then clamping to the model's levels. The core resolver gains an option to skip only the agent's own `thinkingDefault`. Existing clients can ignore the field; the Swift and Kotlin protocol contracts are unchanged. The protocol changelog is release-owned, so this description records the schema change.
- Restricted model views (a model selection policy) drop `thinkingInheritedDefault` along with the other thinking fields, because it is resolved from the agent's hidden model. Their `thinkingDefault` is the agent's own override, so with an override and no inherited level the option reads plain **Inherit default** and names no level.
- The **Inherit default (level)** label shows `thinkingInheritedDefault`, or the agent's resolved level when it has no override. Example: global Low, a per-model param of High and an agent override of Medium give "Inherit default (High)", which is what clearing produces.
- Level names come from one helper, `thinkingLevelLabel` in `ui/src/lib/chat/thinking-level-label.ts`, which this page and the Models page share. It has its own module so it stays out of chat boot JS (the Control UI performance check counts every byte there). It uses the `quickSettings.model.thinkingLevels.*` translations through each page's reactive translator. The five standard levels that had no key (Minimal, Extra high, Adaptive, Maximum, Ultra) gain canonical English, and the translation pipeline supplies other locales. Provider-specific levels keep their own label.
- A saved level that the current model does not offer stays visible and selected, but greyed out, instead of being rewritten.
- The row reads the real config even when the model catalog restricts model choices, because thinking is not a model choice.
- Before config has loaded, or for users who cannot read config, the row is disabled and shows the resolved level the way the read-only row did.

**Known gaps:**

- The level list belongs to the agent's saved model. Right after changing the primary model, the list still shows the old model's levels until the agent list refreshes. Any level picked meanwhile is valid config, and the Gateway clamps it to the new model at run time.
- On a model whose only level is a harness Ultra, an agent with an Ultra override shows "Inherit default (Ultra)", though clearing it leaves no default. This is rare, and the level is visible and recoverable.

## Evidence

Live run on an isolated Gateway built from this branch, inside a macOS VM, with made-up config: agent `coder` on a stand-in reasoning model. A headless browser drove the Control UI, and the script checked the config file after each step.

Before choosing: the menu offers `Inherit default (Medium)`, `Off`, `Minimal`, `Low`, `Medium`, `High`, `Ultra`.
This frame is from the run before the label-only fix; that fix does not change this frame.

Before

![Before](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/daniel-lxs/screenshots/8556c6104607f3ea3219925c637a008914529c98/images/2026/11/ceb177c8-6cca-4499-a032-5dade5beed5f.png)

After

![After](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/daniel-lxs/screenshots/8556c6104607f3ea3219925c637a008914529c98/images/2026/11/c8a71488-9023-4d9d-b278-7c958bc0880a.png)

After choosing **High**, the config file has `agents.entries.coder.thinkingDefault: "high"` and `agents.defaults` is unchanged; after a page reload the row still shows High:



Choosing **Inherit default** again removes the key from `agents.entries.coder`; after a reload the row reads Inherit default (Medium):



Second live run, same VM setup: global Low, a per-model `params.thinking` of High, and coder's own Medium.
- **Upgrade from latest stable (2026.11.3):** stable shows the read-only row. The update runs `openclaw doctor --fix --non-interactive` with this build, then starts on the same state. coder's entry and the defaults are unchanged. `agents.list` reports `thinkingDefault: "medium"` and `thinkingInheritedDefault: "high"`, and the inherit option reads "Inherit default (High)". Choosing it removes the override, and after a reload the agent resolves to High.
- **Model-restricted operator:** a trusted-proxy person whose role has `modelPolicy.allow: ["standin/stand-in"]` and admin scope. The projected roster carries the override as `thinkingDefault` with no inherited field, and the inherit option reads plain "Inherit default".





Tests and checks:
- `ui/src/pages/agents/panels-overview.test.ts`: 21 passed; `ui/src/pages/agents/model-config.test.ts`: 13 passed; the Models page view, locale and page tests and `ui/src/lib/chat/thinking.test.ts` pass with the shared helper. They cover the levels offered, saving and clearing, inherited labels (global Low, per-model High and override Medium labelled "Inherit default (High)"; the same override on a restricted roster labelled plain "Inherit default"), a saved level the model does not offer, a restricted model catalog, and the disabled state without config. The tests that pinned the row as a read-only fact were replaced.
- `src/gateway/session-utils.agent-models.test.ts`: `agents.list` reports `thinkingInheritedDefault: "high"` for that case and omits it for an agent without an override; the real restricted projection of that roster drops the field and reports `thinkingDefault: "medium"`. The UI and Gateway tests each fail without their fix and pass with it.
- `src/gateway/session-utils-model.thinking-default.test.ts`, `src/gateway/server-methods/agents-list.test.ts` and `packages/gateway-protocol/src/schema/agents-models-skills.test.ts`: pass.
- `pnpm tsgo:ui`, `pnpm tsgo:core`, the gateway test typecheck, oxlint and format on the touched files, `pnpm ui:i18n:verify` and `pnpm protocol:check` (Swift and Kotlin contracts unchanged): pass. In a German locale the selector reads "Inherit default (Hoch)", "Aus", "Niedrig", "Mittel", "Hoch".
- Not run: the full test suite (left to CI).

Cards are horizontal: the illustration fills the left side of the card edge to edge, on the same gradient and with the same dark-theme art as before, and the name (with its badge beside it), description and buttons sit on the right. A section with an odd number of cards leaves the last cell empty.

A card's first action now uses the theme's primary button, and the other actions use the normal secondary button. The watch cards, whose only action is Docs, keep it secondary. The Community label and its three links now sit on one line at the bottom, as compact buttons with their existing icons.

On narrow columns the cards stack one per row, and at phone widths the illustration moves back above the text. Cards keep the theme's corner radius. The hero headline and paragraph strings are no longer used, so they've been removed.

prs.title: fix: tell include users how to update without deleting their disabled heartbeat
prs.body:
Related: #200224

## What Problem This Solves

If your agents config lives in an included file (`$include`) and still contains the retired heartbeat settings, updates to 2026.11.5 are refused with "agents.defaults: unrecognized key", and you are told to run `openclaw doctor --fix`. The installed version's Doctor can't retire those settings, so users deleted the disabled heartbeat instead, and the installed version immediately fell back to its default 30-minute heartbeat.

## User Impact

User impact: the refusal now names the legacy settings, says not to remove them, and gives the path we verified: temporarily combine the included files into one `openclaw.json`, retry the update, then split the config again. A disabled heartbeat stays disabled through the whole process.

## Why This Change Was Made

Automatic legacy repair during an update never rewrites included files (`canPlanAutomaticConfigRepair` declines any config with includes), so this refusal is by design for now. The generic hint pointed at a repair that can't run here. The include-owned roster case already had specific guidance; this adds the same kind of guidance for any other legacy field behind includes. Whether update repair should learn to rewrite included files is a separate decision.

## Evidence

Live on Crabbox AWS Linux, with npm installs and a multi-agent roster (`main`, `ops`) using `agents.defaults.heartbeat = { agentId: "main", every: "" }`:

| From → to | Config layout | Result |
|---|---|---|
| 2026.11.4 → 2026.11.5 | heartbeat in `openclaw.json` | Update succeeds; health reports heartbeat disabled; 0 enabled heartbeat automations |
| 2026.11.4 → 2026.11.5 | agents in `$include` | Refused with the reporter's exact text (`unrecognized key <key>` plus the generic doctor hint) |
| 2026.11.4 → 2026.11.5 | include consolidated into `openclaw.json` first | Update succeeds; heartbeat stays disabled; 0 enabled heartbeat automations |

**Patched CLI, end to end.** On Crabbox, this head was built as a package and updated from installed 2026.11.4 with the agents config in `$include`. The update was still refused before any change, the Gateway stayed healthy on 11.4, and the heartbeat stayed disabled. The CLI now prints:

```text
Update refused: configuration is invalid at $OPENCLAW_STATE_DIR/openclaw.json.
- agents.defaults: unrecognized key <key>
The update migrates agents.defaults.heartbeat automatically only in a single-file config, and this config uses includes. Keep these settings as they are; do not remove them, because the installed version can then change behavior (a removed disabled heartbeat falls back to the default heartbeat). Back up the root config and included files, temporarily consolidate the included files into one openclaw.json, correct any other errors listed above, and retry the update. After it succeeds and `openclaw config validate` passes, split the config back into includes.
```

The new admission test fails on base, showing the generic hint, and passes with the fix. Config-failure and failure-report consumers pass 23/23. One existing case, `unsafe TMPDIR`, fails identically on base and head on macOS (a local temp-dir snapshot difference) and is left to Linux CI. autoreview came back scoped-clean (P2), and an independent Codex review found nothing.

Production change: +7/-1 in `src/cli/update-cli/update-command-config-failure.ts`.

prs.title: fix: plugin tools lose native conversation IDs on CLI backends
prs.body:
Closes #200186

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes plugin tools losing the current conversation's native ID when a run uses a CLI backend.

## User Impact

Plugin tools receive the host's raw conversation ID on the CLI loopback path, as they already do on embedded runs. The delivery target remains separate, and an unavailable native ID stays absent.

## Why This Change Was Made

Both CLI grant creation and Gateway tool resolution dropped this existing context field. Forwarding the host-provided `chatId` through those two points restores the documented plugin contract without inferring identity from a delivery target, session key, or client header.

## Evidence

Local focused validation: **112 tests passed across five files**. Core production types, Gateway test types, targeted lint/format, test-line budget (+160/400), and staged diff checks passed. Independent P0-P3 review found no actionable issues in the byte-verified four-file patch and supplied source context.

The broad `check:changed --staged --delegate-compilers` run passed its initial guards but was stopped during whole-repository SQLite analysis when local memory was exhausted. Its remaining lanes are deferred to PR CI; the full command is not claimed as passed.

The regression loads a temporary plugin, creates an admitted CLI grant, authenticates against the real local MCP HTTP server, and invokes the plugin tool. Native ID and delivery target deliberately differ. A second invocation omits the native ID while retaining the same delivery target.

On base `54cb172fb2adf6f77c936c80e3a7ee82cb74e135`, the regression failed at the plugin result:

```text
Expected: {"nativeChannelId":"native-room-123","target":"channel:delivery-456"}
Received: {"nativeChannelId":null,"target":"channel:delivery-456"}
```

No external channel or model credentials were used; this proves the local CLI-grant/MCP/plugin path, not a live Claude or Slack turn. Broad CI remains separate from local focused validation.


With the fix, the real HTTP responses satisfy both cases:

```json
{"nativeChannelId":"native-room-123","target":"channel:delivery-456"}
{"nativeChannelId":null,"target":"channel:delivery-456"}
```

<details>
<summary>Local validation commands and results</summary>

```text
node scripts/run-vitest.mjs run src/agents/cli-runner/mcp-grant-context.test.ts src/gateway/mcp-http.test.ts src/gateway/tool-resolution.test.ts src/agents/openclaw-tools.plugin-context.test.ts src/gateway/mcp-http.plugin-context.test.ts --maxWorkers=1
unit-fast:    1 file,  15 passed
gateway:      3 files, 89 passed
agents-core:  1 file,   8 passed
```

The new integration case took 81.1 seconds on this Windows host, excluding cold worker compilation. An earlier attempt hit the wrapper's 15-minute no-output watchdog during compilation; the successful run used `OPENCLAW_VITEST_NO_OUTPUT_TIMEOUT_MS=3600000`. No test assertions or test timeouts were relaxed.

```text
node scripts/run-tsgo.mjs -p tsconfig.core.json --incremental --tsBuildInfoFile .artifacts/tsgo-cache/core.tsbuildinfo
node scripts/run-tsgo.mjs -p test/tsconfig/tsconfig.core.test.gateway-root.json
node scripts/run-oxlint.mjs --tsconfig config/tsconfig/oxlint.core.json <the four changed files>
node scripts/run-format.mts --check <the four changed files>
node --import ./scripts/tsx.mjs scripts/check-test-lines-ratchet.mts --staged --base HEAD
git diff --cached --check
```

All checks above passed against the patch before commit. The comparison base was `54cb172fb2adf6f77c936c80e3a7ee82cb74e135`.

</details>
## Live CLI proof follow-up

The current-head review requests a shipped Gateway turn in which a real CLI backend invokes the plugin tool. That proof is still missing. This host has no available Claude or Gemini CLI backend, so the local HTTP regression above is the only execution evidence for this path. It must not be read as a live model or external-channel test. The existing CI approval request also remains pending; no cloud test pass is claimed.

prs.title: fix(ui): a connection that died during an app switch recovers late after switching back
prs.body:
Fixes #199875

### What Problem This Solves

When the Control UI's Gateway socket stops delivering frames without closing while you are in another app, the page looks the same after you come back, and nothing the Gateway sends arrives. In live runs the reply appeared 17.9 s after the return on the chat page, and the UI replaced the socket 41 s and 56 s after it on the model setup page. On return, the page-activation check only replaces a socket that is closed or already silent past the 60 s tick window. A socket whose last frame is a few seconds old is left to the inbound-silence watchdog: after 60 s of silence, or 5 s after a request goes unanswered, it sends a `health` probe and gives it 10 s to answer. On the chat page the composer reloads its Talk settings on every window focus; on a dead socket those requests go unanswered, so the watchdog probes about 5 s after the return. Pages without the composer send nothing on return, so they wait for the 60 s silence window or for some later request to go unanswered.

### What changes

- On `visibilitychange` back to visible or window `focus`, if the socket still counts as healthy, `GatewayBrowserClient.probeOnWake()` sends the watchdog's `health` probe (`probe: false`) right away. It keeps the watchdog's 10 s deadline.
- Any inbound frame keeps the socket. The activity hook clears the pending probe as soon as a frame arrives, so an answer that lands in the same millisecond as the previous frame also counts.
- If nothing arrives within 10 s, the watchdog closes the socket (`inbound silence probe timeout`) and the reconnect supervisor replaces it.
- The probe deadline has its own timer, so the socket closes at 10 s rather than at the watchdog's next once-a-second check. After a failed probe the replacement connects at once; if that replacement fails too, reconnects back off as usual, starting at 800 ms.
- Switching back again while a probe is running keeps that probe and its deadline, so repeated focus events cannot hold a dead socket open.
- A socket that is closed, or already silent past the tick window, is replaced at once on return, as before.

### Impact

- Chat page: a reply that finished while you were away appeared 10.4 s after the return, against 17.9 s on `main` (one live run each).
- Model setup page: a socket that stopped delivering frames during an app switch was replaced 10.2 s and 10.2 s after the return, against 41.2 s and 56.1 s on `main` (two live runs each).
- A healthy socket stays open: in both model setup page runs the return's `health` probe was answered within 0.03 s, and no new connection opened in the 40 s that followed. This path closes a socket only if nothing at all arrives for 10 s after the return, the same deadline the watchdog uses.
- Each return to the window while connected sends one `health` request.

### Evidence

**Live runs, model setup page.** An isolated Gateway (`gateway run`, auth off, channels off, no model configured, so the Control UI opens on model setup) and the Control UI in Chrome for Testing, in a macOS VM. The `main` builds come from `05bc22f` with `main`'s two UI files and the PR builds from this PR's head, `7b1fb79`; they differ only in the changed UI files; the served bundle was checked for `probeOnWake` before each run. A test proxy between the page and the Gateway logged every WebSocket and frame, and on command stopped forwarding on the open socket in both directions without closing it. It also removed the WebSocket compression offer so it could read frames. App switch: Finder brought to the front for 5 s, then Chrome again. Each run did a healthy switch first, then a switch with the socket cut off. Run 2 cut it off 1 s after a tick, so the socket's last frame was recent at the return.

| `main` | 2 | no probe, no reconnect | 45.1 s | 55.1 s | 56.1 s |
| This PR | 1 | probe answered in 0.03 s, no reconnect | 0.03 s | 10.0 s | 10.2 s |
| This PR | 2 | probe answered in 0.02 s, no reconnect | 0.03 s | 10.1 s | 10.2 s |

Times are from the proxy log, counted from the moment Chrome came back to the front ("new connection ready" is the replacement socket's `hello-ok`). On `main`, run 1's probe came 60 s after the socket's last frame; run 2's came 5 s after a page request went unanswered. Screenshots of the page 40 s after the healthy return, 3 s after the dead-socket return and after recovery were pixel-identical in all four runs, so the page itself showed nothing either way.

**Live runs, chat page.** The same setup plus a stand-in model that holds its reply until the socket has been cut, so the reply finishes while you are away. ## What Problem This Solves

When a helper finishes while its parent is busy, an internal completion receipt can appear above the composer as an empty **Queued** message, with an inappropriate remove action.

## User Impact

## Why This Change Was Made

prs.title: fix(agents): never fail a turn on the soft compaction threshold
prs.body:
## Problem

Between tool rounds, the embedded runner stops the attempt (`MidTurnPrecheckSignal`) when projected occupancy crosses the client maintenance threshold (for example 204,000 of a 272,000-token window). Recovery then decides whether it can compact and continue the transcript. When it cannot (`replay_unsafe`), the user sees "Context overflow: prompt too large for the model" for a request that would have fit the real window, and has to press Continue.

Production evidence (one Odin gateway, two days): 73 mid-turn precheck aborts with median estimate 207k and p90 215k against a 272k window, none near the window, and no provider-side overflow rejections. One user-visible failure: estimate 206,084 vs threshold 204,000, last batch a Code Mode `wait` returning `status: "waiting"`. Recovery rejected it because only Code Mode `exec` was recorded as parking a run, so `parkedCodeModeRun` was false. The next run compacted 206,029 → 14,530 without trouble.

## Fix

1. **Threshold pressure no longer fails a turn.** `checkMidTurnPrecheck` asks recovery's own question (`canCompactAndContinueMidTurn`, now shared by the boundary and `attempt-recovery`) before stopping for reserve-based pressure. It uses live subscription evidence for the current batch. If compaction could not continue the batch and the request fits the hard window (the same nominal full-window check as today's hard admission), the request is sent and compaction waits for a later boundary or the end of the turn. The run still stops for a request over the window, with the existing overflow copy.
2. **A Code Mode `wait` that parks its run counts as parked.** `codeModeExecToolNames` becomes `codeModeControlToolNames` and includes the marked `exec` and `wait` controls (`isCodeModeControlTool`). Plain tools named `exec` or `wait` are excluded. This feeds the completion handler (`codeModeSuspended`), the conditional `sessions_yield` check in `attempt.ts` and the worker runtime.
3. These protections are unchanged: the hard window, the asynchronous-tool rejection, and the rule that compaction may not rotate the session while Code Mode work is parked.

The boundary predicate trusts subscription evidence only after every call in the current batch has a terminal record. Subscription events trail the agent loop in order, so incomplete evidence makes it defer compaction rather than stop the turn.

Consistent with #189810, #189891 and #190017: hard admission and the soft maintenance threshold remain. This PR only stops the soft threshold from failing a turn that compaction cannot safely continue.

## Tests

- `attempt-context-guards.test.ts`: proactive (measured occupancy) pressure that fits the window is sent when the batch cannot continue after compaction, and still signals when it can. Red on base.
- `attempt-midturn-precheck.test.ts` (real session/request flow): deferred pressure sends the second request; a deferred request over the window still stops. Red on base for the deferral row.
- `attempt-client-tools.test.ts`: the marked Code Mode controls yield `{exec, wait}`; plain `exec`/`wait` yield none. Red on base.
- `embedded-agent-subscribe.handlers.tools.test.ts`: a marked `exec` or `wait` returning `waiting` parks; unmarked ones do not.
- `run.midturn-precheck-retry.test-support.ts`: exec waiting → wait waiting compacts and continues with no error; a replay-unsafe stop shows overflow copy (it is now reached only for a real over-window request).

## Evidence

- Targeted suites pass: context guards, mid-turn precheck, client tools, handlers.tools, shared run integration (including the mid-turn retry file), attempt recovery, execution phase, code-mode bridge lifecycle, tool usage, cron session lifecycle, Talk client-native control, Code Mode continuation.
- `attempt-stream-custody.test.ts` and `attempt.sessions-yield.test.ts` have the same 13 local failures on the unmodified base. They are environmental and were left for CI.
- Type check (`tsrs`) of core plus the agents/cron/gateway test projects shows no errors in touched files. Oxfmt and oxlint pass on touched files, except a `max-lines` count on `attempt-stream-prepare.ts` that this one-line rename does not change.

## Known gaps

- No isolated-Gateway end-to-end run against a real 200k-token conversation. Proof is at the owning boundaries plus the outer run loop.
- If threshold-triggered compaction is attempted and fails, or exhausts its attempts, the turn still surfaces compaction guidance. Handling that would need a carried deferral flag across attempts. Left as follow-up.
- The native ChatGPT V2 boundary fallback (`chatgpt-v2-compaction.ts`) still signals at its soft trigger. That path is not involved in this incident.

prs.title: fix(agents): only a request that cannot fit may fail a turn
prs.body:
Supersedes #200483. Thanks @fuller-stack-dev for finding this and for the first fix; this PR applies the same rule to every route that had the bug.

## The rule

Only a request that cannot fit the model window may fail a turn. Any other context-pressure signal only schedules maintenance, and maintenance runs only at a boundary where the current tool batch can continue.

## What was wrong

Five independent paths stopped or failed a turn on a reserve-based soft threshold even when the request still fit:

| Path | Before | After |
|---|---|---|
| Mid-turn check (`checkMidTurnPrecheck`, #73499/#168338/#190017) | soft threshold → `MidTurnPrecheckSignal` → recovery; a failed compaction surfaced "Auto-compaction failed" | `maintenance` only at a settled boundary; send otherwise |
| Prompt preflight (`attempt-prompt-preflight`) | reserve budget → precheck failure | `overflow` only when over the window |
| ChatGPT V2 fallback (#168401) | soft fallback threw even while tool calls were pending | soft fallback only at a settled boundary |
| Reply pre-turn compaction (`runSessionCompactionIfNeeded`, #49479/#130863) | failed threshold compaction failed the turn | fails only if the prompt cannot fit |
| CLI post-turn compaction (`cli-compaction`) | failed threshold compaction failed the command | fails only if the next prompt cannot fit |

Production evidence (gateway logs, 2026-11-16..17): 79 context-pressure stops across team-metal (62), Peanutto (15) and HamVerBot (2). 44 were soft-threshold stops whose request fit the window. Every stop was logged as an `embedded_run_agent_end` `context_overflow` failure.

## Fix

`src/agents/context-pressure.ts` is the single owner:

| request > window | maintenance due | boundary safe | declined this run | decision |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| yes | any | any | any | `overflow` (recovery may fail the turn) |
| no | yes | yes | no | `maintenance` (compact, always continue) |
| no | yes | yes | yes | send |
| no | yes | no | any | send (deferred) |
| no | no | any | any | send |

- A boundary is safe when every tool call has a result, no tool item is active, no tool started background work, no Code Mode run is parked (its `wait` is bound to the session that compaction may rotate), and no approval prompt is waiting.
- `MidTurnPrecheckRequest.pressure` and `preflightRecovery.pressure` are required, so recovery cannot turn maintenance into a failed turn.
- Maintenance that cannot reduce context is declined for the rest of the run, so it is not retried at every request.
- Maintenance stops are no longer logged as `context_overflow` agent failures, nor as `livenessState=blocked`.

## Evidence

**Real-model E2E**, `openai/gpt-6.1-sol` (272k window, 204k client threshold, `responsesServerCompaction: false`). A 182k-token seed turn, then four sequential `exec` calls; the soft check fires at an estimated 211.6k tokens with the batch settled.

| Journey | base `237e3e4fe0d1` | head |
|---|---|---|
| settled batch; client compaction has nothing to summarize | turn **failed**: "Auto-compaction failed before the next model request. Try again or run /compact." (`kind=compaction_failure`) | turn **completed**: `HERON-5521, 0493` (correct); log `pressure=maintenance` → `[context-maintenance] declined … continuing` |
| settled batch; compaction model unavailable | turn **failed**, same text | turn **completed**: `HERON-5521, 0493` |

Head runs use a dist built from `a69e3de`; base is a dist of `237e3e4fe0d1` (`ocx base merge-base`). Raw stderr and replies are below.

Base also logged `embedded run agent end … failoverReason=context_overflow` for each; head logged none.

<details><summary>Captured E2E output (openclaw agent --local, gpt-6.1-sol; head built from a69e3de)</summary>

**base / settled**:
```
[agent/embedded] embedded run agent end: runId=24267729-7e73-44ec-a958-c2707d0a10ee isError=true model=gpt-6.1-sol provider=openai failoverReason=context_overflow
[agent/embedded] [context-overflow-midturn-precheck] sessionKey=agent:main:explicit:cp-base-settled-1794935543 provider=openai/gpt-6.1-sol route=compact_only estimatedPromptTokens=211627 promptBudgetBeforeReserve=204000 overflowTokens=7627 toolResultReducibleChars=0 effectiveReserveTokens=68000
```

prs.body:
Related: #149678

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes PowerShell completion suggesting options and option values after `--`, such as offering `--json` for `openclaw cron show -- --j`.

## User Impact

PowerShell users can enter positional arguments after `--` without misleading flag suggestions. Subcommands and PowerShell's normal file completion remain available. Regenerate the installed completion script to pick up the fix.

## Why This Change Was Made

Track the option terminator while resolving the command path, using the existing option metadata to distinguish required operands, optional operands, and attached short-option values. A required operand that happens to be `--` must not terminate option parsing. This brings PowerShell in line with the existing Bash behavior.

## Evidence

Refreshed the branch against upstream `bb78f2bdab1a` and resolved conflicts in the existing PowerShell generator. The resolution preserves upstream cursor-prefix handling, required-operand suppression, literal quoting, and the existing terminator regression suite. Added an exact 72-line allocation for that unchanged test file under the current budget policy. Independent review through P3 found no actionable issue.

Before applying the terminator repair, 3 of the 9 shipped-CLI probes failed on `5f2266225373a48bd5527e5f90d06f0e2981a18e` (current main plus the independent quoted-assignment fix). The repaired head passes all probes, including required operands and completion in the middle of a quoted word.

Built `2845cbefe83bdc2d95725cd6bd3bea10a5f10e68` with `pnpm build qaRuntime`, then generated the script through `pnpm --silent openclaw completion --shell powershell` with isolated home/config/state. prs.title: improve: reduce memory used by limited file reads
prs.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Reading a small range from a UTF-8 file could decode and normalize the entire file buffer before selecting the requested lines. This created transient string allocations proportional to file size, even for a 50-line read.

## User Impact

Limited UTF-8 reads use substantially less temporary memory and CPU, with identical text, line totals, cursor behavior, and continuation notices. No settings or migrations are required. UTF-16, Windows code-page selection, binary/image detection, and custom string decoders retain their existing behavior.

Large ordinary local files already stream through the existing page reader. Buffer-only backends still fetch the complete file; this change removes unnecessary text conversion after that read. Reads without an explicit line limit retain bulk decoding for complete-selection totals and CPU parity.

## Why This Change Was Made

The existing capture owner now locates the selected UTF-8 byte range and counts lines before decoding that range once. The existing string scanner continues to own text and cursor details. This adds 50 runtime lines to preserve exact EOF totals without a second pager or cache. The filesystem dependency, mutation queue, and sandbox cancellation paths are unchanged.

## Evidence

The new real-tool regression fails on base `8f80fe08cad63e890008668c6f482a81aa12e2ea` because a two-line request decodes 240,000 bytes; it passes with the fix. All 97 focused tests pass, with one Linux-only proc-file test skipped on macOS. There are 92 exact-result comparisons covering BOMs, UTF-16LE/BE, malformed UTF-8, CRLF, cursors, long lines, and EOF, plus equality for every measured page. Codex autoreview found no actionable P0–P2 findings.

Acceptance: compare two independently loaded base arms A1/A2 with B, using identical synthetic files and exact serialized output equality. Require lower allocation than both controls on affected reads, lower CPU on the expensive cases, and no material end-to-end regression. Five interleaved warm samples of ten reads cover 10 KiB–50 MiB, LF/CRLF, offset 1/limit 50 and offset 75/limit 200. Allocation includes collected JavaScript objects and is measured separately from unprofiled CPU; it excludes native Buffer storage. Measurements are on Node 26.12.1, macOS arm64, not a production storage-latency claim.

Representative first-page results through the real filesystem-backed buffered read tool:

| File | Allocation MB/read A1 / A2 → B | CPU ms/read A1 / A2 → B |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 256 KiB LF | 0.794 / 0.802 → **0.215** | 1.447 / 1.460 → **1.337** |
| 256 KiB CRLF | 1.561 / 1.557 → **0.221** | 1.656 / 1.608 → **1.414** |
| 50 MiB LF | 119.938 / 120.043 → **0.334** | 112.018 / 115.202 → **56.643** |
| 50 MiB CRLF | 172.760 / 172.863 → **0.367** | 169.917 / 166.686 → **59.204** |

The 50 MiB decode/capture owner alone falls from 78.328/78.078 to 14.737 ms CPU for LF and 155.130/154.077 to 15.972 ms for CRLF. Small-file and already-streaming local controls show no material end-to-end regression; no speedup is claimed for them. The longer default-read control (seven samples of 100 reads, 2 MiB) is 7.560/8.107 → 7.727 ms CPU for LF and 7.742/7.699 → 7.709 ms for CRLF. An initial default-read regression was removed before this version.

Wall-time distributions (ms/read, median [min–p95] of five batch means; p95 is the maximum at this sample count):

| File | A1 | A2 | B |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 10 KiB LF | 0.276 [0.251–0.312] | 0.271 [0.225–0.342] | 0.260 [0.251–0.301] |
| 256 KiB LF | 0.473 [0.409–0.487] | 0.443 [0.424–0.465] | 0.412 [0.339–0.485] |
| 51200 KiB LF | 81.446 [81.001–83.704] | 81.741 [80.502–85.826] | 28.105 [26.714–28.631] |
| 51200 KiB CRLF | 94.300 [74.639–94.879] | 92.708 [75.890–93.937] | 28.717 [28.614–29.224] |

Reproduce with the committed workload:

```sh
node --expose-gc --import ./scripts/tsx.mjs scripts/perf/read-tool-decode-measure.ts --baseline 8f80fe08cad63e890008668c6f482a81aa12e2ea --mode timing
node --expose-gc --import ./scripts/tsx.mjs scripts/perf/read-tool-decode-measure.ts --baseline 8f80fe08cad63e890008668c6f482a81aa12e2ea --mode allocation
node --expose-gc --import ./scripts/tsx.mjs scripts/perf/read-tool-decode-measure.ts --baseline 8f80fe08cad63e890008668c6f482a81aa12e2ea --mode timing --pages default --sizes 2097152 --samples 7 --iterations 100
```

Validation: focused read, image, retention, source-work, encoding, sandbox, cancellation, and prompt-stability suites; `pnpm check:changed --staged` plus successful reruns of its corrected test-type and lint checks; exact-head CI [run 44141270064, attempt 2](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/44141270064) passed. Hosted Codex and ClawSweeper reviewed head `73501a0d1f1d1feb690cd00b1b4f44488ee18f3f` with no findings or open checklist items. Attempt 1 lost one shard during runner setup to an Ubuntu Git-mirror HTTP 503; a diagnosed failed-jobs-only retry passed, with no source change or test failure. No changed modules are imported by the Control UI.

prs.title: fix(ui): divide usage throughput by active time instead of session span
prs.body:
Closes #200627

## What Problem This Solves

The Usage throughput tiles say "tokens per minute of active time", but divided by the summed wall-clock span of every session in range — a few sessions left open for days pushed the real rate down by orders of magnitude (the reporter measured 87.3 tok/min where the active-time math gives ~14,098). The tiles now divide by the assistant-turn active time that the same response already ships.

- Problem: `ui/src/pages/usage/view.tsx` computed `throughputTokensPerMin` and `throughputCostPerMin` from `overview.durationMs` (`lastActivity - firstActivity` per session), which includes every idle gap between turns.
- Solution: divide by the recorded assistant-turn active time — `aggregates.latency.avgMs * count`, or the matching `dailyLatency` buckets when days are selected — and keep the tile's empty value when no latency samples exist.
- What changed: `usageActiveMs` and `usageThroughputStats` helpers in `ui/src/pages/usage/metrics.ts`, consumed by `view.tsx`; regression tests in `metrics.test.ts`.
- What did NOT change: the "avg session" figure (wall clock is correct for that label), `durationMs`/`durationCount` themselves, any runtime field, and the hint texts (they already say active time).

## Why This Change Was Made

The reporter's primary ask: honor the documented active-time denominator using data already shipped, rather than re-labeling the tile as wall clock or adding a new runtime signal (#136857 stays separate).

- Best fix: yes — no new field, no new query; `aggregates.latency` is populated by the same rollup on current main.
- Alternative: correcting the hint to say wall-clock was the reporter's fallback, but the tile would then measure how long sessions stayed open, not how fast the model worked.
- Risk / non-goals: ranges whose sessions report no latency samples render the existing empty value instead of a rate; selected-row latency behavior follows the same aggregates the insights card already displays.

## User Impact

The throughput tiles now match their label: operators comparing model speed across ranges see tokens/cost per minute of actual assistant activity instead of numbers deflated by idle session spans.

## Evidence

Runtime check of the shipped helper with the issue's measurement shape (91 turn samples, avg 155,981 ms; for the reporter's own totals this denominator is the ~236.6 active minutes behind their ~14,098 tok/min figure):

```text
$ node --import tsx -e "import('./ui/src/pages/usage/metrics.ts').then(m => console.log(m.usageThroughputStats({ totals: { totalTokens: 14098000, totalCost: 21.5 }, latency: { count: 91, avgMs: 155981 } })))"
{
  throughputTokensPerMin: 59593.056945298566,
  throughputCostPerMin: 0.09088173672321742
}
```

Regression in `metrics.test.ts` asserts the same active-time denominator, and that missing/zero-sample latency keeps both rates `undefined` instead of dividing by the session span:

```text
✓ metrics.test.ts > divides throughput by active time from recorded turn durations
✓ metrics.test.ts > scopes the active-time denominator to the selected days
✓ metrics.test.ts > keeps throughput empty without latency samples instead of dividing by the session span
```

Per review, a day-filtered selection now takes the denominator from the matching `dailyLatency` buckets (one active minute on the selected day divides only that day's usage) instead of the full-range aggregate, which previously mixed unselected days' activity into the rate.

What was not tested: the Control UI rendering itself (labels unchanged; the tile already renders the existing empty value for `undefined` rates).

## AI Assistance

This PR is AI-assisted. Used `git grep` over the usage page to find the single computation site in `view.tsx`, extracted the denominator into `usageThroughputStats` in `metrics.ts`, and validated with `node --import tsx` plus `vitest`. The implementer understands the code: active time is `aggregates.latency.avgMs * count`, already shipped by the shared rollup. All evidence above is from real local runtime execution.
