prs.title: feat: connect OpenClaw to GBrain with one plugin install
prs.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Connecting OpenClaw to [GBrain](https://github.com/garrytan/gbrain) today takes a separate install, a hand-written `mcp.servers` entry, a bearer key minted by hand and a service you keep alive yourself. The `gbrain-context-engine` plugin GBrain ships never selects a brain on multi-agent hosts, and on ClawHub `gbrain` returns only unofficial skills.

## User Impact

User impact: on a machine with Bun 1.4.4 or newer, install the GBrain plugin (one click in the Control UI, or `openclaw plugins install`) and the agent can recall from your brain about a minute later. You do not edit config, mint a key or set up a service yourself. Without Bun, the plugin shows the one command that installs it (Linux also needs `unzip`); OpenClaw does not install Bun. Docker users add one Compose overlay, whose GBrain image includes Bun.

## Why This Change Was Made

GBrain stays the owner of its own install, brain, service and upgrades. The new external plugin `extensions/gbrain` only connects OpenClaw to it:

- A Gateway service runs GBrain's own commands once: `bun install -g`, `gbrain init --pglite`, `gbrain mcp expose`. These install the launchd or systemd user service.
- It mints a bearer key through GBrain's owner API and writes one static streamable-HTTP `mcp.servers.gbrain` entry. Static means cron, heartbeat and subagent runs see it too.
- Every 60 s it checks the connection. A rotated or revoked key is replaced automatically. When the service is down, the plugin reports it with the next command to run. It never restarts the service: that stays with launchd, systemd or Compose.
- It leaves alone any existing `mcp.servers.gbrain` that points elsewhere or uses env templates.
- Docker: `deploy/gbrain/compose.yaml` runs GBrain as its own service on the project network. The brain volume is mounted read-only into the Gateway.
- No core or Plugin SDK changes. The plugin declares no config options.

GBrain's per-turn context hook (`gbrain setup openclaw`) stays opt-in. MCP alone recalled without prompting in every run below.

**Config budget +21 (`plugin`):** these are the generic `plugins.entries.gbrain.*` keys (`enabled`, `config`, `hooks.*`, `llm.*`, `subagent.*`) that the baseline counter writes once for every bundled plugin id (187 × 21). GBrain adds no options of its own. Counting the shared template once is a separate change to the counter.

## Evidence

**Control UI (host with Bun): one click, no consent dialog, recall 58.7 s after the click.** Packed candidate Gateway, plugin served from a local ClawHub fixture (not published yet), real model.

| Before | Installing | Installed | Recall |
|---|---|---|---|
| ![GBrain plugin page before install](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/45dfbbd0-7f37-415d-bcc8-74333c7788a2) | ![Install progress](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/132917e4-a007-4a7f-8e5e-5fdc36d65600) | ![GBrain installed and connected](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/28084efc-0430-44e5-a9df-a1bbb2bb872e) | ![Agent recalls the Sandpiper vault code from GBrain](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/5285b917-b213-4101-ba24-b1d574f8d699) |

Screencast (1 click → installed → connected 4.3 s → recall from a new session):

https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/0d5dc907-4fb1-4265-b84c-0b497d0f4e53

Timeline: clicked install 0 s → `mcp.servers.gbrain` connected 4.3 s → question sent 4.9 s → recalled 58.7 s. Clicks: 1.

**Clean hosts, live model, every step exit 0:**

| | macOS 15 VM | Ubuntu VM (systemd user) | Docker (`ghcr.io/openclaw/openclaw:latest` + overlay) |
|---|---|---|---|
| User actions | install + Bun command | install + `apt install unzip` + Bun command | `-f deploy/gbrain/compose.yaml` + install |
| Connected | 60 s after Bun | 54 s after Bun | 0 s |
| Recall after Gateway restart, codeword never shown to the session | ✅ 55 s | ✅ 64 s | ✅ 58 s |
| `brain.pglite` holders with 2 concurrent sessions | 1 | 1 | 1 |
| `mcp probe gbrain` | 8 tools | 8 tools | 8 tools |
| Stop service / kill serve / rotate key / `gbrain upgrade` → recall | ✅ ✅ ✅ ✅ | ✅ ✅ ✅ ✅ | ✅ ✅ ✅ ✅ |
| Uninstall keeps service and brain, removes install record | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ |

- Docker run: in the concurrent step, turn A answered the codeword correctly after 6 code-mode bridge calls, but its receipt listed no tool names, so the harness flagged it. The receipt gap is a separate issue.
- New live lane: `pnpm test:docker:gbrain`. The host driver is `scripts/e2e/lib/gbrain/host-e2e.sh`.
- `pnpm test extensions/gbrain` (unit), Docker plan test, `ocx build --dts` and the packed-tarball check pass at `a4c2d20`. The latest commit changes only the Docker lane script, which the final Docker run used.

<details><summary>Bugs found by the e2e runs and fixed here</summary>

1. Shared network namespace with the Gateway: `getaddrinfo ENOTFOUND gbrain` after a Gateway restart. GBrain now has its own namespace.
2. Linux: `Unit gbrain-serve.service could not be found.` GBrain now gets the user session bus env (minus Gateway identity and credentials).
3. Linux: Bun links under `XDG_CACHE_HOME`; the plugin asks `bun pm bin -g`.
4. Docker: `stable_unreadable … (offline, or no git)`. The sidecar image includes git.
5. Clean Linux: Bun's installer needs `unzip`; the message says so.
</details>

**Local review (ClawSweeper, local range `origin/main...d26de1b79f`):** complete, "patch is correct", 0 findings. Earlier rounds' findings were all fixed, with regression tests in `extensions/gbrain/src/connect.test.ts` where they apply:
- Key refresh kept only URL, transport and bearer; it now keeps the user's other entry settings (`enabled`, `toolFilter`, other headers).
- An `expose --port` move is followed instead of being reported as an external entry.
- Ownership comes from the config file as authored, not the env-expanded runtime config, so `Bearer ${GBRAIN_MCP_TOKEN}` entries stay the user's; entries supplied or changed by an `$include`, and any non-canonical `authorization` header, also stay the user's.
- Both e2e drivers carry the macOS Bash 5.3 heredoc guard and are registered in `portableScripts`.
- Both e2e drivers fail when the GBrain downgrade or upgrade fails or leaves the version unchanged.

The plugin icon is GBrain's own 512×512 app icon from gbrain.io (`assets/icon.png`); the screenshots above predate it and show the generic letter placeholder.

**Maintainer decision on the remaining finding:** the review flags the one-time `bun install -g github:garrytan/gbrain#stable` in the plugin's Gateway service against `extensions/AGENTS.md` ("Runtime never installs deps"). Kept on purpose: that rule covers the plugin's own package dependencies. GBrain is a separate tool with its own installer, its install runs only after the user explicitly installs this plugin, it happens once, and after a failure it retries at most every 10 minutes. Moving it to Doctor would add a step to the one-click setup this PR exists for.

**Known gaps (not in this PR):**
- GBrain upstream: no CLI to mint a key against a running server (the plugin uses the dashboard API), `mcp expose` has no `--bind`, no official container image. Headless Linux needs `loginctl enable-linger` to keep the user service after logout (not tested).
- OpenClaw: MCP startup backoff does not reset when GBrain recovers. `mcp.servers.gbrain` stays after uninstall (`openclaw mcp unset gbrain`).
- Bun is a prerequisite on macOS and Linux. Follow-up: install GBrain from its standalone release binaries (`gbrain-darwin-arm64`, `gbrain-linux-x64`) so neither Bun nor `unzip` is needed; first check that `gbrain upgrade` and `mcp expose` work without Bun and that releases publish checksums.
- Distribution: `@openclaw/gbrain` is an external plugin like Discord and Codex (`publishToClawHub`/`publishToNpm`, npm default install, excluded from the core `openclaw` package). It publishes with the next release; until then the Control UI proof used a local ClawHub fixture. The unscoped ClawHub name `gbrain` belongs to an unofficial upload; this package is scoped.

## What Problem This Solves

Full Release Validation stops before tests on non-root runners because Corepack tries to create `/usr/bin/pnpm` in a protected system directory. [The failing setup job](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/44112065080/job/134142242320) reports `EACCES` from that symlink operation.

## User Impact

CI can prepare pinned pnpm without write access to the system installation. No application behavior changes.

## Why This Change Was Made

Use the existing private shim directory on every operating system when `PNPM_HOME` is unset. Preserve an explicitly supplied directory and publish the selected directory through the existing environment and PATH outputs. Remove the fallback that installs into Corepack's system directory.

## Evidence

- The new action-shell regression fails on the base for Linux with no `PNPM_HOME`; existing Windows and explicit-directory cases pass. The candidate passes all 22 tests in the archive/bootstrap file (10.75 seconds; the three shim cases take 1.84 seconds).
- A separate real Corepack 0.36.0 check reproduces `EACCES` against a read-only installation directory on the base. The candidate creates a valid private pnpm symlink and leaves that directory unchanged. This checks the shim-installation step, not a complete hosted release run.
- Targeted type-aware lint, the scripts test TypeScript project, formatting, workflow validation (including zizmor), and `git diff --check` pass.

Local validation used the qualified native620 checkout at `9623a7e3` with the two candidate files overlaid after matching action, seed, test, helper, manifest, lockfile, and workspace inputs; all original files were restored. This is bounded owner proof, not local execution of the entire `aa5de061` source graph. Current-head PR CI remains broad proof. No dependency or package-manager version changed.

prs.title: fix(ui): iPhone Safari offers AutoFill Contact in the chat composer
prs.body:
Fixes #199088

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes: iPhone Safari shows "AutoFill Contact" over the keyboard, with the user's own name or email as the suggestion, when they tap the chat composer while a nearby message contains words like "name", "email" or "address".

## User Impact

User impact: on iPhone Safari the chat composer opens the normal keyboard with typing suggestions, and no longer offers the user's contact card. The composer's accessible name stays "Chat composer", including in the mention editor.

## Why This Change Was Made

Safari AutoFill reads a field's `<label>` element, and when there is none it guesses the field type from the visible page text around the field; `aria-label` and `autocomplete="off"` do not stop that guess. The composer textarea had only an `aria-label`, and while a reply streams its text sits directly before the composer, so contact-like words in it made Safari treat the composer as a contact field.

The textarea gets a `<label for>` that Safari reads instead of the surrounding text. The label is visually hidden and hidden from assistive technology: `aria-label` stays the accessible name, which the mention editor also copies onto its own textbox.

## Evidence

iOS 27 Simulator, Safari, with a made-up My Info card and the Control UI on the repo's mocked Gateway. Same chat state in both shots: an assistant reply containing "name on the account… work address" is still streaming, and the composer is focused.

Before (main): "AutoFill Contact" in the bar above the keyboard, with the card's name offered.

![Before: AutoFill Contact over the keyboard on main](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/daniel-lxs/screenshots/e4961494f3d7c59752994c44dd9497c0e20f0eb4/images/2026/11/6310a1f0-242d-4f16-8b6d-9dbd537fdbc5.png)

After (this branch): no AutoFill offer.

![After: no AutoFill offer with the label element](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/daniel-lxs/screenshots/e4961494f3d7c59752994c44dd9497c0e20f0eb4/images/2026/11/e1deae87-5130-47ab-af22-b29669fabd80.png)

- The branch showed no AutoFill offer in 2 of 2 simulator runs; main showed it in the same simulator.
- New test `names the composer with a label element` in `ui/src/pages/chat/chat-composer.test.ts`: fails on main, passes with the fix (22 of 22 in the file).
- `chat-composer-overflow.browser.test.tsx`: 13 of 13, three runs in a row. `composer-editor.browser.test.ts`: 55 of 55.
- In headless Chromium the composer is the textbox named "Chat composer" on both builds, and the label adds no node to the accessibility tree.
- Lint and format of the touched files pass.
- Not run: a physical iPhone, a real Gateway, and the full UI and e2e suites (left to CI).

prs.title: fix(android): match Control UI page scheme to the gateway socket
prs.body:
## What Problem This Solves

A discovered gateway on a non-loopback address opens a TLS socket even when its Bonjour record omits `gatewayTls`. The Android Control UI page did not use that decision. It chose `http` or `https` only from `endpoint.tlsEnabled`, so the page stayed on cleartext while the socket was TLS.

The Terminal, dashboard, and desktop screens load that page after the operator session connects. The page origin is where the signing bridge answers a challenge. A cleartext page is the wrong origin for a connection the socket policy already refused to leave on cleartext.

Manual LAN cleartext is unchanged. A stored pin still does not upgrade that page to HTTPS, matching the socket. A manual remote host whose cleartext toggle is off stays on HTTPS, also matching the socket.

## Evidence

API 34 emulator, play debug build, head `8f4143070ae`. The production `ControlUiWebView` loaded a page on the emulator's private LAN address `10.0.2.15`. The discovered endpoint had `tlsEnabled` false and no advertised fingerprint. The manual endpoint used the cleartext toggle.

```console
$ adb -s emulator-5554 shell am instrument -w -r -e class ai.openclaw.app.ui.ControlUiSchemeDeviceTest ai.openclaw.app.debug.test/androidx.test.runner.AndroidJUnitRunner
OK (2 tests)

url=https://10.0.2.15:36997
page=https://10.0.2.15:36997/ wss://10.0.2.15:36997 NATIVE_AUTH

url=http://10.0.2.15:34079
page=http://10.0.2.15:34079/ ws://10.0.2.15:34079 NATIVE_AUTH
```

![Discovered LAN page loaded over HTTPS and installed native auth](https://github.com/SebTardif/openclaw/raw/8f4143070ae6055df10f80e3928f0451d0d38978/apps/android/app/src/androidTest/proof/https-discovered.png)

![Manual LAN cleartext page stayed on HTTP](https://github.com/SebTardif/openclaw/raw/8f4143070ae6055df10f80e3928f0451d0d38978/apps/android/app/src/androidTest/proof/http-manual-lan.png)

## Real behavior proof

- **Behavior or issue addressed:** The Control UI WebView origin follows the socket. A discovered private-LAN host with no gatewayTls advertisement loads HTTPS, and the native auth bridge publishes a wss gateway URL. Manual private-LAN cleartext stays HTTP and publishes a ws URL.
- **Real environment tested:** Android emulator API 34 google_apis arm64, play debug app `ai.openclaw.app.debug`, head `8f4143070ae`. The page host is the emulator guest address 10.0.2.15.
- **Exact steps or command run after this patch:** Installed the play debug apk and ran `adb -s emulator-5554 shell am instrument -w -r -e class ai.openclaw.app.ui.ControlUiSchemeDeviceTest ai.openclaw.app.debug.test/androidx.test.runner.AndroidJUnitRunner`.
- **Evidence after fix:** The WebView document and the screenshots above. Discovered LAN showed `https://10.0.2.15:36997/` plus `wss://10.0.2.15:36997` and `NATIVE_AUTH`. Manual LAN showed `http://10.0.2.15:34079/` plus `ws://10.0.2.15:34079` and `NATIVE_AUTH`.
- **Observed result after fix:** The production WebView loaded the HTTPS page for the discovered case and the HTTP page for manual cleartext. Both documents received the native auth payload for that origin.
- **What was not tested:** A physical phone. This was not a full OpenClaw gateway login. The page is a local document served to the production WebView so the loaded scheme and the installed auth bridge are visible.

## Summary

The page URL is built from the same TLS decision as the gateway socket. No changelog entry.

prs.title: test(ui): trace cached transcript scroll writers
prs.body:
Related: https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/200542

**Diagnostic only — do not merge.** This branch does not fix the transcript jump.

## What Problem This Solves

A cached conversation briefly moves by about 22px while live history refreshes. Geometry captured the jump, but it did not identify the scroll writer. The first writer probe also discarded bundled JavaScript frames, leaving empty stacks.

## User Impact

No intended product change. This temporary test instrumentation identifies the writer in the existing browser scenario.

## Why This Change Was Made

The test retains up to 128 native scrollTop, scrollTo and scrollBy calls and scroll events after the cached reader is ready. Original receivers, arguments, results and exceptions are preserved; cleanup restores the exact native descriptors. Existing geometry fields correlate writes with extent and row placement.

The capped in-page buffer retains Error objects at the original native call site, but formats and filters their stacks only at the final probe read after geometry observation. Error objects are omitted from output. Captured frames accept only allowlisted source paths and strict asset basenames, stripping origins and query strings. Asset frames are then mapped using source maps from the exact active test build. Output contains only allowlisted repository-relative locations and safe symbol names. Missing or invalid maps leave the sanitized asset location and a static status; they cannot replace the geometry failure. Successful tests remain quiet.

## Evidence

- Original broad failure: https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/44127811804/job/134197218887. The extent shrank by 21.609375px before the retained row placement caught up.
- Prior diagnostic head `b9b9572853df92a164acc68589cd6abbaf2b2d86` passed the broad Linux Node cohort: https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/44133703176/job/134218439038 — 106 files, 451 tests, actual shard 6/9 with four workers. This is a nonreproduction, not a fix.
- A bounded local observation using the active build's source maps identified the same correction as `readerAnchor.flush -> scrollBy -> element.scrollTo`. The same 21.609375px extent shrink occurred, but placement landed in the same sampled frame and visible movement stayed at 0.390625px. This identifies a passing-path writer; it does not establish the failing scheduling branch.
- The deferred-stack candidate passes the existing reader/two-rounds/one-appended-pair case: one test passed in 1.109s, five skipped, 14.04s overall. A temporary post-measurement observation still mapped the original caller to `readerAnchor.flush -> scrollBy`; no Error object escaped. This used a qualified owner-input overlay, not a full exact-source Linux run.
- Targeted typed lint, formatting and diff checks pass. In-memory probes cover mapped locations/names, per-asset caching, unchanged inputs, missing build/maps, outside-source filtering, queried frames, deferred stack access, bounded retention, exact exception propagation and descriptor restoration.
- Fresh independent P0–P3 review of the complete candidate found no actionable issues.

The repaired diagnostic head `9259419619f2b5a00863241acca1b92a6e411957` also passed its broad Linux Node cohort: https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/44138758494/job/134236411618 — 106 files and 451 tests in 582.38s, actual shard 6/9 with four workers. The exact reader/two-rounds/one-appended-pair case passed in 4.442s. No failure trace was emitted. This is another nonreproduction; it does not establish that instrumentation has no scheduling effect.

The final deferred-stack head `640725fb39c84bc3522466895b1ff43a8794e193` passed its exact-head broad Linux Node 24.22.1 cohort: https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/44142551879/job/134249877754 — 106 files and 451 tests in 640.89s, actual shard 6/9 with four workers. The exact reader/two-rounds/one-appended-pair case passed in 5.454s. No failure frame or writer payload was emitted. This is another nonreproduction, not a repair.

The natural main recurrence remains unresolved: https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/44136864878/job/134229713064 at `9aed3620` failed the same reader/two-rounds/one-appended-pair case, with scrollTop 6068 → 6046 and the retained row moving before placement caught up. Passing instrumented runs do not invalidate that evidence.

Error allocation and stack capture still occur at the native call; no zero-overhead or causal claim is made. The transient publication ordering remains unresolved. No production fix, timeout increase or assertion weakening is included. Do not merge this branch.

prs.title: fix(gateway): surface the provider failure behind unavailable secret refs
prs.body:
Closes #200175 ## What Problem This Solves Inside a read-only sandbox, any `openclaw` command needing Gateway auth fails with "gateway.auth.token is configured as a secret reference but is unavailable in this command path" plus a Fix line that pushes agents toward credential overrides — while the real failure (`SECRET_PROVIDER_UNAVAILABLE`, the store's cleanup write) is discarded. The provider failure is now preserved as the error's cause and printed on its own line, so agents and operators see that escalation, not new credentials, is the remedy. - Problem: `resolveConfiguredGatewaySecretInput` converts every non-redacted provider error into `GatewaySecretRefUnavailableError(path)`, losing the provider code and cause. - Solution: construct the unavailable error with the underlying resolution error as `cause` and a config-derived `Provider error: (source , provider

)` line; a provider failure now replaces the credential-override advice with provider-recovery guidance. - What changed: `src/gateway/credentials.ts` (optional `cause`/`providerDiagnostic` on the error class, provider-recovery Fix line) and `src/gateway/credentials-secret-inputs.ts` (the conversion site) plus a regression test. - What did NOT change: the redacted-value rethrow, precedence/scan behavior, the engine-selection conversion (which has no underlying provider error), and every consumer of `isGatewaySecretRefUnavailableError`. ## Why This Change Was Made The generic message assumes the ref was merely unresolved, but when resolution ran and the provider failed, the truth is a provider condition — the same conclusion #196160 reached for this function. - Best fix: yes — the provider detail is composed at the secret-inputs layer, so the core error class stays free of secrets-module dependencies. - Alternative: a dedicated error type was rejected; callers already branch on `isGatewaySecretRefUnavailableError` and the code stays stable. - Risk / non-goals: message matching that assumes the exact three-line shape would see an extra line; the guard helpers match on class and `path`, not the message. ## User Impact An agent working inside a sandbox with a store-backed Gateway token reads `Provider error: SECRET_PROVIDER_UNAVAILABLE: ...` in the failure and asks for sandbox escalation (as the issue reporter's agent did once told the truth), instead of trying to set tokens the sandbox cannot store. ## Evidence Focused regression driving the shipped `resolveGatewayCredentialsWithSecretInputs` with a store-backed token whose provider fails: ```text ✓ credentials-secret-inputs.test.ts > resolveGatewayCredentialsWithSecretInputs store refs > keeps the provider failure as the cause of an unavailable store-backed token ``` The test asserts the thrown `GatewaySecretRefUnavailableError.cause` is the provider's `SecretProviderResolutionError`, the message contains the config-derived provider line, and the credential-override advice is replaced by provider recovery. Shipped-path runtime proof — a real exec secret provider failing (exit 1), no mocks, through the shipped resolver: ```text name: GatewaySecretRefUnavailableError message: gateway.auth.token is configured as a secret reference but is unavailable in this command path. Provider error: SECRET_PROVIDER_UNAVAILABLE (source exec, provider default) Fix: restore access to the secret provider and retry; the configured credential itself needs no change. cause: SecretProviderResolutionError code=SECRET_PROVIDER_UNAVAILABLE ``` Per review, the provider diagnostic now carries only the code, source, and provider identity (never the provider's message, which can quote payload-derived text such as a malformed secret file's parse diagnostic), and a provider failure swaps the Fix line for provider recovery guidance. What was not tested: a live read-only sandbox (Codex bubblewrap); the regression reproduces the provider failure at the same resolution boundary the sandbox failure reaches. ## AI Assistance This PR is AI-assisted. Used `git grep` on `GatewaySecretRefUnavailableError` construction sites and `onResolveRefError` to locate the cause-dropping conversion, implemented the optional diagnostic at the secret-inputs layer, and validated with `vitest`. The implementer understands the code: redacted values rethrow, all other provider failures funneled through one conversion that now preserves the cause. All evidence above is from real local runtime execution.

prs.title: fix: stop the candidate Doctor from refusing updates over reordered plugin migration obligations
prs.body:
Related: #200606

## What Problem This Solves

Updating from 2026.11.3 to 2026.11.5 can stop in the candidate Doctor with "Plugin migration obligations changed during migration input publication", even though nothing changed: both plugin lists are identical and `changed=[]`. The update is refused before activation, and there is no step the user can take to get past it.

## User Impact

User impact: candidate Doctor no longer refuses a config repair just because it found a new unfinished plugin migration whose plugin ID sorts before one it was already tracking. When a real conflict does happen, the message now names the obligations that were added or removed and the protected fields that changed.

## Why This Change Was Made

Doctor keeps the obligations it already knew about first and appends new ones. Config publication then compares that list with the stored rows, which are read back in plugin-ID order, and the comparison was order-sensitive. So when a new obligation's ID sorted before a retained one (for example `alpha` found after `zeta` was retained), the same set of obligations looked "changed" and publication was refused. Obligations are one record per plugin, so the comparison now treats them as a set keyed by plugin ID. Real field, membership and duplicate changes still refuse.

The diagnostic no longer reports reason/command rewording, which never refuses publication. It also now reports `<id>:added` and `<id>:removed`, so a membership change hidden by the four-ID summary is visible.

## Evidence

- **Real Doctor flow (red/green):** `runDoctorConfigPreflight` with a retained obligation for `zeta-owner`, a newly unavailable `alpha-owner`, and a legacy config key Doctor rewrites. On base `9122a49bd8a` it fails with exactly the reported shape (`expected=[alpha-owner, zeta-owner], current=[alpha-owner, zeta-owner]`). With the fix it publishes the repaired config and keeps both owners' protected settings.
- **Comparator contract:** reordered identical obligations publish, a changed protected field still refuses, and the diagnostic names added and removed IDs. These are red on base and green on the fix.
- **Sibling suites:** deferred-migration, config IO, and Doctor plugin persistence/verification/inventory suites pass 77/77, and `pnpm tsgo:core` is clean.
- **Reviews:** autoreview is scoped-clean (P2) and an independent Codex review found nothing.
- **Live updates on Crabbox AWS Linux (real npm installs).** Setup: the installed version had recorded an unfinished migration for `zeta-fixture`, `alpha-fixture` is first seen by the candidate Doctor, and a disabled heartbeat makes the candidate Doctor write config. Both base runs fail with the reporter's exact text; both fix runs succeed.

| From | To | Result |
|---|---|---|
| 2026.11.4 | base main `9122a49bd8a` | `candidate-doctor` failed: `expected=[alpha-fixture, zeta-fixture], current=[alpha-fixture, zeta-fixture], changed=[]` |
| 2026.11.3 | base main | Same failure |
| 2026.11.4 | this fix | Succeeded in 277 s, readyz 200, heartbeat still disabled |
| 2026.11.3 | this fix | Succeeded in 274 s, readyz 200 |

Production change: +18/-4 (net +14) across `src/infra/deferred-plugin-migrations.contract.ts` and `src/infra/deferred-plugin-migrations.ts`.

prs.title: fix: prevent queued agent failures after the sending turn ends
prs.body:
Root cause: src/gateway/server-plugin-in-process-dispatch.ts:187 hands an accepted in-process `agent` turn off outside the caller's operator authority and transcript writer, but leaves the sending tool's Gateway caller identity in place. The recipient's required preflight compaction later captures that identity while building its tools, and fails with `agent tool caller authority is no longer active` once the sending turn has ended.

Fixes #158070

## What Problem This Solves

When one agent sends a message to another session with `sessions_send` and does not wait for the reply, the message can be lost. If the receiving session is busy or close to its context limit, it has to compact before it can run the queued message, and by then the sender's turn is usually over. The compaction then fails with `Preflight compaction required but failed: agent tool caller authority is no longer active`, and the message has to be resent by hand.

## User Impact

Fire-and-forget messages between sessions are delivered even when the receiving session needs to compact first.

## Why This Change Was Made

The handoff that starts the receiving turn already drops the sender's operator authority and transcript writer, so the new turn runs under its own admitted authority. It still carried the sender's tool caller identity, and compaction picked that up. The handoff now drops that identity too. Admission still checks the sender: a sender whose authority is gone is refused before the turn is accepted.

## Evidence

Real Gateway with real agents and a deterministic local OpenAI Responses fixture. Session B is busy on a slow turn that reports near-window usage; session A sends to B with `timeoutSeconds: 0` and finishes; B's queued turn needs token preflight compaction.

- main `9122a49bd8a1`, two runs: `preflight compaction failed: agent tool caller authority is no longer active`; the queued message never reaches the model.
- Control on main with `timeoutSeconds: 120` (the sender's turn stays alive): the same compaction succeeds and the message reaches the model, so the failure follows the sender's lifetime.
- This branch, from source and from the full Node build: compaction succeeds and the queued message reaches the model, no authority error.
- `server-plugin-in-process-dispatch.caller-lifetime.test.ts` fails on main for both the host-close and admission-close cases and passes here.
- The same error appears in production logs on a 2026.11.4 Gateway (19 lines in the last 14 days).

Observed lines: https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/177296#issuecomment-6955230238. The author's earlier allowed and revoked authority runs are in the comments above.

Fix and regression test by @johan-eilertsen. Reported by @Angelojiang11, with further traces from @LachieFREEDOM, @nosugarx, @SamuelThornburg, @roboclaw-bot and @jaxonparrott.

Merge danger: two-way door. A revert restores the old behavior; no state, config or contract changes. Blast radius: in-process `agent` launches (`sessions_send`, plugin agent launches).

prs.title: fix(memory-core): bound the forget fts row count by a single sqlite set
prs.body:
Closes #200276

## What Problem This Solves

A single retained session with many indexed chunks made the read-only `openclaw memory forget --dry-run` planning step die with `too many SQL variables` before any deletion report could be produced. The planner now counts the same rows with one bound parameter, so the report succeeds no matter how many chunks the session has.

- Problem: the fts row-count preview built one SQLite placeholder per selected chunk id (`WHERE id IN (?, ?, ...)`), which breaks preparation once the count passes the runtime's `SQLITE_LIMIT_VARIABLE_NUMBER`.
- Solution: expand the id set through the existing `sqliteStringSet` helper (single `json_each` bind), exactly like the vec0 count right below it already does.
- What changed: `extensions/memory-core/src/memory-forget-index-read.ts` (fts preview count and native vec0 preview count) and `extensions/memory-core/src/memory-forget-kernel.ts` (`forget.purge` chunk and vector deletes) plus regressions.
- What did NOT change: selection semantics, dry-run read-only behavior, postgres paths, tombstone/purge transaction ordering, and the delete-path guards.

## Why This Change Was Made

The unbounded `IN` list was the only remaining per-id parameterization in the forget planner; the vec0 count already uses `sqliteStringSet`, so the fts count now matches its sibling instead of introducing chunked batching.

- Best fix: yes — reuses the shipped single-bind helper rather than adding a new batching mechanism.
- Alternative: batching the count across slices (as `deleteMemoryIndexSources` does) was considered, but it needs summation across queries; the set expansion is one query and one snapshot.
- Risk / non-goals: no behavior change under the bind limit; `chunkIds` is still fully enumerated in JS (unchanged scope, per the issue).

## User Impact

`memory forget --dry-run --json` produces its preview for sessions with very large indexed chunk counts instead of failing with `too many SQL variables`; real deletions and everything else are untouched.

## Evidence

Focused regressions (same harness as the neighboring planner tests, 34,000 chunks for one selected session):

```text
✓ memory-forget.sources.test.ts > counts fts and vector rows past the sqlite bind-variable limit for one selected session
    plan.chunks = 34000, plan.ftsRows = 34000, plan.vectorRows = 34000
✓ memory-forget.sources.test.ts > applies a forget past the sqlite bind-variable limit without stranding chunks
    preview artifacts.indexChunks = 34000; apply leaves memory_index_chunks = 0 rows and memory_index_chunks_vec = 0 rows
```

Red checks on base (fix files reverted): the preview test fails with `too many SQL variables`, and the apply test fails after the tombstone commits — the exact stranded-tombstone failure the purge fix removes. The vec0 count and purge deletes now use the same single-bind helper as their fts/sibling kernels.

## AI Assistance

This PR is AI-assisted. Used `git grep` and the existing `sqliteStringSet` call sites to locate the root cause, and per review bounded the vector preview count and the purge deletes in `memory-forget-kernel.ts` as well. The implementer understands the code: every SQLite statement that expands the selected chunk ids into per-id parameters sits on the same oversized-selection path. All evidence above is from real local runtime execution.

prs.title: refactor(workboard): drop the unused claim and observation records
prs.body:
Closes #198705

## What Problem This Solves

Workboard cards carry optional worker claims passed to `workboard_complete` and session-lifecycle observations from #197471. Proof and run attempts already cover the worker report and run outcome. Verification logic also reads claims for claim-linked checks and self-check attribution; this PR intentionally removes those readers with the claim records. #197471 is on main and not in any tag or release.

## User Impact

`workboard_complete` no longer takes a `claims` parameter, and lifecycle sync no longer writes observations. `workboard_verify` works as before: a checker records what it checked, its outcome, and the proof, artifact, or run attempt it covered. Completion, proof statuses, and dependency scheduling are unchanged.

## Why This Change Was Made

Proof already holds the worker's report and run attempts already hold each run's outcome, so the two extra records repeated them while costing a tool parameter every worker run sees, an observation write at the end of every linked run, and per-kind retention inside the card's metadata budget.

- Verifications are stored as `metadata.automation.verifications`, without a `kind` field now that there is one record type. Generic metadata writes still cannot add, edit, or remove them.
- A card keeps its 4 newest verifications, only in room its other records leave, dropping the oldest first; `workboard_verify` returns an error when a new one cannot fit. The separate 6 KiB evidence cap is gone.

### Cards written on main since #197471

Those cards store claims, observations, and verifications together under `metadata.automation.evidence`. The next update to such a card converts it before any trimming runs, with or without a metadata patch (a manual move, lifecycle settlement, a comment, a new verification):

- checker verifications move to `metadata.automation.verifications`, newest 4, without their `kind` and `claimId` fields;
- claims and observations are dropped;
- the `evidence` key is removed, so it never takes room from proof, attempts, comments, or artifacts.

Until a card's next write, reads still return its stored `evidence` list unchanged. No Doctor migration: the old shape only exists on main builds, and nothing shipped with it.

About 165 production lines removed net.

## Evidence

Public retained evidence for `62c6373c5b467446938e95ee6a29bcb493420985`: [artifact index](https://github.com/daniel-lxs/screenshots/blob/dc47f92f37caeb75dc73439598c0d3549203723c/evidence/2026/11/pr-198706-62c6373-df906ec9-e8b0-44ed-82b2-e0b057d938e5/README.md), [redacted terminal output](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/daniel-lxs/screenshots/dc47f92f37caeb75dc73439598c0d3549203723c/evidence/2026/11/pr-198706-62c6373-df906ec9-e8b0-44ed-82b2-e0b057d938e5/terminal-output.txt), and [stored-data comparison](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/daniel-lxs/screenshots/dc47f92f37caeb75dc73439598c0d3549203723c/evidence/2026/11/pr-198706-62c6373-df906ec9-e8b0-44ed-82b2-e0b057d938e5/stored-data-comparison.json). The files include complete redacted Gateway logs, install/build output, harness sources, and Gateway-returned card snapshots from the same VM run.

- Completion/lifecycle: [settled card](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/daniel-lxs/screenshots/dc47f92f37caeb75dc73439598c0d3549203723c/evidence/2026/11/pr-198706-62c6373-df906ec9-e8b0-44ed-82b2-e0b057d938e5/snapshots/fresh-lifecycle.json) → [completed card](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/daniel-lxs/screenshots/dc47f92f37caeb75dc73439598c0d3549203723c/evidence/2026/11/pr-198706-62c6373-df906ec9-e8b0-44ed-82b2-e0b057d938e5/snapshots/fresh-completed.json).
- Verification persistence: [later write / before restart](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/daniel-lxs/screenshots/dc47f92f37caeb75dc73439598c0d3549203723c/evidence/2026/11/pr-198706-62c6373-df906ec9-e8b0-44ed-82b2-e0b057d938e5/snapshots/fresh-verified-after-write.json) → [after restart](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/daniel-lxs/screenshots/dc47f92f37caeb75dc73439598c0d3549203723c/evidence/2026/11/pr-198706-62c6373-df906ec9-e8b0-44ed-82b2-e0b057d938e5/snapshots/fresh-after-restart.json).
- Stable-upgrade stored data: [stable before](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/daniel-lxs/screenshots/dc47f92f37caeb75dc73439598c0d3549203723c/evidence/2026/11/pr-198706-62c6373-df906ec9-e8b0-44ed-82b2-e0b057d938e5/snapshots/stable-before-upgrade.json) → [PR after](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/daniel-lxs/screenshots/dc47f92f37caeb75dc73439598c0d3549203723c/evidence/2026/11/pr-198706-62c6373-df906ec9-e8b0-44ed-82b2-e0b057d938e5/snapshots/upgrade-verified-after-write.json) → [after restart](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/daniel-lxs/screenshots/dc47f92f37caeb75dc73439598c0d3549203723c/evidence/2026/11/pr-198706-62c6373-df906ec9-e8b0-44ed-82b2-e0b057d938e5/snapshots/upgrade-after-restart.json). Existing attempts, proof, and artifacts are identical; the PR snapshot includes a new verdict and comment.
- Main-format stored data: [before first write](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/daniel-lxs/screenshots/dc47f92f37caeb75dc73439598c0d3549203723c/evidence/2026/11/pr-198706-62c6373-df906ec9-e8b0-44ed-82b2-e0b057d938e5/snapshots/legacy-read-before-write.json) → [first-write conversion](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/daniel-lxs/screenshots/dc47f92f37caeb75dc73439598c0d3549203723c/evidence/2026/11/pr-198706-62c6373-df906ec9-e8b0-44ed-82b2-e0b057d938e5/snapshots/legacy-first-write.json) → [after restart](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/daniel-lxs/screenshots/dc47f92f37caeb75dc73439598c0d3549203723c/evidence/2026/11/pr-198706-62c6373-df906ec9-e8b0-44ed-82b2-e0b057d938e5/snapshots/legacy-after-restart.json). The same attempt is settled, the checker verdict is retained without `kind`/`claimId`, and all twelve artifacts remain unchanged.

- `extensions/workboard/src/store-verification.test.ts`:
  - New regression, starting from a main-format card (claim, observation, and verification under `automation.evidence`) seeded through the SQLite store: a manual move to `done` on a nearly full card keeps the settled attempt and all twelve artifacts, carries the verdict into `verifications`, and removes `evidence`; a `{}` metadata patch carries the verdict too. It fails on e395c89b1d1 (the move evicts an artifact to keep the old evidence) and passes on this head.
  - Existing test: a forged verification in raw metadata is stripped on create; a verification too large for a nearly full card is refused; an accepted one survives a later comment, a lifecycle-settled run, and a manual move to `done`; a checker that is the card's own agent gets `checkedOwnWork: true`.
- Targeted Workboard suites: 183 tests passed across six files (`store-verification`, `store`, `store.attempts`, `tools`, `lifecycle-sync`, `gateway`). The rest of the Workboard suite was not run locally.
- Extension and extension-test typecheck, lint, formatting, and the line-cap ratchet: clean.
- Live Gateway proof at `62c6373c5b467446938e95ee6a29bcb493420985`: passed in one private macOS VM, using the repository mock provider and synthetic credentials. A real agent turn settled a linked card to review with a succeeded attempt; `workboard_complete` completed it without claims or observations. A different checker recorded `workboard_verify`; the exact verdict, attempts, proof, and artifacts survived a later comment and Gateway restart.
- Fresh source install/build passed. Published stable `2026.11.3` created and completed a card through the running Gateway; reopening the same state on the PR build preserved attempts, proof, and artifacts. Verification, later-write/restart survival, and a new agent turn/completion passed after upgrade.
- Main-format compatibility: seeded the isolated SQLite store with records constructed by main's production evidence builders (claim, observation, verification). Reads retained `automation.evidence`; the first manual move converted it, preserved the exact checker verdict, settled the existing attempt, and kept all 12 artifacts. An empty metadata patch and Gateway restart preserved the result.
- Scope: real Gateway, SQLite, repo mock inference, WebSocket RPC and HTTP tool invocation. Real inference providers, external channels, UI, PostgreSQL, and the updater command were not exercised. Broad CI and the Workboard owner's product decision remain merge gates.

prs.title: fix(config): stat each agent database preflight side once per row
prs.body:
Closes #200267

## What Problem This Solves

Gateway boot with many agents re-stat every candidate database row against every configured target before the gateway is ready — measured by the reporter as 8.8M main-thread file calls at ~470 agents. The preflight check now answers exact configured claims with a path compare and stats each side once per row, removing the quadratic file-call storm.

- Problem: `isConfiguredAgentDatabaseTarget` runs one `targets.some(...)` whose alias branch calls `fs.statSync` on the target and on the row for every non-matching owned target, and the boot preflight calls it once per row.
- Solution: check exact matches first (no filesystem probes), then walk targets with the row's existence stat hoisted out of the loop (missing rows stop at the first existing target).
- What changed: `src/config/sessions/targets.ts` (function body only — signature and callers untouched) plus focused regression tests.
- What did NOT change: ownership rules, alias detection via `isSameOpenClawAgentDatabasePath`, and the second quadratic (fresh-state missing-suffix probes) noted in the issue.

## Why This Change Was Made

The fix follows the reporter's suggested shape and keeps the loop: rows still string-compare against every target, so only the repeated file calls are removed, not the scan.

- Best fix: yes for this layer — a per-preflight matcher index (the issue's "further step") is a larger change left out.
- Alternative: caching stat results across rows was rejected because the function has no lifecycle to invalidate it.
- Risk / non-goals: a stat or realpath error the stock loop hit on an earlier target is no longer hit when an exact match answers first; the reporter verified equivalence over 4,000 randomized rows (missing files, symlinks, hard links, symlink loop, ENOTDIR).

## User Impact

Gateway startup on states with many agents stops spending tens of seconds of main-thread file probing in the database readiness phase; the `ready` line arrives sooner with no behavioral change to admission answers.

## Evidence

Synthetic 400-row x 400-agentless-target sweep (the boot admission shape: candidate rows against every earlier candidate path), old vs new shape, `fs.statSync` instrumented with a real `node:sqlite`-free runtime script:

```text
rows=400 targets=400
OLD: stat calls=320000  pathname stats=160000  ms=570.1  hits=0
NEW: stat calls=800  pathname stats=400  ms=6.9  hits=0
AGREE: same answers
```

Focused regressions in `src/config/sessions/targets.test.ts`, each failing on base: an exact claim behind an existing compatible target answers with zero `statSync` calls; a missing row stats the pathname exactly once across 40 owned targets (base re-stats it 40 times); symlink aliases still resolve; an unusable (NUL-byte) earlier target no longer fails an exact claim.

```text
✓ src/config/sessions/targets.test.ts > isConfiguredAgentDatabaseTarget > answers an exact configured claim without filesystem probes
✓ src/config/sessions/targets.test.ts > isConfiguredAgentDatabaseTarget > stats a missing candidate row once instead of once per owned target
```

## AI Assistance

This PR is AI-assisted. Used `git grep` on the preflight call sites and the reporter's suggested shape to rework `isConfiguredAgentDatabaseTarget` in `targets.ts`, with `vitest` and a standalone `node` instrumentation script for validation. The implementer understands the code: exact claims short-circuit before any stat and the row's existence check is hoisted out of the target walk. prs.body:
<!--
Required PR title: type: user-facing description.
Keep Allow edits from maintainers enabled so maintainers can help update the branch.
-->

## What Problem This Solves

Personal skill imports require manual downloads and uploads even when a skill and its companion files already have an HTTPS source.

## User Impact

Import an HTTPS `SKILL.md` or archive bundle through **Plugins → Skills → My skills → Import skill**. Recognized GitHub, GitLab, and Gitea/Forgejo folder-link shapes are normalized without a browser hostname allowlist. Companion files, nested relative paths, and binary files use the existing bundle representation. File, folder, ZIP, and ClawHub imports remain available.

Operators can permit private-network downloads with `skills.library.import.allowedOrigins`: exact HTTPS scheme/host/port entries, absent or empty by default. Grants apply to everyone already authorized to import. An explicitly approved loopback-literal origin retains the shared guard's exception; metadata/link-local destinations and unrelated private origins remain protected. This grants network access, not repository authentication: the Gateway still needs corporate DNS/VPN and TLS trust, and browser login cookies or publishing credentials are not forwarded.

Repository archives must fit the existing download/extraction limits before directory selection, so a small skill inside a large repository can fail. Use a smaller direct bundle URL and selected directory in that case. Unknown forge webpages need the explicit archive fallback; ambiguous refs can use the ref/directory overrides.

## Why This Change Was Made

The replacement is a source adapter into the existing guarded HTTP, safe extraction, canonical bundle, scanning, install-policy, and personal-save owners—not a separate installer. The same import RPC gains a closed URL source alternative. Remote files/archives retain truthful third-party, mutable, network source facts rather than being classified as user-authored local files. Current write authority and private-origin grants are checked across awaited work.

The GitHub-only repository importer, chooser, and superseded policy/test plumbing are retired. There is no Git clone/sparse-checkout system, browser host-list expansion, or fetched-script execution. Canonical validator regeneration causes large numbering changes, but independent normalization isolated the semantic change to the import-parameter predicate.

## Evidence

**The complete candidate authority case passed in real CI. The required stable-upgrade case is still blocked; overall CI is partial/failed—not merge-ready.**

The [exact-head run 42318674850](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/42318674850) tested head `4d595fe1b42a39c095203072d3a775432ebe7260`, tree `f7f608e7747663469ee5e76ac611b100e23b908a`; expected, observed and build commits match. Its ZIP SHA-256 was verified as `13cb6b7dc0a3f54923d4c920416a9aa373d9044cf855eb34414094ee86735e62`.

Actual report: `status: partial`, `authorityStatus: passed`, `upgradeStatus: failed`. All nine authority assertions passed:
- Owned HTTPS source and alternate-host reachability.
- Strict private-network default and read-only access reject before any source request.
- Browser → authenticated Gateway → HTTPS → real policy/extraction → SQLite publication, with correct personal ownership and exact nested/text/binary/executable companion bytes.
- Exact-origin and redirect boundaries issue no next request to an ungranted target.
- Real install-policy denial creates no publication.
- Live role revocation during a held redirect: one initial request, zero next requests, no publication.
- Live role revocation during held publication: committed role change causes the exact canonical post-HELLO connection retirement; settled staging/immutable artifact and library-entry counts remain unchanged. Reconnection through the same profile, requesting the original full scopes, receives a genuine correlated server rejection for a fresh import and makes zero outbound requests. A generic close is not counted as an RPC denial.
- Live origin-grant revocation: effective config version changes while the same authenticated connection stays alive; the held request cannot follow the redirect or publish. One initial request, zero next requests; `connectionStable: true`.

The independent enabled watchOS/direct-node TLS consumer also passed both tests on this head. The proof file ran both required cases: candidate authority passed; stable preparation failed. No skip or continue-on-error masks the failure.

**Remaining required proof:** latest-stable settings/skills/two-revision upgrade survival has not run. The November 7 CI attempt was blocked for exact root `openclaw@2026.11.1` under the checked-in seven-day npm cooldown. At the November 17 policy recheck, official npm `latest` was **`openclaw@2026.11.5`**, published **November 17 at 09:59:33.472 UTC**, so the required current-latest baseline is withheld until **November 24 at 09:59:33.472 UTC**. No age-policy exception, older-version substitution, direct-dist fallback or transitive cooldown change was applied. The same policy-respecting completion check is retained for November 24 after eligibility.

The isolated workflow uses pinned exact-head checkout, normal build, real Gateway/HTTPS/policy/SQLite owners and read-only repository permissions. No live Team policy, credentials, services or deployment changed. Both components remain required; the partial result does not turn the overall gate green. The branch also currently has conflicts with main.

The prior importer-owner and UI tests, focused type/lint/format checks and fresh independent source reviews remain supporting evidence, not substitutes for the failed real-runtime checks. The newly added diagnostic/privacy and report-completion contracts have been exercised. Scoped proof tests have their own allocation; the shared test scalar was not raised.

prs.title: fix(ui): clarify usage rates include idle session time
prs.body:
Related: #200627

## What Problem This Solves

The Usage rate tile presents elapsed session spans as active time and can show unpriced usage as free. Selecting individual days also narrows the usage total while retaining each matching session's span across the report range.

## User Impact

The card identifies rates as usage per session-minute and explains the effects of idle time, overlapping sessions, selected days, zero-duration usage, and missing price data. Usage with no known cost is shown as Unpriced instead of $0.00; a genuinely free known-cost rate remains $0.00.

## Why This Change Was Made

The current rate denominator is a sum of elapsed session spans. The tooltip now describes that behavior, including that selecting days can change which sessions match while each matching session retains its full span within the report range. This change does not claim that day-filtered rates use a day-filtered duration or implement an active-time metric. Sampled latency does not necessarily cover the same messages as token and cost totals, so switching to daily latency still needs an owner decision.

## Evidence

- Production-bundle Control UI E2E: five scenarios passed with synthetic data and a mock Gateway, covering desktop, 390px mobile, zh-CN fallback, selected-day behavior and unpriced usage. prs.title: fix(a2a): settle steered tasks with the consuming run's outcome
prs.body:
Closes #200646

## What Problem This Solves

With `messages.queue.mode: "steer"`, an A2A `SendMessage` that arrives while a turn is already running gets its own task id, but nothing ever settles it — a peer polling `GetTask` sees `TASK_STATE_WORKING` forever while the run that consumed the message answers on the host task. Steered tasks now settle with the consuming run's terminal outcome, the same signal `chat.send` uses.

- Problem: `extensions/a2a/src/inbound.ts` has a settlement path for followup tasks (queued reply batches, #183803) but none for the `deferredToActiveRun: "steer"` branch; a steered message's dispatch never receives a final reply, so `store.complete`/`store.fail` never run for it.
- Solution: settle the steered task from the consuming run's terminal outcome (completed with the store's status message, failed with the run failure) — the same signal `chat.send` uses.
- What changed: `extensions/a2a/src/inbound.ts` plus two `inbound.test.ts` cases.
- What did NOT change: followup settlement, the non-deferred completion path, the task store, and core reply-runtime observers.

## Why This Change Was Made

The run's terminal outcome is the only settlement signal a steered dispatch will ever receive: `collectRuntimeMetadata` fans every adopted item's `onAgentRunTerminalOutcome` observer into the consuming run, so the extension can settle without new core hooks.

- Status: the review correctly identified that accepted steering does not yet deliver the terminal callback — `runActiveReplySteer` consumes the parked source without transferring its run observers, so the new settlement branch is reachable only when the consuming run does report the outcome. Threading terminal custody through the steering owner is a core reply-runtime change (observer registry on the live reply operation vs. injection-option passthrough); this PR holds the extension-side settlement and the acceptance bar while that seam gets implemented.
- Alternative: mirroring the host task's artifact text would require cross-task plumbing the extension cannot see (the steered dispatch never receives the final payload).
- Risk / non-goals: no behavior change on the followup and non-deferred paths; the completion is a no-op behind the store's terminal guard.

## User Impact

A2A peers that poll `GetTask` until a terminal state get `TASK_STATE_COMPLETED` (with a status message naming the run's outcome) or `TASK_STATE_FAILED` when the run fails, instead of waiting forever; the task store no longer accumulates permanent `WORKING` rows.

## Evidence

Focused regression driving the shipped `dispatchA2aInbound` against the real `A2aTaskStore`, with the dispatch result reporting `deferredToActiveRun: "steer"` and the run settling after dispatch resolves (as it does live):

```text
✓ inbound.test.ts > A2A channel inbound dispatch > settles a steered task when the consuming run completes
✓ inbound.test.ts > A2A channel inbound dispatch > settles a steered task when the consuming run fails
```

Before the fix the first case leaves the task in `TASK_STATE_WORKING` with no artifacts (the observed 2h44m probe in the issue); after it the task is `TASK_STATE_COMPLETED` with the store's status message and empty artifacts. The failure case keeps the existing `Agent run failed` status.

What was not tested: `collect` queue mode and the live JSON-RPC peer transport; the settlement logic is transport-independent.

## AI Assistance

This PR is AI-assisted. Used `git grep` across `deferredToActiveRun` and the reply-runtime observer wiring to confirm the steered observer fires, then implemented the settlement in `inbound.ts` and validated with `vitest`. The implementer understands the code: `collectRuntimeMetadata` fans adopted items' terminal observers into the consuming run, and the store's terminal guard makes double settlement a no-op. All evidence above is from real local runtime execution.

prs.title: fix(state): Gateway startup defers healthy agents behind two slow schema readers
prs.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Gateway startup can defer almost every agent when two agent databases need a slow schema reader, even when every other store has a valid clean-close seal and could be admitted right away.

## User Impact

On a fleet where one or two agent stores are slow to inspect, only those stores are deferred at startup. The other sealed agents are admitted before the listener binds, instead of waiting for background preparation. The reported Gateway deferred 465 of 470 sealed agents. Startup still never runs more than two schema reader processes, and private fallback snapshots stay inside the same two-copy cap. A store that cannot be deferred still holds the foreground, as before.

## Why This Change Was Made

#195291 orders clean-closed stores first, which fixes the case where unsealed stores sit at the head of the list. On a boot where every store is sealed, that order changes nothing. Two slow readers can still fill both inspection slots past the 5 second startup wait, and the timer then defers every index that has not finished. The startup list also holds each agent database more than once (configured, agent, and persistent registered paths), so later copies of agents that were already inspected were deferred again.

Startup inspection was bounded to two concurrent readers so a large agent fleet does not multiply child processes. That same change, commit 63e7363c / #139878, accepted at most two private fallback snapshots, because each one is a temporary disk copy. Releasing a startup slot when a reader is slow lets sealed stores admit from the in-process cache, while snapshot preparation and cleanup stay inside the two-slot cap until each copy is removed. A third snapshot waits.

This change does four things:

- When the startup wait ends, a slot that is busy on a slow reader is released while that reader keeps running in the background. Its store is deferred as before.
- A store whose clean-close cache is valid is read without waiting on the busy reader process. A store that still needs a reader waits for the existing process instead of starting a third one.
- Later copies of a database already claimed by real path and agent id are skipped before dispatch, so the first copy keeps its place and its result.
- Fallback snapshot preparation and cleanup stay inside those two slots. A third store waits until a copy is removed.

Admission checks, `canDefer`, config, and public types are unchanged.

## Evidence

Shipped Gateway entry point (`openclaw gateway run`). Isolated Linux machine with Node 24.22.1. The fleet was 41 agents created with `openclaw agents add`, all with a valid clean-close seal, plus the default duplicate startup list (the baseline agent `main` cannot be deleted, so the fleet is 41 rather than 40). The two first-sorted stores, `aa-slow-1` and `aa-slow-2`, were made to miss the in-process cache by editing their sealed metadata version. Each build was started three times from the same fleet.

Compared SHAs:

- main: `c1cf9390ac356d96815dde3f6e10903602b149bd`
- this head: `6f31ca28fa29229ed2cb6d6d95cca4145d264e63`

On this machine's SSD, even a 2 GiB store finished schema inspection in about one second, so the 5 second startup wait did not expire. For these measured starts, a test-only 6 second delay was added at the start of the built schema-inspection worker's request handler, identically on both builds, to stand in for slow disk reads. That delay is not product code and was not committed.

| Build | Deferred agents (runs 1 / 2 / 3) | Who was deferred | `schemaProcessCount` | Readiness | `GET /healthz` |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| main | 41 / 41 / 41 | every agent, including a-fast and main | 2 / 2 / 2 | 11477 / 11309 / 11479 ms | 200 `{"ok":true,"status":"live"}` |
| this change | 2 / 2 / 2 | only the two slow stores | 2 / 2 / 2 | 11619 / 11561 / 11618 ms | 200 `{"ok":true,"status":"live"}` |

Readiness took about 11.5 seconds on every run because the slow readers were still in flight (`schemaInspectionCount=0` at the readiness line). The Gateway became ready, nothing wedged, and it served `/healthz` on loopback after bind.

Main run 1, readiness and a sample of the 41 deferral lines:

```text
[gateway] startup phase: cli.bootstrap.admission.database-readiness 11476.9ms ... agentCount=41 schemaProcessCount=2 schemaInspectionCount=0 schemaSnapshotCount=0 ...
[state/agent-admission] Agent aa-slow-1 has not completed startup inspection and preparation. Inspection and writable admission continue after the Gateway listener binds.
[state/agent-admission] Agent aa-slow-2 has not completed startup inspection and preparation. Inspection and writable admission continue after the Gateway listener binds.
[state/agent-admission] Agent agent-01 has not completed startup inspection and preparation. Inspection and writable admission continue after the Gateway listener binds.
... 38 more identical deferral lines, including a-fast and main (41 total)
```

This head, run 1, readiness and the complete deferral set:

```text
[gateway] startup phase: cli.bootstrap.admission.database-readiness 11618.6ms ... agentCount=41 schemaProcessCount=2 schemaInspectionCount=0 schemaSnapshotCount=0 ...
[state/agent-admission] Agent aa-slow-1 has not completed startup inspection and preparation. Inspection and writable admission continue after the Gateway listener binds.
[state/agent-admission] Agent aa-slow-2 has not completed startup inspection and preparation. Inspection and writable admission continue after the Gateway listener binds.
```

The live fleet produced no fallback snapshots (`schemaSnapshotCount=0` on every official start, and no snapshot staging files during startup). The two-copy snapshot cap is therefore covered by the new lifecycle regression test, `keeps fallback snapshot preparation and cleanup within two slots after startup release`, and not by the live run.

Other regression tests that fail on main:

- `defers only slow stores when later targets repeat an already inspected agent`: targets `[a, slow1, slow2, b, a2, b2]`. Main defers `slow1, slow2, b, a2, b2`; with this change, only `slow1, slow2`.
- `reads a clean-close cache while a schema reader child is still busy`: on main the second read throws `Agent schema inspection worker is busy`. With this change, it returns the cached inspection while the child is still running.

These also passed: the scheduler, schema-inspection worker, preflight, lifecycle, prestart, and startup tests, plus `pnpm tsgo:core`, oxlint, and oxfmt on the touched files. The new test lines are covered by an allocation under `config/test-lines-allocations/`.

Closes #195269

prs.title: chore(ci): diagnose committed mention timeout phases
prs.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Diagnostic only — do not merge. The hourly main run timed out while testing a committed human mention, but its log does not identify which request or lifecycle phase stopped progressing.

## User Impact

No user-visible behavior change. This temporary test instrumentation is intended to identify the failing phase on a matching hosted run.

## Why This Change Was Made

Record up to 24 fixed phase labels with elapsed milliseconds, plus title-request and agent-request counts. Emit one bounded record on failure or test abort, including when a suspended request prevents normal cleanup from unwinding. No request content, identifiers, paths, or stacks are recorded.

All existing requests, awaits, assertions, the 120-second test timeout, and the provider hold through the mention ACK remain unchanged. No production code changes.

## Evidence

- Original failure: [hourly main run 44125940128, job 134190601372](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/44125940128/job/134190601372), head `7b0a97a4c96ea05816296f780b7edf0e053260d0`. The committed-mention case timed out after 120074 ms; the stack points to the provider waiting for release. The following case failed during Gateway startup with metadata shutting down. The timing is consistent with cascading teardown, not proof of a separate defect.
- The original job explicitly selected `bun-all` and the pinned Bun `1.4.4-canary.1+191755ec1` on Linux x64. The job used plan concurrency 1. Its actual order was cron (118 files), infra/storage/state (64), Gateway server (79, split 16/16/16/16/15), then commands-light and daemon. The target failed in the third Gateway batch. The encoded Gateway plan set `OPENCLAW_VITEST_MAX_WORKERS=2`; the runner separately reported inner parallelism 1. Local single-case proof does not reproduce this cohort, prior batches, worker setting, or Linux environment.
- One unchanged macOS arm64 pinned-Bun baseline passed. The diagnostic candidate also passed the same isolated case (6349 ms). These are non-reproductions, not evidence of a fix.
- Targeted format, type-aware lint, and Gateway server typecheck passed. The temporary native fixture overlay was restored byte-for-byte afterward.

prs.title: fix: stop long Bun session transcripts from stalling and crash-looping the Gateway
prs.body:
## What Problem This Solves

On Bun, opening a long session for compaction can block the Gateway's main thread for minutes. After 300 s the main-thread stall watchdog SIGKILLs the process. The compaction runs again after the restart, so one large session can crash the Gateway repeatedly.

## User Impact

Gateways on Bun that hold long transcripts open them in seconds instead of stalling, and stop crash-looping. Node behavior is unchanged.

## Why This Change Was Made

`prepareSessionManagerEntries` called `Object.isFrozen(entries)` once per transcript entry, where `entries` is the frozen hydrated history array. V8 answers that in constant time. JavaScriptCore checks every index on each call, so the loop was quadratic in history length. The root's frozen state is now probed once per call. The loop never mutates `entries`, so the result is the same.

## Evidence

- **Microbenchmark, `Object.isFrozen` on a frozen array (per call):** Bun 1.4.4 took 1.8 ms at 10K entries, 4.2 ms at 20K and 8.3 ms at 36,397. A per-entry loop at 36,397 entries therefore costs about 301 s, just over the watchdog limit. Node v26 measures about 0 ms at every size.
- **Profile:** Bun took 103 s to open a 19,336-event transcript for compaction. Of that, 92.9% (95.9 s) was self time in native `isFrozen` under `prepareSessionManagerEntries`. Node opens the same transcript in 9 s.
- **Offline replay:** the deployed build ran under Bun against a native SQLite backup snapshot and opened a 36,397-event session for compaction. Without the change, the main thread was still spinning when the run was killed at 400 s. With it, the session opened in 18.9 s and the event loop stayed responsive.
- **Regression test:** a frozen history root is probed once rather than once per entry, for both owner-sealed and plain-frozen roots. The test fails on the base (66 probes) and passes with the change.
- **Local gates:** the focused codec suite passes (29/29) and `pnpm check:changed` passes, covering typecheck, lint, format, dead exports and guards.
- **Local review:** autoreview with the Claude engine (Codex unavailable on this host) found nothing at P0 or P2 (`scoped-clean`) on base `9122a49bd8a`, head `a3e8ab5768d`.

**Limitation:** Node cannot reproduce the JavaScriptCore cost, so the test pins the number of probes rather than the elapsed time.

prs.title: improve: reduce per-turn work after Responses compaction
prs.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Long OpenAI Responses conversations repeatedly deep-compare unchanged history after compaction. A reparsed checkpoint forces the entire prefix through normalization and projected JSON comparison, creating avoidable allocation and CPU work on every turn.

## User Impact

Responses turns after compaction require less local CPU and allocation. Request bytes, continuation decisions, persisted context hashes, and mutable payload-hook behavior remain unchanged. No configuration or migration is required.

## Why This Change Was Made

Compaction already publishes immutable per-item identities, which incremental prefix hashing consumes. Continuation comparison now consumes the same owner-provided fact. Ordinary frozen items retain reference comparison; edits, opaque/toJSON values, and sparse arrays retain full validation. The comparison lives in the existing JSON projection module to keep the continuation owner within its file-size limit.

No new cache or fingerprint algorithm. Production delta: +19 lines; focused test delta: +41 lines. The remaining growth implements the immutable identity check and its comparison boundary. This change does not claim to remove full hashing on cold or mutable inputs.

## Evidence

A/A/B acceptance was declared in the committed workload before measurement: identical continuation decisions, request deltas and persisted contextUsage/prefixHash; candidate beats both A controls for CPU and allocation on compacted histories, without regressing ordinary history.

Four synthetic histories, eight appended assistant/user turns each, 2,000-entry scale, including reasoning and tool-call/results. Five counterbalanced samples per arm; 640 timed decisions and 96 allocation decisions per sample. V8 sampling includes objects collected by both major and minor GC. Conversion is outside owner timing; these are owner measurements, not Gateway latency or provider cache-hit claims.

| History | Metric per request | A1 | A2 | B |
|---|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Plain | CPU ms, median | 0.17225 | 0.16628 | 0.13627 |
| Plain | Allocation MB, median | 0.00577 | 0.00577 | 0.00651 |
| Checkpoint | CPU ms, median | 2.17330 | 2.14643 | 0.32075 |
| Checkpoint | Allocation MB, median | 2.81234 | 2.80931 | 0.09547 |
| Complete window | CPU ms, median | 1.59184 | 1.57363 | 0.31657 |
| Complete window | Allocation MB, median | 0.78802 | 0.78789 | 0.06439 |

All arms had identical 100% continuation decision hits. Per 32 requests, recursive equality calls fell from 300,384 to 512 for checkpoint histories and from 450,464 to 512 for complete windows. Plain history stayed at 512. Warm historical prefix serialization was already avoided on the baseline; only new response output is encoded by the prefix hasher. Persisted hash parity includes compaction, reasoning and tool history; existing tests cover toJSON evaluation ordering.

The committed workload is `scripts/perf/responses-continuation-equality-measure.ts` (run under `node --expose-gc --import ./scripts/tsx.mjs`, with adjacent baseline continuation and context-usage modules supplied through `--baseline` and `--baseline-context`). The context baseline must import the baseline continuation module. The allocation/work-count guard fails on the original owner and passes with this change. CPU profiling was also collected.

- 78 focused tests passed: retained compaction, prompt/context usage, reasoning updates, and real SSE/WebSocket continuation integration. Five-file command: 38.01 s including compiler preparation; changed test file under 0.1 s.
- Chromium transcript-boundary test: 1 passed. Models/reasoning UI E2E: 9 passed (25.11 s). No UI import of the touched transport modules was found; no new Node-only import was added.
- Codex autoreview through P2: final production logic scoped-clean. The first benchmark concern was checked against the context-usage owner: the compared replay metadata contains the persisted prefixHash. The final review includes that owner.
- Final `pnpm check:changed` passed. [Exact-head CI attempt 2](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/44136688276/attempts/2) passed; attempt 1 failed before tests because the Git PPA returned HTTP 503, and one failed-only retry succeeded. The strengthened fixture also passed its targeted script typecheck and lint.

<details>
<summary>Five-sample spread and host load</summary>

| History/arm | CPU ms min / p95 | Wall ms min / p95 | Allocation MB min / p95 |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| plain/A1 | 0.1540 / 0.1764 | 0.1254 / 0.1491 | 0.0054 / 0.0079 |
| plain/A2 | 0.1620 / 0.1807 | 0.1380 / 0.1473 | 0.0054 / 0.0065 |
| plain/B | 0.1311 / 0.1559 | 0.1173 / 0.1766 | 0.0062 / 0.0069 |
| checkpoint/A1 | 2.1354 / 2.2205 | 1.9408 / 2.0285 | 2.7966 / 2.8249 |
| checkpoint/A2 | 2.1265 / 2.2026 | 1.9442 / 1.9977 | 2.8021 / 2.8290 |
| checkpoint/B | 0.3114 / 0.3238 | 0.3027 / 0.3138 | 0.0936 / 0.0968 |
| window/A1 | 1.5713 / 1.7261 | 1.4540 / 1.6151 | 0.7733 / 0.7945 |
| window/A2 | 1.4745 / 1.6983 | 1.3689 / 1.5905 | 0.7770 / 0.7926 |
| window/B | 0.2891 / 0.3277 | 0.2275 / 0.2632 | 0.0633 / 0.0658 |

Nearest-rank p95 is the maximum for five samples. Node v26.12.1; observed one-minute load 9.81–12.04

</details>

The final workload supplies provider replay provenance for synthetic reasoning and asserts that reasoning survives conversion; its final A/A/B results above supersede the earlier fixture.

Ordinary-history sampled allocation moved from 5.77/5.77 KB to 6.51 KB per request (+0.74 KB, with overlapping five-sample control ranges); work counts stayed identical and CPU improved. No ordinary-history allocation reduction is claimed. Compacted-history B beats both A controls by a wide margin.
