prs.title: fix(mcp): isolate server startup and retries from chat
prs.body:
## Summary

A slow or unresponsive MCP server no longer blocks ordinary chat or delays tools from healthy servers. The gateway reports slow startup after 10 seconds and cancels an unfinished startup attempt after 60 seconds. Tools that become ready during a turn are available on the next model request. Users do not need to send another message to use them.

This is a draft for design review. The change is not ready to merge.

## Benchmarks

### Latest change: use a tool that becomes ready mid-turn

A real gateway and stdio MCP server processed one user message against a local test model endpoint. The first request arrived before the MCP server was ready. The server finished discovery during that request, and the model made a built-in tool call to continue the same turn. We did not send a follow-up message.

| What we measured | Better result | Previous draft `2065ef90f1` | Current draft `bc62a8a82` |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| First chat request reaches the model endpoint | Lower; one paired run, not a latency comparison at scale | 1.22 s | 1.25 s |
| Model can call the newly ready MCP tool | Earlier, with a successful tool result | Not available during the current turn | Available on request 2; request 3 received `pong` |
| Ordered definitions on consecutive requests with no further tool change | Identical | Identical where the list was unchanged | Identical on requests 2 and 3; existing definitions stayed in their original order |

The tool list can change when a tool becomes ready. A model provider may reuse less of the previous prompt on that request. The earlier equal-prefix result does not apply to this transition. No provider cache hit rate was measured.

### Previous change: slow startup, timeout, and chat

**Compare:** draft `47edc783fa` vs. draft `2065ef90f1`. Both ran the same gateway workload on macOS arm64 with Python 3.11, real stdio MCP child processes, and a local model endpoint. The endpoint captures model requests and returns test responses. No external model was called.

**Result:** Chat latency was similar in these runs, and the reusable prompt prefix did not change. The slow server still worked. The unresponsive child exited, and the next attempts started after the expected delays.

| What we measured | Better result | `47edc783fa` | `2065ef90f1` |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **First chat request reaches the model endpoint** with a 12-second MCP startup in the background. Time starts when the client sends the chat message. | **Lower** | 1.14–1.17 s | 1.06–1.21 s |
| **Slow MCP tool becomes available** with the same 12-second startup. Time starts when the gateway process launches. The tool must return `pong`. | **Lower**, with a successful tool call | 13.41–13.75 s; `pong` | 13.33–13.40 s; `pong` |
| **A child that never answers the handshake exits** while the gateway stays running. Time starts when the gateway process launches. | **Lower**; no child left running after cleanup | Still alive after 63 s; no startup deadline | Exited and reported a timeout at 62.86–63.12 s |
| **Wait before restarting an unresponsive child**, measured from timeout cleanup to the next child launch. | **Match the target**, not faster: 15 s, then 30 s | No retry; the original attempt was still running | 15.12 s, then 30.16 s; no overlapping child processes |
| **Reusable prompt prefix** across two model requests for one user input. The MCP tool becomes ready between the requests. | **Higher** for the same workload; **unchanged** is the goal for this timeout change | 5,259 identical tokens | 5,259 identical tokens; same prefix content |

The first two rows show the range of two paired runs. The chat measurement includes gateway and network overhead; the **1-second** limit applies only to how long the gateway waits for initial MCP discovery. The **10-second** slow notice does not cancel the process. The **60-second** deadline starts cancellation; the timeout is visible after transport cleanup. A healthy sibling tool returned `pong` before and after that timeout.

The cache row counts tokens in the **matching start of two requests**, not extra tokens sent or billed. We normalized temporary checkout and workspace paths and used the same tokenizer on both sides. Ordered tool definitions matched byte for byte across all four compared requests. The next user input called the recovered tool. These measurements do **not** show a live provider's cache hit rate.

<details>
<summary>Earlier benchmarks: discovery, reconnect, and the tool list</summary>

These measurements use different earlier versions or prototypes. Each row identifies its comparison; they are not all comparisons with `main` or new runs on the latest commit. The original PR base was `d3bb330f57`.

| What we measured | Better result | Reference | Earlier PR result |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| First chat request reaches the model endpoint while a 12-second MCP server starts | **Lower** | Original `main`: 12.64 s | 1.11–1.13 s |
| Healthy MCP tool becomes available next to an unresponsive peer, using the slower configuration order in two runs | **Lower** | Serial background prototype: 2.91–3.17 s | Per-server discovery: 0.43–0.52 s |
| A 12-second stdio MCP tool becomes available after the gateway launches | **Lower**, with a successful tool call | Draft `f02258e39e`: no tool within 16 s | 13.2–13.7 s; returned `pong` |
| Healthy MCP tool becomes available when four unresponsive servers are configured ahead of it | **Lower** | Draft `f02258e39e`: 11.6–11.7 s | 2.45–2.58 s |
| Hot reload replaces a stalled server: time to a successful tool call | **Lower** | Draft `f02258e39e`: 10.05 s | 0.23 s |
| A healthy server reconnects while another server stalls: time to a successful tool call | **Lower** | Draft `f02258e39e`: 10.01 s | 0.22 s |
| Status requests in 60 seconds while Apps is open and a server is still connecting | **Lower** if Apps still shows the result | Old polling schedule: 61 | 21; same schedule for the first 10 s |
| Reusable prefix with a tool added between two requests in the same turn | **Higher** for the same workload | Live tool list: 4,360 matching tokens | Tool list held for the turn: 5,305 matching tokens |
| Total input tokens in request 1 / request 2 in that same cache test | **Lower** if the requests still support the same task | Live tool list: 5,306 / 5,462 | Tool list held for the turn: 5,305 / 5,423 |
| Discovery time for 4,000 synthetic tool definitions through the connector, with no network | **Lower** | Draft `0c367b5a2d`: 36.48 ms | 28.87 ms; same ordered tool definitions |
| Discovery time with an allowlist that selects 40 of the 4,000 definitions | **Lower** | Draft `0c367b5a2d`: 12.85 ms | 6.72 ms; same result |

The healthy-peer test used the same 2.5-second test timeout on both sides. It measures when a tool becomes available, not when a model answers. The reload and reconnect rows are single paired observations. The Apps row uses a virtual clock. The synthetic discovery values are medians of three interleaved batches, not end-to-end latency. The token rows are local estimates, not provider usage or cache hit rate.

</details>

### Verification

- Recovery follow-up (`3022ed495`): cancelling a tool call while its old connection closes no longer stops background recovery. Reload and shutdown drain that cleanup before proceeding. Apps continues polling after ordinary connection failures and reflects recovery without a page refresh.
- This follow-up passed 392 focused Python tests (one Windows-only case skipped on Linux), 20 WebUI component tests, WebUI type checking/build, focused lint, and the Python import-boundary check. A real HTTP MCP fixture verified cancellation, recovery, reload, and shutdown. A real Chromium browser against the built WebUI and an isolated gateway showed a failed stdio MCP recover without refreshing the page. All test MCP children exited. The full CI and native upgrade matrices were not rerun locally.
- The `bc62a8a82` draft passed 266 focused Python tests, the import-boundary check, and Ruff. In a separate real gateway run, a healthy MCP tool returned `pong` while its peer was stalled. A peer configured to delay startup by 12 seconds later connected and returned `pong`. No test MCP child remained after shutdown.

- A real Chromium browser used the authenticated Gateway and the built Apps page. It showed slow startup, recovery, and timeout, and exposed **Reconnect** for the timed-out server.
- The preceding draft passed **403 Python tests**, **347 Python tests with minimum dependencies**, and **19 WebUI tests**. The Python checks cover transport cleanup, hot reload, request formatting, proxy and redirect safeguards, and protected gateway activation. WebUI type checking and build, import boundary checks, and Ruff also passed.
- Earlier real stdio checks verified that a name conflict could not send a tool call to the wrong server. Renaming and reloading restored the tool under the new name. The timeout follow-up did not re-run the full native packaged-upgrade matrix.

## Before this PR

The gateway waits for MCP connection attempts before it starts the agent. Its readiness hook also waits for another attempt before each turn. A configured MCP process that starts but never replies can delay ordinary chat, even when the user does not need an MCP tool. If a process fails quickly, the next message can start it again. Serial discovery also delays other MCP servers.

Keeping chat off the connection path also lets a server finish discovery during a turn. The next model request uses the live tool list. An earlier draft held additions until the next user input to preserve a longer prompt prefix, but that could hide a useful tool for the rest of a long turn.

## How the draft works

1. **Gateway and MCP lifecycle.** The gateway starts one MCP maintenance task after normal startup admission. It gives initial discovery one shared window of up to one second. It does not wait for MCP in each chat, Dream, or heartbeat run. The provider cancels an unfinished startup attempt after 60 seconds and closes its transport before retrying. Failed attempts retry independently of chat after 15, 30, 60, then at most 120 seconds. The delay resets after a successful connection or a configuration change.
2. **Separate discovery from publication.** The connector opens one server and returns one handle for its capabilities and cleanup. It does not write to a tool registry. The provider permits up to four concurrent stdio process launches. The handshake and discovery do not hold a launch slot or the configuration lock. Each configured server has at most one connection attempt, so stalled servers do not delay healthy ones. A failed server does not publish partial tools. OAuth and the WebUI connection test consume the discovery result directly and keep their own deadlines. Each SDK transport still opens and closes in its owning task.
3. **Use live tool definitions during a turn.** Discovery publishes ready tools immediately. The next model request can use them, even for the same user input. Removed tools stop appearing in the next request, and execution still checks the live registry. Built-in tools stay first, and the order stays deterministic when the registry is unchanged. This change does not alter an in-flight model request or trigger an extra one.
4. **Do not redirect a conflicting tool name.** Two server names can generate the same wrapped tool name. The provider removes the ambiguous name rather than replacing its target. It unregisters each tool by object ownership, not a name prefix. An ambiguous name cannot be reassigned during the gateway's lifetime. Non-conflicting names stay unchanged. Rename one server or tool and reload to use its new name.
5. **Report the active connection.** The provider uses the active connection and attempt tables for status. Reload revokes removed or changed connections and cancels obsolete attempts. It can return a pending result while discovery continues, instead of canceling a healthy slow connection. The gateway reports a slow connection after ten seconds without canceling it. The Apps page checks every second during the first ten polls, then every five seconds while open and visible. It continues to check after startup times out or a connection fails so it can show the next attempt.

The gateway owns startup and shutdown. The connector owns the SDK connection and discovery. `MCPProvider` owns routing, publication, and retries. The existing runner reads the live tool list for each request. `AgentLoop`, `AgentRunner`, provider payload formats, OAuth consent, network policy, and rules for replaying tool operations do not change. No new installed dependency, setting, or on-disk cache is added. At `bc62a8a82`, the production diff was **+516 / −641** Python lines and **+61 / −17** WebUI lines against the draft base; test and documentation changes are separate.

### Reuse existing libraries

- The existing `referencing` library resolves JSON Pointers inside the document. nanobot still moves local targets under `$defs` for model compatibility. Resolution does not retrieve files or URLs.
- AnyIO provides stream iteration and context-manager cleanup. A small receive adapter keeps malformed progress notifications out of SDK logs, which can otherwise include the raw payload.
- Tools, resources, and prompts use one loop over the MCP SDK's page requests. The loop checks repeated cursors and completes a list before publishing it. The SDK's session group does not fetch subsequent pages, so this change does not use it for discovery.
- SSE and Streamable HTTP use the same preflight and HTTPX client setup for URL validation, proxy routing and redirects. Each transport keeps its own request headers, timeout settings, and SDK lifecycle.
- Tool results use SDK content types directly. Images and embedded image blobs still become local artifacts. Python's stable list sort preserves the exact built-ins-first tool order without maintaining two intermediate lists.
- Discovery reuses each wrapped tool name for the allowlist, diagnostics, and registration. The allowlist still runs before tool schemas are normalized. The turn-history owner preserves MCP mention metadata directly; its unused WebUI import shim is removed.

## Compatibility and open decisions

- **Background discovery:** The ten-second reload wait limits the response, not the lifetime of discovery. A slow stdio handshake can finish after the reload returns, without changing `toolTimeout`. A startup attempt still running at 60 seconds is canceled. The gateway waits for the connection owner to close its transport, even if shutdown overlaps the timeout. A server that really needs more than 60 seconds to start now times out. Interactive OAuth and explicit connection tests retain their own deadlines.
- **Intentional change for conflicting names:** Older versions could silently replace a tool with another tool under the same name. The draft disables that name instead. The configuration guide explains how to rename and reload. Restart the gateway after removing a conflict if you need to restore the original name. This does not change stored configuration or existing non-conflicting names.
- **Update continuity:** An earlier macOS arm64 run used the published 0.4.1 native wheel and the actual 0.4.1 updater code with an isolated local feed. It completed both jumps to private `0.4.2.dev0` and `0.4.2.dev1` fixtures from this source. In a separate run, an injected restart failure restored 0.4.1, and the restored installation then updated successfully to `0.4.2.dev1`. An MCP process started but never replied on the candidate gateways. Existing chat history, later writes, restart, the next update, and the shutdown of all fixture MCP children passed. This is not public-feed, signature, or all-platform upgrade evidence. No settings schema, stored chat data, install layout, or update protocol changes.

## Related work

This builds on the existing MCP lifecycle owner and readiness recovery from #5343 and #5535. It preserves the transport cleanup ownership addressed by #3640 and the tool replay safeguards from #6537.

Resolves [NAN-450](https://linear.app/nanobot-ai/issue/NAN-450/mcp-后台连接不阻塞聊天工具就绪后可在当前轮使用).

prs.title: fix(webui): settle completed turns across reconnect paths
prs.body:
## Summary

Fix a WebUI lifecycle-accounting bug that can leave a conversation showing an active response after its turns have completed. When canonical history explicitly confirms an older turn's completion but a newer turn is still running, completion fencing must also settle the older turn's existing ownership record. Otherwise the fence discards the very terminal events that could release that record.

The fix is limited to frontend lifecycle accounting and its history/reconnect callers. Every fresh full-page recovery response supplies named completion facts to the ledger, independently of mount state or whether its content can be adopted. Whole-snapshot adoption has one owner: the mounted transcript, or the background reader when unmounted and the page is eligible and idle. Lifecycle-only settlement retains buffered/late content and independent anonymous recovery. No Gateway execution, cancellation, database, wire API/protocol, dependencies or configuration changes.

## User-visible problem

The reported symptom was a conversation continuing to show the running/Stop-response UI after the backend had finished. Clicking Stop returned `No active task to stop.`. Read-only investigation of that session found persisted turn completions and no corresponding active checkpoint or pending input. The Stop response is consistent with an already-idle backend; this change does not alter that response or force gateway cancellation.

The original browser's WebSocket/HTTP event trace was not recorded, so this PR does **not** claim to establish the unique cause of that historical incident. The ledger defect described below was independently reproduced with the current source, the mounted history hook and a real `ThreadShell` in controlled browser tests. It is a conditional lifecycle race, not a claim that every completed conversation remains active.

## Original revision environment

The following versions describe the author's original revision `21ab11c16`, not the Windows follow-up verification below. The original incident's precise browser cache/bundle state is unknown.

| Component | Local environment |
| --- | --- |
| OS | Ubuntu 24.04.5 LTS (Noble Numbat), x86_64 |
| Kernel | Linux 7.0.0-31-generic |
| Desktop | GNOME Shell 46.0 |
| Browser used for controlled browser verification | Google Chrome 153.0.8010.52 |
| nanobot source | Declared package version 0.4.1; unpatched base `e91906bc3a83c8a3f37ed94ef6c44f750b92b4c1` |
| Installation context | Local source/editable installation; implementation and review performed in isolated source copies, without modifying the running gateway |
| Gateway installation's Python | 3.12.14; the defect reproduction does not require a model call or Python gateway execution |
| Node used for the final revised implementation and independent review | 22.17.1 |
| System-default Node / npm | 18.19.1 / 9.2.0; **not** the runtime used for the final revised verification reported below |
| Git | 2.43.0 |
| React / React DOM | 18.3.1 / 18.3.1 |
| TypeScript | 5.9.3 |
| Vite | 5.4.21 |
| Vitest | 2.1.9 |
| ESLint | 10.4.0 |
| Playwright test runner | 1.64.1 |
| Bun | Unavailable locally; Bun-only checks were not executed |

These are local verification versions, not new dependency requirements or a claim of a fresh lockfile installation. The browser runs used the official Playwright runner with local Google Chrome, not CI's downloaded Chromium. Controlled HTTP/WS fixtures were used, rather than a real gateway/model recovery session.

## Reproduction

### Required event ordering

A deterministic reproduction needs to control the history response and lifecycle events; simply disconnecting and reconnecting does not guarantee this ordering. Use the same client/gateway contract and a mounted conversation with a nonfragment latest-history response.

1. Let the client observe turn `A` running.
2. Complete `A` on the server, but prevent its terminal WebSocket events from reaching this client, for example during a transport gap.
3. Let the client observe a newer turn `B` running, as can happen through reconnect hydration. The client still retains `A`'s unresolved ownership record.
4. Resolve the mounted conversation's latest-history request with `A` explicitly completed and `B` still active. The response includes:

   ```json
   {
     "schemaVersion": 3,
     "projection": "events",
     "completed_turn_ids": ["A"],
     "has_pending_tool_calls": true,
     "active_turn_id": "B",
     "events": [
       {"event": "user_message", "chat_id": "repro", "turn_id": "A", "text": "First task", "starts_turn": true},
       {"event": "message", "chat_id": "repro", "turn_id": "A", "text": "Completed first answer"},
       {"event": "turn_end", "chat_id": "repro", "turn_id": "A"},
       {"event": "user_message", "chat_id": "repro", "turn_id": "B", "text": "Next task", "starts_turn": true}
     ],
     "page": {"before_cursor": null, "has_more_before": false, "user_message_offset": 0}
   }
   ```

5. Because `B` is still active, the mounted history owner cannot settle the entire run from this page. It records a completion fence for `A` instead. Confirm that `B` remains active and can display new output.
6. Deliver `B`'s normal terminal events:

   ```json
   [
     {"event": "turn_end", "chat_id": "repro", "turn_id": "B"},
     {"event": "goal_status", "chat_id": "repro", "turn_id": "B", "status": "idle"}
   ]
   ```

7. Observe the run state and the Stop-response control. Optionally deliver a delayed `turn_end` for `A`; on the unpatched code that event is discarded by the fence and does not clear the stale state.

**Actual result before the fix:** both turns can be recorded as completed while the run remains `active=true`, `unsettled=true`, `startedAt=null`; the UI can continue showing `Stop response`. A new applicable canonical read or local reset can clear it, but the delivered terminal events alone do not repair the residual ownership record.

**Expected result:** settling `A` must preserve active `B` and its output/clock; once `B` ends, the client must become idle (`active=false`, `unsettled=false`, `startedAt=null`). Delayed events for `A` must not stop or reopen `B`.

### Deterministic automated reproduction included in this PR

With the repository's WebUI dependencies installed, run the maintained regressions in an isolated checkout of the current PR:

```bash
cd webui
node node_modules/vitest/vitest.mjs run \
  src/tests/nanobot-client.test.ts \
  src/tests/useReconnectRuns.test.tsx \
  -t 'settles an older completed turn|notifies subscribers when a completion fence|settles a missed old completion|unmounted old completion|independent anonymous recovery' \
  --maxWorkers=1 --minWorkers=1
```

The original four mounted/ledger regressions failed against the original production base. The follow-up first added four regressions against `21ab11c16`: both timings of a newer turn relative to an unmounted full-page read, and independent anonymous recovery with full/fragment responses. All four failed before the follow-up production changes and pass after them. Historical model failure controls are archived separately from the retained current-policy artifact; the default current-implementation checks must have no counterexamples. Do not replace source files in a live installation to reproduce these comparisons.

The hook regression `settles a missed old completion from mounted history while a newer turn remains active` exercises the actual mounted `useNanobotStream` history/reconnect path. The client regressions cover both direct canonical adoption rejected by a newer owner and the fence-only path, plus subscriber updates when the latest completed turn has no terminal WS frame.

## Root cause

`ClientRunLedger.view()` considers a run active while any turn retains an `openOrder`. Previously `fence()` recorded completed IDs and pruned buffered frames, but did not settle their existing turn records. `applyObservation()` then dropped subsequent top-level frames for every fenced ID, including terminal events. This allowed the state to say a turn was completed while retaining its open lifecycle ownership.

The original and first follow-up identified three paths:

- `useNanobotStream` uses fence-only reconciliation when a mounted full history page cannot safely settle the entire current run.
- Canonical adoption records explicit completion fences even if a newer owner prevents accepting the whole snapshot.
- Unmounted full-page reconnect previously returned on active metadata or failed preflight before applying an older turn's explicit completion. This was traced to the reconnect path introduced by #6211; the later fragment path already separated lifecycle settlement from content coverage.

Explicit completion of `A` is authoritative independently of whether the page can settle `B`. The ledger must release only the named completed turn, rather than requiring acceptance of the whole page or waiting for a terminal frame it will subsequently discard.

Broader verification then found a regression in `6af86525c`: publishing a shared pending reconnect page synchronously superseded the mounted owner's read, but that owner reconciled full pages only when `ownRead` was true. The background reader also skipped whole-page adoption while a newer turn was active. The page could render the completed answer without anyone settling its old lifecycle. This was reproduced through the actual hooks/client before the fix. Removing only the `ownRead` condition exposed duplicate idle adoption, so mounted whole-snapshot adoption is assigned exclusively to the transcript owner.

Expanded dynamic-switch checking then found a second concrete hook race: an ineligible mounted recovery page already contains completion A, a newer B prevents cache adoption, and switching away disposes the old history read before React commits the scheduled refresh. B's later terminal leaves A unresolved. An actual-hooks replay failed before the final correction. The correction separates facts from content: fresh full pages always report their explicit completed IDs to the ledger; mount state and content eligibility govern whole-page adoption, not whether those facts are learned.

## Fix and regression protection

- Record lifecycle closure and use the existing settlement primitive for each explicitly completed fenced turn. This removes its ownership record and discards pending sends for that exact chat/turn identity.
- Clear the effective start timestamp only when the completed ID matches the latest named owner. Do not change the newer owner's identity, generation or clock.
- Preserve independent anonymous recovery activity. An unscoped `attached`/`recovery_state` can start a new recovery before its canonical turn ID arrives, while the old `latestTurnId` is still retained. Completing that old named turn must not stop the new anonymous recovery. The existing parameterized tests now cover both event variants with this fence boundary.
- Generalize the existing fragment lifecycle-only operation as `settleCompletedRunLifecycle`. Unmounted full pages use it even when the whole-page preflight rejects adoption, without fully fencing or discarding live content. Mounted fragments retain their transcript-owner handoff.
- Cache adoptable history before notifying completion subscribers. Only an idle snapshot can clear activity without a named identity; a partial named completion preserves independent anonymous recovery.
- Route direct and published non-seed mounted full pages through the same admitted transcript reconciliation. Initial cached seeds are not new lifecycle evidence. Fresh full-page recovery applies named lifecycle evidence even if the mounted transcript cannot adopt the content; background recovery never performs a second mounted whole-snapshot adoption.
- Unify named lifecycle/content completion in the ledger's `completeTurns` transition; coverage selects pruning without duplicating turn ownership mutation. Request cancellation, transcript admission, and observed run state keep distinct owners. The Gateway remains the execution authority.
- Retain late-frame fencing and read-only canonical preflight. No polling, timeout reset or artificial successful Stop response is added.

The PR now contains exactly two single-parent commits: the original contributor commit `21ab11c16` is unchanged, followed by one consolidated maintainer commit. Retained the current-policy models, necessary configurations and portable runner: 12 default positive checks, two separately classified missing-evidence limits and two optional larger products. Verification material decreased by 385 lines overall. The shared `TurnSync` module remains a required dependency of `RevisedTurnSync`, not a standalone historical check.

Fresh TLC runs on the compacted artifact exhausted all 12 default graphs with exit 0, empty queues and no counterexamples; every distinct-state count matches the corresponding pre-cleanup graph. Both retained current-policy limits still produce the expected temporal counterexamples and are not counted as positive results. Committed inputs were checked against the tested copies after CRLF/LF normalization. [Current artifact](https://github.com/IndigoC/nanobot/blob/a7cdf53bea45574ca7aea2052e9d47ae622c0dc3/webui/verification/turn-sync/README.md).

[Consolidated-head CI run 44058004768](https://github.com/HKUDS/nanobot/actions/runs/44058004768) for `a7cdf53be` **passed**, including the required gate. All **3897 unit tests across 214 files** and **592 distinct browser cases exactly once across four shards** passed, with no browser skips/retries. Static checks, production build and every Docker acceptance step passed, including first boot, retained-volume old-image upgrade, Compose startup, default WhatsApp dependencies and runtime permissions. The upgrade report confirms preserved config/history and continued writes on the same volume. The import-checker suite passed with 41 passes and one Windows-only platform skip. - This change covers named completion accounting and mounted/unmounted history handoff. It does not replace the complete reconnect synchronization protocol or claim every stuck-running symptom is fixed.

prs.title: fix(goal): block goals after terminal execution failures
prs.body:
## Why

A sustained goal could remain active after output-limit recovery, repeated empty responses, or another terminal execution failure had already stopped its run. Some refusal and truncated responses were also reported as successful turns.

## What changed

- Settle terminal failures in the gateway's goal execution policy: atomically block only the current active goal, preserve its objective, and record a safe reason and timestamp before notifying clients.
- Preserve terminal runner reasons and report failed model turns, including refusals, content filtering, and exhausted output/empty-response recovery.
- Expose the blocked recap in runtime context so later replies can explain why work stopped.

## Scope

Only terminal-failure state correction. No new goal actions, permission changes, or recovery workflow. Token settings, retry budgets, client protocols, `/stop`, and `/cancel_goal` are unchanged. Retries and recoverable tool errors keep working.

## Tradeoffs

Terminal failures block rather than retry indefinitely. Existing goal tools and recovery behavior remain unchanged; this PR does not add a resume action.

## Blast Radius

Durable goal execution and model-failure reporting use the existing blocked-state projection. Generation checks and an atomic active-state check prevent stale failures from overwriting a replacement session or a closed goal. Hard process crashes and unavailable storage cannot guarantee a persisted transition.

## Verification

- Runner/loop, goal tools, cancellation, sessions, commands, and SDK regression checks: **1136 passed, 3 skipped** on Windows/Python 3.14.
- WebUI goal/wire/background, runtime-context/model-event checks and gateway smoke suite: **59 passed, 1 skipped**.
- Real isolated gateway + local synthetic SSE model: normal completion, `/stop`, exhausted length recovery, reconnect, and status inquiry passed through the public WebSocket interface.
- Full CI lint command, strict BasedPyright, Python import boundaries, and `git diff --check` passed. Full-project/cross-platform CI for the narrowed scope is pending; the running user instance and its configuration were not changed.

Resolves [NAN-455](https://linear.app/nanobot-ai/issue/NAN-455/执行终止性失败时自动阻塞-goal)

issues.body:
### Pre-flight

- [x] Searched existing issues and PRs by `processes.json`, `recover_from_checkpoint`, `_write_checkpoint`, and cross-process adoption, kill or receipt wording.
  - #109984 / #109985 fix in-process ordering and explicitly don't claim cross-process ownership.
  - #31980 is a generic "tracking lost after restart" report.
  - #118710, #117598 and #117054 add no writer identity.
  - #69918 would make the CLI recover from the checkpoint too.
- [x] Confirmed on current `main`
- [ ] `hermes debug share`: N/A. Reproduced with real processes sharing one `HERMES_HOME`.

### Bug Description

Every Hermes process on a profile (gateway, CLI, TUI, dashboard chat, one-shot, cron worker) shares one `processes.json`, and each rewrites the whole file with only its own jobs. After a gateway restart:

1. **The gateway adopts other live processes' background jobs, and SIGKILLs them at its next shutdown.**
2. **When an adopted job finishes, the gateway overwrites the producer's saved result with an empty one**: no output, no exit code.
3. **The gateway's own crash-recovery entries get erased by other writers**, so after a crash its jobs become untracked orphans.

### Steps to Reproduce

A gateway starts a job and crashes. A CLI on the same profile starts a job. The gateway restarts, then shuts down:

```
processes.json after gateway#1 spawn: ['sleep 42076']
processes.json after CLI spawn     : ['sleep 49097']
gateway#1 exited rc= 137 | its job pid 26662 alive: True
{"who": "gateway#2", "recovered": 1, "adopted": [{... "command": "sleep 49097", "session_key": "cli-sess-1" ...}]}
{"who": "gateway#2", "shutdown_kill_all_killed": 1}
AFTER gateway#2 recovery+shutdown: CLI job pid 26838 alive=False | gateway#1 job pid 26662 alive=True (orphan, never recovered)
```

Receipt overwrite: the CLI's job ends with `exit_code 0, output "...RESULT-OK-42"`. The durable receipt the CLI session reads back on resume then says `exit_code: None, output ''`.

### Expected Behavior

Each process owns its checkpoint entries. Recovery adopts only the jobs of processes that are gone. An adopted job never replaces the producer's saved result.

### Actual Behavior

- `tools/process_registry_checkpoint.py`: `_write_checkpoint` writes this process's running jobs over the whole file (last writer wins).
- `recover_from_checkpoint` adopts any live PID whose start time matches, without checking which process wrote the entry. Gateway shutdown then kills everything it adopted.
- `tools/process_registry_results.py`: `save_completed_result` writes a detached session's empty record over the producer's receipt.

### Affected Component

Tools (terminal, file ops, web, code execution, etc.)

### Messaging Platform

All (gateway + any other process on the same profile)

### Operating System

macOS 26 (host independent)

### Python Version

3.11

### Hermes Version

main

### Root Cause Analysis

The checkpoint has been commented "(gateway only)" since 061fa70907, but writes were never restricted to the gateway. b72e373e23 moved saved *results* to one file per producer so "independent one-shot parents cannot overwrite each other's results in the running-PID checkpoint", but the running checkpoint was left shared.

### Proposed Fix

1. Stamp each entry with its writer's PID and start time, and read-merge-write only your own entries under a cross-process lock.
2. On recovery, adopt only entries whose writer is dead.
3. Never let a detached session overwrite an existing receipt.

**What changed.** On 14 October, #106742 (the unified gateway) moved every local conversation into one gateway process. What broke for people, and how serious it is (by area and severity; click to open) **What broke for people.** 319 problems found on `main`, grouped by what people were doing (each problem is counted once): - **Opening and resuming chats (21):** Desktop can't reopen many stored chats: sessions cleaned up at a restart, chats from the API server, cron, subagents, the WebUI, Claude Code imports and bot handoffs, and a root profile's bot chat. A credential rewritten in config strands older sessions, and some large or compressed sessions fail to resume or come back out of order. - **Turns stuck, lost or never stopping (18):** A prompt can wait forever behind a paused session, a finished reply can miss the screen, queued messages can sit until a restart, and a turn keeps running after its window closes. One busy chat can freeze the gateway for everyone, and any local process can silently stop it from saving. - **Several profiles, renames and moves (52):** Renaming a profile or moving to the shared gateway strands old chats. Secrets, settings, ports and fallbacks are read from the wrong profile or not found. Desktop sends requests and lists to the wrong profile, parked or standalone profiles stay offline, and hosts with many profiles stall or restart. - **Messaging bots (27):** Background-task results never reach Discord threads, Slack DMs and relay chats. Progress updates, cron results and webhooks go out through the wrong profile's bot or not at all. Images, files and relay messages are dropped, and a stop or new conversation doesn't fence a command that is already running. - **Scheduled and background work (26):** Kanban cards fail for whole classes of models and providers, die or hang at start, hide why they failed, and never wake the chat that made them. Cron jobs stop their own gateway, are booked as failed during updates, pause while still running, or create an empty session on every tick. - **Desktop and the terminal UI (49):** Desktop doesn't reconnect after the gateway drops, forwarded turns lose their prompts and Stop, pasted screenshots vanish from history, and the context, queue, voice and dictation views show nothing or the wrong thing. Dashboard bulk actions and some remote connections are refused. - **Group Chats, including rooms across computers (28):** In gateway-hosted Group Chats a message or a Stop can be lost, rooms can't be renamed or ended, retries make duplicate rooms, a turn the gateway can't confirm sits until someone presses Stop, and mention suggestions, file sends and rooms with Bots on two computers are gone. - **Windows and WSL (15):** A Desktop or CLI run under another account never attaches, stale Task Scheduler entries or a non-ASCII install path block start-up, updates start the gateway twice, and editor sessions in per-task homes time out. On WSL2 every Kanban card, cron run and subagent dies. - **Starting and updating the gateway (20):** Every client now needs one supervised gateway, so one start-up refusal blocks the CLI, terminal UI and Desktop together: an unpaired WhatsApp adapter, a symlinked database, a root-owned unit file, or a systemd, launchd, Home Manager, Docker or s6 mismatch. Desktop's update dialog fails without saying why. - **The terminal CLI, scripts, editors and API clients (35):** Scripts that pass their own session source, and old sessions resumed with flags, fail at start. The CLI's session lists miss recent chats. Editors lose their environment, MCP servers and session lists, and API clients get stuck sessions, ignored session names and lost messages after a stop. Several commands still start a second copy of Hermes. - **Model and provider picks (14):** Named custom endpoints collapse to a bare provider and fail, model switches crash on chats that follow their profile, picks and fallbacks land on the wrong provider, and reasoning and Fast changes are dropped. - **Tools and plugins (14):** Terminal commands run with the environment and API keys of whichever client started the shared gateway, or lose the client's own variables. Workspace containers are killed mid-run or pile up, and plugin shell calls and some hooks stop working. **How serious it is.** Of the 319 problems, 166 are broken (something fails or gives a wrong result), 124 degraded (silently does less), 9 security and 20 cosmetic. 37 of these are older multiplexing bugs that #106742's update made everyone with several profiles hit. On 10 Nov every row not yet fixed was re-checked against `main` `95fc3e668f`: 13 were partly fixed, and 30 can't be settled by reading the code (they need a live run or an outside service). The worst: - Terminal commands can run with the environment and API keys of whichever client started the shared gateway, so later runs and other profiles inherit them. - Webhooks bound to a profile are accepted (202) but never run. - Desktop still can't reopen some stored chats, and several of these failures came back on builds that contain the earlier fix. - Background results still never reach some chats (a Discord thread fed from two clients, a Desktop chat waiting on a finished `delegate_task`), and Kanban workers die or hang at start on Windows, in some card workspaces and without the review skill. - On Linux, one shell-quoted variable in the session environment stops Desktop from starting the gateway. Hit hardest: installs with several profiles (52 problems) and Desktop and the terminal UI (49). Data loss shows up as messages, replies and background results that never arrive, and as pasted screenshots that vanish from history.

Report here **Report anything you hit with the unified gateway as a comment on this issue**, or link your issue here. Name its ID (for example `RT-30a`) in the PR so it can be ticked off here. ## Contract under test From [#134889](https://github.com/NousResearch/hermes-agent/issues/134889), unchanged: - Queued admissions survive an owner restart and run FIFO, exactly once. - A started admission that loses its owner becomes interrupted and is never replayed automatically. - A retry reuses the original admission identity and committed payload. - Clients read and submit; the gateway is the only canonical writer. - Profile, provider, generation and revision boundaries hold on every transport. Deliberate limits (not bugs), as in #134889: the served profile set is a start-time snapshot (adding a profile needs `hermes gateway restart`), and hosted-room execution across two profiles on one gateway is not live-certified. ## Direction: follow #106742 Every fix here must keep the direction of [#106742](https://github.com/NousResearch/hermes-agent/pull/106742). Put this section in the brief of every sub-agent you start. - One gateway owns every local session: one FIFO, one durable queue, one writer. Fix the gateway path. Don't bring back a client-side agent, a local fallback or a second writer to `state.db`. - Clients only read and submit. A missing capability gets a gateway handler or a named refusal, not client-side state. - Keep the contract above, and profile boundaries on every transport. - Design calls are yours. Pick the option that best fits this design and write the choice and the reason in the PR body. Ask here only when every option would break a rule above. ## Working rules - Branch from current `main`. Reproduce 🟡 rows on `main` first. A row that doesn't reproduce gets no commit: post the evidence (`file:line`, the probe test) here. - Lanes touch different code, so they can run in parallel. Open one PR per lane (split it if it grows), each with a failing test first. - Name the row ID in the PR and reference this issue, as the packages did (`Refs #134889 (GW-19)`). Use `Fixes` only for the row's own report (`Fixes #142942`), never for this issue or #134889. - **An open PR from an outside contributor doesn't cover a row.** Review it. If it's right, finish it on the contributor's branch, or salvage it with `git cherry-pick -x` so they stay its author and add your work on top; use `Co-authored-by` only for code you rebuilt. If it's wrong or stale, fix the row fresh, say why on that PR, and close it with a credit note. - A fix not run against what it targets (Desktop, a gateway serving several profiles, native Windows, an install upgraded from an older version) uses `Refs`, not `Fixes`, and says what still needs a live retest. - 🔵 rows wait for a maintainer decision. issues.body:
Tracking issue for the staged fast-follow named in [#134889](https://github.com/NousResearch/hermes-agent/issues/134889)'s scope note: *"the browser dashboard and Desktop URL / Cloud / SSH modes still talk to standalone `hermes serve`."* [#106742](https://github.com/NousResearch/hermes-agent/pull/106742) (merged Oct 14, `eb75627f`) gave every **local** surface one gateway-owned session authority per profile. This issue tracks moving the remaining entry points onto that same authority and then removing the old in-process session host.

Design: [One Gateway: Entry-Point and Session Ownership Plan](https://gist.github.com/unsupportedpastels/765f9d551ce88ee01630c18367763e75). Profile-multiplexing direction: [#109417](https://github.com/NousResearch/hermes-agent/issues/109417) (one `hermes gateway run` serves every profile).

**Status (Oct 26, after EP-1, first repros and EP-2 baseline):** EP-1 (caller map) is done, traced by code reading on `main` at `edfa1c2a`. It traced EP-8 to EP-11, split EP-11, and added EP-13 to EP-17 and D6. EP-13 and EP-15 are now reproduced in-process on `edfa1c2a` (no live gateway). 16 open rows, 2 verification rows, 6 open decisions. Nothing is in a package yet. EP-2 has a headless baseline (289 tests passed); `verify_parity2.sh` and the manual live checks need rebuilding. Other rows were checked against `main` at `d49e2ebb`; rows marked *needs repro* come from code reading only.

**Update (Nov 7):** merged the three scripted EP-2 rigs (network drop mid-turn #149888, cron→compress→input #149889, SSE approvals #149896; all pass on `main`, no new gaps), the One Core P2 boundary lint (#149895, report-only, fails only on new core/plugin crossings) with agent guidance (#150243), `PluginContext` in its own module with explicit registrars (#149897, #149898), dashboard-auth and secret-source registries on `ProviderRegistry` (#149879), 12 of 19 legacy `SessionState` views removed (#149880, #149892), and the plugin-docs public-import test (#149899). EP-18 (background-service migration) is planned; EP-13 and EP-14 stay held for the cutover.

**Update (Nov 6):** merged the handler ledger (EP-1, #148795), the acceptance harness (EP-2, #148774), the EP-15 fix (#148769), the EP-11a removal (#148775) and the V1/V2 tests (#148777, #148798). EP-13 (#148770) and EP-14 (#148794) are held for the cutover so `main`'s behavior doesn't change before it.

**Scope:** `hermes serve`, standalone `hermes dashboard`, Desktop remote modes (SSH / URL / Cloud), remaining direct agent constructors, and removal of the legacy host. **Out of scope:** the forced-migration campaign (soak, rollback window, `--force`); migrating background services is in scope as EP-18, storage redesign, protocol unification, a replacement browser UI and a mobile client.

## Done on `main` (not tracked here)

- Local Desktop runs `gateway ensure` (`apps/desktop/electron/main.ts`); `5e783bde` removed code that only Desktop's own `serve` reached.
- `session.detach` is wired in `gateway/session_controls.py`.
- `SessionAuthorities` supports `add`/`remove` at runtime (`gateway/session_authorities.py`, `gateway/run_runtime.py`); see V1.
- [#141864](https://github.com/NousResearch/hermes-agent/pull/141864) serves the Desktop webapp (`apps/desktop/dist-webapp`, not `web/`) from the gateway's own listener.

## Contract under test

- Every supported entry point reaches the canonical profile authority; none starts its own session runtime.
- Closing a client removes a viewer. It never stops accepted work.
- Authorized clients can join and leave the same conversation and see the same queue, execution state and pending controls.
- Profile selection resolves an authority inside the multiplexer; `serve -p X` never launches an independent gateway for X.
- Documented callback URLs, profile-scoped auth, `--force` and standalone migration support are unchanged.
- No legacy execution fallback remains at completion.

## Legend

🔴 open, no fix · 🟡 fix PR open · 🟣 fix in review (member PR) · 🔵 waiting on a maintainer decision · ⚪ not reproduced · 🟢 fixed on `main`

## Open findings

### Stage 1: caller map and parity harness (start here)

| ID | Finding | Severity | Status |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| EP-1 | Caller map for `serve`. **Done at `edfa1c2a`.** One FastAPI app runs in two modes, chosen only by `app.state.gateway_runner` (`hermes_cli/web_server_app.py:234`). Only the gateway's own mount sets it (`gateway/run_api.py:96-97`), so every `hermes serve`, `hermes dashboard` and `serve --isolated` runs `standalone_lifespan` with no authority. `serve` never discovers or forwards to a running gateway, except single-session edits over `session.mutate` (`hermes_cli/web_server_sessions.py:188-234`). Results feed D1 to D6 below. **Handler ledger merged in #148795 (`eccfff7b`):** `tests/hermes_cli/serve_handler_ledger.json` lists every serve HTTP route, RPC and WebSocket handler with its owner decision (625 rows, 520 undecided pending D1–D6); `scripts/gen_serve_handler_ledger.py --check` keeps it in sync with `main`. | P1 | 🟢 |
| EP-2 | Parity rigs on the combined tree. **Headless baseline recorded on `edfa1c2a`** (scratch home, one pytest process per file): 31 files, 289 tests passed, about 8 min. Covers entrypoint parity and boot contract (`tests/e2e/core/parity/`), two-tenant gateway and Desktop backend (`tests/e2e/core/tenancy/`), live hot-serve (`tests/gateway/test_multiplex_hot_serve_live.py`, 7), gateway turn liveness (`tests/e2e/core/chaos/test_gateway_turn_liveness.py`, 12), and the profile-isolation, handoff, recovery and admission/replay unit tests. `tests/e2e/core/tenancy/test_routing_truth_table.py` could not run on this host (its guard refuses temp dirs under `~/.hermes`); use the CI `e2e` job result. **Missing:** `verify_parity2.sh` is not in the tree, git history or any linked issue; the #134889 "Verified working" live checks were manual and have no scripts. **Not run here:** Desktop `apps/desktop/e2e/core` (`remote-topology`, `remote-secondary`, `local-gateway-attach`) needs a GUI; CI lane `e2e-desktop-core` runs it. Next: rerun the same file set on every combined-tree candidate; rebuild network drop mid-turn, cron→compress→input and SSE approvals as scripted e2e tests. **Acceptance harness merged in #148774 (`418de33e`):** `tests/e2e/core/serve_ownership/` runs a real `serve` and gateway with one control cell and three `known_failure` cells for the open ownership gaps; `HERMES_E2E_STRICT_ACCEPTANCE=serve-cutover` turns them into hard failures for the cutover. **Scripted rigs merged (Nov 7):** network drop mid-turn (#149888), cron→compress→input (#149889) and SSE approvals (#149896), all green on `main`. | P1 | 🔴 |

### Stages 2–3: `serve` uses the authority

| ID | Finding | Severity | Status |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| EP-3 | With no `gateway_runner`, `serve` selects `standalone_lifespan` and runs agents in-process (`hermes_cli/web_server_app.py:234`; comment at `hermes_cli/main.py:2598`). | P1 | 🔴 (blocked on D1, D2) |
| EP-4 | `/api/ws` sends every RPC to the legacy `server.dispatch` when no authority is present (`tui_gateway/ws.py:362-390`). With an authority, non-session verbs that the authority answers with -32601 still fall back to legacy handlers in-process (`tui_gateway/ws_legacy_fallback.py:53-64`): 100 methods go to the authority, 163 fall back, 16 are blocked. | P1 | 🔴 |
| EP-5 | New work can enter `serve` without going through the authority's admission: [#138750](https://github.com/NousResearch/hermes-agent/issues/138750). The issue's line numbers have drifted; on `edfa1c2a` the console executor is `hermes_cli/web_routers/chat_ws.py:278`, PTY spawn `:552`, action subprocesses `hermes_cli/web_server_gateway.py:475`. | P1 | 🔴 |
| EP-6 | Version skew: a new remote client's `prompt.submit` attachments are refused by an older `serve`: [#144186](https://github.com/NousResearch/hermes-agent/issues/144186). Traced: the retry strips only `submission_id`, then the legacy param model refuses `attachments` with `4000`. | P2 | 🔴 (blocked on D5) |
| EP-13 | Session-bound legacy fallback methods on authority sessions. **Reproduced in-process at `edfa1c2a`:** the authority answers -32601 for all 13, the fallback runs the legacy handler, and the handler can't find the session (authority sessions are never in `server._sessions`). 10 fail with `4001 session not found`; `tools.list` and `toolsets.list` silently ignore the session and return launch-profile data; `insights.get` isn't session-bound (it rejects `session_id` with 4000). Clients gate or translate 11 of the 13 before they reach the wire. Two still reach the server and fail silently: Desktop `image.detach` on chip removal (`apps/desktop/src/app/chat/hooks/use-composer-actions.ts:922`, harmless) and ui-tui `input.detect_drop` for a dropped non-image path (`ui-tui/src/app/useComposerState.ts:339-379`), which pastes raw text instead of an attachment. `handoff.*` and `tools.configure` are refused by name client-side (feature gap). Defensive server fix: keep -32601 for these verbs in `tui_gateway/ws_legacy_fallback.py`, as already done for `session.`/`prompt.`. | P3 | 🔴 |
| EP-14 | `POST /api/cron/jobs/{id}/trigger` (`hermes_cli/web_routers/cron.py:762`) runs the job's agent inside the request thread (`cron/scheduler.py:3373`) outside admission, in both modes; the code marks the path deprecated. `POST /api/cron/fire` already forwards to the gateway. | P2 | 🔴 |
| EP-15 | `POST /api/health/retirement` (`hermes_cli/web_routers/status.py:160`) is live on the gateway listener and declares a busy gateway idle. **Reproduced in-process at `edfa1c2a`** (real dashboard app bound the way `gateway/run_api.py:75-108` binds it, a claimed admission and one running agent; runner and authority are stand-ins): `GET /api/health/idle` returns `idle: true`, `prepare` returns 200 with a token, `commit` returns 200. Afterwards dashboard JSON-RPC answers 5035 "backend is retiring", cron `tick()` dispatches nothing and the fence admits no new work until restart, while the gateway keeps running. Cause: the idle proof (`hermes_cli/web_server_idle_proof.py:39-58`, `hermes_cli/web_server_idle_exit.py:104-136`) reads only the legacy session table, delegation, cron and the fence; it never consults the gateway runner or authority, and nothing under `gateway/` takes the fence. Latent: no in-repo client calls the route, and it needs an owner or local token. Fix direction: refuse when `app.state.gateway_runner` is set, or base idleness on `gateway/run_idle_exit.py:busy_reason` and fail closed. **Fixed by #148769 (`f190892f`):** with a gateway runner mounted, the idle route reports not idle and `prepare`/`commit`/`cancel` are refused; standalone `serve` keeps its idle retirement. | P1 | 🟢 |
| EP-17 | Bulk session REST (bulk delete, delete-empty, prune) writes `state.db` directly under a store-wide lock and returns 409 while a gateway owns the store, with no owner path. | P3 | 🔴 |

### Stage 4: remote Desktop and browser

| ID | Finding | Severity | Status |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| EP-7 | SSH mode starts `serve --isolated` and kills it on disconnect, so closing the client stops accepted work (`apps/desktop/electron/remote-lifecycle.ts:1142-1161`, `apps/desktop/electron/main.ts:9486`). Every disconnect path (quit, connection switch or edit, profile delete, recycle) kills the remote process with no check for a running turn. | P1 | 🔴 (blocked on D4) |
| EP-8 | Desktop URL and Cloud modes reach whatever process the URL names; neither calls `gateway ensure`. The Docker image's dashboard service runs standalone `hermes dashboard` on 9119 (`docker/s6-rc.d/dashboard/run:52-54`). Desktop reads no `gateway_mode` or host role, so it can't tell which backend it reached. Hosted Cloud agents are inferred to match; Cloud infra isn't in this repo. | P1 | 🔴 |
| EP-9 | Standalone `hermes dashboard` chat (the sidebar's `/api/ws`, and the chat terminal when no profile is named) and its session REST use the legacy dispatcher, not the authority. A named profile attaches to the profile's gateway. *Reworded:* `ChatPage` can't reach `serve`, which is headless and doesn't serve `web/` (`hermes_cli/web_server_dashboard.py:126-149`). | P2 | 🔴 (D6) |
| EP-16 | SSH, URL and Cloud remotes send raw method names: the 13 rewrites to `session.mutate` with revision/generation checks in `canonical-protocol.ts` apply only to `native_dial` sockets. `handoff.*` is refused locally but still sent to remotes. **Fixed by #148219 (`7bc10408da`):** Desktop now selects the canonical adapter from `session_authority: true` in `gateway.ready`, so the rewrites and the `handoff.*` refusal apply to any remote that advertises it. SSH still reaches `serve --isolated`, which serves the legacy names (EP-7). | P2 | 🟢 |

### Stage 5: remaining producers

| ID | Finding | Severity | Status |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| EP-10 | The slash worker runs a second `HermesCLI` per session: [#141196](https://github.com/NousResearch/hermes-agent/issues/141196). Standalone backends only (`tui_gateway/methods_tools.py:1070-1086`); the gateway serves `slash.exec` itself (`gateway/session_controls.py:390`). | P2 | 🔴 (D6) |
| EP-11a | `hermes_cli/oneshot.py` `_run_agent` builds a bare `AIAgent`, but it's dead code: its only caller `_run_and_exit_oneshot` is called only from tests, and `-z` goes through `launch_gateway_chat` (`hermes_cli/main.py:3020-3026`). Removal candidate. **Removed by #148775 (`a2db0efb`).** `_exit_after_oneshot` stays (it writes `--cpu-profile` output) and `hermes_cli.oneshot.get_fallback_chain` stays importable. | P3 | 🟢 |
| EP-11b | `prompt.background` (`tui_gateway/methods_prompt.py:1184`) writes a separate `bg_*` session row and skips the gateway's queue check; `preview.restart` (`:1249`) builds `AIAgent` with no session store. Standalone backends only; gateway connections refuse `prompt.*` fallback. | P2 | 🔴 (D6) |

### Stage 6: remove the legacy host (after parity)

| ID | Finding | Severity | Status |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| EP-18 | Users who run `hermes serve` / `hermes dashboard` as an automatic background service need a migration path before removal. Hermes never installs one itself; the shapes are systemd units copied from the docs (`web-dashboard.md:186-197`, `desktop.md:668`) and hand-written launchd plists, Nix `hermes-backend` (NixOS unit, Home Manager user unit and launchd agent; `Restart=always`, `KeepAlive=true`), the Docker image's s6 `dashboard` longrun and the Compose `dashboard` sidecar, Desktop SSH `serve --isolated`, and operator-made Windows autostarts. `hermes update` restarts these but never migrates them, and its unit-name gate misses `hermes-backend`. Hazard: the attach path exits 0 when another backend owns the host, which respawn-loops under those restart policies, so a deprecated entry point must stay in the foreground. Main blocker is listener parity (the gateway serves the webapp on 9120, not the `web/` SPA on 9119, and lacks the Nix session-token file and the `dashboard.public_url` mapping). Proposed: a `serve.host_mode` switch, sentinel mode, `hermes gateway migrate --backends` with dry-run/rollback, and a report-only update hook until the cutover (Linear HACORE-159). | P1 | 🔴 |
| EP-12 | The legacy session host still exists: `tui_gateway/server.py` (2,187 lines), `tui_gateway/agent_factory.py`, `ws_legacy_fallback`. Remove only after EP-3 to EP-18 are green and EP-2 passes. Modules named `tui_gateway` that don't host sessions stay. | P2 | 🔴 (blocked on stages 2–5) |

### Verification (believed done; needs evidence)

| ID | Finding | Severity | Status |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| V1 | Hot-added and removed profiles create and retire authorities. #134889 lists the served profile set as a start-time snapshot, but `main` now has `SessionAuthorities.add`/`remove`, driven by the `serve-profile`, `unserve-profile` and `rescan-profiles` control-socket verbs (`gateway/run_runtime.py:380`, `:459`). **Partly verified on `edfa1c2a`:** `test_multiplex_hot_serve_live.py` (7 passed) drives `rescan-profiles` against a real multiplexer, and unserve is covered at the function level (`test_run_runtime_hot_serve_cleanup.py`). No test sends `serve-profile` or `unserve-profile` by name; add one to the live test, then update #134889's "Deliberate limits". **Verified by #148777 (`02849dba`):** the live test now sends `serve-profile` and `unserve-profile` by name and checks the authority is added and retired (including during a running turn). | P2 | 🟢 |
| V2 | [#109403](https://github.com/NousResearch/hermes-agent/pull/109403), [#109405](https://github.com/NousResearch/hermes-agent/pull/109405) and [#109412](https://github.com/NousResearch/hermes-agent/pull/109412) closed unmerged. Check whether `main` covers each one's piece ([#109404](https://github.com/NousResearch/hermes-agent/pull/109404)'s is covered by `session.detach`). **Checked:** all three pieces are on `main`; #148798 (`e8a469a1`) adds the Desktop tests that were missing. | P3 | 🟢 |

## Decisions to settle

| ID | Decision | EP-1 input | Gates | Status |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| D1 | Which existing startup/discovery path does `serve` reuse, and when does it start the owner versus forward to it? | `gateway_runner` is in-process only, so forwarding means a proxy, and that needs identity forwarding (D2). The evidence favors remote clients attaching to the gateway listener directly (it mounts the same app and auth), with `serve` as a launcher that uses control-socket discovery (`identify`, `session-ticket`). Blockers: `/api/ws` accepts loopback only; no remote ticket path. | EP-3, EP-4, EP-7, EP-8 | 🔵 |
| D2 | Can owner-side authentication preserve current deployments without delegated identity forwarding? | Yes if the gateway authenticates clients itself; it already runs the same auth stack. No if `serve` forwards: tickets, the session token and cookies are process- or origin-bound, so a forwarder collapses every user into one identity. Missing on the gateway: the SSH `--isolated` token and owner nonce, the Desktop env token, the rendezvous-record token, and carrying `dashboard.public_url` to `webapp.public_url`. | EP-3, EP-8 | 🔵 |
| D3 | Which legacy capabilities need mappings before their callers can move? | Of 254 legacy methods: 75 mapped, 14 partial, 163 legacy fallback, 2 refused (`agents.list`, `session.activate`). Gaps: EP-13 (reproduced: 2 client-reachable, both silent); no authority verb tears a session down like `session.close`; host-wide services (pet, projects, MCP, vault, voice, billing, connectors, group replica/peer) run in the owner process outside admission. | stages 2–5 | 🔵 |
| D4 | Which web/SSH changes are inseparable from keeping those entry points supported? | SSH options: (a) run remote `gateway ensure --json` and tunnel to the gateway, with a capability probe and fallback to isolated `serve`; (b) interim: keep isolated `serve` but stop killing it on quit or window close, relying on its 900 s idle retirement and existing reattach. | EP-7, EP-9 | 🔵 |
| D5 | What explicit migration behavior covers version skew and unsupported legacy operations? | No version handshake exists; Desktop infers canonical vs legacy from `?native_dial`. `gateway.capabilities` exists in the contract but no client uses it. Hosted-room peers' `protocol_versions` plus per-capability flags is a working model. | EP-6 | 🔵 |
| D6 | Is authority-less `serve`/`dashboard` still a supported host? If not, fence that backend instead of fixing each producer. | — | EP-9, EP-10, EP-11b, EP-17 | 🔵 |

Open question: [#109417](https://github.com/NousResearch/hermes-agent/issues/109417) closed Sep 21 with no successor found for its forced-migration gates. This tracker doesn't own those gates; it needs to know whether they're met before EP-12.

## Not tracked here

These are separate operational work, not prerequisites for removing the alternate owner: extracting an execution-host interface from the messaging runner, independent adapter supervision, moving storage off the event loop, durable event retention and idle-session eviction.

## Working rules

- Work is grouped into package issues by stage; each package lists its rows, prerequisites, consumers and acceptance evidence.
- Reproduce on current `main` before fixing; no repro means no commit, plus a ⚪ note here.
- PRs use `Refs #<this issue> (EP-n)`, never `Fixes`.
- If an entry point already meets the contract on `main`, mark it 🟢 and leave the code alone.
- Stop and add a 🔵 row when a slice needs a new framework or an unplanned auth/lifecycle policy.

## Found a problem? Report here

Comment on this issue with: `main` SHA, Desktop version if involved, surface and mode (serve / dashboard / SSH / URL / Cloud / browser), OS and topology, steps, expected, actual, and the relevant lines from `gateway.log`, `errors.log` and `desktop.log`. Redact tokens, cookies, tickets and session URLs.

issues.title: Bot Mode: a DM received during a desktop turn cannot be answered — one-reply-path guard assumes a bot-session runner only Bot Chat has

labels.name: type/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working

labels.name: comp/tools
labels.description: Tool registry, model_tools, toolsets

labels.name: tool/file
labels.description: File tools (read, write, patch, search)

labels.name: P2
labels.description: Medium — degraded but workaround exists

issues.body:
## What happens

A Bot Mode DM that arrives during a **desktop-chat** turn cannot be answered.

`tools/bot_mode_dm.py` (v0.23.0, ~line 356):

```python
if (getattr(sender.agent, "_turn_author", None) or {}).get("id") == f"bot:{resolved}":
    # One reply path (#95074): this turn answers @resolved's delivery, whose runner carries the
    # final response back. A second DM races it and lands in their chat as a separate turn.
    return _err(f"@{handle} messaged you this turn and your final response already goes back "
                "to them: put your reply in it instead of messaging them. Do not retry.")
```

The assumption — "this turn's runner carries the final response back" — holds for a **Bot Chat** turn (`gateway/session_bot.py` persists `result['final_response']` and delivers it) and **does not hold for a desktop turn**, which has no such runner.

Net effect on a desktop turn:

* `message_agent` refuses with "Do not retry".
* The final response goes to the human, not to the bot.
* **The bot's message is never answered, and the agent has no tool that can answer it.**

## Reproduction

1. Bot `@peer` DMs an agent whose active session is a desktop chat.
2. The agent calls `message_agent(target="@peer", ...)` to reply.
3. Error: `@peer messaged you this turn and your final response already goes back to them... Do not retry.`
4. The reply only reaches the human. The peer reports being owed a reply.
5. A **new** human message starts a fresh turn where `_turn_author` is no longer the bot, and the same `message_agent` call then succeeds.

Step 5 is what makes this diagnosable: the block is per-turn, not per-conversation.

## Root cause

`agent.turn_author.parse_turn_author()` normalises to `{id, name, is_bot}` — **no surface/platform field**. A Bot Chat turn and a desktop turn are therefore indistinguishable at the guard, so the guard cannot tell whether a runner exists to carry the reply back.

## Suggested fix

Either:

* **(a)** carry a surface/platform field on the turn author (the dispatcher already knows it) and gate the guard on `surface == "bot_chat"`; or
* **(b)** set a marker on the agent **only** from the bot-session runner (the thing that actually persists `final_response`), and gate on that marker's presence rather than on the sender's identity.

(b) is the tighter test: it asks the question the guard actually means — "will something carry my reply back?" — rather than the proxy "did a bot write this turn?"

## Local workaround in use

```python
_allow_explicit = os.environ.get("HERMES_BOT_DM_ALLOW_EXPLICIT", "").strip().lower() in ("1","true","yes")
if not _allow_explicit and (getattr(sender.agent, "_turn_author", None) or {}).get("id") == f"bot:{resolved}":
```

with `HERMES_BOT_DM_ALLOW_EXPLICIT=1` in the profile `.env`. It works, but it is a blunt escape hatch: it also permits the racing second DM that #95074 was filed to prevent.

## Impact

Low severity, high confusion: from the outside it looks like the agent is ignoring its peers, and from the inside there is no available action. It cost several rounds of "did you message X?" in one session, each resolved only by the human sending another message.

issues.title: [Catalog] Add "games" category for game data and community tools

labels.name: comp/plugins
labels.description: Plugin system and bundled plugins

labels.name: P3
labels.description: Low — cosmetic, nice to have

issues.body:
## Summary

Add a new catalog category, `games`, alongside the existing categories
(`desktop`, `memory`, `platform`, `web`, `tools`, `voice`, `automation`, `models`, `general`).

This gives game-related plugins — data readers, trackers, timers and community tools —
a dedicated browse shelf instead of being filed under the catch-all `tools` category.

---

## Motivation

- Game community plugins are a distinct use case: they wrap third-party game APIs,
  expose trackers/timers, and are typically installed by players rather than developers.
- Today such plugins must use `category: tools`, which mixes them into a shelf with
  ~1,200 unrelated entries and makes discovery hard.
- A dedicated category makes the catalog taxonomy match the actual range of plugins
  the community builds.

### Community demand — this is not a one-off plugin

A manual review of the currently published catalog
(`plugins.json`, 2,450 entries) found **19 game-related plugins** under a strict rule:
the plugin's primary purpose is to **play a game, run a game world, or read
game-specific data**. Game-development tools, generic asset/audio utilities,
hardware drivers, streaming setup, and social platforms are excluded.

They are spread across five existing categories instead of sharing a shelf:

| Current category | Game-related plugins found |
|---|---:|
| `desktop` | 7 |
| `general` | 5 |
| `platform` | 3 |
| `tools` | 3 |
| `web` | 1 |
| **Total** | **19** |

Examples of what is currently misfiled:

- **Playable games / companions:** `agent-hold-em`, `agent-inception`,
  `agentic-kingdoms`, `chess-coach`, `gambit`, `hermagotchi`, `hermes-arcade`,
  `hermes-arcade-tui`, `hermes-arena`, `hermes-pokemon`, `hermes-slots`,
  `mahj-trainer`, `popquiz`, `tablekeeper`
- **Game-specific data / platform gateways:** `3ds-platform`, `minecraft-platform`,
  `wow`, `s2docs` (CS2/Deadlock), `thott-bot` (World of Warcraft)

<details>
<summary>Full list — 19 published game-related plugins (strict)</summary>

| Plugin | Current category |
|---|---|
| [`agent-hold-em`](https://github.com/tony-simons-aiowa/agent-hold-em) | desktop |
| [`agent-inception`](https://github.com/ethanwiegert/agent-inception) | desktop |
| [`chess-coach`](https://github.com/oppai/chess-coach) | desktop |
| [`hermes-arena`](https://github.com/JustinPerea/Hermes-arena) | desktop |
| [`hermes-pokemon`](https://github.com/sxuff/hermes-pokemon) | desktop |
| [`hermes-slots`](https://github.com/tuancookiez-hub/hermes-slots) | desktop |
| [`tablekeeper`](https://github.com/kaverimeshram/tablekeeper) | desktop |
| [`agentic-kingdoms`](https://github.com/agenticgamesllc/agent-kit) | general |
| [`hermagotchi`](https://github.com/mojomast/hermagotchi) | general |
| [`hermes-arcade-tui`](https://github.com/Takumixbt/Hermes-Arcade) | general |
| [`mahj-trainer`](https://github.com/jackwallner/mahj) | general |
| [`popquiz`](https://github.com/4n0nn43x/hermes-popquiz) | general |
| [`3ds-platform`](https://github.com/rndaom/Hermes3DS) | platform |
| [`minecraft-platform`](https://github.com/kyssta-exe/hermes-minecraft-gateway) | platform |
| [`wow`](https://github.com/c-pompa/wow-hermes) | platform |
| [`gambit`](https://github.com/itsflownium/gambit-hackathon) | tools |
| [`s2docs`](https://github.com/c-pompa/s2docs) | tools |
| [`thott-bot`](https://github.com/thott-bot/plugin) | tools |
| [`hermes-arcade`](https://github.com/leoresendedop-sys/hermes-arcade) | web |

</details>

In addition, game plugins currently queued in community submissions would also
qualify once the category exists. This is an existing, growing segment of the
catalog — not a special case for a single submission.

---

## Proposal

Add `games` to the canonical category set across the catalog pipeline:

```diff
- desktop | memory | platform | web | tools | voice | automation | models | general
+ desktop | memory | platform | web | tools | voice | automation | models | games | general
```

UI taxonomy entry:

```ts
games: {
  label: 'Games',
  icon: '🎮',
  blurb: 'Game data, trackers and community tools'
}
```

Total categories: **9 → 10**. Existing `models` is preserved.

---

## Scope of Changes

| # | File | Sector | Effect |
|---:|---|---|---|
| 1 | `scripts/validate_plugin_catalog.py` | CI validator | Accept `category: games` |
| 2 | `hermes_cli/plugin_catalog.py` | CLI catalog | `CATALOG_CATEGORIES` includes `games` |
| 3 | `website/scripts/extract-plugins.py` | Docs generator | `byCategory` gains `games` |
| 4 | `apps/shared/src/catalog-browse.ts` | Desktop UI taxonomy | Adds `Games 🎮` shelf |
| 5 | `plugin-catalog/README.md` | Canonical schema | Documents new category |
| 6 | `website/docs/user-guide/features/plugin-catalog.md` | User docs | Updates browse-shelf table |
| 7 | `tests/hermes_cli/test_plugin_catalog.py` | Tests | Asserts `games` is accepted |

Diff: **7 files, 9 insertions, 6 deletions**.

No runtime, gateway, or built-in tool behavior changes.

---

## Verification Performed

| Check | Result |
|---|---|
| Structural catalog validator | PASS on a temporary `category: games` entry |
| CLI taxonomy import | `games: True`, `models: True` |
| Docs generator | `byCategory.games = 1` in a temporary catalog |
| Unit tests | **41 passed** (catalog + extract + rules mirror) |
| Webapp rebuild | Bundle contains the `Games` string |

Coverage lives only in temporary test directories; **no extra entry is added to
`plugin-catalog/`** by this change.

---

## Related Work

- No published catalog entry uses `games` yet.
- After `games` is accepted upstream and the docs feed is republished, open
  community submissions can migrate from `tools` → `games` in small follow-up PRs.
- No plugin code changes are required by this category addition.

---

## Expected Outcome

- `games` becomes a valid catalog category.
- The published `plugins.json` gains a `games` group as soon as one entry uses it.
- The webapp shows a **Games 🎮** browse-shelf filter automatically, driven by feed data.

---

## Notes

- No credentials, tokens, or server IPs are included in this report.
- Verification was performed on a local branch before this issue was opened.
