labels.description: The chat view of the desktop app: composer, sending messages, message rendering, markdown, streaming

issues.body:
## Summary

Bot Mode gives the primary `default` profile a hard-coded mention handle of `@hermes`, even when that profile has a user-chosen display name (for example, `Maia`). Other profiles use their profile name as the handle.

This makes the primary agent visually identifiable as one thing while it must be addressed as another:

```text
Display name: Maia
Mention handle: @hermes
```

## Current behavior

In the bundled Bot Mode plugin, `botHandle()` special-cases the canonical profile:

```js
return (name || '').trim().toLowerCase() === 'default' ? 'hermes' : name
```

`hermes profile rename default Maia` changes the default profile's presentation/display name while retaining `default` as its canonical ID. The mention handle remains `@hermes`.

## Requested behavior

Allow the default profile to have a configurable Bot Mode mention handle, analogous to its configurable display name.

Suggested model:

```text
Canonical profile ID: default       (immutable)
Display name: Maia                 (user-configurable)
Primary mention handle: @maia      (user-configurable)
Legacy alias: @hermes              (preserved)
```

Keeping `@hermes` as an accepted alias preserves existing chats, prompts, and user habits, while allowing named primary agents to have a coherent identity in the Bot Mode roster, @-completion, group-chat prompts, and agent-to-agent delivery notices.

## Acceptance criteria

- The default profile can set a valid, normalized primary Bot Mode handle without changing its canonical ID.
- Bot Mode displays that selected handle instead of hard-coded `@hermes`.
- `@maia` (or the configured handle) resolves to the default profile in @-completion and message routing.
- `@hermes` continues to resolve as a backwards-compatible alias.
- Existing installations retain `@hermes` unless the user elects a custom handle.
- The setting is represented in durable profile metadata/configuration, rather than requiring a local source patch.

## Why this matters

Bot Mode explicitly supports named, persistent agent teams. A first agent with a custom identity should be addressable using the same identity, rather than appearing to be a special exception to the roster's naming model.

issues.title: [Bug]: Compression-exhaustion auto-reset leaves the desktop showing the old segment while the agent runs context-free, and branch then fails with invalid_params

labels.name: type/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working

labels.name: comp/gateway
labels.description: Gateway runner, session dispatch, delivery

labels.name: P2
labels.description: Medium — degraded but workaround exists

labels.name: area/sessions
labels.description: Session lifecycle, resume, persistence, history

labels.name: area/compression
labels.description: Context compression and continuation sessions

issues.body:
## Bug description

When a local-model session overflows its model's context window and a
compression-exhaustion auto-reset fires, the gateway creates a brand-new
child session segment with no carried-over context at all (not even a short
continuation summary). Three problems compound on top of that:

1. **Desktop UI keeps showing the pre-reset transcript.** `get_messages(...,
   include_compacted=True)` continues to project the old/parent segment's
   rows in the displayed transcript, so the user sees an unbroken
   conversation on screen while the live agent is actually running inside
   the brand-new, empty child segment. There is no visible signal that a
   reset happened (same class of problem as #43008, but for the
   compression-exhaustion trigger rather than idle-expiry, and with a
   concrete UI/branch consequence described below).
2. **The agent has zero awareness of what it was doing.** The child segment
   starts with nothing but the next user turn (e.g. a bare "continue"), so
   the model has no memory of the actual task. It is never told a reset
   happened, so it doesn't ask for a recap — it just proceeds, and can
   confidently continue on an entirely unrelated thread it invents or pulls
   from elsewhere in its prompt.
3. **Branch deterministically fails on an affected conversation.** The
   desktop computes its branch's `through_message_id` from the *displayed*
   (parent+child merged) transcript
   (`apps/desktop/src/app/session/hooks/use-session-actions/branch-boundary.ts`).
   But `hermes_state_mutation_branch.py::_branch_boundary` only accepts a
   boundary row that is `active=1` in the exact *physical* target session.
   Any row from before the reset belongs to the parent segment, not the
   child, so the gateway rejects it with a bare `invalid_params` — nothing
   indicates the real cause is "this message lives in a segment this branch
   doesn't continue from."

## Root cause (traced by reading the source this session)

- `gateway/run_turn_persistence.py` (`_hmwa_rotate_exhausted_session`)
  triggers the auto-reset after `compression_exhausted`.
- `hermes_state_local_lineage.py::reset_local_target` creates the new child
  via `_publish_child_session_row(..., system_prompt=None, ...)` — no
  continuation content is ever written into the fresh segment.
- `hermes_state_mutation_branch.py::_branch_boundary` enforces `active=1`
  scoped to the physical target only; it has no way to recognize (or
  explain) a boundary row that belongs to a different, lineage-linked
  segment instead of just being invalid.
- `apps/desktop/src/app/session/hooks/use-session-actions/branch-boundary.ts`
  derives the boundary from the same merged display list the transcript view
  uses, which is exactly where parent-segment rows leak into a branch
  request against the child.

## Reproduction

1. Run a long session on a local model close to its context ceiling (e.g. a
   coding session with large tool outputs) until a turn's prompt exceeds the
   model's context size and compression itself cannot bring it back under
   budget.
2. Observe the auto-reset: `Auto-resetting session ... after compression
   exhaustion` in `gateway.log`, and a new child `session_id` whose first row
   is just the next plain user message.
3. In the desktop, the transcript still shows the full pre-reset history —
   nothing marks where the segment boundary falls.
4. Try to branch from any message that predates the reset. The gateway
   returns `invalid_params` with no further detail.
5. Separately: ask the agent to continue. It has no memory of the actual
   task, because the session silently started over, and may proceed on
   something unrelated instead of recognizing it lost context.

## Expected behavior

- At minimum, the fresh child segment should be seeded with a short,
  automatically generated continuation note (title / last-known-task) —
  the same way a *successful* compression leaves a summary. A *failed*
  compression currently leaves nothing at all.
- The desktop should visibly mark where a reset segment boundary falls in
  the transcript (or disable branching across it), rather than silently
  merging it into one continuous-looking view.
- If a branch boundary is rejected specifically because it names a row
  outside the physical target's lineage, the error should say so (e.g.
  `cross_segment_boundary`) instead of a bare `invalid_params`.

## Related

- #137565 — same trigger (compression-exhaustion auto-reset), different
  downstream symptom (a dropped inbound message rather than a UI/branch
  mismatch).
- #43008 — same class of problem (reset-unawareness), but for idle-expiry
  rather than compression-exhaustion, and without the branch-boundary
  consequence.

issues.title: feat(skills): deterministic opt-in protection for personal skills against agent edits

labels.name: type/feature
labels.description: New feature or request

labels.name: comp/tools
labels.description: Tool registry, model_tools, toolsets

labels.name: tool/file
labels.description: File tools (read, write, patch, search)

labels.name: tool/skills
labels.description: Skills system (list, view, manage)

labels.name: P3
labels.description: Low — cosmetic, nice to have

issues.body:
### Description

I use Hermes daily with personal skills that I build and refine over time, accumulating operational details, configurations, and workflows discovered in the field.

The problem is that **Hermes, by design, encourages the agent to "improve" skills whenever possible**. This is intended behavior, not a bug — the agent does what it's asked to do.

The point is: for some skills this is helpful, for others **it's destructive**. I have skills representing weeks of work — carefully structured, with specific information that should not be touched. In one case, an agent aggressively rewrote a skill, discarding valuable information. I recovered from a backup, but the damage was real.

This cannot be solved with soft prompts or instructions to the AI. An agent can ignore guidelines, especially in complex multi-step contexts. **We need deterministic, tool-level protection.**

### Requirements

- **Absolute block, not a suggestion** — protection must be enforced at the tool level (skill_manager_tool.py), not in AI prompts. A protected skill must be unmutable: no patch, edit, overwrite, or delete, period.
- **Opt-in, per-skill** — not all skills need protection. Only the ones the user explicitly chooses. Some skills must remain editable for ongoing improvements.
- **Simple CLI** — `hermes skills protect <name>` to lock, `hermes skills protect <name> --unprotect` to unlock
- **Opt-in at creation time (bonus)** — when the agent creates a new skill (e.g. on "save this procedure as a skill"), it could ask the user: "Do you want to make it read-only (protected) or leave it editable?" This prevents forgetting to protect a skill right after creation.
- **Robust mechanism** — corruption-proof marker (e.g. .protected dotfile, not YAML frontmatter) to avoid any risk of SKILL.md corruption

### Related PR

- **#36924** — `feat(skills): protect skills from agent edits via .protected dotfile`
  *Implemented exactly this: `hermes skills protect` CLI, .protected dotfile marker, block in skill_manager_tool.py. Was closed by the author without merge or explanation. Would be ideal to revive and adapt it, potentially integrating the creation-time opt-in question.*

### Why it matters

For anyone seriously using Hermes with personal skills built over time, **knowing that certain skills cannot be touched** is the bare minimum to trust the system. Protection must be opt-in because not all skills need to be locked down — some must remain editable for the agent to improve them. **The choice belongs to the user, not the agent.**

issues.title: gateway: housekeeping malloc_trim blocks 37-88 s on a swap-heavy host and drops every connected kanban worker

labels.name: type/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working

labels.name: comp/gateway
labels.description: Gateway runner, session dispatch, delivery

labels.name: area/config
labels.description: Config system, migrations, profiles

labels.name: P2
labels.description: Medium — degraded but workaround exists

issues.body:
## Summary

On a swap-heavy Linux host, the messaging gateway's housekeeping `malloc_trim(0)` (`gateway/run.py::_housekeeping_memory_trim` → `hermes_cli.mem_trim.trim_memory`) blocks the gateway process for **37–88 seconds per call**. During one such stall, every connected kanban worker turn is lost at once.

## Evidence (live gateway, generation gen-fe159c2e, Python 3.14.7, glibc, Fedora 44)

Host: 16 GB RAM, about 13 GB of 32 GB swap in use, load1 ≈ 14.

`agent.log`, consecutive housekeeping trims:

```
06:06:33 memory trim: reason=messaging gateway housekeeping malloc_trim=1 rss_kib=503296->1004468 ... threads=86 duration_ms=50713.3
06:10:21 ... duration_ms=37746.4
06:14:01 ... duration_ms=88069.6
06:17:33 ... rss_kib=418308->980236 ... duration_ms=71567.0
```

RSS **doubles** during the trim (503 MB → 1004 MB). `malloc_trim` walks the arenas and faults swapped-out heap pages back in, so the call is bound by swap-in I/O rather than CPU.

What one stall did (06:05:42 → 06:06:33):
- three `agent.managed_worker` processes aborted at 06:06:23 with SIGABRT in `_Py_Finalize` → `_io__Buffered_close_impl` → `_enter_buffered_busy`. That is the "could not acquire lock for <_io.BufferedWriter name='<stdout>'> at interpreter shutdown" fatal error, raised while they exited after losing the gateway;
- at 06:06:33 the gateway logged `Managed worker lost: managed_worker_failed` ×3 and `EOFError` ×1, followed by a burst of `tui_gateway.ws: ws send failed … WebSocketDisconnect` and `ws response send failed … method=worker.persist`;
- the workers printed "⚠️ No reply: Hermes couldn't save this conversation" at 06:06:05, and at 06:08:46 four kanban worker runs exited with `Kanban owner refused: Gateway disconnected; turn outcome is unknown`.

## Expected

The trim is housekeeping. It should never block the gateway long enough to drop connected workers.

## Suggested direction

Any one of these would do:
- run the trim off the event-loop thread with a wall-clock budget, and skip or back off it while the process has significant swapped-out memory (`VmSwap` in `/proc/self/status`);
- or skip it when the last trim took longer than a threshold;
- or default `context.memory_trim.enabled` to off when swap usage is high.

Workaround in use: `context.memory_trim.enabled: false`. It is read on every attempt, so no restart is needed.

Related: #145999 (event-loop block → 30 s liveness watchdog), #143174 (RSS ratchet / trims), #140158 (trim log level).

issues.body:
## Summary

On Windows, the Electron **main process** of the desktop app stalls for 2.1–3.9 seconds
repeatedly (every ~1–4 minutes) while the user is actively using the app, typically once per
message send / turn start. During each stall the main process consumes **zero CPU**, has zero sampled system disk queue / page-ins, no observed child-process creations, and no observed store-lock directory —
consistent with a blocking wait, but not sufficient to identify a syscall or thread stack (e.g.
`Atomics.wait`-style sleep loops or a blocking system-service call such as DPAPI/LSASS).
The UI is completely unresponsive for the duration. No data loss or corruption observed.

Minute-scale "lagged" entries in the same log are a **separate, excluded class**: they match
Modern Standby sleep/wake intervals on this machine (verified against Kernel-Power events) and
are not part of this report.

## Environment

- Hermes Agent v0.23.2+14.g40d1e95 (2026.9.24), upstream `40d1e95f37e409f9f618f32c170661c66b86a4f4`, install method `git`,
  updated 2026-11-17 09:09 local. This is the captured installed build, not a claim about latest upstream main at filing time.
- Windows 11 Insider build 28020, x64, 32 GB RAM (3–7 GB free during captures), Modern Standby (S0) machine.
- Bundled Python 3.14.9; OpenAI SDK 2.54.0.
- Third-party AV present: Huorong (`hipsdaemon.exe` / `hipstray.exe`). Possible amplifier, **not tested**.
- Session store: `state.db` ≈ 450 MB, 340 sessions, largest single session ≈ 14 MB (context for payload sizes;
  stalls are zero-CPU, so not compute-bound on these payloads).
- Gateway runs as a separate resident Python process; desktop connects over local HTTP/WS.

## Symptom pattern

- Only while the UI is in use (typing, sending messages, switching sessions). Idle windows of 5+ minutes
  show no second-scale stalls.
- Cadence during use: one stall every ~70–250 s; each 2.1–3.9 s.
- Onset correlates with turn start: e.g. stall 17:25:43.823–17:25:46.863 begins ~1 s after the gateway
  logs a new turn (agent.log 17:25:42.846–42.954, tool-registry checks / credential-pool probe).
- Several durations cluster at 3.0–3.2 s, close to `LOCK_WAIT_MS = 3000` in
  `apps/desktop/electron/gateway-connections-store.ts`; others reach 3.8–3.9 s (above that cap).

### Second-scale stall log (2026-11-17, desktop.log `[diagnostics] main-process event loop lagged`)

| observed at | lag ms | stall window (expected tick → observed) |
|---|---|---|
| 09:48:47.430 | 3859 | 09:48:43.571 → 09:48:47.430 |
| 09:53:37.473 | 3344 | 09:53:34.129 → 09:53:37.473 |
| 09:54:43.278 | 2210 | 09:54:41.068 → 09:54:43.278 |
| 09:56:54.025 | 2550 | 09:56:51.475 → 09:56:54.025 |
| 10:17:31.793 | 2927 | 10:17:28.866 → 10:17:31.793 |
| 10:19:44.627 | 3637 | 10:19:40.990 → 10:19:44.627 |
| 12:09:16.833 | 2127 | 12:09:14.706 → 12:09:16.833 |
| 12:18:04.581 | 3483 | 12:18:01.098 → 12:18:04.581 |
| 12:31:12.362 | 2598 | 12:31:09.764 → 12:31:12.362 |
| 12:55:50.441 | 2912 | 12:55:47.529 → 12:55:50.441 |
| 13:14:02.796 | 3066 | 13:13:59.730 → 13:14:02.796 |
| 14:19:40.500 | 3946 | 14:19:36.554 → 14:19:40.500 |
| 16:30:07.137 | 3108 | 16:30:04.029 → 16:30:07.137 |
| 16:33:18.813 | 3208 | 16:33:15.605 → 16:33:18.813 |
| 16:34:31.832 | 2354 | 16:34:29.478 → 16:34:31.832 |
| 16:35:42.612 | 3887 | 16:35:38.725 → 16:35:42.612 |
| 16:38:54.601 | 3247 | 16:38:51.354 → 16:38:54.601 |
| 16:42:01.947 | 2850 | 16:41:59.097 → 16:42:01.947 |
| 16:43:11.677 | 2837 | 16:43:08.840 → 16:43:11.677 |
| 16:47:28.688 | 2840 | 16:47:25.848 → 16:47:28.688 |
| 16:51:28.891 | 3818 | 16:51:25.073 → 16:51:28.891 |
| 16:55:20.914 | 3786 | 16:55:17.128 → 16:55:20.914 |
| 17:13:26.669 | 2299 | 17:13:24.370 → 17:13:26.669 |
| 17:25:46.863 | 3040 | 17:25:43.823 → 17:25:46.863 |
| 17:29:16.797 | 3114 | 17:29:13.683 → 17:29:16.797 |
| 17:32:55.268 | 3448 | 17:32:51.820 → 17:32:55.268 |

(Last four captured live by a 1 s / 100 ms monitor; the rest from desktop.log.)

## Evidence

### E1 — During a stall: main CPU = 0, disk queue = 0, page faults = 0

Per-second sampling of the main process (PID 29124) CPU delta, `\PhysicalDisk(_Total)\Current Disk Queue
Length`, `\Memory\Pages Input/sec` across the 17:25:43.823–46.863 stall (2 s granularity due to counter
query cost; each line's delta covers the preceding interval):

```
17:25:30 main=0.56 diskq=0.0 pagesIn=8
17:25:32 main=0.53 diskq=0.0 pagesIn=335
17:25:34 main=0.47 diskq=0.0 pagesIn=984
17:25:36 main=0.66 diskq=0.0 pagesIn=2
17:25:38 main=0.41 diskq=0.0 pagesIn=0
17:25:40 main=0.38 diskq=0.0 pagesIn=16
17:25:42 main=0.27 diskq=0.0 pagesIn=1
17:25:44 main=0.41 diskq=0.0 pagesIn=0     <- interval straddles stall onset (43.823)
17:25:46 main=0.00 diskq=0.0 pagesIn=0     <- fully inside stall: zero CPU, zero I/O, zero faults
17:25:48 main=0.16 diskq=0.0 pagesIn=9
17:25:50 main=0.22 diskq=0.0 pagesIn=28
```

A 1 s monitor of the same process printed CPU-spike lines (>0.2 cores/s) continuously before
(17:25:27–42: 0.20–0.38) and after (17:25:54+: 0.20–0.30) the stall, and **none during** it.
=> Consistent with low-CPU blocking rather than sustained compute during this sample. These are process/system counters, not a main-thread stack or per-process I/O trace; they cannot completely exclude synchronous I/O or other waits.

### E2 — No child process spawn and no store-lock hold during stalls

A polling watch (nominal 100 ms sleep for lock paths; process census and log tail every fourth iteration, plus CIM execution time)
covering the 17:32:51.820–55.268 stall recorded **no** `gateway-connections.json.lock` /
`gateway-connection-tokens.json.lock` appearance and **no** new child of the main process:

```
17:32:55.533 LOG ... lagged 3448ms (expected tick ...971820, observed ...975268)
17:33:06.478 SPAWN pid=19016 parent=29124 name=hermes.exe cmd=...\.hermes\bin\hermes.exe --version
17:33:06.488 SPAWN pid=20320 parent=29124 name=git.exe cmd=...git.exe rev-list --count 40d1e95f...
17:34:01.606 SPAWN pid=7276  parent=29124 name=hermes.exe cmd=...hermes.exe --version
17:34:01.608 SPAWN pid=36984 parent=29124 name=git.exe cmd=...git.exe status --porcelain -b -u --null --untracked
17:34:16.420 SPAWN pid=30416 parent=29124 name=git.exe
17:35:49.856 SPAWN pid=32612 parent=29124 name=git.exe
17:36:03.404 SPAWN pid=33400 parent=29124 name=git.exe
17:36:15.503 SPAWN pid=38712 parent=29124 name=git.exe cmd=...git.exe status --porcelain -b -u --null --untracked
17:36:31.503 SPAWN pid=32816 parent=29124 name=git.exe
```

=> No corresponding child process or lock directory was observed. Polling can miss short-lived processes/locks, and cannot exclude a wait on an existing child or a blocking filesystem/system-service call. This narrows hypotheses but does not conclusively rule them out.
Note the separate observation: main spawns `git status --porcelain -b -u --null --untracked` about every
15 s and `hermes.exe --version` + `git rev-list` about every 60 s. Whether those are sync or async was not
determined; their timestamps do not align with the captured stalls.

### E3 — Not system sleep

Kernel-Power events 16:25–17:00 contain only the 16:29:00 wake (Id 566 session 172→174, Id 507 exit,
reason Input Mouse). No power event at any second-scale stall onset in that window.
By contrast the minute-scale lags DO align with sleep: e.g. lag 810852 ms observed 14:33:17.391
(expected tick 14:19:46.539) matches standby entry ~14:19:40 (Id 507 "Restricted Standby Battery Drain
Budget Exceeded") → wake 14:33:17 (Id 507 Lid). Those are sleep durations reported by the timer
diagnostic, excluded from this issue.

### E4 — Trigger correlation with turn start / store touch

agent.log at the onset of the E1 stall:

```
17:25:42,846 INFO tools.registry: check_fn _a2a_tools_available returned False ...
17:25:42,925 INFO agent.auxiliary_client: Vision auto-detect: using main provider codekey-gpt (gpt-6.1-sol)
17:25:42,946 INFO agent.credential_pool: credential pool xai-oauth: no available entries ...
```

i.e. a user message began a turn ~1 s before the main thread froze. Stalls occur only during active use.

### E5 — Post-wake ticket bootstrap failures (related, separate symptom)

After wakes, desktop.log shows `Gateway ticket bootstrap failed` at `TicketBridge.receive/dispose`
(e.g. 12:07:24, 14:33:17) followed by backend connect timeouts. `TicketBridge`
(`apps/desktop/electron/local-gateway-python.ts:61–153`) is fully async (spawn + pipe events + Promise,
10 s dispose timeout at :96), so it cannot itself block the main loop; it explains the post-wake error
burst and helper respawns (a replacement ticket helper python was spawned 17:08:13, coincident with a
133 s post-wake lag), not the second-scale stalls.

## Hypotheses investigated (sampling limitations apply)

| Hypothesis | Verdict | Evidence |
|---|---|---|
| Main-thread compute (JSON/IPC of large payloads) | not supported by these samples; not conclusively excluded | E1: zero CPU during stall |
| Disk I/O congestion / sync file read | not supported by these samples; not conclusively excluded | E1: disk queue 0, pagesIn 0 |
| Memory pressure / paging | not supported by these samples; not conclusively excluded | E1: pagesIn 0; 3–7 GB free |
| Modern Standby micro-sleep | not supported by these samples; not conclusively excluded | E3: no power events at onsets |
| Sync child_process (PowerShell liveness probe, git, hermes --version) | not observed during captured stalls | E2: no spawns during stalls |
| `withStoreLockSync` lock contention (sleepSync loop) | not observed during captured stalls | E2: lock dirs never present at 100 ms |
| TicketBridge async wait | async implementation; no direct blocking stack captured | async Promise/pipe design, E5 |

## Remaining suspect (unverified)

One unverified possibility is a blocking system-service call on the main thread, including
**synchronous secret decryption (Electron `safeStorage` / Windows DPAPI → LSASS RPC)** on the
connection/token store read path (`decrypt` dependency, `gateway-connections-store.ts:98`,
`native-token-store`), executed per store touch (per turn / per refresh). Such a wait shows zero CPU in
the calling process, no disk queue, no children, no lock hold — exactly E1+E2. Pinning the exact syscall
requires admin ETW stack sampling, not yet performed.

## Code pointers (at upstream 40d1e95f)

Candidate synchronous-wait sites for instrumentation; none has been proven responsible for these stalls:

1. `apps/desktop/electron/gateway-connections-store.ts:127`
   `const sleepSync = (ms) => Atomics.wait(new Int32Array(new SharedArrayBuffer(4)), 0, 0, ms)`
   used by `withStoreLockSync` (:181–216): sync `fs.mkdirSync` lock + `sleepSync(LOCK_POLL_MS=20)` retry
   until `LOCK_WAIT_MS=3000` (:62–64). Lock is shared with the Python writer
   (`hermes_cli/gateway_connections.py:122` via `ui_preferences._store_lock`).
2. `apps/desktop/electron/desktop-installation.ts:41–44` `waitForRepair()` = `Atomics.wait(..., 25)`;
   :56–75 comment states the holder-liveness probe on Windows is "a PowerShell of up to 15 s,
   ... blocking the main thread".
3. Sync `fs.readFileSync` + `JSON.parse` store reads (`readDoc`, :134–158) and the `decrypt` dependency
   (:98) on the same path — candidates for the zero-CPU system-service wait.

## Reproduction

1. Windows, desktop app with a large session history (hundreds of sessions / hundreds of MB state.db).
2. Use the app normally: send messages, switch sessions.
3. Watch `logs/desktop.log` for `[diagnostics] main-process event loop lagged 2000–4000ms` entries
   every 1–4 minutes; each onset follows a turn start by ~1 s.
4. Correlate with per-second main-process CPU (expect 0 during the stall) and a polling watch of
   `gateway-connections.json.lock` / child spawns (expect neither).
   Helper scripts were used locally (sampling details below; no external attachment is required) (PowerShell, run with `-ExecutionPolicy Bypass -File`):
   `freeze_watch2.ps1` (1 s CPU-spike + lag tail), `combined_watch.ps1` (100 ms lock/spawn/lag),
   `lock_watch.ps1` (lock hold durations), `measure_idle.ps1 -Target <pid>` (idle IO/CPU baseline).

## Suggested fix directions

- Move store lock acquisition, secret decryption, and holder-liveness probes off the main thread
  (worker thread + async IPC), or make the lock wait async with cancellation; never `Atomics.wait`
  on the Electron main thread.
- Cache decrypted token material in memory with a TTL instead of decrypting per store touch.
- Make the ~15 s `git status --porcelain -u` and ~60 s `hermes --version`/`rev-list` polls async and
  debounced; they are additional main-thread spawn candidates.
- Make post-wake ticket bootstrap non-blocking and retry-with-backoff instead of dispose-on-timeout
  storms (E5).

## Limitations

- Exact blocking syscall not pinned (needs admin ETW); the DPAPI/LSASS suspect is inference from the
  zero-CPU signature plus code path, not direct observation.
- Single machine; Huorong AV present and untested as an amplifier (exclusion experiment not run).
- Minute-scale lags excluded as sleep; mid-scale (10–65 s) lags cluster immediately after wakes/boots
  and are treated as post-wake recovery, not analyzed here.

## Related reports and scope

- #151348: similar Windows Electron main-process stalls, attributed there to the no-console git Python host. This capture has no observed coincident child creation; the same cause is not established or fully excluded.
- #139859: main-process stall followed by process death; this report concerns recoverable 2–4 s stalls, with no crash observed.
- #140492: startup-only stall on macOS; these captures are during normal active Windows use.
- #153046: Python gateway event-loop blocking; the watchdog here explicitly reports the Electron main process.
- #145979: our earlier streaming GPU issue; this is separate main-process event-loop latency, not a demonstrated rendering/GPU cause.

## Evidence provenance and privacy

Diagnostic notes and polling scripts were collected locally using Qoder. The reporter's local desktop.log was independently checked at filing time: the 17:25:46.863 / 3040 ms and 17:32:55.268 / 3448 ms entries are present, along with subsequent 2554 ms and 2583 ms entries at 17:37:07.204 and 17:38:43.544. CPU/lock observations above are the saved capture notes; no ETW trace, main-thread stack, or raw counter output file was supplied. No credentials, full configuration, private chat text, or database are uploaded. All capture times are local China Standard Time (UTC+08:00).

The combined watcher checks two lock paths after a nominal 100 ms sleep, and runs a Win32_Process census every fourth iteration (actual intervals include CIM overhead). The CPU watcher samples process cumulative CPU at nominal 1 s intervals and only prints deltas above 0.2 seconds. Absence of a printed spike alone is not proof of exactly zero CPU; the explicit 0.00 sample in E1 is the stronger observation.

issues.body:
## Goal
Hosted Hermes serves many tenants from **one shared process**. Tenants do not get a process each.

Nothing tenant-controlled runs in that process:
- tenant code runs in a remote sandbox;
- only Nous-curated plugins and MCP servers load in-process; plugins and MCP servers a user adds run only inside that agent's sandbox (item L);
- a tenant supplies data only: prompts, tool arguments, skill text, and files moved through the sandbox.

So the risk inside the process is trusted Hermes code mixing up state between tenants, not hostile code. The design closes that risk with four boundaries that sit outside Python's object graph:

| Resource | Boundary | Where it lives |
|---|---|---|
| Data | Postgres row-level security pinned to the turn's scope; a query that forgets the scope sees zero rows | storage port (D–E) |
| Secrets | a store keyed by scope; nothing tenant-owned in `os.environ` | secret port (F) |
| Execution | a remote sandbox per agent | sandbox port (H) |
| In-memory state | a lint plus frozen registries plus a canary test | A, J |

**Scope of this issue:** hermes-agent core only. Core defines each interface, ships a **local backend that behaves exactly as Hermes does today**, adds a conformance suite that any backend must pass, and enforces the hosted-mode rules. The hosted backends are separate plugins built by Ben: Postgres/RLS storage, the Postgres turn-admission lease, the encrypted secret store, the blob bucket, the Sprites sandbox and the signed-frame verifier.

## Vocabulary (already in code after #141877, module `hermes_scope`)
- `Scope(tenant, agent, actor)` is bound for every activity: turns, cron ticks, eviction, boot probes and RPC handlers.
  - `actor` is `Principal(id)`, a tenant member, or `System(reason)`, e.g. `System("boot")` or `System("cron")`.
- `TurnScope` adds `session_id` and `turn_id`. Only turn paths build one.
- A local install runs as `Scope("local", <profile home path>, LOCAL_OWNER)`.
- `hermes_scope.current_scope()` returns the bound scope.
- `agent.runtime_scope.bind_profile_scope` / `bind_state` are the only ways to bind one.
- `ScopeSwitchRefused` is raised when hosted code tries to change agent mid-activity.
- **Rule for every interface below:** it reads tenant, agent and actor from the bound scope, never from a path, `HERMES_HOME`, a tool argument or a frame field. Calling a hosted backend with no scope bound returns nothing or raises. It never falls back to a default.

## Ownership key: every stored record carries (tenant, subject, agent)
**Ownership chain:** Tenant → (Principal | Group) → Agent.
- Every agent has exactly one owner: a **principal** (a personal agent) or a **group** (a shared agent: a support bot, a collaborative desktop agent, a shared chat-platform agent). Hermes Cloud already does this: an org owner or admin can reassign an agent to the org or one of its groups (`AgentIdentity`).
- A personal agent is not shared by default. Its owner may share it (Hermes Cloud's `MEMBERS`, `GROUPS` or `ORG` access); a teammate's turn then runs on it as that teammate, without the right to administer it. Hermes Cloud's hosted agents already default to `CREATOR_ONLY`.
- Everyone who interacts with an agent is an authorised tenant member. There is no guest actor in v1.

Every record in every store (D, E, F and the D6 registry) carries `tenant_id`, `subject_id` and `agent_id`. The subject is a principal or a group. Either of the last two may be `NULL`, meaning "applies to all" within the tenant. That gives four levels:

| Level | `subject_id` | `agent_id` | Example |
|---|---|---|---|
| participant-on-agent | principal P | X | P's own conversations with agent X; files from those conversations; P's `USER.md` on a group agent |
| agent | NULL | X | X's API keys, memory, skills, cron jobs, user plugins switched on (everything that is per agent today) |
| owner-wide | the owner (principal or group) | NULL | a secret or skill a person or group sets once for all the agents it owns |
| tenant-wide | NULL | NULL | an org-wide secret or skill |

- **Agent-level records never name the owner** (`subject_id` is NULL whoever owns the agent). This keeps the owner's own conversations on X (participant-on-agent, `(owner, X)`) from colliding with X's records. It also means moving an agent between owners (person to group, group to group) rewrites no rows: only resolution changes. The owner is stored once, on the agent.
- **The scope carries the owner and whether the activity may administer the agent.** These are `Scope.owner: Principal | Group` and `Scope.can_administer: bool` (done in #149200).
  - Hosted: the identity verifier (C) takes both from the connector's signed claim. Hermes stores no group memberships; the connector owns them, as it owns tenants.
  - Local: the owner is `LOCAL_OWNER`, and it may administer.
  - A record's level is decided by the store, from the scope, never by a caller-supplied id.
- **Reads resolve through one documented policy function in core,** with the same precedence for every store and every kind of owner. When principal P runs a turn on agent X owned by O:
  1. participant-on-agent `(P, X)`, only for per-participant kinds (conversations, conversation files, and `USER.md` on a group agent);
  2. agent `(NULL, X)`;
  3. owner-wide `(O, NULL)`;
  4. tenant-wide `(NULL, NULL)`.

  A member's own owner-wide records never apply to a group's agent, because that agent's owner is the group, not the member. Changing the policy later is a change to this one function and its tests, not to any schema or backend.
- **`USER.md`:** per participant whenever more than one person uses the agent (a group agent, or a personal agent its owner shared), so the agent keeps separate facts about each person; agent level on an unshared personal agent.
- **Writes** say their level explicitly. Who may write:
  - agent level, **through a turn** (memory, skills and the other learning the agent does today): anyone whose turn runs on the agent;
  - agent level, **administration** (keys, settings, plugins and MCP servers, cron, deletion): a scope with `can_administer`. The claim decides it; in Hermes Cloud that is a personal agent's owner, and the org's owners and admins for an agent owned by the org or a group;
  - owner-wide: the principal, for a personal owner; the org's owners and admins, for a group;
  - tenant-wide: a tenant admin;
  - participant-on-agent: that participant.

  Any other write is refused, and the refusal never reveals whether the target exists.
- **Local backends** store only the agent level until M (today's files and SQLite, where every agent is owned by `LOCAL_OWNER`). They declare that, and they refuse writes at other levels with a clear error. The conformance suite tests resolution against backends that declare all four levels, and tests the refusal against backends that don't. Both are real tests, never skips.
- **Ownership invariants**, part of every store's conformance suite:
  - P's participant-on-agent records are invisible to another member of the same group agent;
  - an owner-wide record of O resolves on every agent O owns and on no other agent; in particular, a member's own owner-wide records never resolve on a group agent;
  - a turn without `can_administer` can update the agent's memory and skills but cannot change its keys, settings, plugins or cron;
  - moving an agent between owners changes resolution only at step 3 and moves no rows;
  - a write at a level the actor may not write is refused.

## Ground rules for every PR
1. **Local behaviour does not change.** The local backend is today's code moved behind the interface, and the existing suite stays green.
2. **Each interface is a plugin kind,** following `plugins/AGENTS.md`.
   - It is selected by config.
   - Core never imports a hosted backend.
   - Hosted mode refuses to boot if a required backend is missing (B).
3. **Each interface ships a conformance suite** in core.
   - It is parametrized over backends: the local one in CI, and plugins import and run the same suite.
   - It includes the isolation invariants listed under each item.
4. **Tests merge green.**
   - The PR body shows each isolation test failing against a deliberately broken backend (scope pin removed, guard bypassed).
   - No xfail/skip tests.
   - A test that needs a service it cannot reach **fails**, never skips.
5. One PR per item. Items can be split per family where noted.

## Review and merge order
Each PR is stacked on the one before it, so review and merge them in this order. After each merge, the next PR is rebased onto main and its full suite is re-run on the new head before it merges.

| # | PR | What it does | State |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | NousResearch/hermes-agent#141373 | Renames `session_contract.Principal` to `SessionActor`, so `Principal` means a tenant member | Merged |
| 2 | NousResearch/hermes-agent#141809 | Kanban worker spawn binds the assignee's whole scope; a routed worker's environment comes from an explicit allowlist that keeps the instance's config deployment and managed dir | MERGED 2026-11-11 |
| 3 | NousResearch/hermes-agent#141877 | One `Scope` value for home, secrets and terminal policy; HX014. Merged with main; fixes a cold cross-profile Remote Config read | MERGED 2026-11-11 |
| 4 | NousResearch/hermes-agent#149200 | `Scope` names the agent's owner and whether the activity may administer it; every turn carries its claim fence | MERGED 2026-11-11 |
| 5 | NousResearch/hermes-agent#149924 | H. A hosted agent's tools reach only its own sandbox: deny-by-default tool allowlist, one host-feature switch, scoped process streams, required idle suspension | MERGED 2026-11-11 |
| 6 | NousResearch/hermes-agent#149940 | A. Refuse shared mutable state on the hosted path (HX015 over the hosted import graph, with a ratchet) and freeze registries after hosted boot | Review only its own commits: `git diff dd51609e4e 4597282515` (reviewer approved after 6 rounds) |
| 7 | NousResearch/hermes-agent#151553 | D1/G. ### C. Inbound identity verifier → #141877, B
- **Interface:** `IdentityVerifier.verify(frame) -> VerifiedTurn | Refusal`, given the raw relay inbound frame. `VerifiedTurn` carries the proven identity only; turn admission adds the session, turn and fence when it builds the `TurnScope` (`VerifiedTurn.turn_scope(session, turn, fence)`), because a signature cannot issue a fence.
  - It returns `tenant`, `agent`, the agent's `owner` (a principal or a group), whether the actor may administer the agent, and `actor=Principal(id)`, all taken from a claim the connector signed, plus the session and turn ids.
  - A principal with no access to the agent is refused, the same as an unknown agent.
  - The verifier, not core, owns the signature scheme and keys.
- **Core:** the relay intake calls the verifier once per inbound frame and binds the returned `TurnScope` for the whole turn.
  - Fields in the frame body that assert a tenant, principal, group, owner, administration right or agent are ignored. Only the verified claim counts.
  - **The connector sends no per-turn claim today.** An inbound frame is `{type:"inbound", event, bufferId?}`; the only authentication is the HMAC token checked when the gateway's socket connects, and tenant and agent come from the connector's record for that socket. (The seal in `gateway/session_ingress_context.py` is Hermes sealing its own record, not a connector signature.) The claim is new work on both sides; the proposed wire contract is the optional, additive `claim` described in "Connector dependency" below.
- **Local:** no verifier. The scope stays `(local, <profile>, LOCAL_OWNER)`, exactly as today.
- **Hosted:**
  - an unsigned, invalid or expired claim is dropped, never routed to a default tenant or agent;
  - a frame for an agent the verifier does not admit produces the same response as an unknown agent, byte for byte.
- **Gates, with a stub verifier:**
  - forged-claim test;
  - the claim decides administration: a claim without it cannot change the agent's keys or plugins;
  - a body-asserted tenant is refused;
  - an unknown agent and a foreign agent are indistinguishable;
  - a route miss drops the frame.

- **Connector dependency (NousResearch/gateway-gateway; the connector owner's work, not this handover's). In review as drafts: NousResearch/gateway-gateway#448 (claim signing, JWKS, owner/admins on the access sync) and NousResearch/hermes-portal#2064 (NAS sends owner/admins, behind a flag that stays off until the connector ships).** The verifier needs the connector to mint, per delivered inbound frame, a signed claim carrying `v, iss, aud, exp, jti, tenant, agent, actor, owner{kind: principal|group, id}, admin: bool`, bound to the event by a hash. Proposed shape, all additive within `contract_version 1`:
  - an optional `claim` key on the inbound frame (Hermes ignores unknown keys today), advertised as `supports_turn_claim` in the capability descriptor; Ed25519 signature with a published JWKS, fetched by Hermes only from its configured issuer (the claim's `iss` is checked against it, never used to find keys);
  - minted in `RelaySession.deliverInbound`, which both the live path and the buffered drain go through, per already-admitted target (the delivery gate's admitted set is unchanged; the tenant-leakage matrix must stay green);
  - access: the actor is the owner, or reaches the agent through its access setting (an owner's share, or membership of the owning group); anyone else gets no claim, and Hermes refuses the frame;
  - `admin`: the owner of a personal agent; for an agent owned by the org or a group, the org's owners and admins (as Hermes Cloud decides today). NAS sends it, so the connector needs no role table.
- **Where the agent's owner comes from.** Hermes Cloud already lets an org OWNER or ADMIN reassign an agent to the org or to one of its groups: NAS keeps an `AgentIdentity` (kind `ORG` or `GROUP`) whose service-account user becomes the agent's `createdById`, and that user is what the connector stores as the agent's `creator`. So the connector already knows the owner; the claim maps a creator that is an `AgentIdentity` user to `owner{kind: group, id}` (or the org), and any other creator to `owner{kind: principal, id}`. The connector needs that mapping from NAS (the identity kind and group id), not a new ownership table.
- **Unverified authors are refused in hosted mode** (decided). The `any` and `allow-list` channel policies admit platform users with no proven tenant principal; such an author has no actor, so the connector mints no claim and the hosted verifier refuses the turn. The connector's channel gate is unchanged (it also governs agents that are not hosted).

### D. Storage port → #141877. Split into D1–D6, one PR per table family. D1 and G land together: the lease and fence live in D1's tables, and D1's writes check them. **D1 in review: NousResearch/hermes-agent#151553, NousResearch/hermes-agent#151554, NousResearch/hermes-agent#151555**
- **Interface:** one port per family, with operations at the level today's call sites use, not SQL.
  - Every operation runs inside a **transaction pinned to the bound scope**: the backend receives `(tenant, agent, owner, actor)` at transaction start, from the scope. Every row carries the ownership key above.
  - The port exposes no way to pin anything else.
  - **Two pin levels:**
    - non-turn activities (cron ticks, eviction, boot probes, RPC handlers) bind a `Scope` and pin `(tenant, agent, owner, actor)`;
    - turns bind a `TurnScope`, and the pin also carries `session_id`, `turn_id` and the turn's **fence**: the lease token G issued when this replica claimed the turn (`runtime_generation` + `owner_epoch`).
  - **Fenced writes:** every write to session-owned data runs in a transaction whose fence the backend checks against the session's current lease, in the same transaction. Session-owned data means messages, session state, admissions, compression results, child sessions, and conversation files in E. A replica that lost the lease (paused, partitioned, slow) has its write rejected, never applied. A turn-path write with no fence is refused.
  - **Stateless across replicas:** a backend holds no per-agent or per-profile connection, path or cache in the process. Connections come from a shared pool and are pinned per transaction, so any replica can run any agent's turn. In-process caches follow A's scope-keyed rule.
  - The local backend is today's SQLite (`hermes_state*.py`, `kanban.db`, `cron/`).
  - **`assert_isolating()`:** a backend method that hosted boot (B) calls. A Postgres backend fails it when its role is a superuser or has `BYPASSRLS`.
- **Families:**
  - **D1 sessions/messages,** including child sessions, `response_store`, pending messages, `session_admissions` and runtime generations (`hermes_state_runtime.py`).
    - Conversations are participant-on-agent records: rows carry the participant's `subject_id` and the participant set, and a principal sees only conversations it takes part in.
    - Direct messages and per-user group sessions belong to one participant. Shared threads admit all participants. This follows today's session-key rules: `group_sessions_per_user`, `thread_sessions_per_user`.
    - A `System` actor sees no conversations unless a named, documented exception admits it (e.g. compression, retention).
  - **D2 memory**: `MEMORY.md` at agent level. `USER.md` is at agent level on a personal agent and per participant on a group agent (see "Ownership key").
  - **D3 skills index**, at agent level, with tenant-wide skills resolving through the policy.
  - **D4 cron jobs and ticks**, at agent level. Each job also records the principal who created it.
    - The fire claim (`cron.jobs.claim_job_for_fire`: at-most-once compare-and-set, today a file lock on `jobs.json`) and the execution audit (`cron.executions`) move behind the port with the same semantics, so `CronScheduler` providers keep working unchanged.
  - **D5 kanban** boards, tasks, events and notify subscriptions, at agent level.
  - **D6 user extension registry** (user plugins and MCP servers, plus their per-agent switches): owner-wide or tenant-wide entries, switched on per agent; see L.
- **Conformance and isolation invariants.** The suite runs as the application role:
  - with no scope pinned, every read returns nothing and every write fails;
  - tenant B and agent B never see A's rows, and a foreign row is indistinguishable from a missing one;
  - a write carrying a superseded fence (two replicas, the lease moved) is rejected and leaves no partial state; a turn-path write with no fence is refused;
  - two replicas running the same agent's different sessions at the same time never block or corrupt each other;
  - pinning an agent never widens the tenant;
  - a prune or retention sweep pinned to A never deletes B's rows, and an unpinned sweep deletes nothing;
  - delegated child sessions: B cannot see or move A's; a child cannot delegate further; no child crosses agents;
  - **D2:** caps refuse before the write;
  - **D3:** another tenant's or agent's skill is indistinguishable from a missing one;
  - **D4:** A cannot list, trigger or re-point B's jobs, and a tick pinned to A never fires B's due job;
  - **D5:** B's task is never dispatched into A, a worker cannot leave its board, and B's notify targets are invisible to A.

- **This is not the cron trigger.** `cron.scheduler_provider.CronScheduler` (built-in ticker, Chronos) decides *when* a cron job fires. That fire then enters this port as one more producer. A Chronos fire calls `fire_due`, which claims the job and runs `run_one_job`, which admits a `cron:<job>:<execution>` input through `gateway/session_cron.py`.
- **Puts behind one port** the profile owner lock (`gateway/runtime_ownership.py`, `gateway.lock`) and `SessionAuthority`'s admission store (`gateway/session_authority.py` over `session_admissions`).
- **Local backend:** today's file lock and SQLite.
- **Hosted (plugin):** a Postgres lease per session instead of per profile; N replicas, and any replica can claim any session.
- **The lease token goes into the `TurnScope`** (`TurnScope.fence`, done in #149200). D's backends check it on every session-owned write, so fencing holds in storage itself, not only at admission.
- **Contract both backends must satisfy, as the conformance suite:**
  - one FIFO per session for every producer (messaging, relay, webhooks, cron, kanban, API);
  - claims fenced by `runtime_generation` + `owner_epoch`, so a stale owner's write is rejected;
  - a turn whose owner dies becomes `unknown` and is **never** replayed automatically;
  - one writer per session, also with two replicas;
  - recovery resumes after a crash.
- **Also:** `agent.managed_worker` accepts a `TurnScope` in its bootstrap frame, so a deployment can run turns out of process by changing config, not code. Its per-turn latency and RSS must be measured before that switch is offered.

A fire for an agent the token does not name is refused, the same as an unknown job;

- **Invariants, with a stub provider:**
